These dark beasts with white tusks are mine, more than a hundred, covered with golden nets. Remembering my fathers and grandfathers, O young man, I say, 'These very ones I will give away.'

Susīmajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Susīma Jātaka, the third.

164. Gijjhajātakaṃ (2-2-4)

164. The Gijjha Jātaka (2.2.4)

27.

27.

Yaṃ nu gijjho yojanasataṃ, kuṇapāni avekkhati;

Kasmā jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhasi.

A vulture, they say, can see a carcass from a hundred yojanas away. Why then, having come upon a net and a snare, do you not perceive it?

28.

28.

Yadā parābhavo hoti, poso jīvitasaṅkhaye;

Atha jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhatīti.

When a being is facing ruin, at the destruction of its life, then, even having come upon a net and a snare, it does not perceive it.

Gijjhajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Gijjha Jātaka, the fourth.

165. Nakulajātakaṃ (2-2-5)

165. The Nakula Jātaka (2.2.5)

29.

29.

Sandhiṃ katvā amittena, aṇḍajena jalābuja;

Vivariya dāṭhaṃ sesi sayasi (sī. syā. pī.), kuto te bhayamāgataṃ.

O womb-born one, having made an alliance with the enemy, the egg-born one, you sleep with fangs bared. From where has fear come to you?

30.

30.

Saṅketheva saṅkateva (ka.) amittasmiṃ, mittasmimpi na vissase;

Abhayā bhayamuppannaṃ, api mūlāni kantatīti mūlaṃ nikantatīti (sī.).

One should be suspicious of an enemy, and one should not trust even a friend. Fear that has arisen from a place of safety cuts one even to the roots.

Nakulajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Nakula Jātaka, the fifth.

166. Upasāḷakajātakaṃ (2-2-6)

166. The Upasāḷaka Jātaka (2.2.6)

31.

31.

Upasāḷakanāmāni upasāḷhakanāmānaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), sahassāni catuddasa;

Asmiṃ padese daḍḍhāni, natthi loke anāmataṃ.

Fourteen thousand named Upasāḷaka have been cremated in this place. In the world, there is no deathless state.

32.

32.

Yamhi [T 1.0058] saccañca dhammo ca, ahiṃsā saṃyamo damo;

Etaṃ ariyā sevanti, etaṃ loke anāmatanti.

In whom there is truth and Dhamma, non-harming, restraint, and self-control—this one the noble ones attend upon. This, in the world, is the deathless state.

Upasāḷakajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Upasāḷaka Jātaka, the sixth.

167. Samiddhijātakaṃ (2-2-7)

167. The Samiddhi Jātaka (2.2.7)

33.

33.

Abhutvā [M 1.0042] bhikkhasi bhikkhu, na hi bhutvāna bhikkhasi;

Bhutvāna bhikkhu bhikkhassu, mā taṃ kālo upaccagā.

Without having enjoyed sensual pleasures, O monk, you live the homeless life; you do not live it after having enjoyed them. First enjoy sensual pleasures, O monk, then live the homeless life. Let not the time for this pass you by.

34.

34.

Kālaṃ [V 1.0039] vohaṃ na jānāmi, channo kālo na dissati;

Tasmā abhutvā bhikkhāmi, mā maṃ kālo upaccagāti.

I do not know the time of death; that time is concealed, it is not seen. Therefore, without having first enjoyed sensual pleasures, I live the homeless life, lest the time for practice pass me by.

Samiddhijātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Samiddhi Jātaka, the seventh.

168. Sakuṇagghijātakaṃ (2-2-8)

168. The Sakuṇagghi Jātaka (2.2.8)

35.

35.

Seno balasā patamāno, lāpaṃ gocaraṭhāyinaṃ;

Sahasā ajjhappattova, maraṇaṃ tenupāgami.

A hawk, swooping down with force upon a quail standing in its feeding ground, swiftly seized it and thereby met its own death.

36.

36.

Sohaṃ nayena sampanno, pettike gocare rato;

Apetasattu modāmi, sampassaṃ atthamattanoti.

Endowed with wisdom, delighting in my ancestral feeding grounds, I rejoice, free from enemies, seeing my own welfare.

Sakuṇagghijātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Sakuṇagghi Jātaka, the eighth.

169. Arakajātakaṃ (2-2-9)

169. The Araka Jātaka (2.2.9)

37.

37.

Yo ve mettena cittena, sabbalokānukampati;

Uddhaṃ [T 1.0059] adho ca tiriyaṃ, appamāṇena sabbaso.

Whoever, with a mind of loving-kindness, has compassion for the entire world—above, below, and across—boundlessly and in all ways.

38.

38.

Appamāṇaṃ hitaṃ cittaṃ, paripuṇṇaṃ subhāvitaṃ;

Yaṃ pamāṇakataṃ kammaṃ, na taṃ tatrāvasissatīti.

When there is a boundless, beneficial mind, complete and well-developed, any limited karma that was done does not remain there.

Arakajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Araka Jātaka, the ninth.

170. Kakaṇṭakajātakaṃ (2-2-10)

170. The Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka (2.2.10)

39.

39.

Nāyaṃ pure uṇṇamati unnamati (syā.), toraṇagge kakaṇṭako;

Mahosadha vijānāhi, kena thaddho kakaṇṭako.

This chameleon at the gateway's top was not arrogant before. O Mahosadha, find out why this chameleon has become so stiff.

40.

40.

Aladdhapubbaṃ laddhāna, aḍḍhamāsaṃ kakaṇṭako;

Atimaññati rājānaṃ, vedehaṃ mithilaggahanti.

Having obtained what was never obtained before, a treasure of half a māsa, this chameleon despises the king, Vedeha, lord of Mithilā.

Kakaṇṭakajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Kakaṇṭaka Jātaka, the tenth.

Santhavavaggo dutiyo.

The Second Chapter on Familiarity.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for this chapter:

Atha [M 1.0043] indasamāna sapaṇṇakuṭi, susimuttama gijjha jalābujako;

Upasāḷaka bhikkhu salāpavaro, atha mettavaro dasapuṇṇamatīti.

Then Indasamāna, Sapaṇṇakuṭi (Santhava), the excellent Susīma, Gijjha, and Jalābujaka (Nakula); Upasāḷaka, Bhikkhu (Samiddhi), and Salāpavara (Sakuṇagghi); then Metta (Araka), and the excellent tenth to complete the list (Kakaṇṭaka).

3. Kalyāṇavaggo

3. The Chapter on Goodness

171. Kalyāṇadhammajātakaṃ (2-3-1)

171. The Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka (2.3.1)

41.

41.

Kalyāṇadhammoti [T 1.0060][V 1.0040] yadā janinda, loke samaññaṃ anupāpuṇāti;

Tasmā na hiyyetha hīyetha (sī.) naro sapañño, hiriyāpi santo dhuramādiyanti.

O ruler of men, when in the world one attains the designation 'one of good qualities,' a wise person should therefore not fall away from it. The virtuous take up the burden through moral shame and moral dread.

42.

42.

Sāyaṃ samaññā idha majja pattā, kalyāṇadhammoti janinda loke;

Tāhaṃ samekkhaṃ idha pabbajissaṃ, na hi matthi chando idha kāmabhogeti.

O ruler of men, today in this world I have attained that designation, 'one of good qualities.' Carefully considering it, I shall go forth in this world. Indeed, I have no desire for the enjoyment of sensual pleasures here.

Kalyāṇadhammajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Kalyāṇadhamma Jātaka, the first.

172. Daddarajātakaṃ (2-3-2)

172. The Daddara Jātaka (2.3.2)

43.

43.

Ko nu saddena mahatā, abhinādeti daddaraṃ;

Taṃ sīhā nappaṭinadanti kiṃ sīhā nappaṭinadanti (sī. pī.), na sīhā paṭinadanti (ka.), ko nāmeso migādhibhū.

Who with a great sound makes the Daddara mountain resound? The lions do not roar back at that sound; what is the name of this lord of beasts?

44.

44.

Adhamo migajātānaṃ, siṅgālo tāta vassati;

Jātimassa jigucchantā, tuṇhī sīhā samacchareti.

Dear son, the jackal, the basest of the animal species, is howling. Loathing its kind, the lions remain silent.

Daddarajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Daddara Jātaka, the second.

173. Makkaṭajātakaṃ (2-3-3)

173. The Makkaṭa Jātaka (2.3.3)

45.

45.

Tāta [T 1.0061][M 1.0044] māṇavako eso, tālamūlaṃ apassito;

Agārakañcidaṃ atthi, handa demassagārakaṃ.

Father, this ascetic is leaning on the palmyra stump. We have this fire-hut. Come, let us give the fire-hut to him who has come.

46.

46.

Mā kho tvaṃ tāta pakkosi, dūseyya no agārakaṃ;

Netādisaṃ mukhaṃ hoti, brāhmaṇassa susīlinoti.

Dear son, do not call him, lest he should ruin our dwelling. The face of a virtuous ascetic is not like this.

Makkaṭajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Makkaṭa Jātaka, the third.

174. Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātakaṃ (2-3-4)

174. The Dubbhiyamakkaṭa Jātaka (2.3.4)

47.

47.

Adamha te vāri pahūtarūpaṃ, ghammābhitattassa pipāsitassa;

So dāni pitvāna pītvāna (sī. pī.) kiriṅkarosi kikiṃkarosi (sī. syā. pī.), asaṅgamo pāpajanena seyyo.

To you, afflicted by heat and thirsty, I gave abundant water. Now, having drunk, you make the 'kiri-kiri' sound. Non-association with a wicked person is indeed better.

48.

48.

Ko te suto vā diṭṭho vā, sīlavā nāma makkaṭo;

Idāni kho taṃ ohacchaṃ ūhacca (sī. pī.), ohaccaṃ (syā.), uhajjaṃ (ka.), esā asmāka dhammatāti.

O brahmin, where have you heard or seen that there exists a monkey that is virtuous? Now I shall defecate upon your head. This is our nature.

Dubbhiyamakkaṭajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Dubbhiyamakkaṭa Jātaka, the fourth.

175. Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātakaṃ (2-3-5)

175. The Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka (2.3.5)

49.

49.

Sabbesu [V 1.0041] kira bhūtesu, santi sīlasamāhitā;

Passa sākhāmigaṃ jammaṃ, ādiccamupatiṭṭhati.

It seems that among all beings, there are those endowed with virtue. Look at this base monkey; he is worshipping the sun.

50.

50.

Nāssa sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha;

Aggihuttañca [T 1.0062] uhannaṃ ūhantaṃ (sī.), ūhanaṃ (syā.), ūhanti (pī.), uhadaṃ (ka.), dve ca bhinnā kamaṇḍalūti.

You do not know his virtue; not knowing, you praise him. Our fire-hut has been defecated in, and two water pots have been broken.

Ādiccupaṭṭhānajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Ādiccupaṭṭhāna Jātaka, the fifth.

176. Kaḷāyamuṭṭhijātakaṃ (2-3-6)

176. The Kaḷāyamuṭṭhi Jātaka (2.3.6)

51.

51.

Bālo [M 1.0045] vatāyaṃ dumasākhagocaro, paññā janinda nayimassa vijjati;

Kaḷāyamuṭṭhiṃ kalāyamuṭṭhiṃ (sī. pī.) avakiriya kevalaṃ, ekaṃ kaḷāyaṃ patitaṃ gavesati.

O ruler of men, this tree-branch dweller is indeed a fool; there is no wisdom in him. Having scattered a whole handful of peas, he searches for the one pea that has fallen.

52.

52.

Evameva mayaṃ rāja, ye caññe atilobhino;

Appena bahuṃ jiyyāma, kaḷāyeneva vānaroti.

Even so, O king, we and others who are excessively greedy lose much for the sake of little, just like the monkey with the pea.

Kaḷāyamuṭṭhijātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Kaḷākamuṭṭhi Jātaka, the sixth.

177. Tindukajātakaṃ (2-3-7)

177. The Tinduka Jātaka (2.3.7)

53.

53.

Dhanuhatthakalāpehi, nettiṃ savaradhāribhi;

Samantā parikiṇṇamha, kathaṃ mokkho bhavissati.

By those with bows and quivers in hand, by those who bear excellent swords, we are surrounded on all sides. How will there be liberation for us?

54.

54.

Appeva bahukiccānaṃ, attho jāyetha koci naṃ;

Atthi rukkhassa acchinnaṃ, khajjathaññeva tindukanti.

Perhaps for those with many duties, some other matter might arise. The fruit of the tree is continuous; you may eat the Tinduka fruit as you wish.

Tindukajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Tinduka Jātaka, the Seventh.

178. Kacchapajātakaṃ (2-3-8)

178. The Kacchapa Jātaka (2-3-8)

55.

55.

Janittaṃ [T 1.0063] me bhavittaṃ me, iti paṅke avassayiṃ;

Taṃ maṃ paṅko ajjhabhavi, yathā dubbalakaṃ tathā;

178. ‘This is my birthplace, this is my dwelling place,’ thinking thus, I dwelt in the mire. That mud has overwhelmed me, just as a weak person is overwhelmed.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi bhaggava, suṇohi vacanaṃ mama.

I tell you this, Bhaggava; listen to my words.

56.

56.

Gāme vā yadi vā raññe, sukhaṃ yatrādhigacchati;

Taṃ janittaṃ bhavittañca, purisassa pajānato;

Whether in a village or in a forest, wherever one attains happiness, that is the birthplace and the dwelling place for a discerning person.

Yamhi jīve tamhi gacche, na niketahato siyāti.

Where one can live, there one should go; one should not be destroyed by attachment to one's dwelling.

Kacchapajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kacchapa Jātaka, the Eighth.

179. Satadhammajātakaṃ (2-3-9)

179. The Satadhamma Jātaka (2-3-9)

57.

57.

Tañca [V 1.0042] appañca ucchiṭṭhaṃ, tañca kicchena no adā;

Sohaṃ brāhmaṇajātiko, yaṃ bhuttaṃ tampi uggataṃ.

And that food was little and leftover, and that he gave to me with difficulty. I am of brahmin birth; what was eaten, even that was vomited up.

58.

58.

Evaṃ [M 1.0046] dhammaṃ niraṃkatvā nirākatvā (?) ni + ā + kara + tvā, yo adhammena jīvati;

Satadhammova lābhena, laddhenapi na nandatīti.

179. Thus, one who, having rejected the Dhamma, lives unrighteously, like Satadhamma, finds no joy even in the gain that is acquired.

Satadhammajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Satadhamma Jātaka, the Ninth.

180. Duddadajātakaṃ (2-3-10)

180. The Duddada Jātaka (2-3-10)

59.

59.

Duddadaṃ dadamānānaṃ, dukkaraṃ kamma kubbataṃ;

Asanto nānukubbanti, sataṃ dhammo durannayo.

The ignoble do not imitate those who give what is hard to give and do a difficult deed; the Dhamma of the good is difficult to understand.

60.

60.

Tasmā satañca asataṃ, nānā hoti ito gati;

Asanto [T 1.0064] nirayaṃ yanti, santo saggaparāyaṇāti parāyanā (syā. ka.).

Therefore, for the good and the ignoble, the destination from here is different; the ignoble go to hell, while the good have heaven as their destination.

Duddadajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

180. The Duddada Jātaka, the Tenth.

Kalyāṇavaggo tatiyo.

The Kalyāṇa Chapter, the Third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Susamaññamigādhibhū māṇavako, vāripahūtarūpādiccupaṭṭhānā;

Sakaḷāyasatindukapaṅka puna, satadhamma sududdadakena dasāti.

Susamañña, Migādhibhū, Māṇavako, Vāripahūtarūpa, Ādiccupaṭṭhānā, Sakaḷāya, Satinduka, Paṅka puna, Satadhamma, and with Sududdadaka make ten.

4. Asadisavaggo

The Asadisa Chapter

181. Asadisajātakaṃ (2-4-1)

181. The Asadisa Jātaka (2-4-1)

61.

61.

Dhanuggaho asadiso, rājaputto mahabbalo;

Dūrepātī akkhaṇavedhī, mahākāyappadālano.

The archer Asadisa, a prince of great strength, is a far-shooter, an unerring marksman, a piercer of great masses.

62.

62.

Sabbāmitte raṇaṃ katvā, na ca kañci viheṭhayi;

Bhātaraṃ sotthiṃ katvāna, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamīti.

Having made war on all his enemies, he harmed no one; having made his brother secure, he undertook the life of restraint.

Asadisajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

4. The Asadisa Jātaka, the First.

182. Saṅgāmāvacarajātakaṃ (2-4-2)

182. The Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka (2-4-2)

63.

63.

Saṅgāmāvacaro [V 1.0043][M 1.0047] sūro, balavā iti vissuto;

Kiṃ [T 1.0065] nu toraṇamāsajja, paṭikkamasi kuñjara.

181. You are a traverser of the battlefield, a hero, famed as strong; why now, O elephant, having reached the archway, do you retreat?

64.

64.

Omadda khippaṃ palighaṃ, esikāni ca abbaha ubbaha (syā.), abbhuha (ka.);

Toraṇāni ca madditvā, khippaṃ pavisa kuñjarāti.

Quickly crush the crossbar, pull up the posts, and having trampled the archways, enter quickly, O elephant!

Saṅgāmāvacarajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Saṅgāmāvacara Jātaka, the Second.

183. Vālodakajātakaṃ (2-4-3)

183. The Vālodaka Jātaka (2-4-3)

65.

65.

Vālodakaṃ apparasaṃ nihīnaṃ, pitvā pītvā (sī. pī.) mado jāyati gadrabhānaṃ;

Imañca pitvāna rasaṃ paṇītaṃ, mado na sañjāyati sindhavānaṃ.

For donkeys, having drunk the inferior Vālodaka of little flavor, intoxication arises; but for the Sindh horses, having drunk this excellent juice, intoxication does not arise.

66.

66.

Appaṃ pivitvāna nihīnajacco, so majjatī tena janinda puṭṭho phuṭṭho (sī. syā.), muṭṭho (ka.);

Dhorayhasīlī ca kulamhi jāto, na majjatī aggarasaṃ pivitvāti.

182. O Janinda, that one of low birth, being afflicted by that, becomes intoxicated having drunk but a little. But the one of enduring nature, born in a good family, does not become intoxicated even having drunk the foremost juice.

Vālodakajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Vālodaka Jātaka, the Third.

184. Giridattajātakaṃ (2-4-4)

184. The Giridatta Jātaka (2-4-4)

67.

67.

Dūsito giridattena giridantena (pī.), hayo sāmassa paṇḍavo;

Porāṇaṃ pakatiṃ hitvā, tassevānuvidhiyyati nuvidhīyati (sī. pī.).

Corrupted by the horse-trainer Giridatta, Paṇḍava, the royal horse of King Sāma, having abandoned its former graceful nature, now imitates his very limp.

68.

68.

Sace [T 1.0066] ca tanujo poso, sikharākāra siṅgārākāra (syā.) kappito;

Ānane naṃ taṃ (sī. syā. pī.) gahetvāna, maṇḍale parivattaye;

And if a man, suitable for it and with well-groomed hair and beard, having taken it by the muzzle, should walk it around in the training ring,

Khippameva pahantvāna, tassevānuvidhiyyatīti.

183. The horse, having quickly abandoned its limping, will then imitate that very man.

Giridattajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Giridatta Jātaka, the Fourth.

185. Anabhiratijātakaṃ (2-4-5)

185. The Anabhirati Jātaka (2-4-5)

69.

69.

Yathodake [M 1.0048] āvile appasanne, na passati sippikasambukañca;

Sakkharaṃ vālukaṃ macchagumbaṃ, evaṃ āvilamhi āvile hi (sī.) citte;

Just as in water that is turbid and unclear, one does not see the oysters and snails, the gravel and sand, and the shoals of fish; so too, when the mind is turbid,

Na passati attadatthaṃ paratthaṃ.

He does not see his own welfare and the welfare of others.

70.

70.

Yathodake [V 1.0044] acche vippasanne, so passati sippikasambukañca;

Sakkharaṃ vālukaṃ macchagumbaṃ, evaṃ anāvilamhi citte;

Dear son, just as in water that is clear and perfectly serene, a person sees the oysters and snails, the gravel and sand, and the shoals of fish; so too, when the mind is untroubled,

So passati attadatthaṃ paratthanti.

that person sees his own welfare and the welfare of others.

Anabhiratijātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Anabhirati Jātaka, the Fifth.

186. Dadhivāhanajātakaṃ (2-4-6)

186. The Dadhivāhana Jātaka (2-4-6)

71.

71.

Vaṇṇagandharasūpeto[T 1.0067], amboyaṃ ahuvā pure;

Tameva pūjaṃ labhamāno, kenambo kaṭukapphalo.

186. O wise one, this mango tree was formerly endowed with color, fragrance, and taste. While still receiving that very same honor, for what reason does the mango now have bitter fruit?

72.

72.

Pucimandaparivāro, ambo te dadhivāhana;

Mūlaṃ mūlena saṃsaṭṭhaṃ, sākhā sākhā sākhaṃ (syā. ka.) nisevare nivīsare (ka.);

O King Dadhivāhana, your royal mango tree is surrounded by neem trees. Its root is intertwined with their roots; their branches penetrate its branches.

Asātasannivāsena, tenambo kaṭukapphaloti.

Through association with the unpleasant, for that reason the mango has bitter fruit.

Dadhivāhanajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Dadhivāhana Jātaka, the Sixth.

187. Catumaṭṭhajātakaṃ (2-4-7)

187. The Catumaṭṭha Jātaka (2-4-7)

73.

73.

Ucce viṭabhimāruyha, mantayavho rahogatā;

Nīce oruyha mantavho, migarājāpi sossati.

O young hamsas, having climbed a high branch, confer in a secluded place; but if you descend to a low place and confer, the king of beasts will also hear.

74.

74.

Yaṃ suvaṇṇo suvaṇṇena yaṃ supaṇṇo supaṇṇena (sī. syā. pī.), devo devena mantaye;

Kiṃ tettha catumaṭṭhassa, bilaṃ pavisa jambukāti.

That which a golden one confers with a golden one, a divine one with a divine one—what is that to you, O catumaṭṭha? Enter your hole, jackal!

Catumaṭṭhajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

187. The Catumaṭṭha Jātaka, the Seventh.

188. Sīhakotthujātakaṃ (2-4-8)

188. The Sīhakotthu Jātaka (2-4-8)

75.

75.

Sīhaṅgulī [M 1.0049] sīhanakho, sīhapādapatiṭṭhito;

So sīho sīhasaṅghamhi, eko nadati aññathā.

Father, this one has the toes of a lion, the claws of a lion, and stands on the paws of a lion. That lion, alone in an assembly of lions, cries out differently. What lion is this?

76.

76.

Mā [T 1.0068] tvaṃ nadi rājaputta, appasaddo vane vasa;

Sarena kho mā (ka.) taṃ jāneyyuṃ, na hi te pettiko saroti.

Do not cry out, O prince. Dwell silently in the forest. For by your voice they would know you; indeed, your voice is not that of your father.

Sīhakotthujātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Sīhakotthu Jātaka, the Eighth.

189. Sīhacammajātakaṃ (2-4-9)

189. The Sīhacamma Jātaka (2-4-9)

77.

77.

Netaṃ sīhassa naditaṃ, na byagghassa na byagghassa na ca (ka.) dīpino;

Pāruto sīhacammena, jammo nadati gadrabho.

188. This is not the sound of a lion, nor of a tiger, nor of a leopard; clothed in a lion's skin, a wretched donkey brays.

78.

78.

Cirampi [V 1.0045] kho taṃ khādeyya, gadrabho haritaṃ yavaṃ;

Pāruto sīhacammena, ravamānova dūsayīti.

For a long time, indeed, the donkey could have eaten green barley; clothed in a lion's skin, by braying, it destroyed itself.

Sīhacammajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Sīhacamma Jātaka, the Ninth.

190. Sīlānisaṃsajātakaṃ (2-4-10)

190. The Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka (2-4-10)

79.

79.

Passa saddhāya sīlassa, cāgassa ca ayaṃ phalaṃ;

Nāgo nāvāya vaṇṇena, saddhaṃ vahatupāsakaṃ.

Behold this fruit of faith, virtue, and generosity: the Nāga, in the form of a boat, carries the faithful lay follower.

80.

80.

Sabbhireva samāsetha, sabbhi kubbetha santhavaṃ;

Satañhi sannivāsena, sotthiṃ gacchati nhāpitoti.

189. One should associate only with the wise; one should make friendship with the wise. For by dwelling with the wise, the barber attains well-being.

Sīlānisaṃsajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Sīlānisaṃsa Jātaka, the Tenth.

Asadisavaggo catuttho.

The Asadisa Chapter, the Fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Dhanuggaha [T 1.0069] kuñjara apparaso, giridattamanāvilacittavaraṃ;

Dadhivāhana jambūka sīhanakho, haritayava nāgavarena dasāti.

190. Dhanuggaha, Kuñjara, Apparasa, Giridatta, the excellent untroubled mind, Dadhivāhana, Jambūka, Sīhanakha, Haritayava, and with the excellent Nāga—these are the ten.

5. Ruhakavaggo

The Ruhaka Chapter

191. Ruhakajātakaṃ (2-5-1)

191. The Ruhaka Jātaka (2-5-1)

81.

81.

Api [M 1.0050] ambho (syā. ka. sī.) ruhaka chinnāpi, jiyā sandhīyate puna;

Sandhīyassu purāṇiyā, mā kodhassa vasaṃ gami.

O Ruhaka, though a bowstring is cut, it is joined together again. Be reconciled with your former wife; do not fall under the power of anger.

82.

82.

Vijjamānesu vākesu vijjamānāsu maruvāsu (sī.), vijjamānāsu marūdvāsu (pī.), vijjamānesu kārisu;

Aññaṃ jiyaṃ karissāmi, alaññeva purāṇiyāti.

Since there are fibers and since there are craftsmen, I will make another bowstring. Enough of the old one!

Ruhakajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Ruhaka Jātaka, the First.

192. Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakaṃ (2-5-2)

192. The Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka (2-5-2)

83.

83.

Itthī siyā rūpavatī, sā ca sīlavatī siyā;

Puriso taṃ na iccheyya, saddahāsi mahosadha.

A woman might be beautiful, and she might also be virtuous, yet a man might not desire her. Do you believe this, Mahosadha?

84.

84.

Saddahāmi [V 1.0046] mahārāja, puriso dubbhago siyā;

Sirī [T 1.0070] ca kāḷakaṇṇī ca, na samenti kudācananti.

I believe it, great king. A man might be unfortunate, for Fortune and Misfortune never come together.

Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

5. The Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka, the Second.

193. Cūḷapadumajātakaṃ (2-5-3)

193. The Cūḷapaduma Jātaka (2-5-3)

85.

85.

Ayameva sā ahamapi ahampi (sī. syā. pī.), ahasmi (ka.) so anañño, ayameva so hatthacchinno anañño;

Yamāha “komārapatī mama”nti, vajjhitthiyo natthi itthīsu saccaṃ.

191. This is that very woman, and I am that very man, none other. This is that very one with severed hands, none other. She who said, ‘He is my youthful husband’—women are to be condemned; there is no truth in women.

86.

86.

Imañca jammaṃ musalena hantvā, luddaṃ chavaṃ paradārūpaseviṃ;

Imissā ca naṃ pāpapatibbatāya, jīvantiyā chindatha kaṇṇanāsanti.

Having struck this wretch with a pestle—this cruel corpse, this violator of others' wives—you must also, for this woman's wicked devotion to her husband, cut off her ears and nose while she is still alive.

Cūḷapadumajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Cūḷapaduma Jātaka, the Third.

194. Maṇicorajātakaṃ (2-5-4)

194. The Maṇicora Jātaka (2-5-4)

87.

87.

Na [M 1.0051] santi devā pavasanti nūna, na hi nūna santi idha lokapālā;

Sahasā karontānamasaññatānaṃ, na hi nūna santī paṭisedhitāro.

Surely there are no gods, or they must be away; surely there are no world-guardians here. For of those who act rashly and without restraint, there are surely none to prevent them.

88.

88.

Akāle vassatī tassa, kāle tassa na vassati;

Saggā [T 1.0071] ca cavati ṭhānā, nanu so tāvatā hatoti.

For him, it rains out of season, and in season it does not rain. He falls from his heavenly state. Is he not thereby afflicted?

Maṇicorajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Maṇicora Jātaka, the Fourth.

195. Pabbatūpattharajātakaṃ (2-5-5)

195. The Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka (2-5-5)

89.

89.

Pabbatūpatthare pabbatapatthare (sī. syā. pī.) ramme, jātā pokkharaṇī sivā;

Taṃ siṅgālo apāpāyi apāpāsi (sī. syā. pī.), jānaṃ sīhena rakkhitaṃ.

On a delightful mountain plateau, a pleasant pond with cool water came to be; knowing it was guarded by a lion, should a jackal have drunk from it?

90.

90.

Pivanti ce pivanti ve (sī.), pivantiva (pī.), pivanteva (?) mahārāja, sāpadāni mahānadiṃ;

Na tena anadī hoti, khamassu yadi te piyāti.

Great king, if beasts of prey drink from the great river, it does not thereby cease to be a river. Forgive her, if she is dear to you.

Pabbatūpatthara pabbatapatthara (sī. syā. pī.) jātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Pabbatūpatthara Jātaka, the fifth.

196. Valāhakassajātakaṃ (2-5-6)

196. The Valāhakassa Jātaka (2-5-6)

91.

91.

Ye na kāhanti ovādaṃ, narā buddhena desitaṃ;

Byasanaṃ te gamissanti, rakkhasīhiva vāṇijā.

Those people who do not follow the advice taught by the Buddha will come to ruin, like the merchants at the hands of the ogresses.

92.

92.

Ye [V 1.0047] ca kāhanti ovādaṃ, narā buddhena desitaṃ;

Sotthiṃ pāraṃ gamissanti, valāheneva vālāheneva (sī. pī.) vāṇijāti.

But those people who follow the advice taught by the Buddha will safely reach the further shore, like the merchants with the cloud-horse.

Valāhakassa vālāhassa (sī. pī.) jātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Valāhakassa Jātaka, the sixth.

197. Mittāmittajātakaṃ (2-5-7)

197. The Mittāmitta Jātaka (2-5-7)

93.

93.

Na naṃ umhayate disvā, na ca naṃ paṭinandati;

Cakkhūni cassa na dadāti, paṭilomañca vattati.

On seeing him, he does not smile, nor does he welcome him; he does not give him his eyes, and he behaves in a contrary way.

94.

94.

Ete [T 1.0072][M 1.0052] bhavanti ākārā, amittasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā;

Yehi amittaṃ jāneyya, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍitoti.

These are the signs established in an enemy, by which a wise person, having seen and heard, may recognize an enemy.

Mittāmittajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Mittāmitta Jātaka, the seventh.

198. Rādhajātakaṃ (2-5-8)

198. The Rādha Jātaka (2-5-8)

95.

95.

Pavāsā āgato tāta, idāni nacirāgato;

Kaccinnu tāta te mātā, na aññamupasevati.

Dear son, I have returned from abroad, having just now arrived. I hope, dear son, that your mother does not attend upon another.

96.

96.

Na kho panetaṃ subhaṇaṃ, giraṃ saccupasaṃhitaṃ;

Sayetha poṭṭhapādova, mummure mummure (syā.), maṃ pure (ka.) mummurasaddo thusaggimhi kukkuḷe ca vattatīti sakkatābhidhānesu upakūthitoti upakūsitoti (sī. syā. pī.), upakūlito (ka.).

Father, wise ones do not utter a speech connected with truth if it is not well-spoken. One who speaks thus would have to lie in hot embers, like Poṭṭhapāda who spoke before.

Rādhajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Rādha Jātaka, the eighth.

199. Gahapatijātakaṃ (2-5-9)

199. The Gahapati Jātaka (2-5-9)

97.

97.

Ubhayaṃ me na khamati, ubhayaṃ me na ruccati;

Yācāyaṃ koṭṭhamotiṇṇā, nāddasaṃ iti bhāsati.

Both are not agreeable to me, both do not please me: that this one, having entered the storeroom when asked, says, 'I did not see it.'

98.

98.

Taṃ taṃ gāmapati brūmi, kadare appasmi jīvite;

Dve māse saṅgaraṃ katvā kāraṃ katvāna (sī. pī.), saṃkaraṃ katvā (ka.), maṃsaṃ jaraggavaṃ kisaṃ;

Village headman, I tell you this: in this short and wretched life, having made an agreement for two months, you give the meat of a lean, old bull;

Appattakāle codesi, tampi mayhaṃ na ruccatīti.

You demand payment before the appointed time has arrived; that too does not please me.

Gahapatijātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Gahapati Jātaka, the ninth.

200. Sādhusīlajātakaṃ (2-5-10)

200. The Sādhusīla Jātaka (2-5-10)

99.

99.

Sarīradabyaṃ [T 1.0073] vuḍḍhabyaṃ vaddhabyaṃ (sī. pī.), sojaccaṃ sādhusīliyaṃ;

Brāhmaṇaṃ teva pucchāma, kannu tesaṃ vanimhase vaṇimhase (sī. pī.).

Beauty of form, seniority, noble birth, and good virtue: Brahmin, we ask you, which of them should we choose?

100.

100.

Attho [V 1.0048] atthi sarīrasmiṃ, vuḍḍhabyassa namo kare;

Attho atthi sujātasmiṃ, sīlaṃ asmāka ruccatīti.

There is value in physical beauty, and one should pay homage to seniority; there is value in being well-born, but it is virtue that is pleasing to us.

Sādhusīlajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Sādhusīla Jātaka, the tenth.

Ruhakavaggo pañcamo.

The Ruhaka Chapter, the fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Apiruhaka [M 1.0053] rūpavatī musalo, pavasanti sapañcamapokkharaṇī;

Atha muttimavāṇija umhayate, ciraāgata koṭṭha sarīra dasāti.

Ruhaka, the Beautiful Woman, the Club, Away on a Journey, and the Pond as the fifth; then the Merchant's Release, Smiles, Long-Awaited Arrival, the Storeroom, and the Body make ten.

6. Nataṃdaḷhavaggo

6. The Daḷha Chapter

201. Bandhanāgārajātakaṃ (2-6-1)

201. The Bandhanāgāra Jātaka (2-6-1)

101.

101.

Na taṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, yadāyasaṃ dārujapabbajañca babbajañca (sī.);

Sārattarattā maṇikuṇḍalesu, puttesu [T 1.0074] dāresu ca yā apekkhā.

The wise do not say that bond is strong which is made of iron, of wood, or of babbaja grass. That passionate attachment to jeweled earrings, and that longing for sons and wives—

102.

102.

Etaṃ daḷhaṃ bandhanamāhu dhīrā, ohārinaṃ sithilaṃ duppamuñcaṃ;

Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrā, anapekkhino kāmasukhaṃ pahāyāti.

—this, the wise say, is a strong bond: dragging down, pliant, yet hard to release. Having cut this bond too, the wise go forth, without longing, having abandoned the pleasure of sensual desires.

Bandhanāgārajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Bandhanāgāra Jātaka, the first.

202. Keḷisīlajātakaṃ (2-6-2)

202. The Keḷisīla Jātaka (2-6-2)

103.

103.

Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca, hatthayo hatthino (sī.), hatthiyo (syā. pī.) pasadā migā;

Sabbe sīhassa bhāyanti, natthi kāyasmi tulyatā.

Swans, curlews, and peacocks, elephants and spotted deer—all are afraid of the lion; in physical form there is no equality.

104.

104.

Evameva manussesu, daharo cepi paññavā;

So hi tattha mahā hoti, neva bālo sarīravāti.

So too among humans: even if one is young, should he be wise, he is truly great among them, not the fool who is merely large in body.

Keḷisīlajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Keḷisīla Jātaka, the second.

203. Khaṇḍajātakaṃ (2-6-3)

203. The Khaṇḍa Jātaka (2-6-3)

105.

105.

Virūpakkhehi me mettaṃ, mettaṃ erāpathehi me;

Chabyāputtehi me mettaṃ, mettaṃ kaṇhāgotamakehi ca.

My loving-kindness is with the Virūpakkhas, my loving-kindness with the Erāpathas; my loving-kindness is with the Chabyāputtas, and my loving-kindness with the Kaṇhāgotamakas.

Apādakehi [V 1.0049][M 1.0054] me mettaṃ, mettaṃ dvipādakehi me;

Catuppadehi me mettaṃ, mettaṃ bahuppadehi me.

My loving-kindness is with the footless, my loving-kindness with the two-footed; my loving-kindness is with the four-footed, my loving-kindness with the many-footed.

Mā [T 1.0075] maṃ apādako hiṃsi, mā maṃ hiṃsi dvipādako;

Mā maṃ catuppado hiṃsi, mā maṃ hiṃsi bahuppado.

Let not the footless harm me, let not the two-footed harm me; let not the four-footed harm me, let not the many-footed harm me.

Sabbe sattā sabbe pāṇā, sabbe bhūtā ca kevalā;

Sabbe bhadrāni passantu, mā kañci kiñci (syā. ka.) pāpamāgamā.

May all beings, all that breathe, all creatures without exception, see what is auspicious; may no evil whatsoever befall anyone.

106.

106.

Appamāṇo buddho, appamāṇo dhammo;

Appamāṇo saṅgho, pamāṇavantāni sarīsapāni sirisapāni (sī. syā. pī.);

Ahivicchikasatapadī, uṇṇanābhi uṇṇānābhi (sī. syā. pī.) sarabūmūsikā.

Immeasurable is the Buddha, immeasurable is the Dhamma, immeasurable is the Saṅgha; but limited are creeping things: snakes, scorpions, centipedes, spiders, lizards, and mice.

Katā me rakkhā katā me parittā, paṭikkamantu bhūtāni;

Sohaṃ namo bhagavato, namo sattannaṃ sammāsambuddhānanti.

Protection has been made by me, a safeguard has been made by me; let the beings depart. I pay homage to the Blessed One, homage to the seven Perfectly Enlightened Ones.

Khaṇḍajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Khaṇḍa Jātaka, the third.

204. Vīrakajātakaṃ (2-6-4)

204. The Vīraka Jātaka (2-6-4)

107.

107.

Api vīraka passesi, sakuṇaṃ mañjubhāṇakaṃ;

Mayūragīvasaṅkāsaṃ, patiṃ mayhaṃ saviṭṭhakaṃ.

O Vīraka, do you see the bird, sweet-voiced, with a neck like a peacock's, my husband Saviṭṭhaka?

108.

108.

Udakathalacarassa pakkhino, niccaṃ āmakamacchabhojino;

Tassānukaraṃ saviṭṭhako, sevāle paliguṇṭhito matoti.

Imitating a bird that moves on water and land, one that always feeds on raw fish, Saviṭṭhaka lies shrouded in moss, dead.

Vīrakajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Vīraka Jātaka, the fourth.

205. Gaṅgeyyajātakaṃ (2-6-5)

205. The Gaṅgeyya Jātaka (2-6-5)

109.

109.

Sobhati maccho gaṅgeyyo, atho sobhati yāmuno sobhanti macchā gaṅgeyyā, atho sobhanti yāmunā (syā. pī.);

Catuppadoyaṃ [T 1.0076] puriso, nigrodhaparimaṇḍalo;

A Ganges fish is splendid, and a Yamunā fish is splendid; but this four-footed being, round as a banyan tree,

Īsakāyata īsamāyata (ka.) gīvo ca, sabbeva atirocati.

and with a slightly long neck, surpasses them all.

110.

110.

Yaṃ [M 1.0055] pucchito na taṃ akkhāsi akkhā (sī. syā. pī.), aññaṃ akkhāsi akkhāti (syā. pī.) pucchito;

Attappasaṃsako poso, nāyaṃ asmāka ruccatīti.

When asked one thing, he does not speak of that; being asked, he speaks of something else. A person who praises himself—this one is not pleasing to us.

Gaṅgeyyajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Gaṅgeyya Jātaka, the fifth.

206. Kuruṅgamigajātakaṃ (2-6-6)

206. The Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka (2-6-6)

111.

111.

Iṅgha [V 1.0050] vaddhamayaṃ vaddhamayaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) pāsaṃ, chinda dantehi kacchapa;

Ahaṃ tathā karissāmi, yathā nehiti luddako.

Come, tortoise, sever this leather snare with your teeth; I shall act in such a way that the hunter will not come.

112.

112.

Kacchapo pāvisī vāriṃ, kuruṅgo pāvisī vanaṃ;

Satapatto dumaggamhā, dūre putte apānayīti.

The tortoise entered the water, the Kuruṅga deer entered the forest; the woodpecker from the treetop led its young far away.

Kuruṅgamigajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka, the sixth.

207. Assakajātakaṃ (2-6-7)

207. The Assaka Jātaka (2-6-7)

113.

113.

Ayamassakarājena, deso vicarito mayā;

Anukāmaya kāmena anukāmayavanukāmena (sī. pī.), piyena patinā saha.

This is the place where I wandered, together with my dear and beloved husband, King Assaka.

114.

114.

Navena sukhadukkhena, porāṇaṃ apidhīyati apithīyati (sī. pī.), apithiyyati (syā.);

Tasmā assakaraññāva, kīṭo piyataro mamāti.

New pleasure and pain conceal the old; therefore, the worm is dearer to me than King Assaka.

Assakajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Assaka Jātaka, the seventh.

208. Susumārajātakaṃ (2-6-8)

208. The Susumāra Jātaka (2-6-8)

115.

115.

Alaṃ [T 1.0077] metehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi ca;

Yāni pāraṃ samuddassa, varaṃ mayhaṃ udumbaro.

Enough for me of those mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits on the other shore of the sea; better for me is the fig tree.

116.

116.

Mahatī vata te bondi, na ca paññā tadūpikā;

Susumāra suṃsumāra (sī. syā. pī.) vañcito mesi, gaccha dāni yathāsukhanti.

Great indeed is your body, but your wisdom is not befitting it. O crocodile, you have been deceived by me; go now as you please.

Susumārajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Susumāra Jātaka, the eighth.

209. Kukkuṭajātakaṃ (2-6-9)

209. The Kukkuṭa Jātaka (2-6-9)

117.

117.

Diṭṭhā [M 1.0056] mayā vane rukkhā, assakaṇṇā vibhīṭakā vibhedakā (syā. ka.);

Na tāni evaṃ sakkanti, yathā tvaṃ rukkha sakkasi.

I have seen trees in the forest, the Assakaṇṇa and the Vibhīṭaka; but they cannot move in the way that you, O tree, can move.

118.

118.

Purāṇakukkuṭo kakkaro (sī. syā. pī.) ayaṃ, bhetvā pañjaramāgato;

Kusalo vāḷapāsānaṃ, apakkamati bhāsatīti.

This old rooster, having broken its cage, has come; skilled in horse-hair snares, he departs and speaks.

Kukkuṭa kakkara (sī. syā. pī.) jātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Kukkuṭa Jātaka, the ninth.

210. Kandagalakajātakaṃ (2-6-10)

210. The Kandagalaka Jātaka (2-6-10)

119.

119.

Ambho [V 1.0051] ko nāma yaṃ rukkho, sinnapatto sīnapatto (sī. pī.) sakaṇṭako;

Yattha ekappahārena, uttamaṅgaṃ vibhijjitaṃ visāṭikaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), vighāṭitaṃ (sī. niyya).

Sir, what is the name of this tree, with small leaves and thorns, on which a head was split with a single blow?

120.

120.

Acāri vatāyaṃ vitudaṃ vanāni, kaṭṭhaṅgarukkhesu asārakesu;

Athāsadā [T 1.0078] khadiraṃ jātasāraṃ jātisāraṃ (ka.), yatthabbhidā garuḷo uttamaṅganti.

Indeed, this noble bird roamed, pecking at pithless trees in the forest, which are mere heaps of firewood. Then he came upon the Khadira, which is naturally hard-wooded, where the garuḍa split his head.

Kandagalaka kandalaka (ka.) jātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Kandagalaka Jātaka, the tenth.

Nataṃdaḷhavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Daḷha Vagga, the sixth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse thereof:

Daḷhabandhana haṃsavaro ca puna, virūpakkha saviṭṭhaka macchavaro;

Sakuruṅga saassaka ambavaro, puna kukkuṭako garuḷena dasāti.

Daḷhabandhana and the excellent swan; again, Virūpakkha, Saviṭṭhaka, and the excellent fish; Sakuruṅga with Assaka and the excellent mango; again the cock, with the Garuḷa—thus there are ten.

7. Bīraṇathambhavaggo

7. The Bīraṇathambha Vagga

211. Somadattajātakaṃ (2-7-1)

211. The Somadatta Jātaka (2-7-1)

121.

121.

Akāsi yoggaṃ dhuvamappamatto, saṃvaccharaṃ bīraṇathambhakasmiṃ;

Byākāsi saññaṃ parisaṃ vigayha, na niyyamo tāyati appapaññaṃ.

Being vigilant, he constantly undertook his practice for a whole year at the Bīraṇatthambaka charnel ground; having entered the assembly, he declared something else. A vow does not protect one of little wisdom.

122.

122.

Dvayaṃ [M 1.0057] yācanako tāta, somadatta nigacchati;

Alābhaṃ [T 1.0079] dhanalābhaṃ vā, evaṃ dhammā hi yācanāti.

Dear Somadatta, a petitioner meets with two outcomes: either failure to get wealth or its attainment. For such is the nature of asking.

Somadattajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Somadatta Jātaka, the first.

212. Ucchiṭṭhabhattajātakaṃ (2-7-2)

212. The Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka (2-7-2)

123.

123.

Añño uparimo vaṇṇo, añño vaṇṇo ca heṭṭhimo;

Brāhmaṇī tveva pucchāmi, kiṃ heṭṭhā kiñca uppari.

The appearance above is one thing, and the appearance below is another. O Brahmin lady, I ask you indeed: what is below, and what is above?

124.

124.

Ahaṃ naṭosmi bhaddante, bhikkhakosmi idhāgato;

Ayañhi koṭṭhamotiṇṇo, ayaṃ so yaṃ tvaṃ (ka.) gavesasīti.

Noble sir, I am an actor; I have come here as a mendicant. This one has entered the storeroom; this is he whom you seek.

Ucchiṭṭhabhattajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Ucchiṭṭhabhatta Jātaka, the second.

213. Bharujātakaṃ (2-7-3)

213. The Bharu Jātaka (2-7-3)

125.

125.

Isīnamantaraṃ [V 1.0052] katvā, bharurājāti kururājāti (ka.) me sutaṃ;

Ucchinno saha raṭṭhehi raṭṭhena (sī. pī.), sarājā vibhavaṅgato.

Having created a division among the seers, King Bharu—so I have heard—was uprooted along with his kingdom; that king came to ruin.

126.

126.

Tasmā hi chandāgamanaṃ, nappasaṃsanti paṇḍitā;

Aduṭṭhacitto bhāseyya, giraṃ saccupasaṃhitanti.

Therefore the wise do not praise succumbing to partiality. With a mind free from malice, one should utter speech connected with the truth.

Bharujātakaṃ kururātakaṃ (ka.) tatiyaṃ.

The Bharu Jātaka, the third.

214. Puṇṇanadījātakaṃ (2-7-4)

214. The Puṇṇanadī Jātaka (2-7-4)

127.

127.

Puṇṇaṃ nadiṃ yena ca peyyamāhu, jātaṃ [T 1.0080] yavaṃ yena ca guyhamāhu;

Dūraṃ gataṃ yena ca avhayanti, so tyāgato tyābhato (syā. ka.) paheḷigāthābhāvo manasi kātabbo handa ca bhuñja brāhmaṇa.

He by whom they call a full river drinkable, and by whom they call grown barley a hiding place, and by whom they call back one who has gone far—he has come to you. Come now, brahmin, and eat.

128.

128.

Yato maṃ saratī rājā, vāyasampi pahetave;

Haṃsā koñcā mayūrā ca haṃsakoñcamayūrānaṃ (ka. aṭṭha. pāṭhantaraṃ), asatīyeva pāpiyāti.

Since the king remembers me, so as to send even a crow, and for swans, herons, and peacocks, not remembering would be truly wicked.

Puṇṇanadījātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Puṇṇanadī Jātaka, the fourth.

215. Kacchapajātakaṃ (2-7-5)

215. The Kacchapa Jātaka (2-7-5)

129.

129.

Avadhī [M 1.0058] vata attānaṃ, kacchapo byāharaṃ giraṃ kacchapova pabyāharaṃ (syā.), kacchapo so pabyāharaṃ (ka.);

Suggahītasmiṃ kaṭṭhasmiṃ, vācāya sakiyāvadhi.

Alas, the turtle killed himself by uttering speech; while on the firmly grasped stick, he was slain by his own words.

130.

130.

Etampi disvā naravīriyaseṭṭha, vācaṃ pamuñce kusalaṃ nātivelaṃ;

Passasi bahubhāṇena, kacchapaṃ byasanaṃ gatanti.

Having seen this, O best of heroic men, one should utter speech that is skillful and not untimely. Do you not see how through excessive talk the turtle met with disaster?

Kacchapajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Kacchapa Jātaka, the fifth.

216. Macchajātakaṃ (2-7-6)

216. The Maccha Jātaka (2-7-6)

131.

131.

Na māyamaggi tapati, na sūlo sādhutacchito;

Yañca maṃ maññate macchī, aññaṃ so ratiyā gato.

The fire does not burn me, nor does the well-sharpened stake; but what my mate thinks of me—that he has gone to another for pleasure—

132.

132.

So [T 1.0081] maṃ dahati rāgaggi, cittaṃ cūpatapeti maṃ;

Jālino muñcathāyirā maṃ, na kāme haññate kvacīti.

that is what burns me, a fire of passion that torments my mind. Release me, noble fishermen! Let no one anywhere be slain on account of sensual pleasures.

Macchajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Maccha Jātaka, the sixth.

217. Seggujātakaṃ (2-7-7)

217. The Seggu Jātaka (2-7-7)

133.

133.

Sabbo [V 1.0053] loko attamano ahosi, akovidā gāmadhammassa seggu;

Komāri ko nāma komārikā nāma (ka.), komāriko nāma (syā. pī.) tavajja dhammo, yaṃ tvaṃ gahitā pavane parodasi.

The whole world was glad, but you, Seggu, are unskilled in the village custom. Maiden, what is this way of yours today, that you weep aloud, having been seized in the forest?

134.

134.

Yo dukkhaphuṭṭhāya bhaveyya tāṇaṃ, so me pitā dubbhi vane karoti;

Sā kassa kandāmi vanassa majjhe, yo tāyitā so sahasaṃ karotīti.

He who should be a shelter for me when afflicted by suffering, my own father, harms me in the forest. To whom shall I cry in the middle of the woods? My own protector is committing violence.

Seggujātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Seggu Jātaka, the seventh.

218. Kūṭavāṇijajātakaṃ (2-7-8)

218. The Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka (2-7-8)

135.

135.

Saṭhassa [M 1.0059] sāṭheyyamidaṃ sucintitaṃ, paccoḍḍitaṃ paṭikūṭassa kūṭaṃ;

Phālañce khādeyyuṃ adeyyuṃ (sī. pī.) mūsikā, kasmā kumāraṃ kulalā na no (sī. syā. pī.) hareyyuṃ.

This counter-deceit against the deceitful one was well-conceived, a counter-fraud set against the fraudulent. If mice could eat a ploughshare, why would hawks not carry off a boy?

136.

136.

Kūṭassa [T 1.0082] hi santi santīdha (ka.) kūṭakūṭā, bhavati bhavanti (ka.) cāpi nikatino nikatyā;

Dehi puttanaṭṭha phālanaṭṭhassa phālaṃ, mā te puttamahāsi phālanaṭṭhoti.

For the fraudulent, there are those who are fraudulent in return; and for the deceitful, there are those who practice counter-deceit. O man who has lost a son, give the ploughshare to the one who has lost a ploughshare. Let not the one who has lost the ploughshare take your son.

Kūṭavāṇijajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka, the eighth.

219. Garahitajātakaṃ (2-7-9)

219. The Garahita Jātaka (2-7-9)

137.

137.

Hiraññaṃ me suvaṇṇaṃ me, esā rattiṃ divā kathā;

Dummedhānaṃ manussānaṃ, ariyadhammaṃ apassataṃ.

'My silver! My gold!'—such is the talk, night and day, of foolish people who do not see the Noble Dhamma.

138.

138.

Dve dve gahapatayo gehe, eko tattha amassuko;

Lambatthano veṇikato, atho aṅkitakaṇṇako;

In the house are two householders; among them, one is beardless, has pendulous breasts, has braided hair, and moreover, has pierced ears;

Kīto dhanena bahunā, so taṃ vitudate jananti.

Bought with much wealth, that one torments the person.

Garahitajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Garahita Jātaka, the ninth.

220. Dhammadhajajātakaṃ (2-7-10)

220. The Dhammadhaja Jātaka (2-7-10)

139.

139.

Sukhaṃ jīvitarūposi, raṭṭhā vivanamāgato;

So ekako rukkhamūle araññasmiṃ (sī. syā. pī.), kapaṇo viya jhāyasi.

You appear to be one who lives happily, having come from the inhabited country to the wilderness. Sitting alone at the foot of a tree, you ponder like one who is wretched.

140.

140.

Sukhaṃ [V 1.0054] jīvitarūposmi, raṭṭhā vivanamāgato;

So ekako rukkhamūle, kapaṇo viya jhāyāmi;

I am one who lives happily, having come from the inhabited country to the wilderness. Sitting alone at the foot of a tree, I ponder like one who is wretched,

Sataṃ [T 1.0083] dhammaṃ anussaraṃti.

remembering the Dhamma of the good.

Dhammadhajajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Dhammadhaja Jātaka, the tenth.

Bīraṇathambhavaggo sattamo.

The Bīraṇathambha Chapter, the seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary:

Atha [M 1.0060] bīraṇathambhavaro ca naṭo, bharurājavaruttamapuṇṇanadī;

Bahubhāṇi aggipavane mūsikā, sahalambatthano kapaṇena dasāti.

The excellent Bīraṇathambha and the Dancer, the excellent King Bharu and the Full River; the Much-Talking One, the Mice in the fire-wind, the Reproached One, together with the Miserable One, make ten.

8. Kāsāvavaggo

8. The Kāsāva Chapter

221. Kāsāvajātakaṃ (2-8-1)

221. The Kāsāva Jātaka (2-8-1)

141.

141.

Anikkasāvo kāsāvaṃ, yo vatthaṃ paridahissati paridahessati (sī. pī.);

Apeto damasaccena, na so kāsāvamarahati.

Whoever, being impure and devoid of self-control and truth, would don the ochre robe, is not worthy of the ochre robe.

142.

142.

Yo ca vantakasāvassa, sīlesu susamāhito;

Upeto damasaccena, sa ve kāsāvamarahatīti.

But he who has purged his impurities, is well-established in the virtues, and is endowed with self-control and truth—he is truly worthy of the ochre robe.

Kāsāvajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Kāsāva Jātaka, the first.

222. Cūḷanandiyajātakaṃ (2-8-2)

222. The Cūḷanandiya Jātaka (2-8-2)

143.

143.

Idaṃ [T 1.0084] tadācariyavaco, pārāsariyo yadabravi porāṇācariyobravi (ka.);

Māsu tvaṃ akari akarā (sī. pī.) pāpaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ pacchā kataṃ tape.

This was that word of the teacher, which the Pārāsariya spoke: ‘Do not commit an evil deed, which, having been done, would later burn you.’

144.

144.

Yāni karoti puriso, tāni attani passati;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ;

Whatever deeds a person does, those he sees in himself. The doer of good experiences good, and the doer of evil, evil;

Yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phalanti.

Whatever kind of seed one sows, that is the kind of fruit one reaps.

Cūḷanandiyajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Cūḷanandiya Jātaka, the second.

223. Puṭabhattajātakaṃ (2-8-3)

223. The Puṭabhatta Jātaka (2-8-3)

145.

145.

Name [V 1.0055] namantassa bhaje bhajantaṃ, kiccānukubbassa kareyya kiccaṃ;

Nānatthakāmassa kareyya atthaṃ, asambhajantampi na sambhajeyya.

One should bow to one who bows and associate with one who associates. One should perform the task for one who carries out one's tasks. One should not perform the task for one who does not desire one's welfare; one should not associate with one who does not associate.

146.

146.

Caje [M 1.0061] cajantaṃ vanathaṃ na kayirā, apetacittena na sambhajeyya;

Dijo dumaṃ khīṇaphalanti ñatvā, aññaṃ samekkheyya mahā hi lokoti.

One should abandon one who abandons and form no attachment. One should not associate with a person who is estranged in heart. A bird, knowing a tree is barren of fruit, seeks another, for the world is vast.

Puṭabhattajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Puṭabhatta Jātaka, the third.

224. Kumbhilajātakaṃ (2-8-4)

224. The Crocodile Jātaka (2-8-4)

147.

147.

Yassete [T 1.0085] caturo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattati.

Whoever possesses these four principles, O king of monkeys, just as you do—truthfulness, wisdom, fortitude, and generosity—overcomes his enemy.

148.

148.

Yassa cete na vijjanti, guṇā paramabhaddakā;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so nātivattatīti.

But for whom these virtues are not found, O supremely virtuous one—truthfulness, wisdom, fortitude, and generosity—he does not overcome his enemy.

Kumbhilajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Crocodile Jātaka, the fourth.

225. Khantivaṇṇajātakaṃ (2-8-5)

225. The Praise of Patience Jātaka (2-8-5)

149.

149.

Atthi me puriso deva, sabbakiccesu byāvaṭo vāvaṭo (ka.);

Tassa cekoparādhatthi, tattha tvaṃ kinti maññasi.

Your Majesty, I have a man who is diligent in all tasks. He has one fault. In that matter, what is your opinion?

150.

150.

Amhākampatthi puriso, ediso idha vijjati;

Dullabho aṅgasampanno, khantirasmāka ruccatīti.

We, too, have such a man; such a one exists here. Rare is a person endowed with all good qualities; for us, patience is pleasing.

Khantivaṇṇajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Praise of Patience Jātaka, the fifth.

226. Kosiyajātakaṃ (2-8-6)

226. The Owl Jātaka (2-8-6)

151.

151.

Kāle nikkhamanā sādhu, nākāle sādhu nikkhamo;

Akālena hi nikkhamma, ekakampi bahujjano;

Going forth at the right time is good; going forth at the wrong time is not good. For a multitude, having gone forth at the wrong time against even a single person, achieves no purpose,

Na kiñci atthaṃ joteti, dhaṅkasenāva kosiyaṃ.

just as a flock of crows does against an owl.

152.

152.

Dhīro ca vidhividhānaññū, paresaṃ vivarānugū;

Sabbāmitte [T 1.0086] vasīkatvā, kosiyova sukhī siyāti.

But the wise one, who knows the right method and procedure, who is attentive to the openings of his foes, having subdued all his enemies, may live happily like the owl.

Kosiyajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Owl Jātaka, the sixth.

227. Gūthapāṇajātakaṃ (2-8-7)

227. The Dung-Beetle Jātaka (2-8-7)

153.

153.

Sūro [V 1.0056][M 1.0062] sūrena saṅgamma, vikkantena pahārinā;

Ehi nāga nivattassu, kiṃ nu bhīto palāyasi;

A hero meets a hero, a valiant one a mighty striker! Come, elephant, turn back! Why do you flee in fear?

Passantu aṅgamagadhā, mama tuyhañca vikkamaṃ.

Let the people of Aṅga and Magadha see the prowess of both you and me.

154.

154.

Na taṃ pādā vadhissāmi, na dantehi na soṇḍiyā;

Mīḷhena taṃ vadhissāmi, pūti haññatu pūtināti.

I will not slay you with my feet, nor with my tusks, nor with my trunk. I will slay you with my excrement. Let the foul be slain by the foul!

Gūthapāṇajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Dung-Beetle Jātaka, the seventh.

228. Kāmanītajātakaṃ (2-8-8)

228. The Kāmanīta Jātaka (2-8-8)

155.

155.

Tayo giriṃ antaraṃ kāmayāmi, pañcālā kuruyo kekake ca kurayo kekaye ca (sī.);

Tatuttariṃ taduttariṃ (ka.) brāhmaṇa kāmayāmi, tikiccha maṃ brāhmaṇa kāmanītaṃ.

I desire the three mountain-like realms, the Pañcālas, the Kurus, and the Kekakas. Even beyond that, O brahmin, I desire. Heal me, O brahmin, for I am afflicted by desire.

156.

156.

Kaṇhāhidaṭṭhassa karonti heke, amanussapaviṭṭhassa amanussavaddhassa (sī. pī.), amanussaviṭṭhassa (syā.) karonti paṇḍitā;

Na kāmanītassa karoti koci, okkantasukkassa [T 1.0087] hi kā tikicchāti.

Some can cure one bitten by a black serpent, and the wise can cure one possessed by a non-human. But no one can cure a person afflicted by desire. For what cure is there for one who has transgressed wholesome principles and entered into the unwholesome?

Kāmanītajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kāmanīta Jātaka, the Eighth.

229. Palāyitajātakaṃ (2-8-9)

229. The Palāyita Jātaka (2-8-9)

157.

157.

Gajaggameghehi hayaggamālibhi, rathūmijātehi sarābhivassebhi sarābhivassabhi (syā. sī. aṭṭha.), sarābhivassibhi (?);

Tharuggahāvaṭṭa dhanuggahāvaṭṭa (ka.) daḷhappahāribhi, parivāritā takkasilā samantato.

Let Takkasilā be surrounded on all sides: by clouds that are excellent elephants, by heroes riding the finest horses, by hosts of chariot-warriors like the waves of the ocean, by those who rain down arrows, and by those wielding bows, whirling and striking fiercely.

158.

158.

abhidhāvathā ca patathā ca, vividhavinaditā ca dantibhi; vattatajja tumulo ghoso, yathā vijjutā jaladharassa gajjatoti; (sī. pī. ka.) Abhidhāvatha [M 1.0063] cūpadhāvatha ca abhidhāvathā cuppatathā ca (syā.), vividhā vināditā vināditattha (ka.) vadantibhi;

Vattatajja tumulo ghoso yathā, vijjulatā jaladharassa gajjatoti abhidhāvathā ca patathā ca, vividhavinaditā ca dantibhi; vattatajja tumulo ghoso, yathā vijjutā jaladharassa gajjatoti; (sī. pī. ka.).

Charge and attack! Make diverse sounds together with the elephants! Let a tumultuous roar arise today, like the thunder of a rain cloud with flashing lightning.

Palāyitajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Palāyita Jātaka, the Ninth.

230. Dutiyapalāyitajātakaṃ (2-8-10)

230. The Second Palāyita Jātaka (2-8-10)

159.

159.

Dhajamaparimitaṃ anantapāraṃ, duppasahaṃdhaṅkehi sāgaraṃva sāgaramiva (sī. syā. pī.);

Girimivaanilena duppasayho duppasaho (sī. pī. ka.), duppasaho ahamajjatādisena.

The banners are immeasurable. Like the ocean with its endless shore, which is difficult for crows to overcome, and like a mountain, which is difficult for the wind to shake, so am I today difficult to overcome by one such as you.

160.

160.

Mā [T 1.0088] bāliyaṃ vilapi vippalapi (bahūsu) na hissa tādisaṃ, viḍayhase viḷayhase (sī. pī.) na hi labhase nisedhakaṃ;

Āsajjasi gajamiva ekacārinaṃ, yo taṃ padā naḷamiva pothayissatīti.

O fool, do not lament your foolishness; it will not be as you think. You are consumed by passion, for you find no one to restrain you. You approach a solitary elephant, which will crush you with its foot as if you were a reed.

Dutiyapalāyitajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Second Palāyita Jātaka, the Tenth.

Kāsāvavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Kāsāva Chapter, the Eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Varavatthavaco [V 1.0057] dumakhīṇaphalaṃ, caturodhammavaraṃ purisuttama;

Dhaṅkamagadhā ca tayogirināma, gajaggavaro dhajavarena dasāti.

The Excellent Cloth, the Tree with Withered Fruit, the Four Excellent Dhammas, the Supreme Person; The Crow and Magadha, the one named Three Mountains, the Excellent Elephant, and with the Excellent Banner make ten.

9. Upāhanavaggo

9. The Chapter on the Sandal

231. Upāhanajātakaṃ (2-9-1)

231. The Sandal Jātaka (2-9-1)

161.

161.

Yathāpi [M 1.0064] kītā purisassupāhanā, sukhassa atthāya dukhaṃ udabbahe;

Ghammābhitattā thalasā papīḷitā, tasseva pāde purisassa khādare.

Just as a man’s bought sandal, meant for his comfort, might bring him suffering; scorched by the heat and pressed by the hard ground, it might bite that very man’s foot.

162.

162.

Evameva [T 1.0089] yo dukkulīno anariyo, tammāka tamhāka (sī.), tumhāka (syā. pī.) vijjañca sutañca ādiya;

Tameva so tattha sutena khādati, anariyo vuccati dupāhanūpamoti pānadūpamoti (sī. pī.).

Even so, whichever ignoble person of low birth acquires knowledge and learning from a teacher, he then harms that very teacher with that learning. Such an ignoble one is said to be like a bad sandal.

Upāhanajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Sandal Jātaka, the First.

232. Vīṇāguṇajātakaṃ (2-9-2)

232. The Lute-String Jātaka (2-9-2)

163.

163.

Ekacintito yamattho, bālo apariṇāyako;

Na hi khujjena vāmena, bhoti saṅgantumarahasi.

This matter must have been conceived by you alone. Indeed, the fool is no leader. O lady, you ought not to associate with a crooked hunchback.

164.

164.

Purisūsabhaṃ maññamānā, ahaṃ khujjamakāmayiṃ;

Soyaṃ saṃkuṭito seti, chinnatanti yathā viṇāti thuṇāti (sī.).

Thinking he was a bull among men, I desired the hunchback. But now he lies all curled up, like a lute with a broken string.

Vīṇāguṇajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Lute-String Jātaka, the Second.

233. Vikaṇṇajātakaṃ (2-9-3)

233. The Vikaṇṇa Jātaka (2-9-3)

165.

165.

Kāmaṃ yahiṃ icchasi tena gaccha, viddhosi mammamhi mamasmi (ka.) vikaṇṇakena;

Hatosi bhattena suvāditena savāditena (sī. syā. pī.), lolo ca macche anubandhamāno.

Go wherever you wish! You have been pierced in a vital spot by my barbed spear. Being greedy while pursuing the fish, you have been slain by the well-flavored bait.

166.

166.

Evampi [M 1.0065] lokāmisaṃ opatanto, vihaññatī [T 1.0090] cittavasānuvattī;

So haññati ñātisakhāna majjhe, macchānugo soriva suṃsumāroti susumāro (ka.).

Even so, one who follows the sway of his mind, falling for the bait of the world, is afflicted. He is afflicted in the midst of his kinsmen, just like that crocodile that came to ruin while pursuing fish.

Vikaṇṇajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Vikaṇṇa Jātaka, the Third.

234. Asitābhūjātakaṃ (2-9-4)

234. The Asitābhū Jātaka (2-9-4)

167.

167.

Tvameva [V 1.0058] dānimakara makari (syā.), makarā (ka. sī.), yaṃ kāmo byagamā tayi;

Soyaṃ appaṭisandhiko, kharachinnaṃva renukaṃ rerukaṃ (sī. pī.).

You yourself have now brought this about: the desire I had for you has departed. It is now without possibility of rejoining, like an elephant's tusk severed by a saw.

168.

168.

Atricchaṃ atricchā (sī. syā. pī.) atilobhena, atilobhamadena ca;

Evaṃ hāyati atthamhā, ahaṃva asitābhuyāti.

Through excessive craving and greed, and the intoxication of great greed, a covetous person falls away from their welfare, just as I have fallen away from Asitābhū.

Asitābhūjātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Asitābhū Jātaka, the Fourth.

235. Vacchanakhajātakaṃ (2-9-5)

235. The Vacchanakha Jātaka (2-9-5)

169.

169.

Sukhā gharā vacchanakha, sahiraññā sabhojanā;

Yattha bhutvā pivitvā ca, sayeyyātha anussuko.

Happy are homes, O Vacchanakha, endowed with gold and with food, where, having eaten and drunk, you may lie down without exertion.

170.

170.

Gharā nānīhamānassa, gharā nābhaṇato musā;

Gharā nādinnadaṇḍassa, paresaṃ anikubbato anikrubbato (ka.);

A home does not endure for one who is indolent, nor for one who refrains from speaking falsely, nor for one who does not inflict punishment and oppress others.

Evaṃ chiddaṃ durabhisambhavaṃ durabhibhavaṃ (sī. pī.), ko gharaṃ paṭipajjatīti.

Who would undertake to manage such a home, so flawed and difficult to maintain?

Vacchanakhajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Vacchanakha Jātaka, the Fifth.

236. Bakajātakaṃ (2-9-6)

236. The Crane Jātaka (2-9-6)

171.

171.

Bhaddako [T 1.0091] vatayaṃ pakkhī, dijo kumudasannibho;

Vūpasantehi pakkhehi, mandamandova jhāyati.

Indeed, what a fine bird this is, this twice-born one resembling a white water lily! With its wings stilled, it remains pensive, as if weak and gentle.

172.

172.

Nāssa sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha;

Amhe dijo na pāleti, tena pakkhī na phandatīti.

You do not know its character; you praise it without understanding. This twice-born does not protect us; that is why the bird does not stir.

Bakajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Heron Jātaka, the Sixth.

237. Sāketajātakaṃ (2-9-7)

237. The Sāketa Jātaka (2.9.7)

173.

173.

Ko [M 1.0066] nu kho bhagavā hetu, ekacce idha puggale;

Atīva hadayaṃ nibbāti, cittañcāpi pasīdati.

What, O Blessed One, is the reason that, toward certain persons here in this world, the heart is exceedingly calmed and the mind also becomes serene?

174.

174.

Pubbeva sannivāsena, paccuppannahitena vā;

Evaṃ taṃ jāyate pemaṃ, uppalaṃva yathodaketi.

Through having lived together in the past or through some benefit in the present, in that way love is born, just as a lotus is born in the water.

Sāketajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Sāketa Jātaka, the Seventh.

238. Ekapadajātakaṃ (2-9-8)

238. The One-Word Jātaka (2.9.8)

175.

175.

Iṅgha [V 1.0059] ekapadaṃ tāta, anekatthapadassitaṃ padanissitaṃ (sī. pī.);

Kiñci saṅgāhikaṃ brūsi, yenatthe sādhayemase.

Come, dear father, speak a single word that points to many meanings. Utter something comprehensive by which we may achieve our aims.

176.

176.

Dakkheyyekapadaṃ tāta, anekatthapadassitaṃ;

Tañca sīlena saññuttaṃ, khantiyā upapāditaṃ;

Skillfulness is the one word, dear son, that points to many meanings. It is connected with virtuous conduct and endowed with patience.

Alaṃ [T 1.0092] mitte sukhāpetuṃ, amittānaṃ dukhāya cāti.

It is sufficient to make friends happy and to bring sorrow to one’s enemies.

Ekapadajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The One-Word Jātaka, the Eighth.

239. Haritamaṇḍūkajātakaṃ (2-9-9)

239. The Green Frog Jātaka (2.9.9)

177.

177.

Āsīvisampi maṃ āsīvisaṃ mamaṃ (sī. pī.) santaṃ, paviṭṭhaṃ kumināmukhaṃ;

Ruccate haritāmātā, yaṃ maṃ khādanti macchakā.

O green friend, does it please you that the fish are eating me, a water snake who has entered the mouth of the fish-trap?

178.

178.

Vilumpateva puriso, yāvassa upakappati;

Yadā caññe vilumpanti, so vilutto vilumpatīti viluppatīti (?).

A man plunders only for as long as it is advantageous for him. But when others plunder him, he, the plundered one, is in turn destroyed.

Haritamaṇḍūkajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Green Frog Jātaka, the Ninth.

240. Mahāpiṅgalajātakaṃ (2-9-10)

240. The Great Piṅgala Jātaka (2.9.10)

179.

179.

Sabbo jano hiṃsito piṅgalena, tasmiṃ mate paccayā paccayaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) vedayanti;

Piyo nu te āsi akaṇhanetto, kasmā nu tvaṃ rodasi dvārapāla.

All the people were oppressed by Piṅgala; now that he is dead they feel joy. Was he dear to you, the one with tawny eyes? Why then do you weep, O gatekeeper?

180.

180.

Na [M 1.0067] me piyo āsi akaṇhanetto, bhāyāmi paccāgamanāya tassa;

Ito gato hiṃseyya maccurājaṃ, so hiṃsito āneyya puna idha.

The one with tawny eyes was not dear to me; I fear his return. Having gone from here, he might harm the King of Death, and he, being harmed, might bring him back here again.

181.

181.

Daḍḍho vāhasahassehi, sitto ghaṭasatehi so;

Parikkhatā [T 1.0093] ca sā bhūmi, mā bhāyi nāgamissatīti.

He was burned with a thousand cartloads of firewood and doused with a hundred pots of water. That burial ground has also been dug up. Do not be afraid; he will not return.

Mahāpiṅgalajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Great Piṅgala Jātaka, the tenth.

Upāhanavaggo navamo.

The Sandal Chapter, the ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Varupāhana khujja vikaṇṇakako, asitābhuya pañcamavacchanakho;

Dija pemavaruttamaekapadaṃ, kumināmukha piṅgalakena dasāti.

The Excellent Sandal, the Hunchback, and the Earless; Asitābhū and fifth, the Vacchanakha; the Bird, Love, and the One-Word; the Fish-Trap Mouth, and with Piṅgala make ten.

10. Siṅgālavaggo

10. The Jackal Chapter

241. Sabbadāṭhijātakaṃ (2-10-1)

241. The All-Tusked Jātaka (2.10.1)

182.

182.

Siṅgālo [V 1.0060] mānathaddho ca, parivārena atthiko;

Pāpuṇi mahatiṃ bhūmiṃ, rājāsi sabbadāṭhinaṃ.

The jackal, stiff with pride and desirous of a retinue, attained a great domain; he was the king of all tusked creatures.

183.

183.

Evameva manussesu, yo hoti parivāravā;

So hi tattha mahā hoti, siṅgālo viya dāṭhinanti.

Just so among human beings, whoever has a retinue, he indeed is great in that place, like the jackal among the tusked creatures.

The All-Tusked Jātaka, the first.

242. Sunakhajātakaṃ (2-10-2)

242. The Dog Jātaka (2.10.2)

184.

184.

Bālo [T 1.0094] vatāyaṃ sunakho, yo varattaṃ yo ca yottaṃ (ka.) na khādati;

Bandhanā ca pamuñceyya, asito ca gharaṃ vaje.

What a fool this dog is, who does not chew the strap! He would be freed from his bond, and having eaten, would go home.

185.

185.

Aṭṭhitaṃ [M 1.0068] me manasmiṃ me, atho me hadaye kataṃ;

Kālañca paṭikaṅkhāmi, yāva passupatū jano pasupatujjano (syā. ka.).

It is established in my mind, and it is resolved in my heart. I am awaiting the right time, until the people fall asleep.

Sunakhajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Dog Jātaka, the second.

243. Guttilajātakaṃ (2-10-3)

243. The Guttila Jātaka (2.10.3)

186.

186.

Sattatantiṃ sumadhuraṃ, rāmaṇeyyaṃ avācayiṃ;

So maṃ raṅgamhi avheti, saraṇaṃ me hohi kosiya.

I played the seven-stringed lute, so very sweet and delightful. Now he challenges me on the stage. Be my refuge, O Kosiya!

187.

187.

Ahaṃ taṃ saraṇaṃ samma ahaṃ te saraṇaṃ homi (vi. va. 328), ahamācariyapūjako;

Na taṃ jayissati sisso, sissamācariya jessasīti.

I am your refuge, friend; I am one who venerates teachers. The pupil will not defeat you; you, the teacher, will defeat the pupil.

Guttilajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Guttila Jātaka, the third.

244. Vigaticchajātakaṃ (2-10-4)

244. The Desire-Free Jātaka (2.10.4)

188.

188.

Yaṃ passati na taṃ icchati, yañca na passati taṃ kiricchati;

Maññāmi ciraṃ carissati, na hi taṃ lacchati yaṃ sa icchati.

What he sees, that he does not want; and what he does not see, that he desires. I think he will wander for a long time, for he will not get that which he wants.

189.

189.

Yaṃ labhati na tena tussati, yañca pattheti laddhaṃ hīḷeti;

Icchā hi anantagocarā, vigaticchāna vīticchānaṃ (sī. pī.) namo karomaseti.

He is not satisfied with what he gets; and what he strives for, once gotten, he despises. For desire’s range is endless. We pay homage to those free from desire!

Vigaticcha vīticcha (sī. pī.) jātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Desire-Free Jātaka, the fourth.

245. Mūlapariyāyajātakaṃ (2-10-5)

245. The Root Sequence Jātaka (2.10.5)

190.

190.

Kālo [T 1.0095][V 1.0061] ghasati bhūtāni, sabbāneva sahattanā;

Time devours all beings, together with itself; but the being who devours time has cooked the cooker of beings.

191.

191.

Bahūni narasīsāni, lomasāni brahāni ca;

Gīvāsu paṭimukkāni, kocidevettha kaṇṇavāti.

Many human heads, hairy and large, are placed upon these necks. Is there anyone here with ears?

Mūlapariyāyajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Mūlapariyāya Jātaka, the fifth.

246. Bālovādajātakaṃ (2-10-6)

246. The Jātaka on the Fool's Advice (2-10-6)

192.

192.

Hantvā chetvā jhatvā (sī. pī.), ghatvā (syā.) vadhitvā ca, deti dānaṃ asaññato;

Edisaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjamāno, sa pāpamupalimpati sa pāpena upalippati (sī. pī.).

Having struck, cut, and killed, an unrestrained person gives a gift; one who eats such food is smeared with evil.

193.

193.

Puttadārampi [M 1.0069] ce hantvā, deti dānaṃ asaññato;

Bhuñjamānopi sappañño, na pāpamupalimpatīti.

Even if an unrestrained person gives a gift after having killed his own son and wife, a wise person, though eating it, is not smeared with evil.

Bālovādajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Jātaka on the Fool's Advice, the sixth.

247. Pādañjalījātakaṃ (2-10-7)

247. The Pādañjali Jātaka (2-10-7)

194.

194.

Addhā pādañjalī sabbe, paññāya atirocati;

Tathā hi oṭṭhaṃ bhañjati, uttariṃ nūna passati.

Indeed, Pādañjali surpasses all with wisdom; for he bites his lip, he surely sees what is beyond.

195.

195.

Nāyaṃ dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, atthānatthañca bujjhati;

Aññatra [T 1.0096] oṭṭhanibbhogā, nāyaṃ jānāti kiñcananti.

This one understands neither what is right nor what is not right, neither what is beneficial nor what is not beneficial; apart from biting his lip, he knows nothing at all.

Pādañjalījātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Pādañjali Jātaka, the seventh.

248. Kiṃsukopamajātakaṃ (2-10-8)

248. The Kiṃsuka Simile Jātaka (2-10-8)

196.

196.

Sabbehi kiṃsuko diṭṭho, kiṃnvettha vicikicchatha;

Na hi sabbesu ṭhānesu, sārathī paripucchito.

You have all seen the kiṃsuka tree, so why are you in doubt about it? For the charioteer was not questioned in all instances.

197.

197.

Evaṃ sabbehi ñāṇehi, yesaṃ dhammā ajānitā;

Te ve dhammesu kaṅkhanti, kiṃsukasmiṃva bhātaroti.

Thus, those by whom the teachings are not known with all their knowledges, they indeed have doubts about the teachings, just as the brothers did about the kiṃsuka tree.

Kiṃsukopamajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kiṃsuka Simile Jātaka, the eighth.

249. Sālakajātakaṃ (2-10-9)

249. The Sālaka Jātaka (2-10-9)

198.

198.

Ekaputtako [V 1.0062] bhavissasi, tvañca no hessasi issaro kule;

Oroha dumasmā sālaka, ehi dāni gharakaṃ vajemase.

You will be our only son, and you will be the master of our family. Come down from the tree, Sālaka; come now, let us go home.

199.

199.

Nanu maṃ suhadayoti nanu maṃ hadayeti (sī. pī.) maññasi, yañca maṃ hanasi veḷuyaṭṭhiyā;

Pakkambavane ramāmase, gaccha tvaṃ gharakaṃ yathāsukhanti.

Surely you do not think of me as a dear friend, you who beat me with a bamboo stick? We shall enjoy ourselves in the Pakkamba grove; you go home as you please.

Sālakajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Sālaka Jātaka, the ninth.

250. Kapijātakaṃ (2-10-10)

250. The Monkey Jātaka (2-10-10)

200.

200.

Ayaṃ [T 1.0097][M 1.0070] isī upasamasaṃyame rato, sa tiṭṭhati santiṭṭhati (sī. pī.) sisirabhayena aṭṭito;

Handa ayaṃ pavisatumaṃ agārakaṃ, vinetu sītaṃ darathañca kevalaṃ.

This sage delights in peace and self-control; he stands there afflicted by fear of the cold. Come, let him enter this dwelling to dispel the cold and all his distress.

201.

201.

Nāyaṃ isī upasamasaṃyame rato, kapī ayaṃ dumavarasākhagocaro;

So dūsako rosako cāpi jammo, sacevajemampi sace + āvaje + imampi dūseyyagāranti dūsaye gharanti (sī. syā. pī.).

This is no sage who delights in peace and self-control; this is a monkey that roams the branches of fine trees. He is destructive, irritable, and a scoundrel; if he enters, he will ruin the dwelling.

Kapijātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Monkey Jātaka, the tenth.

Siṅgālavaggo dasamo.

The Jackal Chapter, the tenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Atha rājā siṅgālavaro sunakho, tathā kosiya icchati kālaghaso;

Atha dānavaroṭṭhapi sārathinā, punambavanañca sisirakapi dasāti.

The King, the Excellent Jackal, the Dog; likewise the Owl, Desires, the Time-Devourer; then the Excellent Gift, the Lip, and the Charioteer; again the Mango Grove and the Cold Monkey make ten.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

The summary of the chapters:

Daḷhañca [T 1.0098] vaggaṃ aparena santhavaṃ, kalyāṇavaggāsadiso ca rūhakaṃ;

Nataṃdaḷha bīraṇathambhakaṃ puna, kāsāvupāhana siṅgālakena dasāti.

The Daḷha Chapter, and next the Santhava; the Kalyāṇa Chapter, the Asadisa, and the Rūhaka; the Nataṃdaḷha, the Bīraṇathambha; again, the Kāsāva, the Upāhana, and with the Siṅgāla make ten.

Dukanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Book of Twos is concluded.

3. Tikanipāto

3. The Book of Threes

1. Saṅkappavaggo

1. The Chapter on Intention

251. Saṅkapparāgajātakaṃ (3-1-1)

251. The Jātaka on Lust Born of Intention (3-1-1)

1.

1.

Saṅkapparāgadhotena[T 1.0099][V 1.0063][M 1.0071], vitakkanisitena ca;

Nālaṅkatena bhadrena nevālaṅkatabhadrena (syā.), usukārākatena ca na usukārakatena ca (sī. syā. pī.).

Washed with the lust of intention, and sharpened by thought; unadorned, yet fine, and not made by a fletcher—

2.

2.

Na kaṇṇāyatamuttena, nāpi morūpasevinā;

Tenamhi hadaye viddho, sabbaṅgaparidāhinā.

—not released from a bow drawn to the ear, nor fletched with peacock feathers; by that arrow I am pierced in the heart, which burns through all my limbs.

3.

3.

Āvedhañca na passāmi, yato ruhiramassave;

Yāva ayoniso cittaṃ, sayaṃ me dukkhamābhatanti.

I do not see the wound from which blood might flow. So long as my mind is unmethodical, I myself have brought this suffering.

Saṅkapparāgajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Jātaka on Lust Born of Intention, the first.

252. Tilamuṭṭhijātakaṃ (3-1-2)

252. The Handful of Sesame Jātaka (3-1-2)

4.

4.

Ajjāpi me taṃ manasi sarasi (ka.), yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ tilamuṭṭhiyā;

Bāhāya maṃ gahetvāna, laṭṭhiyā anutāḷayi.

Even today it is on my mind how you, on account of a handful of sesame seeds, seized me by the arm and struck me with a split bamboo stick.

5.

5.

Nanu jīvite na ramasi, yenāsi brāhmaṇāgato;

Yaṃ maṃ bāhā gahetvāna, tikkhattuṃ anutāḷayi.

Surely you do not delight in life, brahmin, that you have come here—you who seized me by the arm and struck me three times.

6.

6.

Ariyo anariyaṃ kubbantaṃ kubbānaṃ (sī. pī.), kubbaṃ (syā.), yo daṇḍena nisedhati;

Sāsanaṃ taṃ na taṃ veraṃ, iti naṃ paṇḍitā vidūti.

When a noble one restrains with punishment one who is acting ignobly, that is instruction, not enmity—so the wise understand it.

Tilamuṭṭhijātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Handful of Sesame Jātaka, the second.

253. Maṇikaṇṭhajātakaṃ (3-1-3)

253. The Jewel-Neck Jātaka (3-1-3)

7.

7.

Mamannapānaṃ [T 1.0100] vipulaṃ uḷāraṃ, uppajjatīmassa maṇissa hetu;

Taṃ te na dassaṃ atiyācakosi, na cāpi te assamamāgamissaṃ.

Abundant and excellent food and drink arise for me because of this jewel. I will not give it to you, for you are one who begs excessively; nor will I come to your hermitage.

8.

8.

Susū [V 1.0064][M 1.0072] yathā sakkharadhotapāṇī, tāsesi maṃ selaṃ yācamāno;

Taṃ te na dassaṃ atiyācakosi, na cāpi te assamamāgamissaṃ.

Just as a youth with a whetted sword in hand might threaten, so you frighten me, begging for this jewel. You are one who begs excessively; I will not give it to you, nor will I come to your hermitage.

9.

9.

Na taṃ yāce yassa piyaṃ jigīse jigiṃse (sī. syā. pī.), desso hoti atiyācanāya;

Nāgo maṇiṃ yācito brāhmaṇena, adassanaṃyeva tadajjhagamāti.

One should not beg for that which is dear to someone whose affection one wishes to win, for one becomes hateful through excessive begging. The Nāga, when begged for his jewel by the brahmin, went out of sight from that time on.

Maṇikaṇṭhajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Jewel-Neck Jātaka, the third.

254. Kuṇḍakakucchisindhavajātakaṃ (3-1-4)

254. The Jātaka of the Sindh Horse and the Bran Mash (3-1-4)

10.

10.

Bhutvā tiṇaparighāsaṃ, bhutvā ācāmakuṇḍakaṃ;

Etaṃ te bhojanaṃ āsi, kasmā dāni na bhuñjasi.

Having eaten leftover grass, having eaten scum and broken rice—this was your food. Why do you not eat now?

11.

11.

Yattha posaṃ na jānanti, jātiyā vinayena vā;

Bahuṃ pahū (sī. pī.), pahuṃ (syā. ka.) tattha mahābramhe, api ācāmakuṇḍakaṃ.

Where they do not recognize a person by birth or by training, there, O great merchant, even scum and broken rice is plenty.

12.

12.

Tvañca [T 1.0101] kho maṃ pajānāsi, yādisāyaṃ hayuttamo;

Jānanto jānamāgamma, na te bhakkhāmi kuṇḍakanti.

But you indeed know me and what kind of excellent horse I am. I, who know my worth, having come to you, who also knows it, will not eat your bran.

Kuṇḍakakucchisindhavajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Jātaka of the Sindh Horse and the Bran Mash, the fourth.

255. Sukajātakaṃ (3-1-5)

255. The Parrot Jātaka (3-1-5)

13.

13.

Yāva so mattamaññāsi, bhojanasmiṃ vihaṅgamo;

Tāva addhānamāpādi, mātarañca aposayi.

So long as that bird knew the measure in its food, it attained a long life and nourished its mother.

14.

14.

Yato ca kho bahutaraṃ, bhojanaṃ ajjhavāhari ajjhupāhari (sī. pī.);

Tato tattheva saṃsīdi, amattaññū hi so ahu.

But when it consumed too much food, it sank right there, for it was one that did not know the measure.

15.

15.

Tasmā mattaññutā sādhu, bhojanasmiṃ agiddhatā agiddhitā (syā. ka.);

Amattaññū hi sīdanti, mattaññū ca na sīdareti.

Therefore, knowing the measure in eating and non-greediness are good. For those who do not know the measure sink, but those who know the measure do not.

Sukajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Parrot Jātaka, the fifth.

256. Jarūdapānajātakaṃ (3-1-6)

256. The Jarūdapāna Jātaka (3-1-6)

16.

16.

Jarūdapānaṃ [M 1.0073] khaṇamānā, vāṇijā udakatthikā;

Ajjhagamuṃ ayasaṃ lohaṃ ajjhagaṃsu ayolohaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), tipusīsañca vāṇijā;

Rajataṃ jātarūpañca, muttā veḷūriyā bahū.

Digging an old well, merchants in need of water came upon iron and copper, tin and lead, silver and gold, and many pearls and beryl.

17.

17.

Te ca tena asantuṭṭhā, bhiyyo bhiyyo akhāṇisuṃ;

Te tatthāsīviso tattha āsīviso (ka.), tatthapāsīviso (syā.) ghoro, tejassī tejasā hani.

But they, not satisfied with that, dug more and more; there a terrible and powerful venomous serpent struck them down with its fiery energy.

18.

18.

Tasmā [T 1.0102][V 1.0065] khaṇe nātikhaṇe, atikhātaṃ atikhaṇaṃ (ka.) hi pāpakaṃ;

Khātena ca khaṇena ca (ka.), khaṇanena (syā.) dhanaṃ laddhaṃ, atikhātena atikhaṇena (ka.) nāsitanti.

Therefore, one should dig, but not dig excessively, for excessive digging is evil. By digging, wealth was obtained; by digging excessively, they were destroyed.

Jarūdapānajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Jarūdapāna Jātaka, the sixth.

257. Gāmaṇicandajātakaṃ (3-1-7)

257. The Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka (3-1-7)

19.

19.

Nāyaṃ gharānaṃ kusalo, lolo ayaṃ valīmukho;

Kataṃ kataṃ kho dūseyya, evaṃdhammamidaṃ kulaṃ.

This one is not skilled in managing or building houses; this wrinkled-faced one is fickle. He would spoil whatever is done; such is the nature of this breed.

20.

20.

Nayidaṃ cittavato lomaṃ, nāyaṃ assāsiko migo;

Siṭṭhaṃ satthaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) me janasandhena, nāyaṃ kiñci vijānati.

This is not the fur of a creature with a mind, nor is this a trustworthy beast. I was instructed thus by my father, King Janasandha: 'This one knows nothing of judgment.'

21.

21.

Na mātaraṃ pitaraṃ vā, bhātaraṃ bhaginiṃ sakaṃ;

Bhareyya tādiso poso, siṭṭhaṃ dasarathena meti.

Such a person should not support his own mother or father, or his own brother or sister. I was instructed thus by my father, King Dasaratha.

Gāmaṇicanda gāmaṇicaṇḍa (sī. pī.) jātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Gāmaṇicanda Jātaka, the seventh.

258. Mandhātujātakaṃ (3-1-8)

258. The Mandhātu Jātaka (3-1-8)

22.

22.

Yāvatā candimasūriyā, pariharanti disā bhanti virocanā virocamānā (ka.);

Sabbeva dāsā mandhātu, ye pāṇā pathavissitā paṭhavinissitā (sī. pī.), paṭhavissitā (syā.).

As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the directions, all living beings who depend on the earth are indeed slaves of Mandhātu.

23.

23.

Na kahāpaṇavassena, titti kāmesu vijjati;

Appassādā dukhā kāmā, iti viññāya paṇḍito.

Not by a rain of treasures is satisfaction found in sensual pleasures. Sensual pleasures are of little delight and are suffering—thus the wise one understands.

24.

24.

Api [M 1.0074] dibbesu kāmesu, ratiṃ so nādhigacchati;

Taṇhakkhayarato [T 1.0103] hoti, sammāsambuddhasāvakoti.

He finds no delight even in divine sensual pleasures; the disciple of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One delights in the destruction of craving.

Mandhātujātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Mandhātu Jātaka, the eighth.

259. Tirīṭavacchajātakaṃ (3-1-9)

259. The Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka (3-1-9)

25.

25.

Nayimassa vijjāmayamatthi kiñci, na bandhavo no pana te sahāyo;

Atha kena vaṇṇena tirīṭavaccho tirīṭivaccho (syā. ka.), tedaṇḍiko bhuñjati aggapiṇḍaṃ.

This one has no accomplishment achieved through knowledge whatsoever; he is not your relative, nor is he your companion. That being so, for what reason does Tirīṭavaccha, the carrier of the triple staff, eat the finest food?

26.

26.

Āpāsu āvāsu (ka.) me yuddhaparājitassa, ekassa katvā vivanasmi ghore;

Pasārayī kicchagatassa pāṇiṃ, tenūdatāriṃ dukhasaṃpareto.

When I was defeated in battle, alone, and had fallen into a well in distress, he, taking pity on me in that fierce, waterless forest, stretched out his hand. For that reason, though overcome by suffering, I was able to ascend.

27.

27.

Etassa [V 1.0066] kiccena idhānupatto, vesāyino visayā jīvaloke;

Lābhāraho tāta tirīṭavaccho, dethassa bhogaṃ yajathañca yajatañca (sī. pī.), yajitañca (syā.) yaññanti.

By his deed, I have returned here to the world of the living from the realm of Yama. Dear son, Tirīṭavaccha is worthy of gain. Give him wealth and perform a sacrifice.

Tirīṭavacchajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Tirīṭavaccha Jātaka, the ninth.

260. Dūtajātakaṃ (3-1-10)

260. The Dūta Jātaka (3-1-10)

28.

28.

Yassatthā [T 1.0104] dūramāyanti, amittamapi yācituṃ;

Tassūdarassahaṃ dūto, mā me kujjha kujjhi (sī. pī.) rathesabha.

For whose sake beings go far to beg even from an enemy—I am the messenger of that belly. Do not be angry with me, O excellent king.

29.

29.

Yassa divā ca ratto ca, vasamāyanti māṇavā;

Tassūdarassahaṃ dūto, mā me kujjha kujjhi (sī. pī.) rathesabha.

Under whose control people come, both day and night—I am the messenger of that belly. Do not be angry with me, O excellent king.

30.

30.

Dadāmi [M 1.0075] te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ, gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena;

Dūto hi dūtassa kathaṃ na dajjaṃ, mayampi tasseva bhavāma dūtāti.

I give you, brahmin, a thousand red cows together with a bull. For how could a messenger not give to a messenger? We too are messengers of that very same one.

Dūtajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Dūta Jātaka, the tenth.

Saṅkappavaggo paṭhamo.

The First Chapter on Thought.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for that chapter:

Usukāravaro tilamuṭṭhi maṇi, hayarāja vihaṅgama āsiviso;

Janasandha kahāpaṇavassa puna, tiriṭaṃ puna dūtavarena dasāti.

The excellent arrow-maker, the handful of sesame, the jewel; the horse-king, the bird, the venomous serpent; Janasandha, the rain of coins, then Tiriṭa, and then with the excellent messenger—thus there are ten.

2. Padumavaggo

2. The Chapter on the Lotus

261. Padumajātakaṃ (3-2-1)

261. The Paduma Jātaka (3.2.1)

31.

31.

Yathā [T 1.0105] kesā ca massū ca, chinnaṃ chinnaṃ virūhati;

Evaṃ rūhatu te nāsā, padumaṃ dehi yācito.

Just as hair and beard grow back whenever they are cut, so may your nose grow back. Give the lotus, as you are asked.

32.

32.

Yathā sāradikaṃ bījaṃ, khette vuttaṃ virūhati;

Evaṃ rūhatu te nāsā, padumaṃ dehi yācito.

Just as an autumnal seed sown in a field sprouts, so may your nose grow back. Give the lotus, as you are asked.

33.

33.

Ubhopi palapantete vilapantete (syā. ka.), api padmāni dassati;

Vajjuṃ vā te na vā vajjuṃ, natthi nāsāya rūhanā;

Dehi samma padumāni, ahaṃ yācāmi yācitoti.
