These two are merely babbling, 'Perhaps he will give the lotuses!' Whether they speak or not, there is no growing back for a nose. Friend, give the lotuses; I ask, and you are the one being asked.

Padumajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Paduma Jātaka, the first.

262. Mudupāṇijātakaṃ (3-2-2)

262. The Mudupāṇi Jātaka (3.2.2)

34.

34.

Pāṇi [V 1.0067] ce muduko cassa, nāgo cassa sukārito;

Andhakāro ca vasseyya, atha nūna tadā siyā.

If her hand were soft, and if the elephant were well-trained, and if it were dark and it were to rain, then indeed, at that time, it might come to pass.

35.

35.

Analā [M 1.0076] mudusambhāsā, duppūrā tā duppūrattā (ka.) nadīsamā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

Insatiable, of gentle speech, and difficult to fill like rivers; knowing that they cause one to sink, the wise person should avoid them from afar.

36.

36.

Yaṃ etā upasevanti, chandasā vā dhanena vā;

Jātavedova saṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippaṃ anudahanti nanti.

Whomever they associate with, whether through desire or for wealth, they quickly burn him up, just as fire burns its own abode.

Mudupāṇijātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Mudupāṇi Jātaka, the second.

263. Cūḷapalobhanajātakaṃ (3-2-3)

263. The Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka (3.2.3)

37.

37.

Abhijjamāne [T 1.0106] vārismiṃ, sayaṃ ayaṃ (ka.) āgamma iddhiyā;

Missībhāvitthiyā gantvā, saṃsīdasi saṃsīdati (ka.) mahaṇṇave.

Having come yourself by psychic power over unbroken waters, now, having entered into association with a woman, you are sinking in the great ocean.

38.

38.

Āvaṭṭanī mahāmāyā, brahmacariyavikopanā;

Sīdanti naṃ viditvāna, ārakā parivajjaye.

They are a whirlpool, of great illusion, destroyers of the holy life. Knowing that they cause one to sink, the wise person should avoid them from afar.

39.

39.

Yaṃ etā upasevanti, chandasā vā dhanena vā;

Jātavedova saṃ ṭhānaṃ, khippaṃ anudahanti nanti.

Whomever they associate with, whether through desire or for wealth, they quickly burn him up, just as fire burns its own abode.

Cūḷapalobhana cullapalobhana (sī. syā. pī.) jātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Cūḷapalobhana Jātaka, the third.

264. Mahāpanādajātakaṃ (3-2-4)

264. The Mahāpanāda Jātaka (3.2.4)

40.

40.

Panādo nāma so rājā, yassa yūpo suvaṇṇayo;

Tiriyaṃ soḷasubbedho soḷasapabbedho (sī. pī.), uddhamāhu uccamāhu (sī. syā. pī.) sahassadhā.

That king was named Panāda, whose palace was made of gold; it was sixteen units in breadth and, they say, a thousandfold in height.

41.

41.

Sahassakaṇḍo satageṇḍu satabhedo (sī. pī.), satabheṇḍu (sī. nissaya), dhajāsu haritāmayo;

Anaccuṃ tattha gandhabbā, cha sahassāni sattadhā.

It had a thousand sections and a hundred tiers, with banners made of green gems; there, six thousand celestial musicians danced in seven groups.

42.

42.

Evametaṃ evameva (ka.) tadā āsi, yathā bhāsasi bhaddaji;

Sakko ahaṃ tadā āsiṃ, veyyāvaccakaro tavāti.

It was just so at that time, Bhaddaji, as you have said. I was Sakka then, your attendant.

Mahāpanādajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Mahāpanāda Jātaka, the fourth.

265. Khurappajātakaṃ (3-2-5)

265. The Khurappa Jātaka (3.2.5)

43.

43.

Disvā [V 1.0068][M 1.0077] khurappe dhanuveganunne, khagge [T 1.0107] gahīte tikhiṇe teladhote;

Tasmiṃ bhayasmiṃ maraṇe viyūḷhe, kasmā nu te nāhu chambhitattaṃ.

Having seen the razor-arrows shot with the force of the bow, and the sharp, oil-polished swords being grasped, in that fearful moment with death arrayed, why indeed did no trembling arise in you?

44.

44.

Disvā khurappe dhanuveganunne, khagge gahīte tikhiṇe teladhote;

Tasmiṃ bhayasmiṃ maraṇe viyūḷhe, vedaṃ alatthaṃ vipulaṃ uḷāraṃ.

Having seen the razor-arrows shot with the force of the bow, and the sharp, oil-polished swords being grasped, in that fearful moment with death arrayed, I obtained a vast and sublime joy.

45.

45.

So vedajāto ajjhabhaviṃ amitte, pubbeva me jīvitamāsi cattaṃ;

Na hi jīvite ālayaṃ kubbamāno, sūro kayirā sūrakiccaṃ kadācīti.

With that joy arisen, I overcame my enemies, for my life had already been relinquished. Indeed, a hero who holds an attachment to life would never perform a heroic deed.

Khurappajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Khurappa Jātaka, the fifth.

266. Vātaggasindhavajātakaṃ (3-2-6)

266. The Vātaggasindhava Jātaka (3.2.6)

46.

46.

Yenāsi kisiyā paṇḍu, yena bhattaṃ na ruccati;

Ayaṃ so āgato bhattā tāto (sī. syā. pī.), kasmā dāni palāyasi.

He on whose account you were thin and pale, on whose account your food did not please you—that very lord has come. Why, then, do you now flee?

47.

47.

Sace na kho (syā. ka.) panādikeneva, santhavo nāma jāyati;

Yaso hāyati itthīnaṃ, tasmā tāta palāyahaṃ palāyihaṃ (syā.), palāyitaṃ (ka.).

Dear son, if intimacy arises from the very beginning, a woman's reputation diminishes. Therefore, I flee.

48.

48.

Yassassinaṃ kule jātaṃ, āgataṃ yā na icchati;

Socati [T 1.0108] cirarattāya, vātaggamiva bhaddalīti kundalīti (sī. pī.), gadrabhīti (syā.).

The woman who does not desire a renowned suitor of noble birth who has come to her, grieves for a long time, like Bhaddalī for Vātagga.

Vātaggasindhavajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Vātaggasindhava Jātaka, the sixth.

267. Kakkaṭakajātakaṃ (3-2-7)

267. The Kakkaṭaka Jātaka (3.2.7)

49.

49.

Siṅgīmigo [M 1.0078] āyatacakkhunetto, aṭṭhittaco vārisayo alomo;

Tenābhibhūto kapaṇaṃ rudāmi, mā heva maṃ pāṇasamaṃ jaheyya jaheyyā (pī.) jahā’yye (?).

The golden creature, long-eyed, bone-skinned, water-dwelling, and hairless—by him my mate is overcome, and I weep wretchedly. May he not abandon me, who am as dear as his life.

50.

50.

Ayya na taṃ jahissāmi, kuñjaraṃ saṭṭhihāyanaṃ kuñjara saṭṭhihāyana (sī. pī.);

Pathabyā cāturantāya, suppiyo hosi me tuvaṃ.

Noble one, I will not abandon the sixty-year-old elephant. You are dearer to me than the earth bounded by the four oceans.

51.

51.

Ye kuḷīrā samuddasmiṃ, gaṅgāya yamunāya nammadāya (sī. pī.) ca;

Tesaṃ tvaṃ vārijo seṭṭho, muñca rodantiyā patinti.

Of all the crabs in the ocean, and in the Ganges and the Yamunā, you, O water-born, are the chief. Release the husband of this weeping one!

Kakkaṭaka kuḷīra (ka.) jātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Kakkaṭaka Jātaka, the seventh.

268. Ārāmadūsakajātakaṃ (3-2-8)

268. The Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka (3.2.8)

52.

52.

Yo [V 1.0069] ve sabbasametānaṃ, ahuvā seṭṭhasammato;

Tassāyaṃ edisī paññā, kimeva itarā pajā.

He who was considered the chief of all those gathered—if such is his wisdom, what then of the other folk?

53.

53.

Evameva tuvaṃ brahme, anaññāya vinindasi;

Kathaṃ mūlaṃ adisvāna kathaṃhi mūlaṃ aditvā (syā. pī.), rukkhaṃ jaññā patiṭṭhitaṃ.

Just so, noble one, you censure without knowing. How can one know if a tree is firmly established without having seen its root?

54.

54.

Nāhaṃ [T 1.0109] tumhe vinindāmi, ye caññe vānarā vane;

Vissasenova gārayho, yassatthā rukkharopakāti.

I do not censure you, nor the other monkeys in the forest. Vissasena alone is to be blamed, for whose sake those like you are tree-planters.

Ārāmadūsakajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, the eighth.

269. Sujātajātakaṃ (3-2-9)

269. The Sujāta Jātaka (3.2.9)

55.

55.

Na hi vaṇṇena sampannā, mañjukā piyadassanā;

Kharavācā piyā hoti, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.

A harsh-spoken person, though endowed with beauty, a pleasant voice, and a pleasing appearance, is not dear, neither in this world nor in the next.

56.

56.

Nanu passasimaṃ kāḷiṃ, dubbaṇṇaṃ tilakāhataṃ;

Kokilaṃ saṇhavācena, bahūnaṃ pāṇinaṃ piyaṃ.

Do you not see this dark, ill-favored, and spotted cuckoo? With its gentle voice, it is dear to many living beings.

57.

57.

Tasmā [M 1.0079] sakhilavācassa, mantabhāṇī anuddhato;

Atthaṃ dhammañca dīpeti, madhuraṃ tassa bhāsitanti.

Therefore, one should be of amiable speech, speak with wisdom, and be not arrogant. Whoever illuminates the meaning and the teaching, their speech is sweet.

Sujātajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Sujāta Jātaka, the ninth.

270. Ulūkajātakaṃ (3-2-10)

270. The Ulūka Jātaka (3.2.10)

58.

58.

Sabbehi kira ñātīhi, kosiyo issaro kato;

Sace ñātīhi anuññāto ñātīhanuññāto (sī. pī.), bhaṇeyyāhaṃ ekavācikaṃ.

It seems the owl has been made king by all his kinsmen. If I am permitted by these kinsmen, I would speak a single word.

59.

59.

Bhaṇa samma anuññāto, atthaṃ dhammañca kevalaṃ;

Santi hi daharā pakkhī, paññavanto jutindharā.

Speak, friend, you are permitted; speak only on the meaning and the principle. For there are young birds who are wise and possess radiance.

60.

60.

Na me ruccati bhaddaṃ vo bhadante (ka.), ulūkassābhisecanaṃ;

Akkuddhassa [T 1.0110] mukhaṃ passa, kathaṃ kuddho karissatīti.

May it be well with you, but this consecration of the owl does not please me. Look at his face when he is not angry; what will he do when he is angry?

Ulūkajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Ulūka Jātaka, the tenth.

Padumavaggo dutiyo.

The Paduma Vagga, the Second.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Padumuttama [V 1.0070] nāgasirivhayano, sa-mahaṇṇava yūpa khurappavaro;

Atha bhaddalī kuñjara rukkha puna, kharavāca ulūkavarena dasāti.

The excellent Paduma, the one called Nāgasiri, with the Great Ocean, the Post, and the excellent Razor-arrow; then the Fine Mare, the Elephant, the Tree again, Harsh Speech, and with the excellent Owl—these are the ten.

3. Udapānavaggo

3. The Udapāna Vagga

271. Udapānadūsakajātakaṃ (3-3-1)

271. The Udapānadūsaka Jātaka (3.3.1)

61.

61.

Āraññikassa isino, cirarattaṃ tapassino;

Kicchākataṃ udapānaṃ, kathaṃ samma avāhasi avāhayi (sī. pī.), apāhasi (syā.).

This well was made with difficulty by a forest-dwelling ascetic who has long practiced austerities. Why, friend, have you defiled it?

62.

62.

Esa dhammo siṅgālānaṃ, yaṃ pitvā ohadāmase;

Pitupitāmahaṃ dhammo, na taṃ na naṃ (sī. pī.) ujjhātumarahasi.

This is the nature of jackals: that having drunk, we then excrete. This is the custom of our fathers and grandfathers; you ought not cause it to be abandoned.

63.

63.

Yesaṃ [T 1.0111][M 1.0080] vo ediso dhammo, adhammo pana kīdiso;

Mā vo dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, addasāma kudācananti.

If this is the nature of your custom, of what sort, then, must your non-custom be? May we never see your custom or your non-custom at any time!

Udapānadūsakajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Udapānadūsaka Jātaka, the first.

272. Byagghajātakaṃ (3-3-2)

272. The Byaggha Jātaka (3.3.2)

64.

64.

Yena mittena saṃsaggā, yogakkhemo vihiyyati;

Pubbevajjhābhavaṃ tassa, rukkhe akkhīva paṇḍito.

The wise person should, from the very beginning, guard against being overcome by that friend through association with whom one's well-being is diminished, just as one would guard one's own eye.

65.

65.

Yena mittena saṃsaggā, yogakkhemo pavaḍḍhati;

Kareyyattasamaṃ vuttiṃ, sabbakiccesu paṇḍito.

Towards that friend through association with whom one's well-being increases, a wise person should, in all affairs, conduct oneself as towards oneself.

66.

66.

Etha byagghā nivattavho, paccupetha paccametha (sī. pī.) mahāvanaṃ;

Mā vanaṃ chindi nibyagghaṃ, byagghā māhesu nibbanāti.

Come, O tigers, and return; come back to the great forest. Let not the forest be destroyed and left without tigers; may the tigers not be left without a forest.

Byagghajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Byaggha Jātaka, the second.

273. Kacchapajātakaṃ (3-3-3)

273. The Kacchapa Jātaka (3.3.3)

67.

67.

Ko nu uddhitabhattova udditabhattova (sī.), vaḍḍhitabhattova (syā.), pūrahatthova brāhmaṇo;

Kahaṃ nu bhikkhaṃ acari, kaṃ saddhaṃ upasaṅkami.

Who are you, like one with abundant food served up, like a brahmin with full hands? Where indeed did you go for alms? Which faithful person did you approach?

68.

68.

Ahaṃ [V 1.0071] kapismi dummedho, anāmāsāni āmasiṃ;

Tvaṃ maṃ mocaya bhaddante, mutto gaccheyya pabbataṃ.

I am a foolish monkey; I touched what should not be touched. Release me, Venerable Sir! Once freed, I would go to the mountain.

69.

69.

Kacchapā kassapā honti, koṇḍaññā honti makkaṭā;

Muñca kassapa koṇḍaññaṃ, kataṃ methunakaṃ tayāti.

Tortoises are of the Kassapa clan, and monkeys are of the Koṇḍañña clan. O Kassapa, release the Koṇḍañña, for the act of union has been performed by you.

Kacchapajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Kacchapa Jātaka, the third.

274. Lolajātakaṃ (3-3-4)

274. The Lola Jātaka (3.3.4)

70.

70.

Kāyaṃ balākā sikhinī, corī laṅghipitāmahā;

Oraṃ [T 1.0112] balāke āgaccha, caṇḍo me vāyaso sakhā.

What is this crested crane, this thief with a grandfather who is the sky? Come here, O crane; my friend, the crow, is fierce.

71.

71.

Nāhaṃ balākā sikhinī, ahaṃ lolosmi vāyaso;

Akatvā vacanaṃ tuyhaṃ, passa lūnosmi āgato.

I am not a crested crane; I am a greedy crow. Not having followed your words, see, I have returned plucked bare.

72.

72.

Punapāpajjasī [M 1.0081] samma, sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ;

Na hi mānusakā bhogā, subhuñjā honti pakkhināti.

You will fall into misfortune again, friend, for such is your character. Indeed, human enjoyments are not easily partaken of by birds.

Lolajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Lola Jātaka, the fourth.

275. Rucirajātakaṃ (3-3-5)

275. The Rucira Jātaka (3.3.5)

73.

73.

Kāyaṃ balākā rucirā, kākanīḷasmimacchati;

Caṇḍo kāko sakhā mayhaṃ, yassa tassa (sī. pī.) cetaṃ kulāvakaṃ.

What beautiful crane is this that stays in a crow's nest? Fierce is the crow, my friend, to whom this nest belongs.

74.

74.

Nanu maṃ samma jānāsi, dija sāmākabhojana;

Akatvā vacanaṃ tuyhaṃ, passa lūnosmi āgato.

Surely you know me, friend, a bird that feeds on millet? Not having followed your words, see, I have returned plucked bare.

75.

75.

Punapāpajjasī samma, sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ;

Na hi mānusakā bhogā, subhuñjā honti pakkhināti.

You will fall into misfortune again, friend, for such is your character. Indeed, human enjoyments are not easily partaken of by birds.

Rucirajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Rucira Jātaka, the fifth.

276. Kurudhammajātakaṃ (3-3-6)

276. The Kurudhamma Jātaka (3-3-6)

76.

76.

Tava saddhañca sīlañca, viditvāna janādhipa;

Vaṇṇaṃ añjanavaṇṇena, kāliṅgasmiṃ nimimhase vinimhase (syā.), vanimhase (ka.).

O ruler of men, having known your faith and virtue, we wish to exchange gold in the land of Kalinga for the royal elephant of the color of collyrium.

77.

77.

Annabhaccā [T 1.0113] cabhaccā ca, yodha uddissa gacchati;

Sabbe te appaṭikkhippā, pubbācariyavaco idaṃ.

Those supported by food and those supported by wages, and the warrior who goes forth on a mission—all of them are not to be rejected. This is the word of the ancient teachers.

78.

78.

Dadāmi [V 1.0072] vo brāhmaṇā nāgametaṃ, rājārahaṃ rājabhoggaṃ yasassinaṃ;

Alaṅkataṃ hemajālābhichannaṃ, sasārathiṃ gacchatha yena kāmanti.

I give to you, brahmins, this glorious elephant, worthy of a king and fit for a king’s use, adorned and covered with a golden net. With its driver, go wherever you please.

Kurudhammajātakaṃ kurudhammajātakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Kurudhamma Jātaka, the sixth.

277. Romakajātakaṃ (3-3-7)

277. The Romaka Jātaka (3-3-7)

79.

79.

Vassāni [M 1.0082] paññāsa samādhikāni, vasimha selassa guhāya romaka;

Asaṅkamānā abhinibbutattā abhinibbutacittā (syā. ka.), hatthatta hatthattha (syā.) māyanti mamaṇḍajā pure.

For more than fifty years, O Romaka, we have dwelt in the cave of this mountain. Before, the egg-born, being unafraid and with peaceful minds, would come into my hand.

80.

80.

Te dāni vakkaṅga kimatthamussukā, bhajanti aññaṃ girikandaraṃ dijā;

Na nūna maññanti mamaṃ yathā pure, cirappavutthā atha vā na te ime.

O Vakkaṅga, why now are those twice-born so eager to frequent another mountain gorge? Surely they do not regard me as they did before. Are they not the ones who have dwelt here long? Or perhaps these are not they.

81.

81.

Jānāma taṃ na mayaṃ sampamūḷhā na maya’masma mūḷhā (sī. pī.), soyeva tvaṃ te mayamasma nāññe;

Cittañca [T 1.0114] te asmiṃ jane paduṭṭhaṃ, ājīvikā ājīvaka (sī. syā.), ājīvika (pī.) tena tamuttasāmāti.

We know you; we are not deluded. You are that very one, and we are those very ones, not others. Your mind toward this folk is corrupted; because of your livelihood, we are afraid of you.

Romakajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Romaka Jātaka, the seventh.

278. Mahiṃsarājajātakaṃ (3-3-8)

278. The Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka (3-3-8)

82.

82.

Kimattha kamattha (sī. pī.) mabhisandhāya, lahucittassa dubbhino dūbhino (sī. pī.);

Sabbakāmadadasseva duhasseva (sī. syā. pī.), rahasseva (ka.), imaṃ dukkhaṃ titikkhasi.

For what reason do you tolerate this suffering from that fickle-minded, malevolent one, as if you were one who grants all desires?

83.

83.

Siṅgena nihanāhetaṃ, padasā ca adhiṭṭhaha;

Bhiyyo bhīyo (sī.) bālā pakujjheyyuṃ, no cassa paṭisedhako.

Strike him down with your horn, and trample him with your hoof. If there is no one to prevent it, fools will offend even more.

84.

84.

Mamevāyaṃ maññamāno, aññepevaṃ aññampevaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) karissati;

Te naṃ tattha vadhissanti, sā me mutti bhavissatīti.

Thinking others to be just like me, he will treat them in the same way. They will kill him there, and that will be my release.

Mahiṃsarājajātakaṃ mahisajātakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Mahiṃsarāja Jātaka, the eighth.

279. Satapattajātakaṃ (3-3-9)

279. The Satapatta Jātaka (3-3-9)

85.

85.

Yathā [M 1.0083] māṇavako panthe, siṅgāliṃ vanagocariṃ;

Atthakāmaṃ pavedentiṃ pavadantiṃ (pī.), anatthakāmāti maññati;

Anatthakāmaṃ satapattaṃ, atthakāmoti maññati.

Just as a young man on the path regards the forest-roaming she-jackal, who wishes for his welfare and makes it known, as one who wishes him ill; and regards the woodpecker, who wishes him ill, as one who wishes him well.

86.

86.

Evameva idhekacco, puggalo hoti tādiso;

Hitehi vacanaṃ vutto, paṭigaṇhāti vāmato.

In just the same way, here in this world a certain person is of such a kind: when spoken to with words for his welfare, he takes them in a contrary way.

87.

87.

Ye [T 1.0115][V 1.0073] ca kho naṃ pasaṃsanti, bhayā ukkaṃsayanti vā ca (sī. pī.);

Tañhi so maññate mittaṃ, satapattaṃva māṇavoti.

And those who praise him, or exalt him out of fear, he indeed considers to be his friends, just as the young man did the woodpecker.

Satapattajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Satapatta Jātaka, the ninth.

280. Puṭadūsakajātakaṃ (3-3-10)

280. The Puṭadūsaka Jātaka (3-3-10)

88.

88.

Addhā hi nūna migarājā, puṭakammassa kovido;

Tathā hi puṭaṃ dūseti, aññaṃ nūna karissati.

Indeed, the monkey king is surely skilled in making leaf-wrappers! For he so spoils the wrapper, he will surely make another.

89.

89.

Na me mātā vā pitā vā, puṭakammassa kovido;

Kataṃ kataṃ kho dūsema, evaṃ dhammamidaṃ kulaṃ.

Neither my mother nor my father was skilled in making leaf-wrappers. We just ruin whatever has been made; such is the nature of our family.

90.

90.

Yesaṃ vo ediso dhammo, adhammo pana kīdiso;

Mā vo dhammaṃ adhammaṃ vā, addasāma kudācananti.

If this is your nature, what must your bad practice be like? May I never see your nature or your bad practice at any time!

Puṭadūsakajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Puṭadūsaka Jātaka, the tenth.

Udapānavaggo araññavaggo (sī. pī. ka.) tatiyo.

The Udapāna Chapter, the third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Udapānavaraṃ vanabyaggha kapi, sikhinī ca balāka ruciravaro;

Sujanādhiparomakadūsa puna, satapattavaro puṭakamma dasāti.

The excellent Well, the Forest Tiger, the Monkey, the Peacock and the Crane, the excellent Rucira; again Sujanādhipa, Romaka, the Spoiler, the excellent Satapatta, and Basket-work are the ten.

4. Abbhantaravaggo

4. The Abbhantara Chapter

281. Abbhantarajātakaṃ (3-4-1)

281. The Abbhantara Jātaka (3-4-1)

91.

91.

Abbhantaro [T 1.0116][M 1.0084] nāma dumo, yassa dibyamidaṃ phalaṃ;

Bhutvā dohaḷinī nārī, cakkavattiṃ vijāyati.

There is a tree named Abbhantara, which has this divine fruit; having eaten it, a woman with a pregnancy craving gives birth to a wheel-turning monarch.

92.

92.

Tvampi tvañca (sī. pī.), tvaṃ hi (ka.) bhadde mahesīsi, sā cāpi cāsi (sī. pī.) patino piyā;

Āharissati te rājā, idaṃ abbhantaraṃ phalaṃ.

You too, good lady, are a chief queen, and you are dear to your husband; therefore, the king will bring you this Abbhantara fruit.

93.

93.

Bhatturatthe parakkanto, yaṃ ṭhānamadhigacchati;

Sūro attapariccāgī, labhamāno bhavāmahanti.

A hero who strives for his master's welfare and sacrifices himself attains a certain position. May I be one who obtains that position.

Abbhantarajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Abbhantara Jātaka, the first.

282. Seyyajātakaṃ (3-4-2)

282. The Seyya Jātaka (3-4-2)

94.

94.

Seyyaṃso [V 1.0074] seyyaso hoti, yo seyyamupasevati;

Ekena sandhiṃ katvāna, sataṃ vajjhe macce (ka.), bajjhe (ka. aṭṭha.) amocayiṃ.

One who is superior becomes more so by associating with the superior. By making an alliance with one such person, I freed a hundred who were condemned to death.

95.

95.

kasmā…pe… saggaṃ na gaccheyya (katthaci) Tasmā sabbena lokena, sandhiṃ katvāna ekato ekako (sī. syā. pī.);

Pecca saggaṃ nigaccheyya kasmā…pe… saggaṃ na gaccheyya (katthaci), idaṃ suṇātha kāsiyā kāsayo (sī. pī.).

“Therefore, having made an alliance together with the entire world, one may go to heaven after death. Hear this, O people of Kasi!”

96.

96.

Idaṃ vatvā mahārājā, kaṃso bārāṇasiggaho;

Dhanuṃ kaṇḍañca tūṇiñca (sī. pī.) nikkhippa, saṃyamaṃ ajjhupāgamīti.

Having said this, the great king Kaṃsa, the conqueror of Bārāṇasī, laid down his bow and arrow and undertook the life of restraint.

Seyyajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Seyya Jātaka, the second.

283. Vaḍḍhakīsūkarajātakaṃ (3-4-3)

283. The Carpenter-Boar Jātaka (3-4-3)

97.

97.

Varaṃ [T 1.0117] varaṃ tvaṃ nihanaṃ pure cari, asmiṃ padese abhibhuyya sūkare;

So dāni eko byapagamma jhāyasi, balaṃ nu te byaggha na cajja vijjati.

“Formerly, having overcome the boars in this region, you roamed about slaying the very best of them. Now, having withdrawn, you brood alone. O tiger, is your strength not to be found today?”

98.

98.

Ime [M 1.0085] sudaṃ imassu tā (syā. ka.) yanti disodisaṃ pure, bhayaṭṭitā leṇagavesino puthu;

Te dāni saṅgamma vasanti ekato, yatthaṭṭhitā duppasahajjame duppasahajjime (syā.) mayā.

“Formerly, stricken by fear, these went separately in all directions seeking shelter. Now they have gathered and dwell together. Standing thus united, they are difficult for me to overcome today.”

99.

99.

Namatthu saṅghāna samāgatānaṃ, disvā sayaṃ sakhya vadāmi abbhutaṃ;

Byagghaṃ migā yattha jiniṃsu dāṭhino, sāmaggiyā dāṭhabalesu muccareti.

“Homage to the assembled multitudes! Having seen it myself, I declare this wonderful friendship: where tusked beasts have conquered a tiger. Through unity, they are freed from the power of the tusked one.”

Vaḍḍhakīsūkarajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Carpenter-Boar Jātaka, the third.

284. Sirijātakaṃ (3-4-4)

284. The Jātaka on Fortune (3-4-4)

100.

100.

Yaṃ ussukā saṅgharanti, alakkhikā bahuṃ dhanaṃ;

Sippavanto asippā ca, lakkhivā tāni bhuñjati.

“Whatever great wealth the unlucky, whether skilled or unskilled, accumulate through their striving, the one with good fortune enjoys it.”

101.

101.

Sabbattha [T 1.0118] katapuññassa, aticcaññeva pāṇino;

Uppajjanti bahū bhogā, appanāyatanesupi.

“For one who has made merit, surpassing all other beings, abundant wealth arises everywhere, even from unlikely sources.”

102.

102.

Kukkuṭo kukkuṭa (sī. pī.), kukkuṭā (sī. nissaya, saddanīti) maṇayo daṇḍo, thiyo ca puññalakkhaṇā;

Uppajjanti apāpassa, katapuññassa jantunoti.

“A cock, jewels, a staff, and women with auspicious marks arise for a person who is without evil, for a being who has made merit.”

Sirijātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Jātaka on Fortune, the fourth.

285. Maṇisūkarajātakaṃ (3-4-5)

285. The Jewel-Boar Jātaka (3-4-5)

103.

103.

Dariyā [V 1.0075] satta vassāni, tiṃsamattā vasāmase;

Haññāma hañchema (sī. pī.), hañchāma (?) maṇino ābhaṃ, iti no mantanaṃ ahu.

“For seven years we have been dwelling in this mountain cleft, some thirty of us. ‘Let us destroy the radiance of the jewel!’—this was our counsel.”

104.

104.

Yāvatā maṇiṃ ghaṃsāma yāva yāva nighaṃsāma (sī. pī.), bhiyyo vodāyate maṇi;

Idañca dāni pucchāma, kiṃ kiccaṃ idha maññasi.

“The more we rub the jewel, the more brightly it shines. And so now we ask: what do you think should be done in this matter?”

105.

105.

Ayaṃ maṇi veḷūriyo, akāco vimalo vipulo (ka.) subho;

Nāssa sakkā siriṃ hantuṃ, apakkamatha sūkarāti.

“This jewel is a beryl, flawless, immaculate, and bright. It is not possible to destroy its splendor. Depart, you boars!”

Maṇisūkara maṇighaṃsa (ka.) jātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Jewel-Rubbing Jātaka, the fifth.

286. Sālūkajātakaṃ (3-4-6)

286. The Sālūka Jātaka (3-4-6)

106.

106.

Mā [M 1.0086] sālūkassa pihayi, āturannāni bhuñjati;

Appossukko bhusaṃ khāda, etaṃ dīghāyulakkhaṇaṃ.

“Do not envy Sālūka; he eats food that leads to death. Being free from anxiety, eat your chaff. This is the mark of a long life.”

107.

107.

Idāni so idhāgantvā, atithī yuttasevako;

Atha dakkhasi sālūkaṃ, sayantaṃ musaluttaraṃ.

“Just now the servant appointed for the guests will come here; then you shall see Sālūka, him with the pestle-like upper lip, lying dead.”

108.

108.

Vikantaṃ [T 1.0119] vikattaṃ (sī.), vikantiyamānaṃ chindiyamānaṃti attho sūkaraṃ disvā, sayantaṃ musaluttaraṃ;

Jaraggavā vicintesuṃ, varamhākaṃ bhusāmivāti.

Having seen the crying boar with the pestle-like upper lip lying dead, the old oxen reflected: 'Our chaff is indeed better!'

Sālūkajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Sālūka Jātaka, the sixth.

287. Lābhagarahajātakaṃ (3-4-7)

287. The Jātaka on Censuring Gain (3-4-7)

109.

109.

Nānummatto nāpisuṇo, nānaṭo nākutūhalo;

Mūḷhesu labhate lābhaṃ, esā te anusāsanī.

“Not being mad nor a slanderer, not an actor nor meddlesome, a being obtains gain among the deluded—this is the instruction given to you.”

110.

110.

Dhiratthu taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena adhammacariyāya (sī. syā.) vā.

“Shame on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, brahmin, which is a livelihood obtained through self-destruction or by unrighteous conduct.”

111.

111.

Api ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Esāva jīvikā seyyo seyyā (sī. syā. pī.), yā cādhammena esanāti.

“Even if one must take up a bowl and wander as a homeless one, that very livelihood is better than any seeking of wealth that is unrighteous.”

Lābhagarahajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Jātaka on Censuring Gain, the seventh.

288. Macchuddānajātakaṃ (3-4-8)

288. The Fish-Portion Jātaka (3-4-8)

112.

112.

Agghanti [V 1.0076] macchā adhikaṃ sahassaṃ, na so atthi yo imaṃ saddaheyya;

Mayhañca assu idha satta māsā, ahampi taṃ macchuddānaṃ kiṇeyyaṃ.

“The fish are worth more than a thousand, but there is no one who would believe this. If I had seven māsakas here, I too would buy that portion of fish.”

113.

113.

Macchānaṃ bhojanaṃ datvā, mama dakkhiṇamādisi;

Taṃ dakkhiṇaṃ sarantiyā, kataṃ apacitiṃ tayā.

“Having given food to the fish, you designated a religious gift for me. I, remembering that religious gift and the veneration performed by you, have guarded your wealth.”

114.

114.

Paduṭṭhacittassa [T 1.0120][M 1.0087] na phāti hoti, na cāpi taṃ naṃ (sī. syā.) devatā pūjayanti;

Yo bhātaraṃ pettikaṃ sāpateyyaṃ, avañcayī dukkaṭakammakārīti.

There is no prosperity for one with a corrupt mind, nor do the deities honor him—he who, being a doer of evil deeds, has cheated his brother of the paternal inheritance.

Macchuddānajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Fish-Portion Jātaka, the eighth.

289. Nānāchandajātakaṃ (3-4-9)

289. The Jātaka on Various Wishes (3-4-9)

115.

115.

Nānāchandā mahārāja, ekāgāre vasāmase;

Ahaṃ gāmavaraṃ icche, brāhmaṇī ca gavaṃ sataṃ.

“Great king, we have diverse wishes though we live in a single house. I desire a choice village, and the brahmin woman desires a hundred cows.”

116.

116.

Putto ca ājaññarathaṃ, kaññā ca maṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Yā cesā puṇṇikā jammī, udukkhalaṃbhikaṅkhati.

“My son desires a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds, and my daughter-in-law a jeweled earring; and as for this wretched slave-girl Puṇṇikā, she longs for a mortar and pestle.”

117.

117.

Brāhmaṇassa gāmavaraṃ, brāhmaṇiyā gavaṃ sataṃ;

Puttassa ājaññarathaṃ, kaññāya maṇikuṇḍalaṃ;

Yañcetaṃ puṇṇikaṃ jammiṃ, paṭipādethudukkhalanti.

“Provide a choice village for the brahmin, a hundred cows for the brahmin woman, a chariot drawn by thoroughbreds for the son, a jeweled earring for the daughter-in-law, and for the wretched slave-girl Puṇṇikā, a mortar.”

Nānāchandajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Jātaka on Various Wishes, the ninth.

290. Sīlavīmaṃsakajātakaṃ (3-4-10)

290. The Jātaka on Testing Virtue (3-4-10)

118.

118.

Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ, sīlaṃ loke anuttaraṃ;

Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññati.

“Virtue, it is said, is truly excellent; virtue is supreme in the world. Behold, a serpent of terrible venom is not harmed because he is virtuous.”

119.

119.

Sohaṃ sīlaṃ samādissaṃ, loke anumataṃ sivaṃ;

Ariyavuttisamācāro[T 1.0121], yena vuccati sīlavā.

I shall undertake that virtue, approved by the wise and safe, on account of which one who practices the conduct of the noble is called 'virtuous' in the world.

120.

120.

Ñātīnañca piyo hoti, mittesu ca virocati;

Kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ, upapajjati sīlavāti.

The virtuous one is dear to his kinsmen and shines among his friends. After the breaking up of the body, he is reborn in a good destination.

Sīlavīmaṃsakajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Jātaka on Testing Virtue, the tenth.

Abbhantaravaggo catuttho.

The Abbhantara Chapter, the fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that chapter:

Duma [V 1.0077][M 1.0088] kaṃsavaruttamabyagghamigā, maṇayo maṇi sālukamavhayano;

Anusāsaniyopi ca macchavaro, maṇikuṇḍalakena kirena dasāti.

The Tree, the Best Choice, the Tiger and Deer; the Jewels, the Jewel, and Sālūka by name; the Instruction and the Choice Fish; with the Jeweled Earring and 'Reportedly'—these are the ten.

5. Kumbhavaggo

5. The Chapter on the Pot

291. Surāghaṭajātakaṃ (2-5-1)

291. The Jātaka on the Liquor Pot (2-5-1)

121.

121.

Sabbakāmadadaṃ kumbhaṃ, kuṭaṃ laddhāna dhuttako;

Yāva naṃ anupāleti, tāva so sukhamedhati.

291. A drunkard, having obtained a pot that grants all desires, for as long as he guarded it, for so long did he attain happiness.

122.

122.

Yadā matto ca ditto ca, pamādā kumbhamabbhidā;

Tadā naggo ca pottho ca, pacchā bālo vihaññati.

When, drunk and arrogant, through heedlessness he broke the pot, then afterwards that fool, naked and in rags, is afflicted.

123.

123.

Evameva yo dhanaṃ laddhā, pamatto amattā (sī.), amatto (pī.) paribhuñjati;

Pacchā [T 1.0122] tappati dummedho, kuṭaṃ bhitvāva kuṭaṃ bhinnova (sī. pī.), kuṭabhinnova (?) dhuttakoti.

In the very same way, one of little wisdom who gains wealth and enjoys it heedlessly, afterwards grieves, like the drunkard who broke the pot.

Surāghaṭa bhadraghaṭa (sī. pī.), bhadraghaṭabhedaka (syā.) jātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Jātaka on the Liquor Pot, the first.

292. Supattajātakaṃ (3-5-2)

292. The Supatta Jātaka (3-5-2)

124.

124.

Bārāṇasyaṃ bārāṇassaṃ (sī. pī.) mahārāja, kākarājā nivāsako nivāsiko (sī. pī.);

Asītiyā sahassehi, supatto parivārito.

In Bārāṇasī, O great king, dwelt the crow-king Supatta, attended by eighty thousand crows.

125.

125.

Tassa dohaḷinī bhariyā, suphassā bhakkhitumicchati macchamicchati (sī. pī.);

Rañño mahānase pakkaṃ, paccagghaṃ rājabhojanaṃ.

292. His wife, Suphassā, had a pregnancy craving and desired to eat the very costly royal food cooked in the king’s great kitchen.

126.

126.

Tesāhaṃ pahito dūto, rañño camhi idhāgato;

Bhattu apacitiṃ kummi, nāsāyamakaraṃ makariṃ (sī. nissaya) vaṇanti.

I am their sent messenger, and I have come here as a doer of harm to the king. Thinking, 'I will pay homage to my master,' I inflicted a wound upon the cook's nose.

Supattajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Supatta Jātaka, the second.

293. Kāyanibbindajātakaṃ (3-5-3)

293. The Jātaka on Disenchantment with the Body (3-5-3)

127.

127.

Phuṭṭhassa [M 1.0089] me aññatarena byādhinā, rogena bāḷhaṃ dukhitassa ruppato;

Parisussati khippamidaṃ kaḷevaraṃ, pupphaṃ yathā paṃsuni ātape kataṃ.

Afflicted by some disease, greatly pained and tormented by sickness, this body of mine quickly withers away, like a delicate flower placed in the sun upon the sand.

128.

128.

Ajaññaṃ [V 1.0078] jaññasaṅkhātaṃ, asuciṃ sucisammataṃ;

Nānākuṇapaparipūraṃ, jaññarūpaṃ apassato.

Ignoble, it is reckoned noble; impure, it is considered pure. Full of various kinds of corpses, it appears delightful to one who does not see.

129.

129.

Dhiratthumaṃ [T 1.0123] āturaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, jegucchiyaṃ assuciṃ byādhidhammaṃ;

Yatthappamattā adhimucchitā pajā, hāpenti maggaṃ sugatūpapattiyāti.

293. Fie on this ailing, putrid body, disgusting, impure, and subject to disease! In which beings, heedless and utterly infatuated, lose the path to a good destination.

Kāyanibbinda kāyavicchanda (sī.), kāyavicchinda (pī.) jātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Jātaka on Disenchantment with the Body, the third.

294. Jambukhādakajātakaṃ (3-5-4)

294. The Jātaka on the Rose-Apple Eater (3-5-4)

130.

130.

Koyaṃ bindussaro vaggu, saravantāna pavadantāna (sī. pī.) muttamo;

Accuto jambusākhāya, moracchāpova kūjati.

Who is this with a full, pleasant voice, the best among those endowed with voice? Unmoving on the rose-apple branch, he calls out like a young peacock.

131.

131.

Kulaputtova jānāti kulaputto pajānāti (syā. ka.), kulaputtaṃ kulaputte (sī. pī.) pasaṃsituṃ;

Byagghacchāpasarīvaṇṇa, bhuñja samma dadāmi te.

A clansman knows how to praise a clansman. O you whose complexion is like a tiger cub’s, eat, friend, I give this to you.

132.

132.

Cirassaṃ vata passāmi, musāvādī samāgate;

Vantādaṃ kuṇapādañca, aññamaññaṃ pasaṃsaketi.

After a long time, indeed, I see liars met together: an eater of vomit and an eater of corpses praising one another.

Jambukhādakajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

294. The Jātaka on the Rose-Apple Eater, the fourth.

295. Antajātakaṃ (3-5-5)

295. The Jātaka on the Worst (3-5-5)

133.

133.

Usabhasseva te khandho, sīhasseva vijambhitaṃ;

Migarāja namo tyatthu, api kiñci labhāmase.

Your shoulder is like a bull’s, your majestic bearing is like a lion’s. Homage be to you, O king of beasts! Might we perhaps obtain something?

134.

134.

Kulaputtova jānāti, kulaputtaṃ pasaṃsituṃ;

Mayūragīvasaṅkāsa, ito pariyāhi vāyasa.

A clansman knows how to praise a clansman. O you with a neck like a peacock’s, come here, crow!

135.

135.

Migānaṃ [T 1.0124][M 1.0090] siṅgālo kotthuko (sī. pī.), koṭṭhuko (syā.) anto, pakkhīnaṃ pana vāyaso;

Eraṇḍo anto rukkhānaṃ, tayo antā samāgatāti.

The jackal is the worst among beasts, and the crow among birds; the castor-oil plant is the worst among trees. The three worst things have come together.

Antajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Jātaka on the Worst, the fifth.

296. Samuddajātakaṃ (3-5-6)

296. The Samudda Jātaka (3-5-6)

136.

136.

Ko nāyaṃ ko nvāyaṃ (syā.) loṇatoyasmiṃ, samantā paridhāvati;

Macche makare ca vāreti, ūmīsu ca vihaññati.

295. What bird is this that runs all around in the salt water, wards off fish and makaras, and is distressed by the waves?

137.

137.

Anantapāyī sakuṇo, atittoti disāsuto;

Samuddaṃ pātumicchāmi, sāgaraṃ saritaṃ patiṃ.

I am the bird, famous in all directions as 'the insatiable one,' the one who drinks endlessly. I wish to drink the ocean, the sea, the lord of rivers.

138.

138.

So [V 1.0079] ayaṃ hāyati ceva, pūrate ca mahodadhi;

Nāssa nāyati pītanto, apeyyo kira sāgaroti.

This great ocean both ebbs and fills, and its end is not found by drinking. Truly, the sea is said to be impossible to drink dry.

Samuddajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Samudda Jātaka, the sixth.

297. Kāmavilāpajātakaṃ (3-5-7)

297. The Kāmavilāpa Jātaka (3-5-7)

139.

139.

Ucce sakuṇa ḍemāna, pattayāna vihaṅgama;

Vajjāsi kho tvaṃ vāmūruṃ, ciraṃ kho sā karissati sarissati (ka.).

O bird, flying high, with wings for your vehicle, moving through the air! Please speak to the woman with beautiful thighs; she will think it has been a long time.

140.

140.

Idaṃ kho sā na jānāti, asiṃ sattiñca oḍḍitaṃ;

Sā caṇḍī kāhati kodhaṃ, taṃ me tapati no idaṃ no idha (sī. syā. pī.).

296. She does not know of this stake, set up like a sword and spear. That fierce woman will become angry with me for being so long; that torments my mind, not this.

141.

141.

Esa [T 1.0125] uppalasannāho, nikkhañcussīsakohitaṃ nikkhamussīsake kataṃ (sī. pī.), nikkhañcussīsake kataṃ (syā.);

Kāsikañca muduṃ vatthaṃ, tappetu dhanikā piyāti dhanakāmiyāti (syā. pī.), dhanakāmikāti (sī.).

This lotus-like adornment, the golden ornament, and the soft cloth from Kasi—this much is placed at the head of the bed. Taking it, may this beloved wife who desires wealth be satisfied.

Kāmavilāpajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Kāmavilāpa Jātaka, the seventh.

298. Udumbarajātakaṃ (3-5-8)

298. The Udumbara Jātaka (3-5-8)

142.

142.

Udumbarā cime pakkā, nigrodhā ca kapitthanā;

Ehi nikkhama bhuñjassu, kiṃ jighacchāya miyyasi.

These udumbara figs are ripe, and these banyans and wood-apples too. Come, come out and eat! Why do you die of hunger?

143.

143.

Evaṃ [M 1.0091] so suhito hoti, yo vuḍḍhamapacāyati;

Yathāhamajja suhito, dumapakkāni māsito.

Thus is one who reveres an elder well-satisfied, just as I today am well-satisfied, having eaten the ripe fruits of the tree.

144.

144.

Yaṃ vanejo vanejassa, vañceyya kapino kapi;

Daharo kapi daharopi taṃ na (sī. pī.), daharopi na (syā.) saddheyya, na hi jiṇṇo jarākapīti.

Whatever a forest-dwelling monkey might say to deceive another forest-dwelling monkey, a young monkey might believe it, but surely not an old, decrepit monkey.

Udumbarajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Udumbara Jātaka, the eighth.

299. Komāraputtajātakaṃ (3-5-9)

299. The Komāraputta Jātaka (3-5-9)

145.

145.

Pure tuvaṃ sīlavataṃ sakāse, okkantikaṃ okkandikaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) kīḷasi assamamhi;

Karohare karohi re (ka.) makkaṭiyāni makkaṭa, na taṃ mayaṃ sīlavataṃ ramāma.

Formerly, in the hermitage, you played intrusively in the presence of the virtuous. O monkey, you perform your monkey-tricks! We do not delight in that virtuous conduct of yours.

146.

146.

Sutā [T 1.0126] hi mayhaṃ paramā visuddhi, komāraputtassa bahussutassa;

Mā dāni maṃ maññi tuvaṃ yathā pure, jhānānuyutto viharāmi jhānānuyuttā viharāma (sī. pī.) āvuso.

For the supreme purity of the very learned Komāraputta has been heard by me. Friend, do not think of me now as you did before. I dwell devoted to jhāna.

147.

147.

Sacepi selasmi vapeyya bījaṃ, devo ca vasse na hi taṃ virūḷhe neva hi taṃ ruheyya (sī. pī.), na hi taṃ virūhe (?);

Sutā hi te sā paramā visuddhi, ārā tuvaṃ makkaṭa jhānabhūmiyāti.

Even if one were to sow seed on a rock, and even if the god were to send rain, it would surely not sprout. That supreme purity of yours is only something you have heard of. You are far, monkey, from the ground of jhāna.

Komāraputtajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Komāraputta Jātaka, the ninth.

300. Vakajātakaṃ (3-5-10)

300. The Vaka Jātaka (3-5-10)

148.

148.

Parapāṇarodhā [V 1.0080] parapāṇaghāte (syā.), parapāṇarocaṃ (ka.) jīvanto, maṃsalohitabhojano;

Vako vataṃ samādāya, upapajji uposathaṃ.

A wolf, living by obstructing the life-breath of others, an eater of flesh and blood, undertook a vow and entered upon the Uposatha.

149.

149.

Tassa sakko vataññāya, ajarūpenupāgami;

Vītatapo ajjhappatto, bhañji lohitapo tapaṃ.

Sakka, having known his vow, approached in the form of a goat. The wolf pounced, his austerity gone; the blood-drinker broke his ascetic practice.

150.

150.

Evameva [M 1.0092] idhekacce, samādānamhi dubbalā;

Lahuṃ karonti attānaṃ, vakova ajakāraṇāti.

Just so, some here are weak in their resolution; they make themselves contemptible on account of a goat, just like the wolf.

Vakajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Vaka Jātaka, the tenth.

Kumbhavaggo pañcamo.

The Kumbha Vagga, the fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of this chapter:

Varakumbha [T 1.0127] supattasirivhayano, sucisammata bindusaro cusabho;

Saritaṃpati caṇḍi jarākapinā, atha makkaṭiyā vakakena dasāti.

The Surāghaṭa, Supatta, Kāyanibbinda, and Jambukhādaka; the Anta, Samudda, Kāmavilāpa, and Udumbara; then the Makkaṭi along with the Vaka make ten.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Now the summary of the chapters:

Saṅkappo padumo ceva, udapānena tatiyaṃ;

Abbhantaraṃ ghaṭabhedaṃ, tikanipātamhilaṅkatanti.

The Saṅkappa, the Paduma, and the Udapāna as the third; the Abbhantara and the Kumbha: these adorn the Book of Threes.

Tikanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Book of Threes is finished.

4. Catukkanipāto

4. The Book of the Fours

1. Kāliṅgavaggo

1. The Kāliṅga Chapter

301. Cūḷakāliṅgajātakaṃ (4-1-1)

301. The Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka

1.

1.

Vivarathimāsaṃ [T 1.0128][V 1.0081][M 1.0093] vivaratha imāsaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) dvāraṃ, nagaraṃ pavisantu pavisituṃ mayā; (ka.) aruṇarājassa;

Sīhena susiṭṭhena, surakkhitaṃ susatthena, surakkhitaṃ (sī. pī.), susiṭṭhena (ka.) nandisenena.

Open the gate for these princesses; let them enter the city of King Aruṇa, well-protected by Nandisena, who is like a lion and well-disciplined.

2.

2.

Jayo kaliṅgānamasayhasāhinaṃ, parājayo anayo ajayo (syā.), anvito (ka.) assakānaṃ;

Icceva te bhāsitaṃ brahmacāri, na ujjubhūtā vitathaṃ bhaṇanti.

Victory to the Kaliṅgas, who endure the unendurable; defeat and ruin to the Assakas. Thus, O holy man, was it spoken by you; for the upright do not speak falsely.

3.

3.

Devā musāvādamupātivattā, saccaṃ dhanaṃ paramaṃ tesu tathaṃ pemakaraṃ nu (ka.), tathaṃ paramaṃ karaṃ nu (syā.) sakka;

Taṃ te musā bhāsitaṃ devarāja, kiṃ vā paṭicca maghavā mahinda.

The gods have transcended false speech; truth is their supreme treasure, O Sakka. That was spoken falsely by you, O king of gods. For what reason, O Maghavā, Mahinda?

4.

4.

Nanu te sutaṃ brāhmaṇa bhaññamāne, devā na issanti purisaparakkamassa;

Damo samādhi manaso abhejjo adejjo (sī. pī.), abhijjo (ka.), abyaggatā [T 1.0129] nikkamanañca nikkhamanañca (sī.) kāle;

Daḷhañca viriyaṃ purisaparakkamo ca, teneva āsi vijayo assakānanti.

Brahmin, have you not heard it said: the gods are not masters of human striving? For the Assakas there was self-control, unbreakable concentration of mind, serenity, and timely action, and firm energy and human striving. By that alone was there victory for the Assakas.

Cūḷakāliṅgajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka, the first.

302. Mahāassārohajātakaṃ (4-1-2)

302. The Mahāassāroha Jātaka

5.

5.

Adeyyesu dadaṃ dānaṃ, deyyesu nappavecchati;

Āpāsu byasanaṃ patto, sahāyaṃ nādhigacchati.

One who gives to the unworthy and does not offer to the worthy, upon meeting with misfortune, does not find a friend.

6.

6.

Nādeyyesu [M 1.0094] dadaṃ dānaṃ, deyyesu yo pavecchati;

Āpāsu byasanaṃ patto, sahāyamadhigacchati.

One who does not give to the unworthy but offers to the worthy, upon meeting with misfortune, finds a friend.

7.

7.

Saññogasambhogavisesadassanaṃ, anariyadhammesu saṭhesu nassati;

Katañca ariyesu ca ajjavesu, mahapphalaṃ hoti aṇumpi tādisu.

The benefit seen from special association and intimacy perishes in the case of the deceitful and those of ignoble ways. But even a little done for the noble, the upright, and such-like ones, has great fruit.

8.

8.

Yo pubbe katakalyāṇo, akā loke sudukkaraṃ;

Pacchā kayirā na vā kayirā, accantaṃ pūjanārahoti.

One who has formerly done good, who did in the world what is very difficult to do—whether later he does so or not, he is certainly worthy of honor.

Mahāassārohajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Mahāassāroha Jātaka, the second.

303. Ekarājajātakaṃ (4-1-3)

303. The Ekarāja Jātaka

9.

9.

Anuttare [T 1.0130][V 1.0082] kāmaguṇe samiddhe, bhutvāna pubbe vasī ekarāja;

So dāni dugge narakamhi khitto, nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ.

Ekarāja, having formerly enjoyed unsurpassed and abundant sensual pleasures, you lived as a sole king. Now, cast into a harsh hell, why do you not abandon your former complexion and strength?

10.

10.

Pubbeva khantī ca tapo ca mayhaṃ, sampatthitā dubbhisena dabbasenā (sī. pī.) ahosi;

Taṃ dāni laddhāna kathaṃ nu rāja, jahe ahaṃ vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ.

O Dubbhisena, formerly patience and austerity were aspired to by me. Having now obtained them, O king, how could I abandon my former complexion and strength?

11.

11.

Sabbā kirevaṃ pariniṭṭhitāni, yasassinaṃ paññavantaṃ visayha;

Yaso ca laddhā purimaṃ uḷāraṃ, nappajjahe vaṇṇabalaṃ purāṇaṃ.

Indeed, all things are thus accomplished for one who is glorious, wise, and persevering. And having obtained lofty, former glory, one should not abandon one's former complexion and strength.

12.

12.

Panujja dukkhena sukhaṃ janinda, sukhena vā dukkhamasayhasāhi;

Ubhayattha santo abhinibbutattā, sukhe ca dukkhe ca bhavanti tulyāti.

Having driven out pleasure with pain, O lord of men, or pain with pleasure, one endures the unendurable. The good, being of extinguished nature, are the same in both pleasure and in pain.

Ekarājajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Ekarāja Jātaka, the third.

304. Daddarajātakaṃ (4-1-4)

304. The Daddara Jātaka (4-1-4)

13.

13.

Imāni [T 1.0131][M 1.0095] maṃ daddara tāpayanti, vācāduruttāni manussaloke;

Maṇḍūkabhakkhā udakantasevī, āsīvisaṃ maṃ avisā sapanti.

304. O Daddara, these ill-spoken words in the human world torment me. The non-venomous young ones curse me, a venomous serpent, calling me a 'frog-eater' and a 'water-dweller'.

14.

14.

Sakā raṭṭhā pabbājito, aññaṃ janapadaṃ gato;

Mahantaṃ koṭṭhaṃ kayirātha, duruttānaṃ duruttāni (ka.) nidhetave.

Driven from one's own country and gone to another land, one should make a great storehouse in which to deposit ill-spoken words.

15.

15.

Yattha posaṃ na jānanti, jātiyā vinayena vā;

Na tattha mānaṃ kayirātha, vasamaññātake jane.

Where they do not know a person by birth or by discipline, one should not seek honor there while living among unknown people.

16.

16.

Videsavāsaṃ vasato, jātavedasamenapi jātavedabhayenapi (ka.);

Khamitabbaṃ sapaññena, api dāsassa tajjitanti.

For one living in a foreign land, a wise person should endure even the threatening of a slave, though one may be like fire itself.

Daddarajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Daddara Jātaka, the fourth.

305. Sīlavīmaṃsanajātakaṃ (4-1-5)

305. The Jātaka on the Investigation of Virtue (4-1-5)

17.

17.

Natthi loke raho nāma, pāpakammaṃ pakubbato;

Passanti vanabhūtāni, taṃ bālo maññatī raho.

There is no such thing as a secret place in the world for one who commits an evil deed. The forest spirits see it, yet the fool thinks it is a secret.

18.

18.

Ahaṃ raho na passāmi, suññaṃ vāpi na vijjati;

Yattha aññaṃ suññaṃ (syā. ka.) na passāmi, asuññaṃ hoti taṃ mayā.

305. I see no secret place, nor is any empty place to be found. Where I do not see another, that place is not empty of me.

19.

19.

Dujjacco ca sujacco ajacco (pī.) ca, nando ca sukhavaḍḍhito sukhavacchako (sī.), sukhavacchano (syā. pī.);

Vejjo [T 1.0132] ca addhuvasīlo atha sīlo (ka.) ca, te dhammaṃ jahu matthikā.

Dujjacca and Sujacca, Nanda and Sukhavaḍḍhita, Vajja and Sīla—they, desiring a woman, abandoned the principle.

20.

20.

Brāhmaṇo [V 1.0083] ca kathaṃ jahe, sabbadhammāna pāragū;

Yo dhammamanupāleti, dhitimā saccanikkamoti.

But how could a brahmin abandon the principle, one who has gone to the far shore of all principles? He who protects the Dhamma is steadfast, endowed with truth and effort.

Sīlavīmaṃsanajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka, the fifth.

306. Sujātajātakaṃ (4-1-6)

306. The Sujāta Jātaka (4-1-6)

21.

21.

Kimaṇḍakā [M 1.0096] ime deva, nikkhittā kaṃsamallake;

Upalohitakā vaggū, taṃ te (pī.) me akkhāhi pucchito.

O king, what are these round things, placed in a bronze bowl? They are reddish and beautiful. Being asked, please tell me of what fruit they are.

22.

22.

Yāni pure tuvaṃ devi, bhaṇḍu nantakavāsinī;

Ucchaṅgahatthā pacināsi, tassā te koliyaṃ phalaṃ.

O queen, the fruit which you formerly gathered—with shaven head, wearing worn-out clothes, and with your hands in the fold of your garment—this is that very koliya fruit of yours.

23.

23.

Uḍḍayhate na ramati, bhogā vippajahanti taṃ vippajahanti’maṃ (?);

Tatthevimaṃ paṭinetha, yattha kolaṃ pacissati.

306. She is consumed by pride and finds no delight; pleasures abandon her. Lead her back to that very place where she will gather jujube fruits.

24.

24.

Honti hete mahārāja, iddhippattāya iddhimattāya (ka.) nāriyā;

Khama deva sujātāya, māssā māsu (ka.) kujjha rathesabhāti.

These things happen, great king, for a woman who has attained prosperity. Forgive Sujātā, O king; do not be angry with her, O bull among charioteers.

Sujātajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Sujāta Jātaka, the sixth.

307. Palāsajātakaṃ (4-1-7)

307. The Palāsa Jātaka (4-1-7)

25.

25.

Acetanaṃ brāhmaṇa assuṇantaṃ, jāno ajānantamimaṃ palāsaṃ;

Āraddhaviriyo dhuvaṃ appamatto, sukhaseyyaṃ [T 1.0133] pucchasi kissa hetu.

O brahmin, knowing it to be insentient, unhearing, and unknowing, for what reason do you, with aroused energy, constantly and heedfully, ask this Palāsa tree about a comfortable life?

26.

26.

Dūre suto ceva brahā ca rukkho, dese ṭhito bhūtanivāsarūpo;

Tasmā namassāmi imaṃ palāsaṃ, ye cettha bhūtā te te ca (sī. pī.) dhanassa hetu.

This tree is renowned from afar and large; it stands in a prominent place and is a dwelling for spirits. Therefore, for the sake of wealth, I pay homage to this Palāsa tree and to the spirits who dwell herein.

27.

27.

So te karissāmi yathānubhāvaṃ, kataññutaṃ brāhmaṇa pekkhamāno;

Kathañhi āgamma sataṃ sakāse, moghāni te assu pariphanditāni.

O brahmin, showing my gratitude, I will act for you according to my power. For how, having come into the presence of the good, could your strivings be in vain?

28.

28.

Yo [M 1.0097] tindukarukkhassa paro puro (ka.) pilakkho pilakkhu (sī. pī.), milakkhu (ka.), parivārito pubbayañño uḷāro;

Tassesa mūlasmiṃ nidhi nikhāto, adāyādo gaccha taṃ uddharāhīti.

307. Beyond the Tinduka tree stands a magnificent, surrounded Pilakkha tree, honored with ancient sacrifices. At its root a treasure is buried, which is without an heir. Go and dig it up.

Palāsajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Palāsa Jātaka, the seventh.

308. Sakuṇajātakaṃ (4-1-8)

308. The Sakuṇa Jātaka (4-1-8)

29.

29.

Akaramhasa te kiccaṃ, yaṃ balaṃ ahuvamhase;

Migarāja namo tyatthu, api kiñci labhāmase.

We have performed your task with what strength we possessed. O king of beasts, homage to you. Might we obtain even a little something?

30.

30.

Mama [V 1.0084] lohitabhakkhassa, niccaṃ luddāni kubbato;

Dantantaragato santo, taṃ bahuṃ yampi jīvasi.

That you are still alive, having been between the teeth of me, who consumes blood and constantly commits cruel deeds, is a great thing indeed.

31.

31.

Akataññumakattāraṃ[T 1.0134], katassa appaṭikārakaṃ;

Yasmiṃ kataññutā natthi, niratthā tassa sevanā.

Association with one who is ungrateful, a non-doer of good, one who does not repay a deed done, and in whom no gratitude is found—such association is fruitless.

32.

32.

Yassa sammukhaciṇṇena, mittadhammo na labbhati;

Anusūya anusuyya (sī. pī.) manakkosaṃ, saṇikaṃ tamhā apakkameti.

From one by whom the nature of a friend is not obtained even through a good deed done in their presence, one should gently withdraw, without envy and without reviling.

Sakuṇajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

308. The Sakuṇa Jātaka, the eighth.

309. Chavakajātakaṃ (4-1-9)

309. The Chava Jātaka (4-1-9)

33.

33.

Sabbamidaṃ carimaṃ kataṃ carimavataṃ (sī. pī.), ubho dhammaṃ na passare;

Ubho pakatiyā cutā, yo cāyaṃ mantejjhāpeti mantajjhāyati (sī.), sajjhāpayati (pī.);

Yo ca mantaṃ adhīyati.

All this that is done is a base deed. Both he who teaches the sacred texts and he who learns the sacred texts—both fail to see what is right; both have fallen from their natural state.

34.

34.

Sālīnaṃ odanaṃ bhuñje, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na sevāmi, dhammaṃ isīhi sevitaṃ.

I eat the rice of the Sāli grain, pure and with a meat relish; therefore, I do not practice this Dhamma that is followed by the seers.

35.

35.

Paribbaja mahā loko mahābrahme (ka.), pacantaññepi pāṇino;

Mā taṃ adhammo ācarito, asmā kumbhamivābhidā.

The world is vast; go wander elsewhere, O brahmin. Other beings also cook. Do not practice unrighteousness. Just as a stone shatters a pot, may unrighteousness not shatter you.

36.

36.

Dhiratthu [M 1.0098] taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vāti.

Shame on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O brahmin, that livelihood which arises either through ruin or through the practice of unrighteousness.

Chavakajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Chavaka Jātaka, the ninth.

310. Seyyajātakaṃ (4-1-10)

310. The Seyya Jātaka (4-1-10)

37.

37.

Sasamuddapariyāyaṃ[T 1.0135], mahiṃ sāgarakuṇḍalaṃ;

Na icche saha nindāya, evaṃ seyya sayha (sī. syā. pī.) vijānahi.

I would not desire the earth, with its surrounding ocean and the great sea as its earring, if it came with censure. Thus, O Seyya, you should know.

38.

38.

Dhiratthu taṃ yasalābhaṃ, dhanalābhañca brāhmaṇa;

Yā vutti vinipātena, adhammacaraṇena vā.

Shame on that gain of fame and gain of wealth, O brahmin, that livelihood which arises either through ruin or through the practice of unrighteousness.

39.

39.

Api ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Sāyeva jīvikā seyyo, yā cādhammena esanā.

Even if, having taken up a bowl, a homeless one should wander for alms, that very livelihood is better than any seeking that is done through unrighteousness.

40.

40.

Api [V 1.0085] ce pattamādāya, anagāro paribbaje;

Aññaṃ ahiṃsayaṃ loke, api rajjena taṃ varanti.

Even if, having taken up a bowl, a homeless one should wander in the world without harming any other being, that life is more excellent even than kingship.

Seyyajātakaṃ sayhajātakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) dasamaṃ.

The Seyya Jātaka, the tenth.

Kāliṅgavaggo vivaravaggo (sī. pī.) paṭhamo.

The Kāliṅga Chapter, the first.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Vivarañca adeyya samiddhavaraṃ, atha daddara pāpamahātiraho;

Atha koli palāsavarañca kara, carimaṃ sasamuddavarena dasāti.

The Cūḷakāliṅga Jātaka; the Mahāassaroha and Ekarāja Jātakas; then the Daddara and Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātakas; then the Sujāta Jātaka; and the Palāsa Jātaka; together with the Sakuṇa, Chava, and Seyya Jātakas, make ten.

2. Pucimandavaggo

2. 2. The Pucimanda Chapter

311. Pucimandajātakaṃ (4-2-1)

311. The Pucimanda Jātaka (4.2.1)

41.

41.

Uṭṭhehi cora kiṃ sesi, ko attho supanena supitena (sī.), supinena (pī. ka.) te;

Mā [T 1.0136] taṃ gahesuṃ gaṇheyyuṃ (ka.) rājāno, gāme kibbisakārakaṃ.

Arise, O thief! Why do you sleep? What benefit is there for you in sleeping? May the king's men not seize you, the one who commits cruel deeds in the village.

42.

42.

Yaṃ [M 1.0099] nu nūna (syā.) coraṃ gahessanti, gāme kibbisakārakaṃ;

Kiṃ tattha pucimandassa, vane jātassa tiṭṭhato.

When they seize the thief, the one who commits cruel deeds in the village, what is that to the Pucimanda tree, which has grown and stands in the forest?

43.

43.

Na tvaṃ assattha jānāsi, mama corassa cantaraṃ;

Coraṃ gahetvā rājāno, gāme kibbisakārakaṃ;

Appenti accenti (syā.) nimbasūlasmiṃ, tasmiṃ me saṅkate mano.

O Assattha, you do not know the connection between me and the thief. Having seized the thief who commits cruel deeds in the village, the king's men impale him on a stake of Nimba wood. At that, my mind is filled with apprehension.

44.

44.

Saṅkeyya saṅkitabbāni, rakkheyyānāgataṃ bhayaṃ;

Anāgatabhayā dhīro, ubho loke avekkhatīti.

One should be apprehensive of what is to be apprehended; one should guard against a danger that has not yet come. Fearing future danger, the wise person considers both worlds.

Pucimandajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Pucimanda Jātaka, the first.

312. Kassapamandiyajātakaṃ (4-2-2)

312. The Kassapamandiya Jātaka (4.2.2)

45.

45.

Api kassapa mandiyā, yuvā sapati hanti sampaṭihanti (ka.) vā;

Sabbaṃ taṃ khamate dhīro, paṇḍito taṃ titikkhati.

Indeed, Kassapa, due to dull-wittedness, the young may revile or strike; the wise one endures all that, the learned one is patient with it.

46.

46.

Sacepi santo vivadanti, khippaṃ sandhīyare puna;

Bālā pattāva bhijjanti, na te samathamajjhagū.

Even if the virtuous quarrel, they are quickly reconciled again; fools break like earthen pots—they do not attain peace.

47.

47.

Ete [V 1.0086] bhiyyo samāyanti, sandhi tesaṃ na jīrati;

Yo cādhipannaṃ jānāti, yo ca jānāti desanaṃ.

He who knows his transgression, and he who knows how to confess it—these are reconciled again; their friendship does not decay.

48.

48.

Eso hi uttaritaro, bhāravaho dhuraddharo;

Yo paresādhipannānaṃ[T 1.0137], sayaṃ sandhātumarahatīti.

Indeed, he is more excellent, a bearer of the burden, a carrier of the yoke, who is himself able to reconcile others who have transgressed.

Kassapamandiyajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Kassapamandiya Jātaka, the second.

313. Khantīvādījātakaṃ (4-2-3)

313. The Khantīvādī Jātaka (4.2.3)

49.

49.

Yo te hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi;

Tassa kujjha mahāvīra, mā raṭṭhaṃ vinasā vinassa (ka. sī. syā. ka.) idaṃ.

O great hero, be angry with him who cut off your hands and feet, and your ears and nose. Do not let this kingdom be destroyed.

50.

50.

Yo me hatthe ca pāde ca, kaṇṇanāsañca chedayi;

Ciraṃ jīvatu so rājā, na hi kujjhanti mādisā.

May that king who cut off my hands and feet, and my ears and nose, live long. Indeed, those such as I do not become angry.

51.

51.

Ahū atītamaddhānaṃ ahu atītamaddhāne (syā. pī. ka.), samaṇo khantidīpano;

Taṃ khantiyāyeva ṭhitaṃ, kāsirājā achedayi.

In a time long past, there was an ascetic who illumined patience. Him, established in patience itself, the king of Kāsi mutilated.

52.

52.

Tassa [M 1.0100] kamma kammassa (sī. pī.) pharusassa, vipāko kaṭuko ahu;

Yaṃ kāsirājā vedesi, nirayamhi samappitoti.

Bitter was the result of that harsh deed, which the king of Kāsi experienced, established in hell.

Khantīvādījātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Khantīvādī Jātaka, the third.

314. Lohakumbhijātakaṃ (4-2-4)

314. The Lohakumbhi Jātaka (4.2.4)

53.

53.

Dujjīvitamajīvimha, ye sante yesaṃ no (syā. ka.) na dadamhase;

Vijjamānesu bhogesu, dīpaṃ nākamha attano.

We lived a wicked life, we who did not give even when we had wealth; we did not make a refuge for ourselves.

54.

54.

Saṭṭhi saṭṭhiṃ (syā.) vassasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni sabbaso;

Niraye paccamānānaṃ, kadā anto bhavissati.

For us who are being tormented in hell, sixty thousand years are now completely fulfilled in every way; when will there be an end?

55.

55.

Natthi anto kuto anto, na anto paṭidissati;

Tadā [T 1.0138] hi pakataṃ pāpaṃ, mama tuyhañca mārisā mārisa (sī. syā. pī.).

There is no end. From where could there be an end? An end is not seen. For then, dear sirs, evil was done by me and by you.

56.

56.

Sohaṃ nūna ito gantvā, yoniṃ laddhāna mānusiṃ;

Vadaññū sīlasampanno, kāhāmi kusalaṃ bahunti.

Surely I, having gone from here and obtained a human birth, becoming generous and endowed with virtue, shall perform many meritorious deeds.

Lohakumbhijātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Lohakumbhi Jātaka, the fourth.

315. Sabbamaṃsalābhajātakaṃ (4-2-5)

315. The Sabbamaṃsalābha Jātaka (4.2.5)

57.

57.

Pharusā [V 1.0087] vata te vācā, maṃsaṃ samma (pī. ka.) yācanako asi casi (pī.);

Kilomasadisī kilomassa sadisā (pī.) vācā, kilomaṃ samma dammi te.

Indeed, your words are harsh; you are a beggar for flesh. Your speech is like the fascia; friend, I will give you the fascia.

58.

58.

Aṅgametaṃ manussānaṃ, bhātā loke pavuccati;

Aṅgassa sadisī vācā aṅgassadisī te vācā (ka.), aṅgaṃ samma dadāmi te.

A brother is said to be a limb of a person in this world. Your speech is like a limb; friend, I give you a limb.

59.

59.

Tātāti putto vadamāno, kampeti sammeti (ka.) hadayaṃ pitu;

Hadayassa sadisī hadayassadisī (ka.) vācā, hadayaṃ samma dammi te.

A son, saying 'Father!', makes his father's heart tremble. Your speech is like the heart; friend, I will give you the heart.

60.

60.

Yassa gāme sakhā natthi, yathāraññaṃ tatheva taṃ;

Sabbassa sadisī vācā, sabbaṃ samma dadāmi teti.

For one who has no friend in a village, that village is just like a forest. Your speech is like my whole self; friend, I will give you my all.

Sabbamaṃsalābhajātakaṃ maṃsajātakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) pañcamaṃ.

The Sabbamaṃsalābha Jātaka, the fifth.

316. Sasapaṇḍitajātakaṃ (4-2-6)

316. The Jātaka of the Wise Hare (4.2.6)

61.

61.

Satta [M 1.0101] me rohitā macchā, udakā thalamubbhatā;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasa.

“O brahmin, I have seven rohu fish, drawn from the water onto dry land. This is what I have; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.”

62.

62.

Dussa me khettapālassa, rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ;

Maṃsasūlā [T 1.0139] ca dve godhā, ekañca dadhivārakaṃ;

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasa.

“O brahmin, I have brought the night-meal of the field-guard Dussa: two meat skewers, a roasted monitor lizard, and one pot of curd. This is what I have; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.”

63.

63.

Ambapakkaṃ dakaṃ ambapakkodakaṃ (sī. pī.) sītaṃ, sītacchāyā manoramā sītacchāyaṃ manoramaṃ (sī. syā. pī.);

Idaṃ brāhmaṇa me atthi, etaṃ bhutvā vane vasa.

“O brahmin, I have a ripe mango, cool water, and delightful cool shade. This is what I have; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.”

64.

64.

Na sasassa tilā atthi, na muggā napi taṇḍulā;

Iminā agginā pakkaṃ, mamaṃ maṃsaṃ (ka.) bhutvā vane vasāti.

“The hare has no sesame, no mung beans, nor rice. Having eaten my flesh, cooked by this fire, dwell in the forest.”

Sasapaṇḍitajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Jātaka of the Wise Hare, the sixth.

317. Matarodanajātakaṃ (4-2-7)

317. The Jātaka of Weeping for the Dead

65.

65.

Mataṃ mataṃ eva matamatameva (sī. syā. pī.) rodatha, na hi taṃ rodatha yo marissati;

Sabbepi sabbeva (sī. syā. pī.) sarīradhārino, anupubbena jahanti jīvitaṃ.

“You weep for each one who has died, but you do not weep for one who is yet to die. All who bear a body, in succession, abandon life.”

66.

66.

Devamanussā catuppadā, pakkhigaṇā uragā ca bhogino;

Samhi yamhi (syā.), asmiṃ (pī. ka.) sarīre anissarā, ramamānāva jahanti jīvitaṃ.

“Gods and humans, quadrupeds, flocks of birds, and serpents—all, though endowed with splendor, are powerless over their own body; while still delighting, they abandon life.”

67.

67.

Evaṃ [V 1.0088] calitaṃ asaṇṭhitaṃ, sukhadukkhaṃ manujesvapekkhiya;

Kanditaruditaṃ niratthakaṃ, kiṃ vo sokagaṇābhikīrare.

“Considering this trembling, unstable nature of happiness and suffering among humans, lamentation and weeping are useless. Why do hosts of sorrow overwhelm you?”

68.

68.

Dhuttā ca soṇḍā dhuttā soṇḍā (sī.), dhuttā soṇḍā ca (syā.) akatā, bālā sūrā ayogino bālā sūrā vīrā ayogino (pī.);

Dhīraṃ maññanti bāloti, ye dhammassa akovidāti.

“The profligate, the drunkard, the idle, the foolish, the bold, the undisciplined—those who are unskilled in the Dhamma think a wise person is a fool.”

Matarodanajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Jātaka of Weeping for the Dead, the seventh.

318. Kaṇaverajātakaṃ (4-2-8)

318. The Kaṇavera Jātaka

69.

69.

Yaṃ [T 1.0140][M 1.0102] taṃ vasantasamaye, kaṇaveresu bhāṇusu;

Sāmaṃ bāhāya pīḷesi, sā taṃ ārogyamabravi.

“In the spring season, amidst the red kaṇavera bushes, when you embraced Sāmā with your arm, she spoke to you of her well-being.”

70.

70.

Ambho na kira saddheyyaṃ, yaṃ vāto pabbataṃ vahe;

Pabbatañce vahe vāto, sabbampi pathaviṃ vahe;

Yattha sāmā kālakatā kālaṅkatā (ka.), sā maṃ ārogyamabravi.

“Indeed, sir, it is unbelievable that the wind could carry away a mountain. If the wind were to carry a mountain, it would carry away the entire earth. Just as unbelievable is this: that Sāmā, who is dead, spoke to me of her well-being.”

71.

71.

Na ceva sā kālakatā, na ca sā aññamicchati;

Ekabhattikinī ekabhattā kira (sī. syā.), ekabhattakinī (pī.) sāmā, tameva abhikaṅkhati.

“She is not dead at all, nor does she desire another. Sāmā, who eats but a single meal, longs only for you.”

72.

72.

Asanthutaṃ maṃ cirasanthutena asandhataṃ maṃ cirasandhatena (ka.), nimīni sāmā adhuvaṃ dhuvena;

Mayāpi sāmā nimineyya aññaṃ, ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissanti.

“Sāmā exchanged me, the unacquainted, for one long-acquainted; the uncertain for the certain. I, too, should exchange Sāmā for another; I will go far away from here.”

Kaṇaverajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kaṇavera Jātaka, the eighth.

319. Tittirajātakaṃ (4-2-9)

319. The Tittira Jātaka

73.

73.

Susukhaṃ vata jīvāmi, labhāmi ceva bhuñjituṃ;

Paripantheva tiṭṭhāmi, kā nu bhante gatī mama.

“I live very happily indeed, and I also get things to eat; yet I stand in harm's way. Venerable sir, what will be my fate?”

74.

74.

Mano ce te nappaṇamati, pakkhi pāpassa kammuno;

Abyāvaṭassa bhadrassa, na pāpamupalimpati.

“O bird, if your mind does not incline toward an evil deed, evil does not cling to one who is harmless and virtuous.”

75.

75.

Ñātako no nisinnoti, bahu āgacchate jano;

Paṭicca [T 1.0141] kammaṃ phusati, tasmiṃ me saṅkate mano.

“Thinking, ‘Our relative is sitting there,’ many folk come. On my account, the hunter commits his deed; about that, my mind is anxious.”

76.

76.

Na paṭicca kammaṃ phusati, mano ce nappadussati;

Appossukkassa bhadrassa, na pāpamupalimpatīti.

“The deed does not touch you, though done on your account, if your mind is not corrupted. For one without anxiety, for one who is virtuous, evil does not cling.”

Tittirajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Tittira Jātaka, the ninth.

320. Succajajātakaṃ (4-2-10)

320. The Succaja Jātaka

77.

77.

Succajaṃ [V 1.0089][M 1.0103] vata naccaji, vācāya adadaṃ giriṃ;

Kiṃ hitassa cajantassa, vācāya adada pabbataṃ.

“Indeed, he did not renounce what is easy to renounce, he who did not grant the mountain even by word. What benefit is there for one who is renouncing, yet does not grant the mountain even by word?”

78.

78.

Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

“One should speak of what one does; one should not speak of what one does not do. The wise discern the one who speaks but does not act.”

79.

79.

Rājaputta namo tyatthu, sacce dhamme ṭhito casi;

Yassa te byasanaṃ patto, saccasmiṃ ramate mano.

“O prince, homage to you! You are established in truth and in Dhamma. Though you have met with misfortune, your mind still delights in truth.”

80.

80.

Yā daliddī daliddassa, aḍḍhā aḍḍhassa kittima kittimā (sī. syā. pī.);

Sā hissa paramā bhariyā, sahiraññassa itthiyoti.

“O Kittima, the wife who is poor when her husband is poor and wealthy when he is wealthy—she is truly his supreme wife. For a man with gold and silver to have women is no wonder.”

Succajajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Succaja Jātaka, the tenth.

Pucimandavaggo dutiyo.

The Pucimanda Chapter, the second.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Atha cora sakassapa khantīvaro, dujjīvitatā ca varā pharusā;

Atha [T 1.0142] sasa matañca vasanta sukhaṃ, succajaṃvatanaccajinā ca dasāti.

Then the Pucimanda, Kassapamandiya, and the excellent Khantivādī; the Lohakumbhī and the excellent Sabbamaṃsalābha; then the Sasa and Matarodana, the Kaṇavera and Tittira; together with the Succaja, these are the ten.

3. Kuṭidūsakavaggo

3. The Kuṭidūsaka Chapter

321. Kuṭidūsakajātakaṃ (4-3-1)

321. The Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka

81.

81.

Manussasseva te sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca vānara;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, agāraṃ te na vijjati.

“O monkey, your head is just like a human's, and so are your hands and feet. For what reason, then, do you not have a home?”

82.

82.

Manussasseva me sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca siṅgila siṅgāla (ka.), piṅgala (ṭīkā);

Yāhu seṭṭhā manussesu, sā me paññā na vijjati.

“My head is like a human's, O Siṅgila, and so are my hands and feet. But that which is said to be the highest among humans—that wisdom—is not found in me.”

83.

83.

Anavaṭṭhitacittassa[M 1.0104], lahucittassa dubbhino dūbhino (pī.);

Niccaṃ addhuvasīlassa, sukhabhāvo sucibhāvo (sī.), sukhabhāgo (?) na vijjati.

“For one with an unsteady mind, a fickle mind, who is treacherous to friends; for one of constantly unstable virtue, a state of happiness is not found.”

84.

84.

So [V 1.0090] karassu ānubhāvaṃ, vītivattassu sīliyaṃ;

Sītavātaparittāṇaṃ, karassu kuṭavaṃ kuṭikaṃ (sī. syā.) kapīti.

“Therefore, exert your power and overcome this bad habit. Make a hut, O monkey, for protection from the cold and wind.”

Kuṭidūsaka siṅgālasakuṇa (ka.) jātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Kuṭidūsaka Jātaka, the first.

322. Duddubhajātakaṃ (4-3-2)

322. The Duddubha Jātaka

85.

85.

Duddubhāyati daddabhāyati (sī. pī.) bhaddante, yasmiṃ dese vasāmahaṃ;

Ahampetaṃ na jānāmi, kimetaṃ duddubhāyati.

Venerable sir, in the place where I dwell, it makes a 'duddubha' sound. I do not know what it is that makes this 'duddubha' sound.

86.

86.

Beluvaṃ [T 1.0143] patitaṃ sutvā, duddubhanti daddabhanti (sī.) saso javi;

Sasassa vacanaṃ sutvā, santattā migavāhinī.

Hearing a ripe wood-apple fruit fall with a 'duddubha' sound, the hare fled. Hearing the hare's words, the herd of animals fled in terror.

87.

87.

Appatvā padaviññāṇaṃ, paraghosānusārino;

Panādaparamā bālā, te honti parapattiyā.

Not having attained direct knowledge of the path, fools follow the cries of others. Taking the shouts of others as supreme, they are led by faith in others.

88.

88.

Ye ca sīlena sampannā, paññāyūpasame ratā;

Ārakā viratā dhīrā, na honti parapattiyāti.

But those who are endowed with virtue, delighting in wisdom and the calming of defilements, the wise who are aloof and abstinent, are not led by faith in others.

Duddubhajātakaṃ daddabhajātakaṃ (sī. pī.) dutiyaṃ.

The Duddubha Jātaka, the second.

323. Brahmadattajātakaṃ (4-3-3)

323. The Brahmadatta Jātaka

89.

89.

Dvayaṃ yācanako rāja, brahmadatta nigacchati;

Alābhaṃ dhanalābhaṃ vā, evaṃ dhammā hi yācanā.

O King Brahmadatta, a petitioner meets with two outcomes: either not receiving, or the receipt of wealth. For such is the nature of petitioning.

90.

90.

Yācanaṃ rodanaṃ āhu, pañcālānaṃ rathesabha;

Yo yācanaṃ paccakkhāti, tamāhu paṭirodanaṃ.

Petitioning, they say, is weeping, O bull among the charioteers of the Pañcālas. He who refuses a petition, they say, is weeping in return.

91.

91.

Mā maddasaṃsu rodantaṃ, pañcālā susamāgatā;

Tuvaṃ vā paṭirodantaṃ, tasmā icchāmahaṃ raho.

May the well-assembled Pañcālas not see me weeping, nor you weeping in return by refusing me. Therefore, I desire to be in private.

92.

92.

Dadāmi [M 1.0105] te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ, gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena;

Ariyo hi ariyassa kathaṃ na dajjā dajje (sī.), dajjaṃ (?), sutvāna gāthā tava dhammayuttāti.

I give to you, O brahmin, a thousand red cows, together with a bull. For how could a noble one not give to a noble one, having heard your verses that are in accord with the Dhamma?

Brahmadattajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Brahmadatta Jātaka, the third.

324. Cammasāṭakajātakaṃ (4-3-4)

324. The Cammasāṭaka Jātaka

93.

93.

Kalyāṇarūpo [T 1.0144] vatayaṃ catuppado, subhaddako ceva supesalo ca;

Yo brāhmaṇaṃ jātimantūpapannaṃ, apacāyati meṇḍavaro yasassī.

Beautiful in form indeed is this quadruped, both auspicious and very amiable; he, the glorious and excellent ram, reveres a brahmin endowed with high birth.

94.

94.

Mā [V 1.0091] brāhmaṇa ittaradassanena, vissāsamāpajji catuppadassa;

Daḷhappahāraṃ abhikaṅkhamāno abhikattukāmo (syā.), avasakkatī dassati suppahāraṃ.

O brahmin, do not place trust in a quadruped from a brief sighting. Desiring to strike a heavy blow, it retreats to deliver a well-aimed one.

95.

95.

Ūruṭṭhi ūraṭṭhi (sī.) bhaggaṃ pavaṭṭito patito (sī. syā.) khāribhāro, sabbañca bhaṇḍaṃ brāhmaṇassa brāhmaṇassīdha (ka. sī. pī.), brāhmaṇasseva (ka. sī. syā. ka.) bhinnaṃ;

Ubhopi bāhā paggayha paggayyeva (syā.), paggahīya (?) kandati bāhā paggayya kandati (pī. ka.), abhidhāvatha haññate brahmacārī.

The thigh bone is broken, the shoulder-pole load has fallen, and all the brahmin’s goods are ruined. With both arms raised, he weeps, “Come quickly, the holy man is being killed!”

96.

96.

Evaṃ so nihato seti, yo apūjaṃ pasaṃsati namassati (pī.);

Yathāhamajja pahato, hato meṇḍena dummatīti.

Thus lies he slain who praises one who is unworthy of praise, just as I am struck down today, slain by the foolish ram.

Cammasāṭakajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Cammasāṭaka Jātaka, the fourth.

325. Godharājajātakaṃ (4-3-5)

325. The Godharāja Jātaka

97.

97.

Samaṇaṃ [T 1.0145] taṃ maññamāno, upagacchimasaññataṃ;

So maṃ daṇḍena pāhāsi, yathā assamaṇo tathā.

Thinking him to be an ascetic, I approached that unrestrained one; he struck me with a stick, just as a non-ascetic would.

98.

98.

Kiṃ [M 1.0106] te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā;

Abbhantaraṃ te gahanaṃ, bāhiraṃ parimajjasi.

What use are your matted locks, O witless one? What use your antelope-hide garment? Your interior is a dense thicket, while you merely polish the outside.

99.

99.

Ehi godha nivattassu, bhuñja sālīnamodanaṃ;

Telaṃ loṇañca me atthi, pahūtaṃ mayha pipphali.

Come, iguana, turn back, and eat this porridge of fine rice; I have oil and salt, and I have plenty of long pepper.

100.

100.

Esa bhiyyo pavekkhāmi, vammikaṃ sataporisaṃ;

Telaṃ loṇañca kittesi kintesi (syā. pī.), ahitaṃ mayha pipphalīti.

I shall enter even further into this anthill a hundred persons deep; you speak of oil and salt, but long pepper is unsuitable for me.

Godharājajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Godharāja Jātaka, the fifth.

326. Kakkārujātakaṃ (4-3-6)

326. The Kakkāru Jātaka

101.

101.

Kāyena yo nāvahare, vācāya na musā bhaṇe;

Yaso laddhā na majjeyya, sa ve kakkārumarahati.

He who does not steal with his body, nor speak falsehood with his speech, who, having gained prosperity, is not heedless—he, indeed, is worthy of the Kakkāru celestial flower.

102.

102.

Dhammena vittameseyya, na nikatyā dhanaṃ hare;

Bhoge laddhā na majjeyya, sa ve kakkārumarahati.

One who would seek wealth righteously, and not take riches by deceit; having obtained enjoyments, one should not be heedless—he, indeed, is worthy of the Kakkāru celestial flower.

103.

103.

Yassa cittaṃ ahāliddaṃ, saddhā ca avirāginī;

Eko sāduṃ na bhuñjeyya, sa ve kakkārumarahati.

He whose mind is not fickle like turmeric dye, and whose faith is unfading; who would not eat a delicious meal alone—he, indeed, is worthy of the Kakkāru celestial flower.

104.

104.

Sammukhā vā tirokkhā vā parokkhā vā (pī.), parammukhā (ka.), yo sante na paribhāsati;

Yathāvādī [T 1.0146] tathākārī, sa ve kakkārumarahatīti.

He who does not revile the virtuous, whether in their presence or in their absence; who acts as he speaks—he, indeed, is worthy of the Kakkāru celestial flower.

Kakkārujātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Kakkāru Jātaka, the sixth.

327. Kākavatījātakaṃ (4-3-7)

327. The Kākavatī Jātaka

105.

105.

Vāti [V 1.0092] cāyaṃ vāyaṃ (ka.) tato gandho, yattha me vasatī piyā;

Dūre ito hi kākavatī kākātī (sī.), kākāti (syā. pī.), yattha me nirato mano.

From there blows this fragrance, from where my beloved dwells; far from here is Kākavatī, in whom my mind delights.

106.

106.

Kathaṃ samuddamatarī, kathaṃ atari kepukaṃ kebukaṃ (sī. pī.);

Kathaṃ satta samuddāni, kathaṃ simbalimāruhi.

How did you cross the ocean? How did you cross the Kepuka? How did you traverse the seven seas? How did you climb the Simbali tree?

107.

107.

Tayā samuddamatariṃ, tayā atari kepukaṃ kebukaṃ (sī. pī.);

Tayā satta samuddāni, tayā simbalimāruhiṃ.

By you, I crossed the ocean; by you, I crossed the Kepuka; by you, I traversed the seven seas; by you, I climbed the Simbali tree.

108.

108.

Dhiratthumaṃ [M 1.0107] mahākāyaṃ, dhiratthumaṃ acetanaṃ;

Yattha jāyāyahaṃ jāraṃ, āvahāmi vahāmi cāti.

Fie upon me of great body! Fie upon me, this insentient one! For my own wife, I bring her lover here and carry him away.

Kākavatījātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Kākavatī Jātaka, the seventh.

328. Ananusociyajātakaṃ (4-3-8)

328. The Ananusociya Jātaka

109.

109.

Bahūnaṃ vijjatī bhotī, tehi me kiṃ bhavissati;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, piyaṃ sammillahāsiniṃ.

O lady, she is now among many. With them, what will she be to me? Therefore, I do not grieve for this beloved Sammillahāsinī.

110.

110.

Taṃ taṃ ce anusoceyya, yaṃ yaṃ tassa na vijjati;

Attānamanusoceyya, sadā maccuvasaṃ pataṃ.

If I were to grieve for each and every one who is no more, I should grieve for myself, who is always falling under the sway of death.

111.

111.

Na [T 1.0147] heva ṭhitaṃ nāsīnaṃ, na sayānaṃ na paddhaguṃ patthaguṃ (syā.);

Yāva byāti nimisati, tatrāpi rasatī saratī (sī. syā. pī.) vayo.

Life's decay does not wait for one to be standing, nor sitting, nor lying down, nor walking. Even in the time it takes to open and close the eyes, in that very moment, age diminishes.

112.

112.

Tatthattani vatappaddhe vata panthe (syā.), vata bandhe (ka.) vata + pa-addhe = vatappaddhe, vinābhāve asaṃsaye;

Bhūtaṃ sesaṃ dayitabbaṃ, vītaṃ ananusociyanti cavitaṃ nānusociyanti (syā.), matantaṃ nānusociyaṃ (ka.).

Indeed, when one is bound to this existence, separation is without a doubt. The being that remains should be cherished; one should not grieve for the one who has passed away.

Ananusociyajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Ananusociya Jātaka, the eighth.

329. Kāḷabāhujātakaṃ (4-3-9)

329. The Kāḷabāhu Jātaka

113.

113.

Yaṃ annapānassa pure labhāma, taṃ dāni sākhamigameva gacchati;

Gacchāma dāni vanameva rādha, asakkatā casma dhanañjayāya dhanañcayāya (ka.).

The food and drink that we formerly received, now goes only to the monkey. Let us now go to the forest, Rādha; we are unhonored by Dhanañjaya.

114.

114.

Lābho alābho yaso ayaso ca, nindā pasaṃsā ca sukhañca dukkhaṃ;

Ete aniccā manujesu dhammā, mā soci kiṃ socasi poṭṭhapāda.

Gain and loss, fame and disrepute, blame and praise, and pleasure and pain—these conditions are impermanent among humans. Do not grieve, Poṭṭhapāda; why do you grieve?

115.

115.

Addhā [M 1.0108] tuvaṃ paṇḍitakosi rādha, jānāsi atthāni anāgatāni;

Kathaṃ [T 1.0148] nu sākhāmigaṃ dakkhisāma dakkhiyāma (ka.), dakkhāma (syā.), niddhāvitaṃ niddhāpitaṃ (sī. syā.), nibbāpitaṃ (pī.), nicchadaṃ (ka.) rājakulatova jammaṃ.

Truly, you are wise, Rādha; you know of matters yet to come. How then shall we see that base monkey driven out from the royal household?

116.

116.

Cāleti [V 1.0093] kaṇṇaṃ bhakuṭiṃ karoti, muhuṃ muhuṃ bhāyayate bhāyate (syā.), bhāyāpate (ka.) kumāre;

Sayameva taṃ kāhati kāḷabāhu, yenārakā ṭhassati annapānāti.

He moves his ear and makes a frown; again and again he frightens the young princes. Kāḷabāhu himself will bring about that by which he will be kept far from food and drink.

Kāḷabāhujātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Kāḷabāhu Jātaka, the ninth.

330. Sīlavīmaṃsajātakaṃ (4-3-10)

330. The Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka

117.

117.

Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ, sīlaṃ loke anuttaraṃ;

Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññati.

Virtue, it is said, is truly excellent; virtue is supreme in the world. Behold the serpent of terrible venom: because he is virtuous, he is not harmed.

118.

118.

Yāvadevassahū kiñci, tāvadeva akhādisuṃ;

Saṅgamma kulalā loke, na hiṃsanti akiñcanaṃ.

For as long as it had something, for that long they attacked it. Gathering together in the world, the kites do not harm one who has nothing.

119.

119.

Sukhaṃ nirāsā supati, āsā phalavatī sukhā;

Āsaṃ nirāsaṃ katvāna, sukhaṃ supati piṅgalā.

One without hope sleeps in peace; the fruitfulness of hope is happiness. Having rendered hope hopeless, Piṅgalā sleeps in peace.

120.

120.

Na samādhiparo atthi, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca;

Na paraṃ nāpi attānaṃ, vihiṃsati samāhitoti.

There is no state superior to concentration, neither in this world nor in the next. One who is concentrated harms neither another nor oneself.

Sīlavīmaṃsajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātaka, the tenth.

Kuṭidūsakavaggo tatiyo.

The Kuṭidūsaka Vagga, the third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Samanussa [T 1.0149] -saduddubha-yācanako, atha meṇḍavaruttama-godhavaro;

Atha kāyasakepuka bhotīvaro, atha rādhasusīlavarena dasāti.
