The Siṅgāla, Sakuṇa, Duddubha, and Brahmadatta Jātakas; then the Dhammaṭṭha and Godharāja Jātakas; then the Kakkāru, Kākavatī, and Ananusociya Jātakas; then with the Kāḷabāhu and Sīlavīmaṃsana Jātakas, there are ten.

4. Kokilavaggo

4. The Cuckoo Chapter

331. Kokilajātakaṃ (4-4-1)

331. The Kokila Jātaka

121.

121.

Yo [M 1.0109] ve kāle asampatte, ativelaṃ pabhāsati;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, kokilāyiva atrajo.

Whoever indeed speaks excessively before the time has arrived, that person lies slain, just like the son of the cuckoo.

122.

122.

Na hi satthaṃ sunisitaṃ, visaṃ halāhalāmiva halāhalaṃ iva (pī.);

Evaṃ nikaṭṭhe nikkaḍḍhe (syā.), nikaḍḍhe (ka.) pāteti, vācā dubbhāsitā yathā.

For a well-sharpened weapon does not strike down instantly, nor does halāhala poison, in the same way that ill-spoken speech does.

123.

123.

Tasmā kāle akāle vā akāle ca (sī. syā.), vācaṃ rakkheyya paṇḍito;

Nātivelaṃ pabhāseyya, api attasamamhi vā.

Therefore, a wise person should guard their speech, whether it is the proper time or not. They should not speak excessively, even to one who is their equal.

124.

124.

Yo [V 1.0094] ca kāle mitaṃ bhāse, matipubbo vicakkhaṇo;

Sabbe amitte ādeti, supaṇṇo uragāmivāti.

And that wise person, with wisdom as the forerunner, who speaks measuredly at the proper time, seizes all enemies, just as a supaṇṇa seizes a serpent.

Kokilajātakaṃ kokālikajātakaṃ (sabbattha) paṭhamaṃ.

The Kokila Jātaka, the First.

332. Rathalaṭṭhijātakaṃ (4-4-2)

332. The Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka

125.

125.

Api hantvā hato brūti, jetvā jitoti bhāsati;

Pubbavakkhāyino [T 1.0150] pubbamakkhāyino (sī. syā.) rāja, aññadatthu ekadatthu (sī. pī.) na saddahe.

O king, even having struck himself, one might say, 'I was struck'; having conquered, he might say, 'I am conquered.' One should not place trust in the words of the one who speaks first.

126.

126.

Tasmā paṇḍitajātiyo, suṇeyya itarassapi;

Ubhinnaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā, yathā dhammo tathā kare.

Therefore, one of wise birth should listen to the words of the other as well. Having heard the words of both, one should act in accordance with how the Dhamma is established.

127.

127.

Alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhu.

A lazy householder who enjoys sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained renunciate is not good; a king who acts without deliberation is not good; and if a wise person is prone to anger, that is not good.

128.

128.

Nisamma khattiyo kayirā, nānisamma disampati;

Nisammakārino rāja rañño (sī. syā.), yaso kitti ca vaḍḍhatīti.

A noble should act with deliberation; a ruler should not act without deliberation. O king, for the one who acts with deliberation, both glory and fame increase.

Rathalaṭṭhijātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Rathalaṭṭhi Jātaka, the Second.

333. Pakkagodhajātakaṃ (4-4-3)

333. The Pakkagodha Jātaka

129.

129.

Tadeva [M 1.0110] me tvaṃ vidito, vanamajjhe rathesabha;

Yassa te khaggabaddhassa, sannaddhassa tirīṭino;

Assatthadumasākhāya, pakkā godhā palāyatha.

O bull among chariots, by that very thing you are known to me in the middle of the forest: from you, girt with a sword, clad in armor, and wearing a diadem, a roasted iguana fled from the branch of an Assattha tree.

130.

130.

Name namantassa bhaje bhajantaṃ, kiccānukubbassa kareyya kiccaṃ;

Nānatthakāmassa kareyya atthaṃ, asambhajantampi na sambhajeyya.

One should bow to one who bows; one should attend to one who attends. One should do one's duty for one who does one's duties. One should not act for the benefit of one who desires one's harm. One should not associate with one who does not associate.

131.

131.

Caje [T 1.0151] cajantaṃ vanathaṃ na kayirā, apetacittena na sambhajeyya;

Dijo dumaṃ khīṇaphalanti phalaṃva (ka. sī. syā. ka.), dukanipāte puṭabhattajātakena saṃsandetabbaṃ ñatvā, aññaṃ samekkheyya mahā hi loko.

One should abandon one who abandons and not create longing. One should not associate with a person of estranged mind. A bird, knowing a tree is devoid of fruit, should look for another; for the world is vast indeed.

132.

132.

So te karissāmi yathānubhāvaṃ, kataññutaṃ khattiye khattiyo (syā. ka.) pekkhamāno;

Sabbañca te issariyaṃ dadāmi, yassicchasī tassa tuvaṃ dadāmīti.

I, a noble, considering gratitude, will act for you according to my power. I give you all sovereignty, and I give you whatever you wish.

Pakkagodhajātakaṃ godhajātakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) tatiyaṃ.

The Pakkagodha Jātaka, the Third.

334. Rājovādajātakaṃ (4-4-4)

334. The Rājovāda Jātaka

133.

133.

Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, jimhaṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā tā jimhaṃ gacchanti sabbā gāvī jimhaṃ yanti (sī. syā.), nette jimhaṃ gate sati.

If, among cattle crossing a river, the lead bull goes crookedly, they all go crookedly, the leader having gone crooked.

134.

134.

Evameva [V 1.0095] manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So ce adhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ raṭṭhaṃ dukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti adhammiko.

Just so among humans, whoever is considered the best, if he practices unrighteousness, what need be said of the other people? If the king is unrighteous, the whole country dwells in suffering.

135.

135.

Gavaṃ ce taramānānaṃ, ujuṃ gacchati puṅgavo;

Sabbā gāvī ujuṃ yanti sabbā tā ujuṃ gacchanti (pī. a. ni. 4.70), nette ujuṃ gate sati.

If, among cattle crossing a river, the lead bull goes straight, all the cows go straight, the leader having gone straight.

136.

136.

Evameva [M 1.0111] manussesu, yo hoti seṭṭhasammato;

So sace dhammaṃ carati, pageva itarā pajā;

Sabbaṃ [T 1.0152] raṭṭhaṃ sukhaṃ seti, rājā ce hoti dhammikoti.

Just so among humans, whoever is considered the best, if he practices the Dhamma, what need be said of the other people? If the king is righteous, the whole country dwells in happiness.

Rājovādajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Rājovāda Jātaka, the Fourth.

335. Jambukajātakaṃ (4-4-5)

335. The Jambuka Jātaka (4-4-5)

137.

137.

Brahā pavaḍḍhakāyo so, dīghadāṭho ca jambuka;

Na tvaṃ tattha kule jāto, yattha gaṇhanti kuñjaraṃ.

O jackal, that elephant is great, with a well-developed body and long tusks. You were not born into a family where they seize elephants.

138.

138.

Asīho sīhamānena, yo attānaṃ vikubbati;

Kotthūva kuṭṭhūva (sī.), kutthuva (syā. pī) gajamāsajja, seti bhūmyā anutthunaṃ.

Whoever, not being a lion, presents himself with the pride of a lion, lies lamenting on the ground like a jackal having approached an elephant.

139.

139.

Yasassino uttamapuggalassa, sañjātakhandhassa mahabbalassa;

Asamekkhiya thāmabalūpapattiṃ, sa seti nāgena hatoyaṃ jambuko.

Without considering the inherent stamina and strength of the glorious, supreme individual, of well-developed shoulders and great power, this jackal lies slain by the elephant.

140.

140.

Yo cīdha kammaṃ kurute pamāya, thāmabbalaṃ attani saṃviditvā;

Jappena mantena subhāsitena, parikkhavā so vipulaṃ jinātīti.

Whoever in this world, being wise, performs an action after measuring and knowing the stamina and strength within himself, wins a great result through deliberation, counsel, and well-spoken words.

Jambukajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Jambuka Jātaka, the fifth.

336. Brahāchattajātakaṃ (4-4-6)

336. The Brahāchatta Jātaka (4-4-6)

141.

141.

Tiṇaṃ tiṇanti lapasi, ko nu te tiṇamāhari;

Kiṃ [T 1.0153] nu te tiṇakiccatthi, tiṇameva pabhāsasi.

You prattle, 'Grass, grass!' Who then brought you grass? What need have you for grass, that you speak only of grass?

142.

142.

Idhāgamā brahmacārī, brahā chatto bahussuto;

So me so ve (ka.) sabbaṃ samādāya, tiṇaṃ nikkhippa gacchati.

Here came a holy man, the great Chatta, a man of great learning. Having taken all from me, he leaves the grass and goes.

143.

143.

Evetaṃ hoti kattabbaṃ, appena bahumicchatā;

Sabbaṃ sakassa ādānaṃ, anādānaṃ tiṇassa ca. ( ) (tiṇassa cāṭīsu gato, tattha kā paridevanā) (sī. syā.) (cāṭīsu pakkhipitvāna, tattha kā paridevanā) (ka.)

Thus this should be done by one who desires much from little: the taking of all of his property, and the not-taking of the grass.

144.

144.

Sīlavanto [V 1.0096][M 1.0112] na kubbanti, bālo sīlāni kubbati;

Aniccasīlaṃ dussīlyaṃ dussīlaṃ (pī.), kiṃ paṇḍiccaṃ karissatīti.

The virtuous do not do such things, but a fool engages in bad practices. For one of inconstant virtue, for the immoral one, what can wisdom accomplish?

Brahāchattajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Brahāchatta Jātaka, the sixth.

337. Pīṭhajātakaṃ (4-4-7)

337. The Pīṭha Jātaka (4-4-7)

145.

145.

Na te pīṭhamadāyimhā madāsimha (pī. ka.), na pānaṃ napi bhojanaṃ;

Brahmacāri khamassu me, etaṃ passāmi accayaṃ.

We did not give you a seat, nor drink, nor food. O holy one, please forgive me; I see this as a transgression.

146.

146.

Nevābhisajjāmi na cāpi kuppe, na cāpi me appiyamāsi kiñci;

Athopi me āsi manovitakko, etādiso nūna kulassa dhammo.

I am not offended, nor am I angry, nor was there any displeasure for me. Rather, a thought arose in my mind: 'Surely, such must be the custom of this family.'

147.

147.

Esasmākaṃ kule dhammo, pitupitāmaho sadā;

Āsanaṃ udakaṃ pajjaṃ, sabbetaṃ nipadāmase.

This is the custom in our family, from our fathers and grandfathers always: a seat, water, and water for the feet—all this we offer.

148.

148.

Esasmākaṃ [T 1.0154] kule dhammo, pitupitāmaho sadā;

Sakkaccaṃ upatiṭṭhāma, uttamaṃ viya ñātakanti.

This is the custom in our family, from our fathers and grandfathers always: we respectfully attend upon ascetics and brahmins as if they were our highest kinsmen.

Pīṭhajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Pīṭha Jātaka, the seventh.

338. Thusajātakaṃ (4-4-8)

338. The Thusa Jātaka (4-4-8)

149.

149.

Viditaṃ thusaṃ undurānaṃ undūrānaṃ (ka.), viditaṃ pana taṇḍulaṃ;

Thusaṃ thusaṃ thusaṃ thūlaṃ (sī.) vivajjetvā, taṇḍulaṃ pana khādare.

Known to the mice is the chaff, and known, too, is the rice grain. Having discarded all the chaff, they eat only the rice grain.

150.

150.

Yā mantanā araññasmiṃ, yā ca gāme nikaṇṇikā;

Yañcetaṃ iti cīti ca, etampi viditaṃ mayā.

Whatever counsel there was in the forest, and whatever whispering in the village, and whatever 'this and that' was said—all of that is also known by me.

151.

151.

Dhammena kira jātassa, pitā puttassa makkaṭo;

Daharasseva santassa, dantehi phalamacchidā.

By nature, it is said, the father monkey bit off the testicles of his own son with his teeth while he was still young.

152.

152.

Yametaṃ parisappasi parisabbesi (ka.), ajakāṇova sāsape;

Yopāyaṃ heṭṭhato seti sesi (sī.), etampi viditaṃ mayāti.

That you creep about in the mustard field like a one-eyed goat, and that this one lies in wait below—this too is known by me.

Thusajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Thusa Jātaka, the eighth.

339. Bāverujātakaṃ (4-4-9)

339. The Bāveru Jātaka (4-4-9)

153.

153.

Adassanena [M 1.0113] morassa, sikhino mañjubhāṇino;

Kākaṃ tattha apūjesuṃ, maṃsena ca phalena ca.

Due to the non-appearance of the peacock, the crested one with a pleasant voice, they honored the crow there with meat and with fruit.

154.

154.

Yadā [V 1.0097] ca sarasampanno, moro bāverumāgamā;

Atha [T 1.0155] lābho ca sakkāro, vāyasassa ahāyatha.

And when the peacock, endowed with voice, came to Bāveru, then the gain and honor of the crow diminished.

155.

155.

Yāva nuppajjatī buddho, dhammarājā pabhaṅkaro;

Tāva aññe apūjesuṃ, puthū samaṇabrāhmaṇe.

For as long as the Buddha—the King of Dhamma, the light-maker—does not arise, for so long did others honor many other ascetics and brahmins.

156.

156.

Yadā ca sarasampanno, buddho dhammaṃ adesayi;

Atha lābho ca sakkāro, titthiyānaṃ ahāyathāti.

And when the Buddha, endowed with voice, taught the Dhamma, then the gain and honor of the sectarians diminished.

Bāverujātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Bāveru Jātaka, the ninth.

340. Visayhajātakaṃ (4-4-10)

340. The Visayha Jātaka (4-4-10)

157.

157.

Adāsi dānāni pure visayha, dadato ca te khayadhammo ahosi;

Ito paraṃ ce na dadeyya dānaṃ, tiṭṭheyyuṃ te saṃyamantassa bhogā.

O Visayha, in the past you gave gifts. And for you, the giver, there was the nature of exhaustion of wealth. If from this time onward you were not to give gifts, your wealth would remain, for you who are restraining.

158.

158.

Anariyamariyena sahassanetta, suduggatenāpi akiccamāhu;

Mā vo dhanaṃ taṃ ahu devarāja ahuvā janinda (ka. sī. syā. pī.), yaṃ bhogahetu vijahemu saddhaṃ.

O thousand-eyed one, the Noble Ones say that an ignoble deed is not to be done, even by a noble one who is very poor. O king of gods, may we not have that wealth for the sake of which we might abandon faith.

159.

159.

Yena eko ratho yāti, yāti tenāparo ratho;

Porāṇaṃ nihitaṃ vattaṃ, vattataññeva vaddhaṃ, vaddhataññeva (ka. sī. pī.) vāsava.

By the path one chariot goes, by that path goes a later chariot. The ancient practice has been established by me; let that very practice continue, O Vāsava.

160.

160.

Yadi [T 1.0156] hessati dassāma, asante kiṃ dadāmase;

Evaṃbhūtāpi dassāma, mā dānaṃ pamadamhaseti.

If there is wealth, we shall give. When there is none, what can we give? Even being in this state, we shall give. Let us not be heedless of giving.

Visayhajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Visayha Jātaka, the tenth.

Kokilavaggo kokālikavaggo (ka.) catuttho.

The Kokila Vagga is the fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that chapter is:

Ativelapabhāsati [M 1.0114] jītavaro, vanamajjha rathesabha jimhagamo;

Atha jambu tiṇāsanapīṭhavaraṃ, atha taṇḍula mora visayha dasāti.

The Kokālika, the Rathalaṭṭhi, the Pakkagodha and Rājovāda; then the Jambuka, Brahāchatta, and Pīṭha; then the Thusa, the Bāveru, and the Visayha—these are the ten.

5. Cūḷakuṇālavaggo

5. The Cūḷakuṇāla Chapter

341. Kaṇḍarījātakaṃ (4-5-1)

341. The Kaṇḍarī Jātaka

161.

161.

Narānamārāmakarāsu nārisu, anekacittāsu aniggahāsu ca;

Sabbattha nāpītikarāpi sabba’ttanā’pītikarāpi (sī. syā.) ce siyā siyuṃ (syā.), na vissase titthasamā hi nāriyo.

In women who cause displeasure to men, who are of many minds and difficult to control, one should not place trust. Even if she were pleasing in every way, do not trust her, for women are indeed like a river-ford.

162.

162.

Yaṃ [V 1.0098] ve yañca (syā. ka.) disvā kaṇḍarīkinnarānaṃ kinnarakinnarīnaṃ (syā.), kinnarīkinnarānaṃ (ka.), sabbitthiyo na ramanti agāre;

Taṃ [T 1.0157] tādisaṃ maccaṃ cajitvā bhariyā, aññaṃ disvā purisaṃ pīṭhasappiṃ.

Having seen the case of the Kinnara and his queen, it should be known that all women do not delight in their husband's home. The wife, the Kinnarī, having seen another man, a cripple, abandoned her husband and committed an evil deed with that human-ghost.

163.

163.

Bakassa ca bāvarikassa pāvārikassa (sī.) rañño, accantakāmānugatassa bhariyā;

Avācarī accācari (syā.), anācari (ka.) paṭṭhavasānugassa baddhavasānugassa (sī. syā.), pattavasānugatassa (ka.), kaṃ vāpi itthī nāticare tadaññaṃ.

The wife of King Baka and King Bāvarika, who indulged her every desire, misbehaved with one subservient to her will. What other man, then, would a woman not transgress against?

164.

164.

Piṅgiyānī sabbalokissarassa, rañño piyā brahmadattassa bhariyā;

Avācarī paṭṭhavasānugassa, taṃ vāpi sā nājjhagā kāmakāminīti.

Piṅgiyānī, the beloved wife of King Brahmadatta, ruler of the whole world, misbehaved with a horse-groom who was subservient to her will. That desirer of sensual pleasures did not attain either of them and was thus ruined on both sides.

Kaṇḍarījātakaṃ kinnarījātakaṃ (ka. sī. ka.), kuṇḍalikajātakaṃ (syā.) paṭhamaṃ.

The Kaṇḍarī Jātaka, the first.

342. Vānarajātakaṃ (4-5-2)

342. The Vānara Jātaka

165.

165.

Asakkhiṃ [M 1.0115] vata attānaṃ, uddhātuṃ udakā thalaṃ;

Na dānāhaṃ puna tuyhaṃ, vasaṃ gacchāmi vārija.

Indeed, I was able to lift myself from the water to the land. Now I will not again come under your power, O crocodile.

166.

166.

Alametehi ambehi, jambūhi panasehi ca;

Yāni pāraṃ samuddassa, varaṃ mayhaṃ udumbaro.

Enough of these mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits which are on the other shore of the river. Better for me is the fig.

167.

167.

Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, na khippamanubujjhati;

Amittavasamanveti[T 1.0158], pacchā ca anutappati.

He who does not quickly understand a matter that has arisen falls into the power of his enemies, and later regrets it.

168.

168.

Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, khippameva nibodhati;

Muccate sattusambādhā, na ca pacchānutappatīti.

But he who quickly comprehends a matter that has arisen is freed from the oppression of his enemies and does not later regret it.

Vānarajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Vānara Jātaka, the second, is concluded.

343. Kuntinījātakaṃ (4-5-3)

343. The Kuntinī Jātaka

169.

169.

Avasimha tavāgāre, niccaṃ sakkatapūjitā;

Tvameva dānimakari, handa rāja vajāmahaṃ.

We lived in your house, always honored and revered. Now you yourself have caused this displeasure. Well then, O king, I shall go.

170.

170.

Yo ve kate paṭikate, kibbise paṭikibbise;

Evaṃ taṃ sammatī veraṃ, vasa kuntini māgamā.

Indeed, when a deed has been met with a counter-deed, and an offense with a counter-offense, thus that enmity is appeased. Stay, O Kuntinī, do not go.

171.

171.

Na katassa ca kattā ca, metti mettī (pī.), mittī (ka.) sandhīyate puna;

Hadayaṃ nānujānāti, gacchaññeva rathesabha.

Between the one who has been wronged and the wrongdoer, friendship is not renewed. The heart does not consent; I shall surely go, O lord of chariots.

172.

172.

Katassa ceva kattā ca, metti sandhīyate puna;

Dhīrānaṃ no ca bālānaṃ, vasa kuntini māgamāti.

Between the one who has been wronged and the wrongdoer, friendship is renewed—for the wise, but not for the foolish. Stay, O Kuntinī, do not go.

Kuntinījātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Kuntinī Jātaka, the third, is concluded.

344. Ambajātakaṃ (4-5-4)

344. The Amba Jātaka

173.

173.

Yo [V 1.0099] nīliyaṃ maṇḍayati, saṇḍāsena vihaññati;

Tassa sā vasamanvetu, yā te ambe avāhari.

May she who stole your mangoes come under the power of a man who adorns his dark hair and plucks out the grey with tweezers.

174.

174.

Vīsaṃ vā pañcavīsaṃ paṇṇuvīsaṃ (ka. sī. pī.) vā, ūnatiṃsaṃ va jātiyā;

Tādisā [T 1.0159] pati mā laddhā patiṃ mā laddhā (pī.), pati mā’lattha (?), yā te ambe avāhari.

May she who stole your mangoes, upon reaching twenty, or twenty-five, or twenty-nine years of age, still not find a husband.

175.

175.

Dīghaṃ [M 1.0116] gacchatu addhānaṃ, ekikā abhisārikā;

Saṅkete pati mā adda mā addasa (sī. pī.), yā te ambe avāhari.

May she who stole your mangoes go a long journey, alone, as a woman seeking a lover; and may she not find her lover at the appointed place.

176.

176.

Alaṅkatā suvasanā, mālinī candanussadā;

Ekikā sayane setu, yā te ambe avāharīti.

Adorned, well-dressed, garlanded, and anointed with sandalwood, may she who stole your mangoes lie alone in her bed.

Ambajātakaṃ ambacorajātakaṃ (ka. sī. pī.) catutthaṃ.

The Amba Jātaka, the fourth, is concluded.

345. Gajakumbhajātakaṃ (4-5-5)

345. The Gajakumbha Jātaka

177.

177.

Vanaṃ yadaggi dahati, pāvako kaṇhavattanī;

Kathaṃ karosi pacalaka, evaṃ dandhaparakkamo.

When the fire, the blaze with its black trail, burns the forest, what will you do, O drowsy one, you who are so slow in effort?

178.

178.

Bahūni rukkhachiddāni, pathabyā vivarāni ca;

Tāni ce nābhisambhoma, hoti no kālapariyāyo.

There are many hollows in trees and crevices in the earth. If we cannot reach them, our time will have come.

179.

179.

Yo dandhakāle tarati, taraṇīye ca dandhati;

Sukkhapaṇṇaṃva akkamma, atthaṃ bhañjati attano.

He who hurries at a time for slowness, and is slow at a time for haste, destroys his own welfare, just as one crushes a dry leaf by treading on it.

180.

180.

Yo dandhakāle dandheti, taraṇīye ca tārayi;

Sasīva rattiṃ vibhajaṃ, tassattho paripūratīti.

He who is slow at a time for slowness, and is quick at a time for haste—his purpose is fulfilled, just as the moon grows to fullness day by day.

Gajakumbhajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Gajakumbha Jātaka, the fifth, is concluded.

346. Kesavajātakaṃ (4-5-6)

346. The Kesava Jātaka

181.

181.

Manussindaṃ [T 1.0160] jahitvāna, sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Kathaṃ nu bhagavā kesī, kappassa ramati assame ramatassame (ka.).

Having abandoned the ruler of men, who is endowed with all desirable things, how indeed, O venerable Kesī, do you delight in the hermitage of Kappa?

182.

182.

Sādūnī sādhūni (ka. sī. syā. ka.) ramaṇīyāni, santi vakkhā manoramā;

Subhāsitāni kappassa, nārada ramayanti maṃ.

O Nārada, there are trees that are pleasant, delightful, and charming to the heart. The well-spoken words of Kappa delight me.

183.

183.

Sālīnaṃ odanaṃ bhuñje, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Kathaṃ sāmākanīvāraṃ, aloṇaṃ chādayanti taṃ.

You eat cooked Sāli rice with pure meat sauce. How can the unsalted food of millet and wild rice please you?

184.

184.

Sāduṃ [V 1.0100] vā asāduṃ (pī.) yadi vāsāduṃ, appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ;

Vissattho yattha bhuñjeyya, vissāsaparamā rasāti.

Whether it be savory or unsavory, whether it be little or much, where one eats with trust, that food is good; for trust is the supreme flavor.

Kesavajātakaṃ kesījātakaṃ (ka.) chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Kesava Jātaka, the sixth, is concluded.

347. Ayakūṭajātakaṃ (4-5-7)

347. The Ayakūṭa Jātaka

185.

185.

Sabbāyasaṃ [M 1.0117] kūṭamatippamāṇaṃ, paggayha yo so (pī.) tiṭṭhasi antalikkhe;

Rakkhāya me maṃ (sī.) tvaṃ vihito nusajja, udāhu me cetayase vāyamase (sī. syā.) vadhāya.

You who stand in the sky, brandishing a hammer made entirely of iron and of immense size, are you appointed today for my protection, or do you intend my death?

186.

186.

Dūto ahaṃ rājidha rakkhasānaṃ, vadhāya tuyhaṃ pahitohamasmi;

Indo [T 1.0161] ca taṃ rakkhati devarājā, tenuttamaṅgaṃ na te na hi (ka. sī. pī.), te na (ka.) phālayāmi.

O king, I am a messenger of the Rakkhasas, and I am sent here for your death. But Inda, the king of the devas, protects you; for that reason, I do not split your head.

187.

187.

Sace ca maṃ rakkhati devarājā, devānamindo maghavā sujampati;

Kāmaṃ pisācā vinadantu sabbe, na santase rakkhasiyā pajāya.

If the king of the devas, Indra, Maghavā, the husband of Sujā, protects me, then let all the Pisācas roar as they please. I do not tremble at the offspring of a Rakkhasī.

188.

188.

Kāmaṃ kandantu kantantu (ka.), kaṇḍantu (syā.) kumbhaṇḍā, sabbe paṃsupisācakā;

Nālaṃ pisācā yuddhāya, mahatī sā vibhiṃsikāti vibhesikāti (syā.), vihesikāti (pī.).

Let the Kumbhaṇḍas and all the dust-Pisācas wail as they please. The Pisācas are not capable of battle; that is merely a great frightening display.

Ayakūṭajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Ayakūṭa Jātaka, the seventh.

348. Araññajātakaṃ (4-5-8)

348. The Arañña Jātaka

189.

189.

Araññā gāmamāgamma, kiṃsīlaṃ kiṃvataṃ ahaṃ;

Purisaṃ tāta seveyyaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

Father, having come from the forest to a village, what kind of person, of what virtue and what observance, should I associate with? Being asked, please tell me this.

190.

190.

Yo taṃ vissāsaye tāta, vissāsañca khameyya te;

Sussūsī ca titikkhī ca, taṃ bhajehi ito taṃ bhajeyyāsito (ka.) gato.

Dear son, he who would inspire your trust, and who would approve of your trust in him; who is eager to listen and is patient—having gone from here, you should associate with that person.

191.

191.

Yassa kāyena vācāya, manasā natthi dukkaṭaṃ;

Urasīva patiṭṭhāya, taṃ bhajehi ito gato.

He for whom there is no wrongdoing by body, speech, or mind—having gone from here, associate with him, establishing him in your heart.

192.

192.

Haliddirāgaṃ [M 1.0118] kapicittaṃ, purisaṃ rāgavirāginaṃ;

Tādisaṃ [T 1.0162] tāta mā sevi, nimmanussampi ce siyāti.

Dear son, do not associate with such a person—one whose attachment is like turmeric dye, whose mind is like a monkey's, who is quick to become impassioned and quick to become dispassionate—even if the whole of Jambudīpa were devoid of people.

Araññajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Arañña Jātaka, the eighth.

349. Sandhibhedajātakaṃ (4-5-9)

349. The Sandhibheda Jātaka

193.

193.

Neva itthīsu sāmaññaṃ, nāpi bhakkhesu sārathi;

Athassa sandhibhedassa, passa yāva sucintitaṃ.

O charioteer, there is no common ground for them in regard to females, nor is there common ground in regard to food. And yet, see how well-devised is the plan of this breaker of friendships!

194.

194.

Asi [V 1.0101] tikkhova maṃsamhi, pesuññaṃ parivattati;

Yatthūsabhañca sīhañca, bhakkhayanti migādhamā.

Like a sharp sword in flesh, slander operates, whereby base beasts devour both the bull and the lion.

195.

195.

Imaṃ so sayanaṃ seti, yamimaṃ yayimaṃ (sī. pī.), yimaṃ (ka.) passasi sārathi;

Yo vācaṃ sandhibhedassa, pisuṇassa nibodhati.

O charioteer, he lies in this state that you see, whoever heeds the word of a slanderer, a breaker of friendships.

196.

196.

Te janā sukhamedhanti, narā saggagatāriva;

Ye vācaṃ sandhibhedassa, nāvabodhanti sārathīti.

Those people prosper in happiness, O charioteer, like men who have gone to heaven—they who do not heed the word of a breaker of friendships.

Sandhibhedajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Sandhibheda Jātaka, the ninth.

350. Devatāpañhajātakaṃ (4-5-10)

350. The Devatāpañha Jātaka

197.

197.

Hanti hatthehi pādehi, mukhañca parisumbhati;

Sa ve rāja piyo hoti, kaṃ tena tvābhipassasi mabhipassasi (sī.).

O king, one who strikes with hands and feet, and also strikes the face; he, indeed, is dear. For that reason, whom do you see as dear?

198.

198.

Akkosati yathākāmaṃ, āgamañcassa icchati;

Sa [T 1.0163] ve rāja piyo hoti, kaṃ tena tvābhipassasi.

O king, one who abuses another as he pleases, and yet desires his coming; he, indeed, is dear. For that reason, whom do you see as dear?

199.

199.

Abbhakkhāti abhūtena, alikenābhisāraye;

Sa ve rāja piyo hoti, kaṃ tena tvābhipassasi.

O king, one who accuses with falsehood, and causes one to be reminded with untruth; he, indeed, is dear. For that reason, whom do you see as dear?

200.

200.

Haraṃ annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca;

Aññadatthuharā santā, te ve rāja piyā honti;

Kaṃ tena tvābhipassasīti.

O king, those who take away food and drink, clothing and lodging—though they are indeed takers, they are dear. For that reason, whom do you see as dear?

Devatāpañhajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Devatāpañha Jātaka, the tenth.

Cūḷakuṇālavaggo pañcamo.

The Cūḷakuṇāla Chapter, the fifth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of that chapter:

Narānaṃ [M 1.0119] asakkhivasimhavaro, nīliyamaggivarañca puna;

Puna rasāyasakūṭavaro, tathārañña sārathi hanti dasāti.

The Kinnarī or Vānara Jātaka, the Kuntinī Jātaka, the Amba Jātaka, again the Rājakumbha Jātaka, again the Kesī and Ayakūṭa Jātakas, likewise the Arañña, Sandhibheda, and Devatāpañha Jātakas: these are the ten.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Now, the summary of the chapters:

Kāliṅgaṃ vivaraṃ (bahūsu) pucimandañca, kuṭidūsaka kokilā kuṭidūsaṃ bahubhāṇakaṃ (bahūsu);

Cūḷakuṇālavaggo so, pañcamo suppakāsitoti.

The Kaliṅga Chapter, the Pucimanda Chapter, the Kuṭidūsaka Chapter, the Kokālika Chapter, and that fifth, the Cūḷakuṇāla Chapter—these have been well expounded.

Catukkanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Nipāta of Fours is concluded.

5. Pañcakanipāto

5. The Nipāta of Fives

1. Maṇikuṇḍalavaggo

1. 1. The Maṇikuṇḍala Chapter

351. Maṇikuṇḍalajātakaṃ (5-1-1)

351. 351. The Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka

1.

1.

Jīno [T 1.0164][V 1.0102][M 1.0120] rathassaṃ maṇikuṇḍale ca, putte ca dāre ca tatheva jīno;

Sabbesu bhogesu asesakesu asesitesu (sī. pī.), asesikesu (ka.), kasmā na santappasi sokakāle.

You have lost the chariot and horse, and the jeweled earrings; likewise, you have lost your sons and wives; you have lost all your possessions, without remainder. Why, in this time for sorrow, do you not grieve?

2.

2.

Pubbeva maccaṃ vijahanti bhogā, macco vā te ca ne (pī.), dhane (ka.) pubbataraṃ jahāti;

Asassatā bhogino kāmakāmi, tasmā na socāmahaṃ sokakāle.

O desirer of sensual pleasures, possessions abandon a mortal beforehand, or a mortal abandons them even earlier. The enjoyers of possessions are impermanent. Therefore, I do not grieve in this time for sorrow.

3.

3.

Udeti āpūrati veti pūreti khīyati (syā.) cando, atthaṃ tapetvāna andhaṃ tapetvāna (ka.), atthaṅgametvāna (syā.), ettha “tapetvāna atthaṃ paletī”ti sambandho paleti sūriyo;

Viditā vijitā (syā.) mayā sattuka lokadhammā, tasmā na socāmahaṃ sokakāle.

The moon rises, becomes full, and wanes; the sun, having shone, goes to its setting. O enemy, the ways of the world are known by me; therefore, I do not grieve in this time for sorrow.

4.

4.

Alaso gihī kāmabhogī na sādhu, asaññato [T 1.0165] pabbajito na sādhu;

Rājā na sādhu anisammakārī, yo paṇḍito kodhano taṃ na sādhu.

A lazy householder who indulges in sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained renunciant is not good; a king who acts without consideration is not good; and if a wise person is prone to anger, that is not good.

5.

5.

Nisamma khattiyo kayirā, nānisamma disampati;

Nisammakārino rāja rañño (sī. syā.), yaso kitti ca vaḍḍhatīti.

A noble should act after reflection; a ruler should not act without reflection. O king, for one who acts with reflection, glory and fame increase.

Maṇikuṇḍalajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Maṇikuṇḍala Jātaka, the first.

352. Sujātajātakaṃ (5-1-2)

352. The Sujāta Jātaka

6.

6.

Kiṃ [M 1.0121] nu santaramānova, lāyitvā haritaṃ tiṇaṃ;

Khāda khādāti lapasi, gatasattaṃ jaraggavaṃ.

Why indeed, as if in a hurry, having cut green grass, do you say, 'Eat, eat!' to the old bull whose life is gone?

7.

7.

Na hi annena pānena, mato goṇo samuṭṭhahe;

Tvañca tucchaṃ vilapasi, yathā taṃ dummatī tathā.

A dead bull surely does not get up by food or drink. You lament in vain, just as that foolish person does.

8.

8.

Tatheva tiṭṭhati sīsaṃ, hatthapādā ca vāladhi;

Sotā tatheva tiṭṭhanti so tāta tatheva tiṭṭhati (ka.), maññe goṇo samuṭṭhahe.

The head stands just as before, as do the feet and the tail; the ears also stand just as before. I think the bull might get up.

9.

9.

Nevayyakassa sīsañca sīsaṃ vā (sī. syā. pī.), hatthapādā ca dissare;

Rudaṃ mattikathūpasmiṃ, nanu tvaññeva dummati.

Neither the grandfather's head nor his hands and feet are to be seen. Weeping at an earthen mound, are you not indeed the foolish one?

10.

10.

Ādittaṃ [V 1.0103] vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ osiñci (ka.), sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

Indeed, for me who was blazing with sorrow, like a fire sprinkled with ghee, he has extinguished all my grief, as if dousing it with water.

11.

11.

Abbahī abbūḷhaṃ (sī. syā.), abbhūḷhaṃ (ka.) vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ sokaṃ hadayanissitaṃ (sī. syā.);

Yo [T 1.0166] me sokaparetassa, pitu sokaṃ apānudi.

He who dispelled the sorrow for my father, of me who was overcome by grief; indeed, he has extracted the dart that was lodged in my heart.

12.

12.

Sohaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna māṇava.

Having heard your words, O young man, I am one whose dart has been extracted, free from sorrow, and untroubled. I do not sorrow, nor do I weep.

13.

13.

Evaṃ karonti sappaññā, ye honti anukampakā;

Vinivattenti sokamhā, sujāto pitaraṃ yathāti.

Just as Sujāta delivered his father from sorrow, so too do the wise who are compassionate act; they deliver others from sorrow.

Sujātajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Sujāta Jātaka, the second.

353. Venasākhajātakaṃ (5-1-3)

353. The Venasākha Jātaka (5-1-3)

14.

14.

Nayidaṃ niccaṃ bhavitabbaṃ brahmadatta, khemaṃ subhikkhaṃ sukhatā ca kāye;

Atthaccaye mā ahu sampamūḷho, bhinnaplavo sāgarasseva majjhe.

353. O Prince Brahmadatta, this state of safety, this abundance, and this well-being in the body—all this should not be permanent. When sovereignty is lost, do not be bewildered, like one with a broken boat in the middle of the ocean.

15.

15.

Yāni [M 1.0122] karoti puriso, tāni attani passati;

Kalyāṇakārī kalyāṇaṃ, pāpakārī ca pāpakaṃ;

Yādisaṃ vapate bījaṃ, tādisaṃ harate phalaṃ.

Whatever deeds a man does, those he sees in himself. The doer of good sees good, and the doer of evil sees evil. Whatever kind of seed one sows, that kind of fruit one reaps.

16.

16.

Idaṃ tadācariyavaco, pārāsariyo yadabravi;

Mā su mā ssu (sī. syā. pī.) tvaṃ akari pāpaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ pacchā kataṃ tape.

This is the teacher's word, which the ancient teacher spoke to me: 'Do not do that evil which, having been done, would torment you afterwards.'

17.

17.

Ayameva so piṅgiya so piṅgiyo (syā.), sopi bhiyyo (ka.) venasākho, dhonasākho (ka. sī. pī.) yamhi [T 1.0167] ghātayiṃ khattiyānaṃ sahassaṃ;

Alaṅkate candanasārānulitte, tameva dukkhaṃ paccāgataṃ mamaṃ.

This very tree is that banyan with spreading branches, at which I killed a thousand kings, adorned and anointed with sandalwood essence. That very suffering has returned to me.

18.

18.

Sāmā ca sāmāpi (sī. syā.) kho candanalittagattā gattī (ka. sī. syā. pī.), laṭṭhīva sobhañjanakassa uggatā;

Adisvā adisvāva (sī.) kālaṃ karissāmi ubbariṃ, taṃ me ito dukkhataraṃ bhavissatīti.

My queen is indeed of golden complexion, her body anointed with sandalwood. She is beautiful, like an upward-growing branch of the drumstick tree. Not seeing that queen, I shall die. Not seeing her will be more painful for me than this death.

Venasākhajātakaṃ dhonasākhajātakaṃ (ka. sī. pī.) tatiyaṃ.

The Venasākha Jātaka, the third.

354. Uragajātakaṃ (5-1-4)

354. The Uraga Jātaka (5-1-4)

19.

19.

Uragova tacaṃ jiṇṇaṃ, hitvā gacchati saṃ tanuṃ;

Evaṃ sarīre nibbhoge, pete kālaṅkate sati.

Just as a snake, having abandoned its old skin, goes away from its own body, so it is when the body is without enjoyment, departed, and has passed away.

20.

20.

Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gati.

354. Being cremated, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; whatever destination was his, to that he has gone.

21.

21.

Anavhito [V 1.0104] tato āgā, ananuññāto nānuññāto (ka.) ito gato;

Yathāgato tathā gato, tattha kā paridevanā.

Uncalled, he came from another existence; unpermitted, he has gone from here. As he came, so he has gone. What cause for lamentation is there in that?

22.

22.

Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gati.

Being burned, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; whatever destination was his, to that he has gone.

23.

23.

Sace rode kisā kisī (pī.) assaṃ, tassā me kiṃ phalaṃ siyā;

Ñātimittasuhajjānaṃ[T 1.0168], bhiyyo no aratī siyā.

If I were to weep, I would become thin. What fruit would there be in that for me? For our relatives, friends, and companions, there would be even more discontent.

24.

24.

Ḍayhamāno [M 1.0123] na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gati.

Being burned, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; whatever destination was his, to that he has gone.

25.

25.

Yathāpi dārako candaṃ, gacchantamanurodati;

Evaṃ sampadamevetaṃ, yo petamanusocati.

For one who grieves for the dead, this state of affairs is just like a child who weeps for the moving moon.

26.

26.

Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gati.

Being burned, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; whatever destination was his, to that he has gone.

27.

27.

Yathāpi udakakumbho, bhinno appaṭisandhiyo;

Evaṃ sampadamevetaṃ, yo petamanusocati.

For one who grieves for the dead, this state of affairs is just like a broken water pot that cannot be joined together again.

28.

28.

Ḍayhamāno na jānāti, ñātīnaṃ paridevitaṃ;

Tasmā etaṃ na socāmi, gato so tassa yā gatīti.

Being burned, he does not know the lamentation of his relatives. Therefore, I do not grieve for him; whatever destination was his, to that he has gone.

Uragajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Uraga Jātaka, the fourth.

355. Ghaṭajātakaṃ (5-1-5)

355. The Ghaṭa Jātaka (5-1-5)

29.

29.

Aññe socanti rodanti, aññe assumukhā janā;

Pasannamukhavaṇṇosi, kasmā ghaṭa ghata (sī. pī.) na socasi.

Others grieve and weep, other people have tearful faces; you have a serene facial complexion. Why, O Ghaṭa, do you not grieve?

30.

30.

Nābbhatītaharo soko, nānāgatasukhāvaho;

Tasmā dhaṅka vaṃka (pī.) na socāmi, natthi soke dutīyatā soko dutīyakā (ka.).

Sorrow does not bring back past happiness, nor does it bring future happiness. Therefore, O Dhaṅka, I do not grieve. For sorrow, there is no companionship.

31.

31.

Socaṃ paṇḍu kiso hoti, bhattañcassa na ruccati;

Amittā sumanā honti, sallaviddhassa ruppato.

355. Grieving, one becomes pale and thin, and food is not pleasing to him. Enemies are delighted for one who is afflicted, pierced by the dart of sorrow.

32.

32.

Gāme [T 1.0169] vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Ṭhitaṃ maṃ nāgamissati, evaṃ diṭṭhapado ahaṃ.

Whether in a village or in a forest, whether in a valley or on high ground, that which is established will not come to me. Thus I am one who has seen the state.

33.

33.

Yassattā nālamekova, sabbakāmarasāharo;

Sabbāpi pathavī tassa, na sukhaṃ āvahissatīti.

For one who has friends, not even one is able to bring the taste of all desires. Even the entire earth will not bring happiness to him.

Ghaṭajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Ghaṭa Jātaka, the fifth.

356. Koraṇḍiyajātakaṃ (5-1-6)

356. The Koraṇḍiya Jātaka (5-1-6)

34.

34.

Eko [V 1.0105][M 1.0124] araññe girikandarāyaṃ, paggayha paggayha silaṃ pavecchasi pavejjhasi (syā. sī. aṭṭha.);

Punappunaṃ santaramānarūpo, koraṇḍiya kāraṇḍiya (sī. syā. pī.) ko nu tava yidhattho.

Alone in the forest, O Koraṇḍiya, with a hasty demeanor, you repeatedly take up stones and place them in the mountain gorge. What, now, is your purpose here?

35.

35.

Ahañhimaṃ sāgara sevitantaṃ, samaṃ karissāmi yathāpi pāṇi;

Vikiriya sānūni ca pabbatāni ca, tasmā silaṃ dariyā pakkhipāmi.

I will make this earth, bordered by the ocean, as level as the palm of a hand. Having scattered the plateaus and the mountains, therefore I cast stones into the gorge.

36.

36.

Nayimaṃ mahiṃ arahati pāṇikappaṃ, samaṃ manusso karaṇāya meko;

Maññāmimaññeva dariṃ jigīsaṃ jigiṃsaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), koraṇḍiya [T 1.0170] hāhasi hāyasi (syā. ka.) jīvalokaṃ.

A single man is not able to make this earth level by handiwork. I think that while you are merely seeking to fill this very gorge, O Koraṇḍiya, you will have to abandon this world of the living.

37.

37.

Sace ahaṃ ayaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) bhūtadharaṃ na sakkā sakko (syā. ka.), samaṃ manusso karaṇāya meko;

Evameva tvaṃ brahme ime manusse, nānādiṭṭhike nānayissasi te ne (ka.).

356. O brahmin, if I, a single man, am unable to make the earth level, just so will you be unable to lead these people of diverse views according to your will.

38.

38.

Saṅkhittarūpena bhavaṃ mamatthaṃ, akkhāsi koraṇḍiya evametaṃ;

Yathā na sakkā pathavī samāyaṃ, kattuṃ manussena tathā manussāti.

O Koraṇḍiya, you have stated my purpose with a concise simile. This is just so. Just as it is not possible for a man to make the earth level, so too is it not possible to make men so.

Koraṇḍiyajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Koraṇḍiya Jātaka, the sixth.

357. Laṭukikajātakaṃ (5-1-7)

357. The Laṭukika Jātaka (5-1-7)

39.

39.

Vandāmi taṃ kuñjara saṭṭhihāyanaṃ, āraññakaṃ yūthapatiṃ yasassiṃ;

Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi, mā me vadhī puttake dubbalāya.

I pay homage to you, O king of elephants, sixty years of age, a forest-dweller, leader of the herd, one with a great retinue. With my wings I make the añjali gesture to you. Do not kill the young ones of me, who am weak.

40.

40.

Vandāmi [M 1.0125] taṃ kuñjara ekacāriṃ, āraññakaṃ pabbatasānugocaraṃ;

Pakkhehi taṃ pañjalikaṃ karomi, mā [T 1.0171] me vadhī puttake dubbalāya;

I pay homage to you, O king of elephants, who wanders alone, lives in the forest, and finds food on mountain slopes and plateaus. With my wings I make the añjali gesture to you. Do not kill the young ones of me, who am weak.

41.

41.

Vamissāmi te laṭukike puttakāni, kiṃ me tuvaṃ kāhasi dubbalāsi;

Sataṃ sahassānipi tādisīnaṃ, vāmena pādena papothayeyyaṃ.

O little quail hen, I will kill your young ones. You are weak; what can you do to me? Even a hundred thousand such as you, I could crush with just my left foot.

42.

42.

Na heva sabbattha balena kiccaṃ, balañhi bālassa vadhāya hoti;

Karissāmi te nāgarājā anatthaṃ, yo me vadhī puttake dubbalāya.

Indeed, a deed is not always accomplished by strength, for strength leads to the destruction of a fool. I will bring you harm, O king of elephants, you who killed the young ones of me, who am weak.

43.

43.

Kākañca passa laṭukikaṃ, maṇḍūkaṃ nīlamakkhikaṃ;

Ete nāgaṃ aghātesuṃ, passa verassa verinaṃ;

Tasmā hi veraṃ na kayirātha, appiyenapi kenacīti.

O monks, behold the crow and the quail, the frog and the blue fly. These killed the elephant. See the result of an enemy's enmity! Therefore, one should not create enmity with anyone at all, not even with one who is disliked.

Laṭukikajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Laṭukika Jātaka, the seventh.

358. Cūḷadhammapālajātakaṃ (5-1-8)

358. The Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka (5-1-8)

44.

44.

Ahameva [V 1.0106] dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa;

Etaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, hatthe me deva chedehi.

I alone am the offender, the destroyer of the prosperity of King Mahāpatāpa. O King, release this Dhammapāla; cut off my hands.

45.

45.

Ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa;

Etaṃ muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, pāde me deva chedehi.

I alone am the offender, the destroyer of the prosperity of King Mahāpatāpa. O King, release this Dhammapāla; cut off my feet.

46.

46.

Ahameva dūsiyā bhūnahatā, rañño mahāpatāpassa;

Etaṃ [T 1.0172] muñcatu dhammapālaṃ, sīsaṃ me deva chedehi.

I alone am the offender, the destroyer of the prosperity of King Mahāpatāpa. O King, release this Dhammapāla; cut off my head.

47.

47.

Na hi naha (sī. syā. pī.) ettha ha-kāro khede nūnimassa rañño, mittāmaccā ca vijjare suhadā;

Ye na vadanti rājānaṃ, mā ghātayi orasaṃ puttaṃ.

Surely, for this king, there exist no friends, ministers, or well-hearted ones who would say to the king: 'Do not kill your own-born son.'

48.

48.

Na hi naha (sī. syā. pī.) ettha ha-kāro khede nūnimassa rañño, ñātī mittā ca vijjare suhadā;

Ye na vadanti rājānaṃ, mā ghātayi atrajaṃ puttaṃ.

Surely, for this king, there exist no relatives, friends, or well-hearted ones who would say to the king: 'Do not kill your own son.'

49.

49.

Candanasārānulittā[M 1.0126], bāhā chijjanti dhammapālassa;

Dāyādassa pathabyā, pāṇā me deva rujjhantīti.

The sandalwood-smeared arms of Dhammapāla, the heir of the earth, are being cut; O King, my life-breaths are ceasing!

Cūḷadhammapālajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Cūḷadhammapāla Jātaka, the eighth.

359. Suvaṇṇamigajātakaṃ (5-1-9)

359. The Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka (5-1-9)

50.

50.

Vikkama re haripāda mahāmiga (sī. syā. pī.), vikkama re mahāmiga harīpada (sī. syā. pī.);

Chinda vārattikaṃ pāsaṃ, nāhaṃ ekā vane rame.

Strive, O golden-footed one! Strive, O great deer! Cut the leather-strap snare; I cannot delight alone in the forest.

51.

51.

Vikkamāmi na pāremi, bhūmiṃ sumbhāmi vegasā;

Daḷho vārattiko pāso, pādaṃ me parikantati.

I strive, but I am not able. I kick the ground with force. The leather-strap snare is strong; it cuts all around my foot.

52.

52.

Attharassu palāsāni, asiṃ nibbāha luddaka;

Paṭhamaṃ maṃ vadhitvāna, hana pacchā mahāmigaṃ.

Spread out the leaves, O hunter, and draw your sword. Having first killed me, kill the great deer afterwards.

53.

53.

Na me sutaṃ vā diṭṭhaṃ vā, bhāsantiṃ mānusiṃ migiṃ na me sutā vā diṭṭhā vā, bhāsantī mānusiṃ migī (ṭīkā);

Tvañca bhadde sukhī hohi, eso cāpi mahāmigo.

Never before have I heard or seen a doe speaking with a human voice. May you be happy, good lady, and may this great deer also be happy.

54.

54.

Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Yathāhamajja [T 1.0173] nandāmi, muttaṃ disvā mahāmiganti.

Thus, O hunter, may you rejoice, together with all your kinsmen, just as I rejoice today, seeing the great deer freed.

Suvaṇṇamigajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Suvaṇṇamiga Jātaka, the ninth.

360. Suyonandījātakaṃ (5-1-10)

360. The Suyonandī Jātaka (5-1-10)

55.

55.

Vāti [V 1.0107] gandho timirānaṃ, kusamuddo ca va (syā. pī.) ghosavā;

Dūre ito suyonandī ito hi susandī (sī. syā.), itopi sussondī (pī.), tambakāmā tudanti maṃ.

The scent of the Timira trees wafts, and the small ocean resounds. Far from here is Suyonandī; O Tamba, desires torment me.

56.

56.

Kathaṃ samuddamatari, kathaṃ addakkhi sedumaṃ serumaṃ (sī. syā. pī.);

Kathaṃ tassā ca tuyhañca, ahu sagga agga (sī. syā.) samāgamo.

How did you cross the ocean? How did you see Seduma? How did that meeting between her and you come about?

57.

57.

Kurukacchā bharukacchā (sī. syā. pī.) payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Makarehi abhidā makarehibbhidā (sī.), makarehi’bhidā (syā.), makarehi bhinnā (pī.) nāvā, phalakenāhamaplaviṃ.

The ship of the wealth-seeking merchants who had set out from Kurukaccha was broken by sea-monsters; I floated away on a plank.

58.

58.

Sā [M 1.0127] maṃ saṇhena mudunā, niccaṃ candanagandhinī;

Aṅgena aṅkena (pī. ka.) uddharī bhaddā, mātā puttaṃva orasaṃ.

That good lady, ever fragrant with sandalwood, having comforted me with gentle and soft speech, lifted me with her arms, just as a mother lifts her own-born son.

59.

59.

Sā maṃ annena pānena, vatthena sayanena ca;

Attanāpi ca mandakkhī, evaṃ tamba vijānāhīti.

She, the gentle-eyed one, satisfied me with food and drink, with clothing and bedding, and also with her own person. Thus, O Tamba, you should know.

Suyonandījātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Suyonandī Jātaka, the tenth.

Maṇikuṇḍalavaggo paṭhamo.

The Maṇikuṇḍala Chapter, the first.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse for this:

Atha jinavaro haritaṃ tiṇako, atha [T 1.0174] bhinnaplavo uragova ghaṭo;

Dariyā puna kuñjara bhūnahatā, migamuttamasaggavarena dasāti.

Then the noble conqueror, the green grass; then the broken raft, the one like a snake, the pot; the cavern, again the elephant, the destroyer of prosperity; the best of deer, and with the excellent one not of heaven—these are the ten.

2. Vaṇṇārohavaggo

2. The Chapter on Appearance and Stature

361. Vaṇṇārohajātakaṃ (5-2-1)

361. The Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka (5-2-1)

60.

60.

Vaṇṇārohena jātiyā, balanikkamanena ca;

Subāhu na mayā seyyo, sudāṭha iti bhāsasi.

“In appearance and stature, by birth, and by strength and exertion, do you say, O Sudāṭha, ‘Subāhu is not my superior’?”

61.

61.

Vaṇṇārohena jātiyā, balanikkamanena ca;

Sudāṭho na mayā seyyo, subāhu iti bhāsasi.

“In appearance and stature, by birth, and by strength and exertion, do you say, O Subāhu, ‘Sudāṭha is not my superior’?”

62.

62.

Evaṃ ce maṃ viharantaṃ, subāhu samma dubbhasi;

Na dānāhaṃ tayā saddhiṃ, saṃvāsamabhirocaye.

“Friend Subāhu, if you should betray me while I am living thus in harmony, I now no longer take delight in living together with you.”

63.

63.

Yo [V 1.0108] paresaṃ vacanāni, saddaheyya saddahetha (sī. syā. pī.) yathātathaṃ;

Khippaṃ bhijjetha mittasmiṃ, verañca pasave bahuṃ.

Whoever would believe the words of others as true and real would quickly break with a friend and beget much enmity.

64.

64.

Na [M 1.0128] so mitto yo sadā appamatto, bhedāsaṅkī randhamevānupassī;

Yasmiñca setī urasīva putto, sa ve mitto yo abhejjo parehīti.

He is not a friend who is ever vigilant, suspicious of a break, always looking for a flaw. But he in whom one reposes as a son on a mother’s breast—he is truly a friend, one who cannot be divided by others.

Vaṇṇārohajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Vaṇṇāroha Jātaka, the First.

362. Sīlavīmaṃsajātakaṃ (5-2-2)

362. The Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka (5-2-2)

65.

65.

Sīlaṃ [T 1.0175] seyyo sutaṃ seyyo, iti me saṃsayo ahu;

Sīlameva sutā seyyo, iti me natthi saṃsayo.

Is virtue superior, or is learning superior? This was my doubt. Virtue itself is superior to learning; on this I have no doubt.

66.

66.

Moghā jāti ca vaṇṇo ca, sīlameva kiruttamaṃ;

Sīlena anupetassa, sutenattho na vijjati.

Birth and appearance are in vain; it is virtue that is truly supreme. For one who is not endowed with virtue, there is no benefit from learning.

67.

67.

Khattiyo ca adhammaṭṭho, vesso cādhammanissito;

Te pariccajjubho loke, upapajjanti duggatiṃ.

A warrior who is unrighteous and a merchant who relies on unrighteousness: having departed from the world, both are reborn in a woeful state.

68.

68.

Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Idha dhammaṃ caritvāna, bhavanti tidive samā.

Warriors, brahmins, merchants, workers, outcastes, and scavengers: having practiced the Dhamma here, they become equal in the heavenly world.

69.

69.

Na vedā samparāyāya, na jāti nāpi nopi (pī.) bandhavā;

Sakañca sīlaṃ saṃsuddhaṃ, samparāyāya sukhāya cāti sukhāvahanti (sī. syā.).

The Vedas are not for the next world, nor are birth or relatives. But one’s own purified virtue is for the next world and for happiness.

Sīlavīmaṃsajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Sīlavīmaṃsa Jātaka, the Second.

363. Hirijātakaṃ (5-2-3)

363. The Hiri Jātaka (5-2-3)

70.

70.

Hiriṃ tarantaṃ vijigucchamānaṃ, tavāhamasmī iti bhāsamānaṃ;

Seyyāni kammāni anādiyantaṃ, neso mamanti iti naṃ vijaññā.

363. One who transgresses shame, who is disgusted by friendship, who only says, “I am your friend,” but does not undertake excellent deeds—one should know of him: “This one is not my friend.”

71.

71.

Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ [T 1.0176] bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

What one would do, that one should say; what one would not do, one should not say. The wise discern the one who speaks but does not act.

72.

72.

Na [M 1.0129] so mitto yo sadā appamatto, bhedāsaṅkī randhamevānupassī;

Yasmiñca setī urasīva putto, sa ve mitto yo abhejjo parehi.

He is not a friend who is ever vigilant, suspicious of a break, always looking for a flaw. But he in whom a friend reposes without apprehension, as a son on a mother’s breast—he is truly a friend, one who cannot be divided by others.

73.

73.

Pāmojjakaraṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ, pasaṃsāvahanaṃ sukhaṃ;

Phalānisaṃso bhāveti, vahanto porisaṃ dhuraṃ.

Bearing the manly yoke, one develops a cause for joy, happiness that brings praise, and the fruit and its benefits.

74.

74.

Pavivekarasaṃ [V 1.0109] pitvā, rasaṃ upasamassa ca;

Niddaro hoti nippāpo, dhammappītirasaṃ pivanti.

Having drunk the taste of seclusion and the taste of peace, one becomes free from anguish and free from evil, drinking the taste of joy in the Dhamma.

Hirijātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Hiri Jātaka, the Third.

364. Khajjopanakajātakaṃ (5-2-4)

364. The Khajjopanaka Jātaka (5-2-4)

75.

75.

Ko nu santamhi pajjote, aggipariyesanaṃ caraṃ;

Addakkhi ratti rattiṃ (syā.) khajjotaṃ, jātavedaṃ amaññatha.

Who now, while a blazing fire was present, wandering in search of fire, saw a firefly at night and mistook it for fire?

76.

76.

Svassa gomayacuṇṇāni, abhimatthaṃ tiṇāni ca;

Viparītāya saññāya, nāsakkhi pajjaletave.

364. Upon it he scattered fine cow-dung powder and grass, but striving with distorted perception, he was not able to make it blaze.

77.

77.

Evampi anupāyena, atthaṃ na labhate migo mūgo (syā.);

Visāṇato gavaṃ dohaṃ, yattha khīraṃ na vindati.

Even so, a fool searching by wrong means does not obtain his goal, just as one milking a cow from the horn does not find milk where there is none.

78.

78.

Vividhehi upāyehi, atthaṃ papponti māṇavā;

Niggahena amittānaṃ, mittānaṃ paggahena ca.

By various means, people attain their goals: by the suppression of enemies and by the support of friends.

79.

79.

Senāmokkhapalābhena [T 1.0177] senī mokkhūpalābhena (syā.), vallabhānaṃ nayena ca;

Jagatiṃ jagatipālā, āvasanti vasundharanti.

By obtaining a general and by the policy of the favored, the protectors of the earth rule the world, the bearer of treasures.

Khajjopanakajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Khajjopanaka Jātaka, the Fourth.

365. Ahituṇḍikajātakaṃ (5-2-5)

365. The Ahituṇḍika Jātaka (5-2-5)

80.

80.

Dhuttomhi samma sumukha, jūte akkhaparājito;

Harehi sevehi (pī.) ambapakkāni, vīriyaṃ te bhakkhayāmase.

I am a rogue, friend Sumukha, defeated at dice; fetch ripe mangoes, and let us eat the fruit of your effort.

81.

81.

Alikaṃ vata maṃ samma, abhūtena pasaṃsasi;

Ko te suto vā diṭṭho vā, sumukho nāma makkaṭo.

Truly, friend, you praise me with what is untrue. Your word is indeed false. Where have you heard of or seen a monkey named Sumukha?

82.

82.

Ajjāpi [M 1.0130] me taṃ manasi te maṃ sarasi (ka.), yaṃ maṃ tvaṃ ahituṇḍika;

Dhaññāpaṇaṃ pavisitvā, matto mutto (ka.) chātaṃ hanāsi maṃ.

365. Even today that is in my mind, how you, O snake-charmer, having entered the grain market, being intoxicated, struck me when I was hungry.

83.

83.

Tāhaṃ saraṃ dukkhaseyyaṃ, api rajjampi kāraye;

Nevāhaṃ yācito dajjaṃ, tathā hi bhayatajjito.

Remembering that painful experience, even if you were to grant me a kingdom, I, being begged, would not give, for I was so threatened by danger.

84.

84.

Yañca jaññā kule jātaṃ, gabbhe tittaṃ amacchariṃ;

Tena sakhiñca mittañca, dhīro sandhātumarahatīti.

A wise person should form companionship and friendship with one whom he knows to be of good birth, inherently content, and unselfish.

Ahituṇḍikajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Ahituṇḍika Jātaka, the Fifth.

366. Gumbiyajātakaṃ (5-2-6)

366. The Gumbiya Jātaka (5-2-6)

85.

85.

Madhuvaṇṇaṃ [V 1.0110] madhurasaṃ, madhugandhaṃ visaṃ ahu;

Gumbiyo [T 1.0178] ghāsamesāno, araññe odahī visaṃ.

There was a poison, honey-colored, honey-flavored, and honey-scented. Gumbiya, seeking prey, placed this poison in the wilderness.

86.

86.

Madhu iti maññamānā madhūti maññamānāya (ka.), ye taṃ visamakhādisuṃ visamasāyisuṃ (sī. syā.);

Tesaṃ taṃ kaṭukaṃ āsi, maraṇaṃ tenupāgamuṃ.

Thinking it was honey, those who consumed that poison found it became bitter for them, and by that they came to death.

87.

87.

Ye ca kho paṭisaṅkhāya, visaṃ taṃ parivajjayuṃ;

Te āturesu sukhitā, ḍayhamānesu nibbutā.

But those who, after reflection, avoided that poison, are happy among the afflicted and at peace among those who burn.

88.

88.

Evameva manussesu, visaṃ kāmā samohitā;

Āmisaṃ bandhanañcetaṃ, maccuveso paccuvaso (sī. syā.) guhāsayo.

366. Just so among humans, the collections of sensual pleasures are poison. This is bait and a bond, the domain of death, that which lies in a cave.

89.

89.

Evameva ime kāme, āturā paricārike paricārake (ka.);

Ye sadā parivajjenti, saṅgaṃ loke upaccagunti.

Likewise, those who always avoid these sensual pleasures—which are afflictions and attendants—transcend attachment in the world.

Gumbiyajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Gumbiya Jātaka, the Sixth.

367. Sāḷiyajātakaṃ (5-2-7)

367. The Sāḷiya Jātaka (5-2-7)

90.

90.

Yvāyaṃ sāḷiya sāliya (sī. syā. pī.), sāḷika (?) chāpoti, kaṇhasappaṃ agāhayi;

Tena sappenayaṃ daṭṭho, hato pāpānusāsako.

This one, who caused a black snake to be seized, thinking it was a young myna bird, has been bitten by that snake; this wicked instructor is slain.

91.

91.

Ahantāra ahananta (pī.), aharanta (?) mahantāraṃ, yo naro hantumicchati;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, yathāyaṃ puriso hato.

Whatever man wishes to kill a great one who should not be harmed lies slain in this way, just as this man here is slain.

92.

92.

Ahantāra [M 1.0131] ahananta (sī. syā. pī.), aharanta (?) maghātentaṃ, yo naro hantumicchati;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, yathāyaṃ puriso hato.

Whatever man wishes to harm one who is harmless and should not be harmed, he lies slain in this way, just as this man here is slain.

93.

93.

Yathā paṃsumuṭṭhiṃ puriso, paṭivātaṃ paṭikkhipe;

Tameva [T 1.0179] so rajo hanti, tathāyaṃ puriso hato.

Just as a man might throw a handful of dust against the wind, that very dust harms him; just so is this man slain.

94.

94.

Yo appaduṭṭhassa narassa dussati, suddhassa posassa anaṅgaṇassa;

Tameva bālaṃ pacceti pāpaṃ, sukhumo rajo paṭivātaṃva khittoti.

367. Whoever offends an uncorrupted man, a pure person without blemish, that very evil returns to the fool, like fine dust thrown against the wind.

Sāḷiyajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Sāḷiya Jātaka, the Seventh.

368. Tacasārajātakaṃ (5-2-8)

368. The Tacasāra Jātaka (5-2-8)

95.

95.

Amittahatthatthagatā hatthattagatā (katthaci, sī. niyya), tacasārasamappitā;

Pasannamukhavaṇṇāttha, kasmā tumhe na socatha.

Having fallen into the hands of enemies, bound with bamboo strips, you have serene facial complexions; why do you not grieve?

96.

96.

Na [V 1.0111] socanāya paridevanāya, atthova labbho attho ca labbhā (sī. syā.), atthodha labbhā (a. ni. 5.48) api appakopi;

Socantamenaṃ dukhitaṃ viditvā, paccatthikā attamanā bhavanti.

By sorrowing and by lamenting, not even the slightest benefit is obtained. Knowing one to be sorrowing and afflicted, the enemies become pleased.

97.

97.

Yato ca kho paṇḍito āpadāsu, na vedhatī atthavinicchayaññū;

Paccatthikāssa paccatthikā te (ka.) dukhitā bhavanti, disvā mukhaṃ avikāraṃ purāṇaṃ.

But when a wise man, who knows how to discern what is beneficial, does not waver in the midst of calamities, his adversaries become distressed on seeing his face unchanged, as it was before.

98.

98.

Jappena mantena subhāsitena, anuppadānena paveṇiyā vā;

Yathā [T 1.0180] yathā yattha labhetha atthaṃ, tathā tathā tattha parakkameyya.

By incantation, by counsel, by well-spoken words, by giving bribes, or by citing lineage; in whatever way and in whatever matter one might obtain the benefit, in that very way and in that matter one should strive.

99.

99.

Yato [M 1.0132] ca jāneyya alabbhaneyyo, mayā va mayā vā (syā. ka.) aññena vā esa attho;

Asocamāno adhivāsayeyya, kammaṃ daḷhaṃ kinti karomi dānīti.

And when one knows, 'This benefit is unobtainable either by me or by another,' one should endure without sorrowing, thinking: 'Kamma is firm; what can I do now?'

Tacasārajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Tacasāra Jātaka, the Eighth.

369. Mittavindakajātakaṃ (5-2-9)

369. The Mittavindaka Jātaka (5-2-9)

100.

100.

Kyāhaṃ devānamakaraṃ, kiṃ pāpaṃ pakataṃ mayā;

Yaṃ me sirasmiṃ ohacca uhacca (ka.), uhacca (pī.), cakkaṃ bhamati matthake.

What have I done to the gods? What evil was committed by me, that a wheel, having struck my head, spins upon its crown?

101.

101.

Atikkamma ramaṇakaṃ, sadāmattañca dūbhakaṃ;

Brahmattarañca pāsādaṃ, kenatthena idhāgato.

Having passed beyond the crystal palace, the silver palace, the ruby palace, and the golden palace, for what reason have you come here?

102.

102.

Ito bahutarā bhogā, atra maññe bhavissare;

Iti etāya saññāya, passa maṃ byasanaṃ gataṃ.

With the perception, 'I imagine there will be far more pleasures there than here,' behold me, who has come to ruin.

103.

103.

Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhāhipi ca aṭṭhāhi cāpi (sī. syā.), aṭṭhābhi cāpi (ka.) soḷasa;

Soḷasāhi ca bāttiṃsa, atricchaṃ cakkamāsado;

From four you obtained eight; and from eight, sixteen; and from sixteen, thirty-two. Being excessively greedy, you came upon the wheel.

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake.

Upon the crown of the head of a man smitten by craving, the wheel spins.

104.

104.

Uparivisālā duppūrā, icchā visaṭagāminī upari visālaṃ duppūraṃ, icchāvisadagāminī (sī.);

Ye [T 1.0181] ca taṃ anugijjhanti, te honti cakkadhārinoti.

Craving is vast and hard to fill, wide-spreading in its course. And those who are attached to it become bearers of the wheel.

Mittavindakajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Mittavindaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

370. Palāsajātakaṃ (5-2-10)

370. The Palāsa Jātaka (5-2-10)

105.

105.

Haṃso palāsamavaca, nigrodho samma jāyati;

Aṅkasmiṃ aṅgasmiṃ (ka.) te nisinnova, so te mammāni checchati chijjati (ka.).

The swan spoke to the deva of the Palāsa tree: 'Friend, a banyan tree is growing. Seated in your fork, it will sever your vital spots.'

106.

106.

Vaḍḍhatāmeva vaddhitameva (ka.) nigrodho, patiṭṭhassa bhavāmahaṃ;

Yathā pitā ca mātā ca pitā vā mātā vā (pī.), mātā vā pitā vā (ka.), evaṃ me so bhavissati.

Let the banyan tree grow! I shall be its support, just as a father and a mother are for their children. So it will be to me.

107.

107.

Yaṃ [V 1.0112] tvaṃ aṅkasmiṃ vaḍḍhesi, khīrarukkhaṃ bhayānakaṃ;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāma, vuḍḍhi massa na ruccati.

That which you are raising in your lap is a terrifying milky tree. We now take our leave of you; its growth does not please us.

108.

108.

Idāni [M 1.0133] kho maṃ bhāyeti, mahānerunidassanaṃ;

Haṃsassa anabhiññāya, mahā me bhayamāgataṃ.

Now it frightens me, with its appearance like great Meru. Through not understanding the swan's words, great fear has come upon me.

109.

109.

Na tassa vuḍḍhi kusalappasatthā, yo vaḍḍhamāno ghasate patiṭṭhaṃ;

Tassūparodhaṃ parisaṅkamāno, patārayī mūlavadhāya dhīroti.

The growth of that which, while growing, consumes its own support is not praised by the skillful. Fearing its destructiveness, the wise person should strive for its destruction from the root.

Palāsajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Palāsa Jātaka, the Tenth.

Vaṇṇārohavaggo dutiyo imassuddānaṃ tatiyavaggapariyosāne bhavissati.

The Vaṇṇāroha Chapter, the Second.

3. Aḍḍhavaggo

3. The Half Chapter

371. Dīghītikosalajātakaṃ (5-3-1)

371. The Dīghīti of Kosala Jātaka (5-3-1)

110.

110.

Evaṃbhūtassa te rāja, āgatassa vase vaso (pī. ka.) mama;

Atthi nu koci pariyāyo, yo taṃ dukkhā pamocaye.

O king, for you who are in such a state, having come into my power, is there any way that might free you from suffering?

111.

111.

Evaṃbhūtassa [T 1.0182] me tāta, āgatassa vase tava;

Natthi no koci pariyāyo, yo maṃ dukkhā pamocaye.

Dear one, for me who am in such a state, having come into your power, there is no way that might free me from suffering.

112.

112.

Nāññaṃ sucaritaṃ rāja, nāññaṃ rāja subhāsitaṃ;

Tāyate maraṇakāle, evamevitaraṃ dhanaṃ.

O king, nothing other than good conduct, O king, nothing other than well-spoken words, protects at the time of death. Other wealth is just so.

113.

113.

Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ upanayhanti, veraṃ tesaṃ na sammati.

'He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me.' For those who bind themselves to such thoughts, their enmity is never appeased.

114.

114.

Akkocchi maṃ avadhi maṃ, ajini maṃ ahāsi me;

Ye ca taṃ nupanayhanti, veraṃ tesūpasammati.

'He abused me, he struck me, he defeated me, he robbed me.' For those who do not bind themselves to such thoughts, their enmity is appeased.

115.

115.

Na hi verena verāni, sammantīdha kudācanaṃ;

Averena ca sammanti, esa dhammo sanantanoti.

Indeed, not by enmity are enmities ever appeased here; they are appeased by non-enmity. This is an ancient principle.

Dīghītikosalajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Dīghīti of Kosala Jātaka, the First.

372. Migapotakajātakaṃ (5-3-2)

372. The Fawn Jātaka (5-3-2)

116.

116.

Agārā [V 1.0113] paccupetassa, anagārassa te sato;

Samaṇassa na taṃ sādhu, yaṃ petamanusocasi.

For you, being a recluse who has gone forth from home to homelessness, it is not proper that you grieve for the dead.

117.

117.

Saṃvāsena [M 1.0134] have sakka, manussassa migassa vā;

Hadaye [T 1.0183] jāyate pemaṃ, na taṃ sakkā asocituṃ.

Indeed, Sakka, through living together, whether with a human or a beast, affection is born in the heart. It is not possible not to grieve for that one.

118.

118.

Mataṃ marissaṃ rodanti, ye rudanti lapanti ca;

Tasmā tvaṃ isi mā rodi, roditaṃ moghamāhu santo.

Those who weep and lament, weep for the dead and for the one who will die. Therefore, O sage, do not weep; the virtuous say that weeping is in vain.

119.

119.

Roditena have brahme, mato peto samuṭṭhahe;

Sabbe saṅgamma rodāma, aññamaññassa ñātake.

Indeed, O holy one, if by weeping the departed dead could rise up, we would all gather together and weep for each other's relatives.

120.

120.

Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

Indeed, like sprinkling a fire fed with ghee with water, you have extinguished me, who was burning, and have quenched all my feverish grief.

121.

121.

Abbahi vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

You who have removed the sorrow for my son from me, who was overcome with grief, have indeed extracted the dart that was lodged in my heart.

122.

122.

Sohaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna vāsavāti.

Having heard your words, O Vāsava, I am one with the dart extracted, free from sorrow, and untroubled. I do not grieve, nor do I weep.

Migapotakajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Fawn Jātaka, the Second.

373. Mūsikajātakaṃ (5-3-3)

373. The Mouse Jātaka (5-3-3)

123.

123.

Kuhiṃ gatā kattha gatā, iti lālappatī jano;

Ahameveko jānāmi, udapāne mūsikā hatā.

‘Where has she gone? Where has she gone?’ Thus the people lament. I alone know that the mouse was killed in the well.

124.

124.

Yañcetaṃ yathetaṃ (pī.), yavetaṃ (ka.), yametaṃ (katthaci) iti cīti ca, gadrabhova nivattasi;

Udapāne mūsikaṃ hantvā, yavaṃ bhakkhetumicchasi.

Though you have opportunities to kill from here and there, you turn back like a donkey. Having killed the mouse in the well, you wish to devour the barley.

125.

125.

Daharo cāsi dummedha, paṭhamuppattiko paṭhamuppattito (sī. pī.) susu;

Dīghañcetaṃ [T 1.0184] dīghametaṃ (pī.) samāsajja samāpajja (syā. ka.), na te dassāmi jīvitaṃ.

You are young, O foolish one, a youth in your first age. And you stand holding this long pestle. I will not grant you your life.

126.

126.

Nāntalikkhabhavanena, nāṅgaputtapinena nāṅgaputtasirena (sī. syā. pī.) vā;

Puttena hi patthayito, silokehi pamocito.

I was not freed by a celestial mansion, nor by the affection of a son dear as my own limbs. Though my son desired my death, I was freed by these verses.

127.

127.

Sabbaṃ [V 1.0114] sutamadhīyetha, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhimaṃ;

Sabbassa atthaṃ jāneyya, na ca sabbaṃ payojaye;

Hoti tādisako kālo, yattha atthāvahaṃ sutanti.

One should learn all that is heard—inferior, excellent, and middling. One should know the meaning of it all, but not apply everything. For there comes a time of such a kind when what has been heard is beneficial.

Mūsikajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Mouse Jātaka, the Third.

374. Cūḷadhanuggahajātakaṃ (5-3-4)

374. The Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka (5-3-4)

128.

128.

Sabbaṃ [M 1.0135] bhaṇḍaṃ samādāya, pāraṃ tiṇṇosi brāhmaṇa;

Having taken all your goods, you have crossed to the far shore, O brahmin.

Paccāgaccha lahuṃ khippaṃ, mampi tārehi dānito dānibho (syā.).

Return quickly, swiftly, and ferry me also from here now.

129.

129.

Asanthutaṃ maṃ cirasanthutena, nimīni bhotī addhuvaṃ dhuvena;

Mayāpi bhotī nimineyya aññaṃ, ito ahaṃ dūrataraṃ gamissaṃ.

O lady, you exchanged me, the unacquainted, for the long-acquainted one; you exchanged the impermanent for the permanent. O lady, you might also exchange me for another; I will go very far from here.

130.

130.

Kāyaṃ eḷagalāgumbe eḷagaṇagumbe (ka.), karoti ahuhāsiyaṃ;

Nayīdha naccagītaṃ vā nayidha naccaṃ vā gītaṃ vā (sī. syā. pī.), tāḷaṃ vā susamāhitaṃ;

Anamhikāle anamhakāle (pī.) susoṇi sussoṇi (sī. syā. pī.), kiṃ nu jagghasi sobhane sobhaṇe (pī. ka.).

Who is this in the thicket of sweet-rush grass, laughing so loudly? Here there is neither dancing nor singing, nor well-played cymbals. At a time not for laughter, O beautiful one with lovely hips, why indeed do you laugh?

131.

131.

Siṅgāla bāla dummedha, appapaññosi jambuka;

Jīno [T 1.0185] macchañca pesiñca, kapaṇo viya jhāyasi.

O foolish, witless jackal, you are of little wisdom, O glutton! Having lost both the fish and the meat, you pine like a wretch.

132.

132.

Sudassaṃ vajjamaññesaṃ, attano pana duddasaṃ;

Jīnā patiñca jārañca, maññe tvaññeva mampi tvaññeva (sī. syā.), tvampi maññeva (pī.) jhāyasi.

The fault of others is easy to see, but one's own is difficult to see. Having lost both your husband and your lover, I think it is you who pines.

133.

133.

Evametaṃ migarāja, yathā bhāsasi jambuka;

Sā nūnāhaṃ ito gantvā, bhattu hessaṃ vasānugā.

It is so, O king of beasts, just as you say, O jackal. Surely, having gone from here, I shall be obedient to my husband.

134.

134.

Yo hare mattikaṃ thālaṃ, kaṃsathālampi so hare;

Katañceva kataṃyeva (sī. syā. pī.) tayā pāpaṃ, punapevaṃ karissasīti.

One who would steal an earthen bowl would also steal a bronze one. You have done an evil deed, and you will do so again.

Cūḷadhanuggahajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Cūḷadhanuggaha Jātaka, the Fourth.

375. Kapotajātakaṃ (5-3-5)

375. The Pigeon Jātaka (5-3-5)

135.

135.

Idāni khomhi sukhito arogo, nikkaṇṭako nippatito kapoto;

Kāhāmi dānī hadayassa tuṭṭhiṃ, tathāhimaṃ maṃsasākaṃ baleti.

Now indeed I am happy and healthy, free from trouble; a pigeon has fallen to me! I will now bring satisfaction to my heart, for this meat and vegetable dish gives me strength.

136.

136.

Kāyaṃ [M 1.0136] balākā sikhino, corī laṅghipitāmahā;

Oraṃ balāke āgaccha, caṇḍo me vāyaso sakhā.

Who is this crane, O crested one, O thief, whose grandfather is the sky? Come hither, O crane; my friend, the crow, is fierce.

137.

137.

Alañhi te jagghitāye, mamaṃ disvāna edisaṃ;

Vilūnaṃ sūdaputtena, piṭṭhamaṇḍena piṭṭhamaddena (sī. syā. pī.) makkhitaṃ.

It is not proper for you to laugh, having seen me in such a state: plucked by the cook and smeared with a paste of ground spices.

138.

138.

Sunhāto [V 1.0115] suvilittosi, annapānena tappito;

Kaṇṭhe [T 1.0186] ca te veḷuriyo, agamā nu kajaṅgalaṃ.

You are well-bathed and well-anointed, satisfied with food and drink, and there is a beryl gem at your throat. Have you been to Kajaṅgala?

139.

139.

Mā te mitto amitto vā, agamāsi kajaṅgalaṃ;

Piñchāni tattha lāyitvā, kaṇṭhe bandhanti vaṭṭanaṃ.

Let neither your friend nor your foe go to Kajaṅgala. There, having plucked their feathers, they tie a pot-sherd around their necks.

140.

140.

Punapāpajjasī samma, sīlañhi tava tādisaṃ;

Na hi mānusakā bhogā, subhuñjā honti pakkhināti.

You will fall into such trouble again, friend, for such is your nature. Indeed, human enjoyments are not easy for a bird to partake of.

Kapotajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Pigeon Jātaka, the Fifth.

Aḍḍhavaggo tatiyo.

The Half-Chapter, the Third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Atha vaṇṇa sasīla hiri labhate, sumukhā visa sāḷiyamittavaro;

Atha cakka palāsa sarāja sato, yava bāla kapotaka pannarasāti.

Then the Vaṇṇaroha, Sīlavīmaṃsa, Hiri, and Khajjopanaka; the Sumukha, Visa, Sāḷiya, and Mittavara; then the Cakka, Palāsa, Sarāja, and Sata; the Yava, Bāla, and Kapotaka—these are the fifteen.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Then the summary of the chapters:

Jīnañca vaṇṇaṃ asamaṃvaguppari, sudesitā jātakanti santi vīsati jātaka pañcavīsati (?);

Mahesino brahmacarittamutta-mavoca gāthā atthavatī subyañjanāti.

The Jina, Vaṇṇa, and the unequal chapter following: thus are the twenty-five Jātakas well-taught. The Great Sage declared these meaningful and well-phrased verses to be the supreme, noble practice.

Pañcakanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Book of Fives is concluded.

6. Chakkanipāto

6. The Book of Sixes

1. Avāriyavaggo

1. The Chapter on Avāriya

376. Avāriyajātakaṃ (6-1-1)

376. The Avāriya Jātaka (6-1-1)

1.

1.

Māsu [T 1.0187][V 1.0116][M 1.0137] kujjha bhūmipati, māsu kujjha rathesabha;

Kuddhaṃ appaṭikujjhanto, rājā raṭṭhassa pūjito.

Do not be angry, O lord of the earth; do not be angry, O bull among charioteers. A king who is not angry in return toward one who is angry is honored by the country.

2.

2.

Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Sabbattha anusāsāmi, māsu kujjha māssu kujjhi (sī. pī.) rathesabha.

Whether in a village or in the wilderness, in a valley or on high ground, everywhere I instruct you: do not be angry, O bull among charioteers.

3.

3.

Avāriyapitā nāma, ahu gaṅgāya nāviko;

Pubbe janaṃ tāretvāna, pacchā yācati vetanaṃ;

Tenassa bhaṇḍanaṃ hoti, na ca bhogehi vaḍḍhati.

On the Ganges, there was a ferryman named Avāriyapitā. Having first ferried people across, he would afterwards ask for the fare. Because of this, quarrels arose for him, and he did not prosper in wealth.

4.

4.

Atiṇṇaṃyeva yācassu, apāraṃ tāta nāvika;

Añño hi tiṇṇassa mano, añño hoti pāresino taresino (sī. pī.), tiresino (syā.).

Ask while they have not yet crossed to the far shore, O dear ferryman. For the mind of one who has crossed is different, and the mind of one who wishes to cross is different.

5.

5.

Gāme vā yadi vāraññe, ninne vā yadi vā thale;

Sabbattha anusāsāmi, māsu kujjhittha nāvika.

Whether in a village or in the wilderness, in a valley or on high ground, everywhere I instruct you: do not be angry, O ferryman.

6.

6.

Yāyevānusāsaniyā, rājā gāmavaraṃ adā;

Tāyevānusāsaniyā, nāviko paharī mukhaṃ.

For the very instruction for which the king gave a choice village, for that same instruction, the ferryman struck him in the face.

7.

7.

Bhattaṃ bhinnaṃ hatā bhariyā, gabbho ca patito chamā;

Migova jātarūpena, na tenatthaṃ abandhi sūti avaḍḍhitunti (sī. syā.), avaḍḍhi sūti (?).

The rice bowl was broken, the wife was struck, and the embryo fell to the ground. By that instruction, he did not secure his own welfare, just as a deer is not fashioned from gold.

Avāriyajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Avāriya Jātaka, the First.

377. Setaketujātakaṃ (6-1-2)

377. The Setaketu Jātaka (6-1-2)

8.

8.

Mā [T 1.0188] tāta kujjhi na hi sādhu kodho, bahumpi te adiṭṭhamassutañca;

Mātā pitā disatā disā tāta (syā.), disā tā (pī.) setaketu, ācariyamāhu disataṃ pasatthā.

377. My dear Setaketu, do not be angry, for anger is not good; there is much that is unseen and unheard by you. Mother and father are the eastern direction; the praised ones call the teacher the southern direction.

9.

9.

Agārino [V 1.0117][M 1.0138] annadapānavatthadā annapānavatthadā (syā. ka.), avhāyikā tampi disaṃ vadanti;

Esā disā paramā setaketu, yaṃ patvā dukkhī sukhino bhavanti.

Householders who are givers of food, drink, and clothing are inviters of righteous ascetics and brahmins; this they also call a direction. This is the supreme direction, O Setaketu, having reached which the suffering become happy.

10.

10.

Kharājinā jaṭilā paṅkadantā, dummakkharūpā dumukkharūpā (sī. syā.), dummukkharūpā (pī. ka.) yeme jappanti mante;

Kacci nu te mānusake payoge, idaṃ vidū parimuttā apāyā.

Those who wear rough hides, have matted hair, dirt-caked teeth, and a squalid appearance, who recite sacred chants—I wonder, being established in human practices, do they know this and are they freed from the woeful states?

11.

11.

Pāpāni kammāni katvāna rāja, bahussuto ce na bahussuto neva (sī. syā.) careyya dhammaṃ;

Sahassavedopi na taṃ paṭicca, dukkhā pamuñce caraṇaṃ apatvā.

O king, if one who is very learned, having done evil deeds, does not practice the Dhamma, not having attained right conduct, even one who knows a thousand Vedas is not freed from suffering by relying on them.

12.

12.

Sahassavedopi na taṃ paṭicca, dukkhā pamuñce caraṇaṃ apatvā;

Maññāmi [T 1.0189] vedā aphalā bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇameva caraṇaññeva (sī. syā. pī.) saccaṃ.

Not having attained right conduct, even one who knows a thousand Vedas is not freed from suffering by relying on them. I think the Vedas are fruitless; conduct with self-restraint is the truth itself.

13.

13.

Na heva vedā aphalā bhavanti, sasaṃyamaṃ caraṇameva saccaṃ;

Kittiñhi pappoti adhicca vede, santiṃ puṇeti santaṃ pune’ti (sī. pī.) caraṇena dantoti.

The Vedas are not entirely fruitless, for conduct with self-restraint is the truth itself. One indeed attains fame by mastering the Vedas, but it is through conduct that the tamed one reaches peace.

Setaketujātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Setaketu Jātaka, the Second.

378. Darīmukhajātakaṃ (6-1-3)

378. The Darīmukha Jātaka (6-1-3)

14.

14.

Paṅko ca kāmā palipo ca kāmā, bhayañca metaṃ timūlaṃ pavuttaṃ;

Rajo ca dhūmo ca mayā pakāsitā, hitvā tuvaṃ pabbaja brahmadatta.

Sensual pleasures are a bog, sensual pleasures are a mire, and this has been declared a three-rooted fear; dust and smoke have been proclaimed by me. Having abandoned them, Brahmadatta, go forth!

15.

15.

Gadhito [M 1.0139] gathito (sī.) ca ratto ca adhimucchito ca, kāmesvahaṃ brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpaṃ;

Taṃ nussahe jīvikattho pahātuṃ, kāhāmi puññāni anappakāni.

378. O holy one, I am attached, impassioned, and utterly infatuated with sensual pleasures of a dreadful nature. Desiring this livelihood, I am unable to abandon them. I will perform abundant meritorious deeds.

16.

16.

Yo atthakāmassa hitānukampino, ovajjamāno na karoti sāsanaṃ;

Idameva seyyo iti maññamāno, punappunaṃ [T 1.0190] gabbhamupeti mando.

When advised by a compassionate well-wisher who seeks his welfare, if one does not follow the instruction, thinking, ‘This alone is better,’ that fool enters the womb again and again.

17.

17.

So ghorarūpaṃ nirayaṃ upeti, subhāsubhaṃ muttakarīsapūraṃ;

Sattā sakāye na jahanti giddhā, ye honti kāmesu avītarāgā.

He enters that dreadful hell, filled with urine and excrement, which is fair to some and foul to others. Beings who are greedy for their own bodies do not abandon them, those who are not free from lust for sensual pleasures.

18.

18.

Mīḷhena littā ruhirena makkhitā, semhena littā upanikkhamanti;

Yaṃ yañhi kāyena phusanti tāvade, sabbaṃ asātaṃ dukhameva kevalaṃ.

Smeared with excrement, anointed with blood, and daubed with phlegm, they emerge. Whatever they touch with the body at that very moment is all disagreeable, purely suffering.

19.

19.

Disvā vadāmi na hi aññato savaṃ, pubbenivāsaṃ bahukaṃ sarāmi;

Citrāhi gāthāhi subhāsitāhi, darīmukho nijjhāpayi sumedhanti.

Having seen this for myself, I speak; not from hearing it from another. I remember many past lives. With varied and well-spoken verses, Darīmukha made the wise Sumedha understand.

Darīmukhajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Darīmukha Jātaka, the Third.

379. Nerujātakaṃ (6-1-4)

379. The Neru Jātaka (6-1-4)

20.

20.

Kākolā kākasaṅghā ca, mayañca patataṃ varā vara (ka.) mayantipadassa hi visesanaṃ;

Sabbeva sadisā homa, imaṃ āgamma pabbataṃ.

Ravens and flocks of crows, and we, the best of flying creatures—having come to this mountain, we all become alike in appearance.

21.

21.

Idha [V 1.0118] sīhā ca byagghā ca, siṅgālā ca migādhamā;

Sabbeva [T 1.0191] sadisā honti, ayaṃ ko nāma pabbato.

Here lions and tigers, and jackals, the lowest of beasts, all become alike in appearance. What, indeed, is the name of this mountain?

22.

22.

Imaṃ [M 1.0140] nerūti nerunti (sī. syā.) jānanti, manussā pabbatuttamaṃ;

Idha vaṇṇena sampannā, vasanti sabbapāṇino.

379. People know this as Neru, the best of mountains. Here all living beings dwell, endowed with a golden color.

23.

23.

Amānanā yattha siyā, santānaṃ vā vimānanā;

Hīnasammānanā vāpi, na tattha vasatiṃ vase vasatī vase (syā.), vasa divase (pī.).

Where there is disrespect for the good, or contempt for them, or where the inferior are honored, one should not take up residence there.

24.

24.

Yatthālaso ca dakkho ca, sūro bhīru ca pūjiyā;

Na tattha santo vasanti, avisesakare nare nage (sī. syā. pī.).

Where the lazy and the skilled, the brave and the timid are honored alike, the good do not dwell there among people who make no distinction.

25.

25.

Nāyaṃ neru vibhajati, hīnaukkaṭṭhamajjhime;

Avisesakaro neru, handa neruṃ jahāmaseti.

This Neru does not distinguish between the low, the excellent, and the middling. Neru makes no distinction; come, let us abandon Neru!

Nerujātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Neru Jātaka, the Fourth.

380. Āsaṅkajātakaṃ (6-1-5)

380. The Āsaṅka Jātaka (6-1-5)

26.

26.

Āsāvatī nāma latā, jātā cittalatāvane;

Tassā vassasahassena, ekaṃ nibbattate phalaṃ.

A creeper named Āsāvatī grows in the Cittalatā Grove; after a thousand years, a single fruit is produced from it.

27.

27.

Taṃ devā payirupāsanti, tāva dūraphalaṃ satiṃ;

Āsīseva āsiṃseva (sī. syā. pī.) tuvaṃ rāja, āsā phalavatī sukhā.

The gods wait upon it while it is still a distant fruit. Just so should you hope, O king; for hope, when fruitful, is happiness.
