28.

28.

Āsīsateva āsiṃsetheva (sī. syā. pī.) so pakkhī, āsīsateva āsiṃsetheva (sī. syā. pī.) so dijo;

Tassa cāsā tassevāsā (syā.) samijjhati, tāva dūragatā satī;

Āsīseva tuvaṃ rāja, āsā phalavatī sukhā.

That bird hopes, that twice-born hopes, and its hope is fulfilled, though the goal is far away. Just so should you hope, O king, for hope, when fruitful, is happiness.

29.

29.

Sampesi kho maṃ vācāya, na ca sampesi saṃsesi (ka.) kammunā;

Mālā [T 1.0192] sereyyakasseva, vaṇṇavantā agandhikā.

380. You have pleased me with your words, but you have not pleased me with your deeds, like a Sereyyaka flower, beautiful in color but without fragrance.

30.

30.

Aphalaṃ madhuraṃ vācaṃ, yo mittesu pakubbati;

Adadaṃ avissajaṃ bhogaṃ, sandhi tenassa jīrati.

One who offers sweet but fruitless words to friends, not giving, not bestowing wealth—the bond of friendship with them wears away.

31.

31.

Yañhi kayirā tañhi vade, yaṃ na kayirā na taṃ vade;

Akarontaṃ bhāsamānaṃ, parijānanti paṇḍitā.

One should say what one does; one should not say what one does not do. The wise recognize the one who speaks but does not act.

32.

32.

Balañca vata me khīṇaṃ, pātheyyañca na vijjati;

Saṅke pāṇūparodhāya, handa dāni vajāmahaṃ.

Alas, my strength is exhausted, and I have no provisions for the journey. I fear for the destruction of my life; come now, I must depart.

33.

33.

Etadeva [V 1.0119][M 1.0141] hi me nāmaṃ, yaṃ nāmasmi rathesabha;

Āgamehi mahārāja, pitaraṃ āmantayāmahanti.

My name is indeed what I am, O bull among charioteers. Wait, great king; I must take leave of my father.

Āsaṅkajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Āsaṅka Jātaka, the Fifth.

381. Migālopajātakaṃ (6-1-6)

381. The Migālopa Jātaka (6-1-6)

34.

34.

Na me rucci migālopa, yassa te tādisī gatī;

Atuccaṃ tāta patasi, abhūmiṃ tāta sevasi.

I do not approve of this, Migālopa, this course of yours. You fly too high, my dear; you frequent a land that is not your domain, my dear.

35.

35.

Catukkaṇṇaṃva kedāraṃ, yadā te pathavī siyā;

Tato tāta nivattassu, māssu etto paraṃ gami.

When the earth appears to you like a four-cornered field, from there, my dear, you must turn back; do not go any further than that.

36.

36.

Santi aññepi sakuṇā, pattayānā vihaṅgamā;

Akkhittā vātavegena, naṭṭhā te sassatīsamā.

There are other birds too, winged creatures that go through the sky. Tossed up by the force of the wind, they who thought themselves eternal are destroyed.

37.

37.

Akatvā apanandassa aparaṇṇassa (sī. syā. pī.), pitu vuddhassa sāsanaṃ;

Kālavāte [T 1.0193] atikkamma, verambhānaṃ vasaṃ agā gato (sī.).

Not heeding the instruction of his aged father Apananda, he transgressed beyond the timely winds and came under the power of the Verambha gales.

38.

38.

Tassa puttā ca dārā ca, ye caññe anujīvino;

Sabbe byasanamāpāduṃ, anovādakare dije.

His sons and his wife, and all his other dependents, all met with disaster, because that twice-born one did not take advice.

39.

39.

Evampi idha vuddhānaṃ, yo vākyaṃ nāvabujjhati;

Atisīmacaro atisīmaṃ caro (sī. syā. ka.) ditto, gijjhovātītasāsano;

Sabbe byasanaṃ papponti, akatvā buddhasāsananti.

So too in this Dispensation, one who does not heed the word of the elders, who is arrogant and transgresses the boundaries, like the vulture that went beyond its instruction—they all meet with disaster by not following the teaching of the Buddha.

Migālopajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Migālopa Jātaka, the sixth.

382. Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakaṃ (6-1-7)

382. The Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka (6-1-7)

40.

40.

Kā nu kāḷena vaṇṇena, na cāpi na cāsi (sī.) piyadassanā;

Kā vā tvaṃ kassa vā dhītā, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

382. Who can you be, with your dark complexion, not at all pleasant to see? Who are you, and whose daughter? How are we to know you?

41.

41.

Mahārājassahaṃ dhītā, virūpakkhassa caṇḍiyā;

Ahaṃ kāḷī alakkhikā, kāḷakaṇṇīti maṃ vidū;

Okāsaṃ yācito dehi, vasemu tava santike.

I am the fierce daughter of the great king Virūpakkha. I am Kālī, the unfortunate one; they know me as Kāḷakaṇṇī. Grant the permission I ask; let us dwell in your presence.

42.

42.

Kiṃsīle [M 1.0142] kiṃsamācāre, purise nivisase tuvaṃ;

Puṭṭhā me kāḷi akkhāhi, kathaṃ yathā (sī. pī.) jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

In a person of what virtue, of what conduct, do you take up your abode? Asked by me, Kālī, please tell me, so that we may know you.

43.

43.

Makkhī paḷāsī sārambhī, issukī maccharī saṭho;

So mayhaṃ puriso kanto, laddhaṃ yassa vinassati.

The ungrateful, the spiteful, the contentious, the envious, the miserly, the deceitful—that person is dear to me, one whose gains all perish.

44.

44.

Kodhano [V 1.0120] upanāhī ca, pisuṇo ca vibhedako;

Kaṇḍakavāco aṇḍakavāco (ka. sī. pī.) pharuso, so me kantataro tato.

The angry and the resentful, the slanderer and the divisive, the harsh-spoken and the cruel—such a one is even dearer to me than that.

45.

45.

Ajja [T 1.0194] suveti puriso, sadatthaṃ nāvabujjhati;

Ovajjamāno kuppati, seyyaṃ so atimaññati.

The person who says, ‘Today… tomorrow…,’ not understanding his own welfare; who gets angry when advised and despises his superior—

46.

46.

Davappaluddho devappaluddho (ka.), davappaladdho (pī.) puriso, sabbamittehi dhaṃsati;

So mayhaṃ puriso kanto, tasmiṃ homi anāmayā.

The person who is frivolous and greedy, who falls out with all his friends—that person is dear to me; with him I am perfectly at ease.

47.

47.

Apehi etto tvaṃ kāḷi, netaṃ amhesu vijjati;

Aññaṃ janapadaṃ gaccha, nigame rājadhāniyo.

Go away from here, Kālī! These things are not found among us. Go to another country, to its towns and royal cities.

48.

48.

Ahampi kho taṃ cetaṃ (sī.) jānāmi, netaṃ tumhesu vijjati;

Santi loke alakkhikā, saṅgharanti bahuṃ dhanaṃ;

Ahaṃ devo ca me bhātā, ubho naṃ vidhamāmase.

I too know that these things are not found among you. But there are unfortunate people in the world who accumulate much wealth. My brother, the god Deva, and I—we both destroy it.

49.

49.

Kā nu dibbena vaṇṇena, pathabyā supatiṭṭhitā;

Kā vā tvaṃ kassa vā dhītā, kathaṃ jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

Who can you be, with your divine appearance, so firmly established on the earth? Who are you, and whose daughter? How are we to know you?

50.

50.

Mahārājassahaṃ dhītā, dhataraṭṭhassa sirīmato dhataraṭṭhasirīmato (syā. ka.);

Ahaṃ sirī ca lakkhī ca, bhūripaññāti maṃ vidū;

Okāsaṃ yācito dehi, vasemu tava santike.

I am the daughter of the great king Dhataraṭṭha, the glorious. I am Sirī and Lakkhī; they know me as Bhūripaññā. Grant the permission I ask; let us dwell in your presence.

51.

51.

Kiṃsīle kiṃsamācāre, purise nivisase tuvaṃ;

Puṭṭhā me lakkhi akkhāhi, kathaṃ yathā (sī. pī.) jānemu taṃ mayaṃ.

In a person of what virtue, of what conduct, do you take up your abode? Asked by me, Lakkhī, please tell me, so that we may know you.

52.

52.

Yo [M 1.0143] cāpi sīte athavāpi uṇhe, vātātape ḍaṃsasarīsape ca;

Khudhaṃ khuddaṃ (syā. ka.), khudaṃ (pī.) pipāsaṃ abhibhuyya sabbaṃ, rattintivaṃ yo satataṃ niyutto;

Kālāgatañca [T 1.0195] na hāpeti atthaṃ, so me manāpo nivise ca tamhi.

He who, in cold or in heat, in wind and sun, amidst gadflies and crawling things, overcoming all hunger and thirst, strives constantly day and night, and does not let a timely opportunity pass—that person is pleasing to me, and I dwell with him.

53.

53.

Akkodhano mittavā cāgavā ca, sīlūpapanno asaṭhojubhūto asaṭho ujjubhūto (pī.);

Saṅgāhako sakhilo saṇhavāco, mahattapattopi nivātavutti;

Tasmiṃhaṃ tasmāhaṃ (sī. pī.) pose vipulā bhavāmi, ūmi samuddassa yathāpi vaṇṇaṃ.

Not angry, friendly, and generous, virtuous, honest, and upright; helpful, amiable, and of gentle speech, humble in conduct though he has attained greatness—in such a person I become abundant, just as a wave appears on the surface of the ocean.

54.

54.

Yo cāpi mitte athavā amitte, seṭṭhe sarikkhe atha vāpi hīne;

Atthaṃ carantaṃ athavā anatthaṃ, āvī raho saṅgahameva vatte vatto (syā. ka.).

Vācaṃ na vajjā pharusaṃ kadāci, matassa jīvassa ca tassa homi.

Towards friends or foes, superiors, equals, or inferiors, whether they act for his welfare or not, openly or in secret, he always acts with kindness. He would never utter a harsh word. I am his, whether he is living or dead.

55.

55.

Etesaṃ yo aññataraṃ labhitvā, kantā sirī kantasiriṃ (katthaci), kantaṃ siriṃ (syā.) aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dutiyatatiyapāṭhantarāni majjati appapañño;

Taṃ dittarūpaṃ visamaṃ carantaṃ, karīsaṭhānaṃva karīsajātaṃ va (sī. syā.) vivajjayāmi.

But the foolish person who, having gained delightful fortune, becomes intoxicated with pride—that one of blazing appearance, behaving unevenly, I avoid as I would a dung heap.

56.

56.

Attanā [V 1.0121] kurute lakkhiṃ, alakkhiṃ kurutattanā;

Na [T 1.0196] hi lakkhiṃ alakkhiṃ vā, añño aññassa kārakoti.

By oneself one creates good fortune, by oneself one creates misfortune. For no one can create for another either good fortune or misfortune.

Sirikāḷakaṇṇijātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Sirikāḷakaṇṇi Jātaka, the seventh.

383. Kukkuṭajātakaṃ (6-1-8)

383. The Kukkuṭa Jātaka (6-1-8)

57.

57.

Sucittapattachadana[M 1.0144], tambacūḷa vihaṅgama;

Oroha dumasākhāya, mudhā bhariyā bhavāmi te.

O bird with very wonderful wings and a red crest, descend from the tree branch; I will become your wife for nothing.

58.

58.

Catuppadī tvaṃ kalyāṇi, dvipadāhaṃ manorame;

Migī pakkhī asaññuttā, aññaṃ pariyesa sāmikaṃ.

383. You are a quadruped, O beautiful one; I am a biped, O delightful one. A beast and a bird are not compatible; seek another husband.

59.

59.

Komārikā te hessāmi, mañjukā piyabhāṇinī;

Vinda maṃ ariyena vedena, sāvaya maṃ yadicchasi.

I will be your youthful bride, pleasant-voiced and sweet-spoken. Obtain me by the noble custom, and instruct me as you wish.

60.

60.

Kuṇapādini lohitape, cori kukkuṭapothini;

Na tvaṃ ariyena vedena, mamaṃ bhattāramicchasi.

O eater of carrion, drinker of blood, O thief, slayer of chickens! You do not desire me as a husband by the noble custom.

61.

61.

Evampi caturā cāturā (syā. ka.) nārī, disvāna sadhanaṃ pavaraṃ (sī. syā. pī.) naraṃ;

Nenti saṇhāhi vācāhi, biḷārī viya kukkuṭaṃ.

Even so, clever women, upon seeing a wealthy man, lead him with gentle words, just as the she-cat leads the rooster.

62.

62.

Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, na khippamanubujjhati;

Amittavasamanveti, pacchā ca anutappati.

Whoever does not quickly understand a matter that has arisen falls under the sway of his enemies and afterwards grieves.

63.

63.

Yo ca uppatitaṃ atthaṃ, khippameva nibodhati;

Muccate [T 1.0197] sattusambādhā, kukkuṭova biḷāriyāti.

But whoever quickly understands a matter that has arisen is freed from the oppression of his foes, like the rooster from the she-cat.

Kukkuṭajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Kukkuṭa Jātaka—the eighth.

384. Dhammadhajajātakaṃ (6-1-9)

384. The Dhammadhaja Jātaka (6-1-9)

64.

64.

Dhammaṃ caratha ñātayo, dhammaṃ caratha bhaddaṃ vo bhadda vo (ka.);

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi ca.

Practice the Dhamma, kinsmen! Practice the Dhamma! May it be well with you! One who practices the Dhamma rests happily in this world and in the next.

65.

65.

Bhaddako vatayaṃ pakkhī, dijo paramadhammiko;

Ekapādena tiṭṭhanto, dhammamevānusāsati.

What a virtuous bird this is, a twice-born one, supremely righteous! Standing on one foot, he teaches the very Dhamma.

66.

66.

Nāssa sīlaṃ vijānātha, anaññāya pasaṃsatha;

Bhutvā aṇḍañca potañca chāpe ca (sī. pī.), dhammo dhammoti bhāsati.

384. You do not know his virtue; without knowing, you praise him. Having eaten eggs and young ones, he says, ‘Dhamma! Dhamma!’

67.

67.

Aññaṃ bhaṇati vācāya, aññaṃ kāyena kubbati;

Vācāya no ca kāyena, na taṃ dhammaṃ adhiṭṭhito.

He says one thing with his speech, and does another with his body. With his speech he speaks of the Dhamma, but not with his body; he is not established in that Dhamma.

68.

68.

Vācāya [V 1.0122][M 1.0145] sakhilo manoviduggo, channo kūpasayova kaṇhasappo;

Dhammadhajo gāmanigamāsusādhu gāmanigamāsu sādhusammato (sī.), gāmanigamasādhu (pī.), dujjāno purisena bālisena.

Gentle in speech but treacherous in mind, hidden like a black snake in a pit; bearing the banner of the Dhamma, honored as a saint in village and town, he is difficult for a foolish person to know.

69.

69.

Imaṃ [T 1.0198] tuṇḍehi pakkhehi, pādā cimaṃ viheṭhatha vipothatha (pī.);

Chavañhimaṃ vināsetha, nāyaṃ saṃvāsanārahoti.

Harass this one with your beaks, wings, and feet! Destroy this wretch! He is not fit to dwell with us.

Dhammadhajajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Dhammadhaja Jātaka—the ninth.

385. Nandiyamigarājajātakaṃ (6-1-10)

385. The Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka (6-1-10)

70.

70.

Sace brāhmaṇa gacchesi, sākete sāketaṃ (sī. syā.) ajjunaṃ añjhanaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) vanaṃ;

Vajjāsi nandiyaṃ nāma, puttaṃ asmākamorasaṃ;

Mātā pitā ca te vuddhā, te taṃ icchanti passituṃ.

“Brahmin, if you go to Sāketa, to the Ajjuna Wood, please tell our own true-born son, the one named Nandiya: ‘Your mother and father are old; they wish to see you.’”

71.

71.

Bhuttā mayā nivāpāni, rājino pānabhojanaṃ;

Taṃ rājapiṇḍaṃ avabhottuṃ avabhottaṃ (ka.), nāhaṃ brāhmaṇa mussahe.

“Brahmin, I have eaten the king's provisions, his food and drink. I am not able to be ungrateful for the king's provision.”

72.

72.

Odahissāmahaṃ passaṃ, khurappānissa khurappāṇissa (sī.), khurapāṇissa (pī.), khurappapāṇissa (?) rājino;

Tadāhaṃ sukhito mutto, api passeyya mātaraṃ.

“I will offer my flank to the king's razor-arrow. Then, happy and freed, I might see my mother.”

73.

73.

Migarājā pure āsiṃ, kosalassa niketane niketave (sī. syā. pī.);

Nandiyo nāma nāmena, abhirūpo catuppado.

“Formerly, I was a deer-king in the abode of the Kosala king, Nandiya by name, a handsome quadruped.”

74.

74.

Taṃ maṃ vadhitumāgacchi, dāyasmiṃ ajjune vane;

Dhanuṃ ārajjaṃ ārajjuṃ (niyya), adejjhaṃ (sī. pī.) advedhābhāvaṃ ekībhāvanti attho katvāna, usuṃ sannayha sandhāya (sī. pī.) kosalo.

“The Kosalan king came to kill me in the Ajjuna Wood preserve, having strung his bow and fitted an arrow.”

75.

75.

Tassāhaṃ [M 1.0146] odahiṃ passaṃ, khurappānissa rājino;

Tadāhaṃ [T 1.0199] sukhito mutto, mātaraṃ daṭṭhumāgatoti.

“To that king I offered my flank for his razor-arrow. Then, happy and freed, I came to see my mother.”

Nandiyamigarājajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Nandiyamigarāja Jātaka—the tenth.

Avāriyavaggo paṭhamo.

The Avāriya Chapter—the first.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Atha kujjharathesabha ketuvaro, sadarīmukha neru latā ca puna;

Apananda sirī ca sucittavaro, atha dhammika nandimigena dasāti.

Then Kujjha, Rathesabha, and the excellent Ketu, with Darīmukha, Neru, and Latā again; Apananda, Sirī, and the excellent Sucitta, then Dhammika, and with Nandimiga make ten.

2. Kharaputtavaggo

2. The Kharaputta Chapter

386. Kharaputtajātakaṃ (6-2-1)

386. The Kharaputta Jātaka (6-2-1)

76.

76.

Saccaṃ [V 1.0123] kirevamāhaṃsu, vastaṃ bhastaṃ (sī. pī.), kalakaṃ (syā.), garaṃ (ka.) bāloti paṇḍitā;

Passa bālo rahokammaṃ, āvikubbaṃ na bujjhati.

“Indeed, the wise have said of the goat, ‘It is a fool.’ This is truly so. Behold, the foolish one, acting openly, does not realize it is a deed to be done in secret.”

77.

77.

Tvaṃ khopi tvaṃ nu kho (sī. syā.), tvañca kho (pī.) samma bālosi, kharaputta vijānahi;

Rajjuyā hi rajjuyāsi (pī.) parikkhitto, vaṅkoṭṭho ohitomukho.

“Friend, son of a donkey, know this: you too are a fool, being encircled by a rope along with the yoke, with crooked lips and a downcast face.”

78.

78.

Aparampi samma te bālyaṃ ayampi samma te bālo (ka.), yo mutto na palāyasi;

So ca bālataro samma, yaṃ tvaṃ vahasi senakaṃ.

“This, too, is your foolishness, friend: that being freed, you do not flee. But he is even more foolish, friend, Senaka, whom you carry.”

79.

79.

Yaṃ nu samma ahaṃ bālo, ajarāja vijānahi;

Atha [T 1.0200] kena senako bālo, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

“Friend, king of goats, know indeed that I am a fool. But for what reason is Senaka a fool? Being asked, please explain it to me.”

80.

80.

Uttamatthaṃ labhitvāna, bhariyāya yo padassati bhayiyā yo padassati (pī.), bhayiyā na bhavissati (ka.);

Tena jahissatattānaṃ, sā cevassa na hessati.

“He who, having obtained the highest good, would give it to his wife, will thereby abandon himself, and she will not remain his.”

81.

81.

Na [M 1.0147] ve piyammeti na piyameti (ka.), na piyamedanti (katthaci) janinda tādiso, attaṃ niraṃkatvā piyāni sevati sevaye (?);

Attāva seyyo paramā ca seyyo, labbhā piyā ocitatthena pacchāti.

“Indeed, O king, such a person is not dear, who, having abandoned himself, pursues what is dear. Oneself is indeed best, and supremely best. For a man who has accumulated wealth, a dear wife can be obtained later.”

Kharaputtajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Kharaputta Jātaka—the first.

387. Sūcijātakaṃ (6-2-2)

387. The Sūci Jātaka (6-2-2)

82.

82.

Akakkasaṃ apharusaṃ, kharadhotaṃ supāsiyaṃ;

Sukhumaṃ tikhiṇaggañca, ko sūciṃ ketumicchati.

“Not coarse, not rough, polished on a whetstone, with a well-bored eye; fine and sharp-pointed—who wishes to buy this needle?”

83.

83.

Sumajjañca supāsañca, anupubbaṃ anupubba (sī. syā.) suvaṭṭitaṃ;

Ghanaghātimaṃ paṭithaddhaṃ, ko sūciṃ ketumicchati.

“Well-polished and with a well-bored eye, gradually well-rounded; forged solid and very firm—who wishes to buy this needle?”

84.

84.

Ito dāni patāyanti, sūciyo baḷisāni ca;

Koyaṃ kammāragāmasmiṃ, sūciṃ vikketumicchati.

“From this village now go forth needles and fishhooks; who is this who wishes to sell a needle in a blacksmiths' village?”

85.

85.

Ito satthāni gacchanti, kammantā vividhā puthū;

Koyaṃ kammāragāmasmiṃ, sūciṃ vikketumicchati marahati (sī. syā. pī.).

“From here go forth implements, and many and various kinds of craftwork. Who is this who wishes to sell a needle in a blacksmiths' village?”

86.

86.

Sūciṃ [T 1.0201] kammāragāmasmiṃ, vikketabbā pajānatā;

Ācariyāva jānanti ācariyā sañjānanti (ka.), ācariyā pajānanti (syā.), ācariyāva sañjānanti (pī.), kammaṃ sukatadukkaṭaṃ dukkataṃ (sī. pī.).

“A needle should be sold in a blacksmiths' village by one who knows; for the masters know a work, whether it is well-made or poorly-made.”

87.

87.

Imaṃ [V 1.0124] ce imañca (sī. syā. pī.) te pitā bhadde, sūciṃ jaññā mayā kataṃ;

Tayā ca maṃ nimanteyya, yañcatthaññaṃ ghare dhananti.

“Good lady, if your father should know of this needle made by me, he would invite me with you, and with whatever other wealth there is in the house.”

Sūcijātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Sūci Jātaka—the second.

388. Tuṇḍilajātakaṃ (6-2-3)

388. The Tuṇḍila Jātaka (6-2-3)

88.

88.

Navachannake navachandake (sī. pī.), navacchaddake (syā.) dāni doṇi (ka.), dānaṃ, dāne (katthaci) diyyati, puṇṇāyaṃ doṇi suvāminī ṭhitā;

Bahuke jane pāsapāṇike, no ca kho me paṭibhāti bhuñjituṃ.

“Now in a newly-thatched place it is given, this trough is full, the good mistress stands by; but there are many people with snares in hand, and it does not please me to eat.”

89.

89.

Tasasi [M 1.0148] bhamasi leṇamicchasi, attāṇosi kuhiṃ gamissasi;

Appossukko bhuñja tuṇḍila, maṃsatthāya hi positāmhase posiyāmase (sī. syā. pī.).

“You tremble, you roam, you seek a hiding place; you are without protection—where will you go? Be without anxiety and eat, Tuṇḍila, for we are raised for the sake of our flesh.”

90.

90.

Ogaha rahadaṃ akaddamaṃ, sabbaṃ sedamalaṃ pavāhaya;

Gaṇhāhi navaṃ vilepanaṃ, yassa [T 1.0202] gandho na kadāci chijjati.

“Descend into the mudless lake, wash away all sweat and grime; take up this new unguent, whose fragrance never fades.”

91.

91.

Katamo rahado akaddamo, kiṃsu sedamalanti vuccati;

Katamañca navaṃ vilepanaṃ, yassa gandho na kadāci chijjati.

“What is the mudless lake? What is called ‘sweat and grime’? And what is the new unguent, whose fragrance never fades?”

92.

92.

Dhammo rahado akaddamo, pāpaṃ sedamalanti vuccati;

Sīlañca navaṃ vilepanaṃ, tassa gandho na kadāci chijjati.

“The Dhamma is the mudless lake, evil is called ‘sweat and grime’; and virtue is the new unguent, its fragrance never fades.”

93.

93.

Nandanti sarīraghātino, na ca nandanti sarīradhārino;

Puṇṇāya ca puṇṇamāsiyā, ramamānāva jahanti jīvitanti.

“Those who slay bodies rejoice, but those who bear bodies do not rejoice. On the full moon of the full-moon day, while delighting, they abandon life.”

Tuṇḍilajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Tuṇḍila Jātaka—the third.

389. Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātakaṃ (6-2-4)

389. The Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka (6-2-4)

94.

94.

Siṅgīmigo āyatacakkhunetto, aṭṭhittaco vārisayo alomo;

Tenābhibhūto kapaṇaṃ rudāmi, hare sakhā kissa nu maṃ jahāsi.

“O friend! A golden creature with long eyes, whose skin is bone, who lies in the water, and is hairless—overpowered by it, I weep wretchedly. Why indeed do you abandon me?”

95.

95.

So [T 1.0203][M 1.0149] passasanto mahatā phaṇena, bhujaṅgamo kakkaṭamajjhapatto;

Sakhā sakhāraṃ paritāyamāno, bhujaṅgamaṃ kakkaṭako gahesi.

That serpent, exhaling with its great hood, approached the crab. The crab, a friend protecting his friend, seized the serpent.

96.

96.

Na vāyasaṃ no pana kaṇhasappaṃ, ghāsatthiko kakkaṭako adeyya;

Pucchāmi taṃ āyatacakkhunetta, atha kissa hetumha ubho gahītā.

O long-eyed one, a crab desirous of food should not seize a crow, nor should it seize a black cobra. Yet, for what reason have we both been seized? I ask you this.

97.

97.

Ayaṃ puriso mama atthakāmo, yo maṃ gahetvāna dakāya neti;

Tasmiṃ mate dukkhamanappakaṃ me, ahañca eso ca ubho na homa.

This man who, having taken me, leads me, is my well-wisher. If he dies, great suffering will befall me. Both this man and I shall not prosper.

98.

98.

Mamañca disvāna pavaddhakāyaṃ, sabbo jano hiṃsitumeva micche;

Sāduñca thūlañca muduñca maṃsaṃ, kākāpi maṃ disvāna disva (sī. pī.) viheṭhayeyyuṃ.

Seeing me with my large body, all people would wish only to harm me. Seeing me, one with sweet, plump, and tender flesh, even crows would harass me.

99.

99.

Sacetassa [V 1.0125] hetumha ubho gahītā, uṭṭhātu poso visamāvamāmi visamācamāmi (sī. pī. ka.);

Mamañca kākañca pamuñca khippaṃ, pure [T 1.0204] visaṃ gāḷhamupeti maccaṃ.

If we both have been seized for his sake, let the man arise; I shall draw out the poison. Release me and the crow quickly, before the poison deeply penetrates the man.

100.

100.

Sappaṃ pamokkhāmi na tāva kākaṃ, paṭibandhako paṭibaddhako (sī. pī.) hohiti hoti hi (syā.) tāva kāko;

Purisañca disvāna sukhiṃ arogaṃ, kākaṃ pamokkhāmi yatheva sappaṃ.

I shall release the snake, but not yet the crow. For now, the crow shall be my security. Having seen the man happy and without illness, I shall release the crow just as I released the snake.

101.

101.

Kāko [M 1.0150] tadā devadatto ahosi, māro pana kaṇhasappo ahosi;

Ānandabhaddo kakkaṭako ahosi, ahaṃ tadā brāhmaṇo homi satthāti tatthāti (sī. pī.).

At that time, the crow was Devadatta; the black cobra was Māra; the good crab was Ānanda; and I, the Teacher, was the brahmin at that time.

Suvaṇṇakakkaṭajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Suvaṇṇakakkaṭa Jātaka, the fourth.

390. Mayhakajātakaṃ (6-2-5)

390. The Mayhaka Jātaka (6-2-5)

102.

102.

Sakuṇo mayhako nāma, girisānudarīcaro;

Pakkaṃ pipphalimāruyha, mayhaṃ mayhanti kandati.

A bird named Mayhaka, who frequents mountain slopes and valleys, having climbed a ripe fig tree, cries out, 'Mine! Mine!'

103.

103.

Tassevaṃ vilapantassa, dijasaṅghā samāgatā;

Bhutvāna pipphaliṃ yanti, vilapatveva so dijo.

While he was thus lamenting, flocks of birds gathered; having eaten the fig fruit, they depart, while that bird only continues to lament.

104.

104.

Evameva idhekacco, saṅgharitvā bahuṃ dhanaṃ;

Nevattano na ñātīnaṃ, yathodhiṃ paṭipajjati.

Just so in this world, a certain person, having amassed much wealth, does not use it for himself, nor does he give to his kinsmen, nor does he act according to what is proper.

105.

105.

Na so acchādanaṃ bhattaṃ, na mālaṃ na vilepanaṃ;

Anubhoti [T 1.0205] nānubhoti (syā. ka.) sakiṃ kiñci, na saṅgaṇhāti ñātake.

He does not enjoy clothing or food, nor garlands, nor unguents; he does not enjoy anything even once, nor does he support his kinsmen.

106.

106.

Tassevaṃ vilapantassa, mayhaṃ mayhanti rakkhato;

Rājāno atha vā corā, dāyadā ye va ye ca (syā. ka.) appiyā;

Dhanamādāya gacchanti, vilapatveva so naro.

While that very person is lamenting, 'Mine, mine!' and guarding it, kings, or thieves, or those heirs who are unloved, take his wealth and go. That man is left only to lament.

107.

107.

Dhīro dhīro ca (sī.) bhoge adhigamma, saṅgaṇhāti ca ñātake;

Tena so kittiṃ pappoti, pecca sagge pamodatīti sagge ca modatīti (sī. pī.).

The wise person, having acquired possessions, also supports his kinsmen. By that, he obtains fame, and after passing away, he rejoices in heaven.

Mayhakajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Mayhaka Jātaka, the fifth.

391. Vijjādharajātakaṃ (6-2-6)

391. The Vijjādhara Jātaka (6-2-6)

108.

108.

Dubbaṇṇarūpaṃ tuvamariyavaṇṇī, purakkhatvā purakkhitvā (syā. ka.) pañjaliko namassasi;

Seyyo nu te so udavā udāhu (syā. ka.) sarikkho, nāmaṃ parassattano cāpi brūhi.

You who have a fine complexion, having placed before you a monk of unattractive appearance, you pay homage with hands joined in reverence. Is he superior to you, or is he your equal? Tell me the name of the other and of yourself as well.

109.

109.

Na [M 1.0151] nāmagottaṃ gaṇhanti rāja, sammaggatānujjugatāna samaggatānujjugatāna (syā.), samuggatānujjugatāna (ka.) devā;

Ahañca te nāmadheyyaṃ vadāmi, sakkohamasmī tidasānamindo.

O king, the devas do not grasp the name and clan of those who have gone rightly, who have gone straight. And I shall tell you my name: I am Sakka, the ruler of the devas.

110.

110.

Yo [V 1.0126] disvā bhikkhuṃ caraṇūpapannaṃ, purakkhatvā pañjaliko namassati;

Pucchāmi taṃ devarājetamatthaṃ, ito [T 1.0206] cuto kiṃ labhate sukhaṃ so.

O king of devas, whoever, having seen a monk endowed with virtuous conduct, places him in front and pays homage with hands joined in reverence—I ask you about this matter: when that person passes away from this existence, what happiness does he obtain?

111.

111.

Yo disvā bhikkhuṃ caraṇūpapannaṃ, purakkhatvā pañjaliko namassati;

Diṭṭheva dhamme labhate pasaṃsaṃ, saggañca so yāti sarīrabhedā.

Whoever, having seen a monk endowed with virtuous conduct, places him in front and pays homage with hands joined in reverence, obtains praise in this very life. After the breaking up of the body, he also goes to the heavenly realm.

112.

112.

Lakkhī vata me udapādi ajja, yaṃ vāsavaṃ bhūtapatiddasāma;

Bhikkhuñca disvāna tuvañca sakka, kāhāmi puññāni anappakāni.

Indeed, glory has arisen for me today, in that we have seen Vāsava, the lord of beings. Having seen the monk and you, O Sakka, I shall perform abundant meritorious deeds.

113.

113.

Addhā have sevitabbā sapaññā, bahussutā ye bahuṭhānacintino;

Bhikkhuñca disvāna mamañca rāja, karohi puññāni anappakāni.

Indeed, O king, one should associate with those who are wise, learned, and capable of reflecting on many matters. Having seen the monk and me, perform abundant meritorious deeds.

114.

114.

Akkodhano niccapasannacitto, sabbātithīyācayogo bhavitvā;

Nihacca mānaṃ abhivādayissaṃ, sutvāna devinda subhāsitānīti.

O lord of devas, having heard your well-spoken words, I will become free from anger, with a mind ever serene, devoted to all guests and visitors. Having subdued my pride, I will pay homage.

Vijjādhara dhajaviheṭhaka (sī. pī.), pabbajitaviheṭhaka (syā.) jātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Vijjādhara Jātaka, the sixth.

392. Siṅghapupphajātakaṃ (6-2-7)

392. The Siṅghapuppha Jātaka (6-2-7)

115.

115.

Yametaṃ [T 1.0207][M 1.0152] yamekaṃ (pī.) vārijaṃ pupphaṃ, adinnaṃ upasiṅghasi;

Ekaṅgametaṃ theyyānaṃ, gandhathenosi mārisa.

Venerable sir, in that you smell this water-born flower which was not given, this is one part of theft. You are a fragrance-thief.

116.

116.

Na harāmi na bhañjāmi, ārā siṅghāmi vārijaṃ;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, gandhathenoti vuccati.

I do not take the water-born flower, nor do I break it; I smell it from afar. For what reason, then, am I called a fragrance-thief?

117.

117.

Yoyaṃ bhisāni khaṇati, puṇḍarīkāni bhañjati;

Evaṃ ākiṇṇakammanto, kasmā eso na vuccati.

This person who digs up lotus stalks and breaks the white lotuses—why is this one, so engaged in coarse actions, not called a thief?

118.

118.

Ākiṇṇaluddo puriso, dhāticelaṃva makkhito;

Tasmiṃ me vacanaṃ natthi, tañcārahāmi vattave.

A person replete with coarse and cruel actions is smeared with evil like a wet-nurse's garment. Regarding him, I have nothing to say; but it is you whom I am fit to address.

119.

119.

Anaṅgaṇassa posassa, niccaṃ sucigavesino;

Vālaggamattaṃ pāpassa, abbhāmattaṃva khāyati.

For a faultless person, ever seeking purity, even a hair's tip measure of evil appears as large as a great cloud.

120.

120.

Addhā maṃ yakkha jānāsi, atho maṃ anukampasi;

Punapi yakkha vajjāsi, yadā passasi edisaṃ.

Surely, O yakkha, you know me, and you have compassion for me. O yakkha, should you see such a thing again, please speak.

121.

121.

Neva taṃ upajīvāmi, napi te bhatakāmhase bhatakamhase (sī. pī.), bhatikamhase (syā.);

Tvameva bhikkhu jāneyya, yena gaccheyya suggatinti.

I do not make a living depending on you, nor am I your hired servant. O monk, you yourself should know that path by which one may go to a good destination.

Siṅghapuppha bhisapuppha (sī. pī.), upasiṅghapuppha (syā.) jātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Siṅghapuppha Jātaka, the seventh.

393. Vighāsādajātakaṃ (6-2-8)

393. The Vighāsāda Jātaka (6.2.8)

122.

122.

Susukhaṃ [V 1.0127] vata jīvanti, ye janā vighāsādino;

Diṭṭheva [T 1.0208] dhamme pāsaṃsā, samparāye ca suggatī.

Very happily indeed do they live, those people who are eaters of remnants. They are praiseworthy in this very life, and in the next life, a good destination awaits.

123.

123.

Sukassa suvassa (sī. syā. pī.) bhāsamānassa, na nisāmetha paṇḍitā;

Idaṃ suṇātha sodariyā, amhevāyaṃ pasaṃsati.

O wise ones, O brothers, do you not hear the parrot speaking? Listen to this! This one praises only us.

124.

124.

Nāhaṃ tumhe pasaṃsāmi, kuṇapādā suṇātha me;

Ucchiṭṭhabhojino bhojanā (ka.) tumhe, na tumhe vighāsādino.

I do not praise you, O corpse-eaters, listen to me! You are eaters of leavings; you are not eaters of remnants.

125.

125.

Sattavassā [M 1.0153] pabbajitā, mejjhāraññe majjheraññe (ka.) sikhaṇḍino;

Vighāseneva yāpentā, mayaṃ ce bhoto gārayhā;

Ke nu bhoto pasaṃsiyā.

Having gone forth for seven years, we who have top-knots are in the middle of the forest. Sustaining ourselves only with remnants, if we are blameworthy, O venerable one, who then is to be praised by you?

126.

126.

Tumhe sīhānaṃ byagghānaṃ, vāḷānañcāvasiṭṭhakaṃ;

Ucchiṭṭheneva yāpentā, maññivho vighāsādino.

Eating the remainder left by lions, tigers, and beasts of prey, sustaining yourselves with mere leavings, do not consider yourselves to be 'eaters of remnants'.

127.

127.

Ye brāhmaṇassa samaṇassa, aññassa vā aññassa ca (sī. syā.), aññasseva (pī.) vanibbino vaṇibbino (sī. syā.);

Datvāva datvāna (pī. ka.) sesaṃ bhuñjanti, te janā vighāsādinoti.

Those people who, having given to a brahmin, an ascetic, or another mendicant, eat what is left—those people are eaters of remnants.

Vighāsādajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Vighāsāda Jātaka, the Eighth.

394. Vaṭṭakajātakaṃ (6-2-9)

394. The Vaṭṭaka Jātaka (6.2.9)

128.

128.

Paṇītaṃ bhuñjase bhattaṃ, sappitelañca mātula;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, kiso tvamasi vāyasa.

O uncle crow, you eat excellent food, cooked rice with ghee and oil. That being so, for what reason are you thin?

129.

129.

Amittamajjhe vasato, tesu āmisamesato;

Niccaṃ ubbiggahadayassa, kuto kākassa daḷhiyaṃ.

Dwelling in the midst of enemies, seeking food among them, with a heart ever frightened—how could there be stoutness for a crow?

130.

130.

Niccaṃ ubbegino ubbiggino (syā. ka.), ubbedhino (sī.) kākā, dhaṅkā pāpena kammunā;

Laddho [T 1.0209] piṇḍo na pīṇeti, kiso tenasmi vaṭṭaka.

O quail, crows are always of a frightened mind. The alms-food obtained by an evil deed does not satisfy. For that reason, I am thin.

131.

131.

Lūkhāni tiṇabījāni, appasnehāni bhuñjasi;

Atha kena nu vaṇṇena, thūlo tvamasi vaṭṭaka.

O quail, you eat dry grass seeds that have little oil. That being so, for what reason are you stout?

132.

132.

Appicchā appacintāya, adūragamanena ca;

Laddhāladdhena yāpento, thūlo tenasmi vāyasa.

O crow, by being of few wishes, by having little anxiety, and by not going far, I sustain myself with whatever is obtained. For that reason, I am stout.

133.

133.

Appicchassa [V 1.0128] hi posassa, appacintasukhassa appacintisukhassa (sī. syā. pī.) ca;

Susaṅgahitamānassa susaṅgahitapamāṇassa (sī. syā. pī.), vuttī susamudānayāti.

Indeed, for a person of few wishes, who is happy with little anxiety, and whose mind is well-collected, a livelihood is easy to come by.

Vaṭṭakajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

395. Pārāvatajātakaṃ (6-2-10)

395. The Pārāvata Jātaka (6.2.10)

134.

134.

Cirassaṃ vata passāmi, sahāyaṃ maṇidhārinaṃ;

Sukatā sukatāya (sī. pī.) massukuttiyā, sobhate vata me sakhā.

Indeed, after a long time I see my friend wearing a jewel! With his beard so well-trimmed, my friend truly shines!

135.

135.

Parūḷhakacchanakhalomo[M 1.0154], ahaṃ kammesu byāvaṭo;

Cirassaṃ nhāpitaṃ laddhā, lomaṃ taṃ ajjaṃ hārayiṃ apahārayiṃ (sī. pī.).

With my armpit hair, nails, and body hair overgrown, I was busy with my duties. Having found a barber after a long time, today I had that hair removed.

136.

136.

Yaṃ nu lomaṃ ahāresi, dullabhaṃ laddha kappakaṃ;

Atha kiñcarahi te samma, kaṇṭhe kiṇikiṇāyati idaṃ kaṇṭhe kiṇāyati (ka.), kaṇṭhe kiṃnikilāyati (syā.).

Indeed, having found that hard-to-get barber, you had your hair removed. That being so, friend, what is it that jingles at your neck?

137.

137.

Manussasukhumālānaṃ, maṇi kaṇṭhesu lambati;

Tesāhaṃ [T 1.0210] anusikkhāmi, mā tvaṃ maññi davā kataṃ.

A jewel hangs at the necks of delicate humans. I am imitating them. Do not think it was done for sport.

138.

138.

Sacepimaṃ pihayasi, massukuttiṃ sukāritaṃ;

Kārayissāmi te samma, maṇiñcāpi dadāmi te.

Friend, if you desire this well-done beard trimming, I will have it done for you. I will also give you the jewel.

139.

139.

Tvaññeva maṇinā channo, sukatāya ca massuyā;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāmi, piyaṃ me tava dassananti.

You alone are suited for the jewel and for the well-trimmed beard. The sight of you is dear to me. Now, having taken leave of you, I will go.

Pārāvatajātakaṃ kākajātakaṃ (sī. pī.), maṇijātakaṃ (syā.) dasamaṃ.

The Pārāvata Jātaka, the Tenth.

Kharaputtavaggo senakavaggo (sī. pī.), khuraputtavaggo (syā.), sūcivaggo (ka.) dutiyo.

The Kharaputta Chapter, the Second.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Atha passa sasūci ca tuṇḍilako, miga mayhakapañcamapakkhivaro;

Atha pañjali vārija mejjha puna, atha vaṭṭa kapotavarena dasāti.

Then Kharaputta, Sūci, and Tuṇḍila; Suvattakakkaṭa, Mayhaka, and the excellent bird as the fifth; then Vijjādhara, Sigālapuppha, and Vighāsāda; then again Vaṭṭaka along with the excellent Pārāvata make ten.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Then the summary of the chapters:

Atha vaggaṃ pakittissaṃ, chanipātaṃ varuttame;

Avāriyā ca kharo ca senaka (sī.), sūci ca (syā. ka.), dve ca vuttā subyañjanāti.

Now in the most excellent Book of Sixes, I will announce the chapters. The Avāriya and the Kharaputta are the two chapters that have been well-expounded.

Chakkanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Book of Sixes is finished.

7. Sattakanipāto

7. The Book of Sevens

1. Kukkuvaggo

1. The Kukku Chapter

396. Kukkujātakaṃ (7-1-1)

396. The Kukku Jātaka (7.1.1)

1.

1.

Diyaḍḍhakukkū [T 1.0211][V 1.0129][M 1.0155] udayena kaṇṇikā, vidatthiyo aṭṭha parikkhipanti naṃ;

Sā siṃsapā sasiṃsapā (sī. pī.), sā sīsapā (syā.), yā siṃsapā (ka. sī. niyya) sāramayā apheggukā, kuhiṃ ṭhitā upparito uparito (sī. syā. pī.) na dhaṃsati.

The pinnacle is one and a half cubits in height; eight spans surround it. That pinnacle, made of sissoo heartwood, without sapwood—where is it placed that it does not fall from above?

2.

2.

Yā tiṃsati sāramayā anujjukā, parikiriya pakiriyā (ka.) gopāṇasiyo samaṃ ṭhitā samaṭṭhitā (sī. syā.);

Tāhi susaṅgahitā balasā pīḷitā tā saṅgahitā balasā ca pīḷitā (sī.), tāhi susaṅgahitā balasā ca pīḷitā (syā.), tāhi saṅgahītā balasā ca pīḷitā (pī.), samaṃ ṭhitā upparito na dhaṃsati.

The thirty crooked rafters of heartwood, set evenly in a circle; by them it is well-supported, pressed together by their strength. It stands evenly and does not fall from above.

3.

3.

Evampi mittehi daḷhehi paṇḍito, abhejjarūpehi sucīhi mantibhi;

Susaṅgahīto siriyā na dhaṃsati, gopāṇasī bhāravahāva kaṇṇikā.

So too, a wise king, well-supported by strong, unbreakable, and pure friends and counselors, does not fall from glory, just as the pinnacle is supported by the load-bearing rafters.

4.

4.

Kharattacaṃ bellaṃ yathāpi satthavā, anāmasantopi karoti tittakaṃ;

Samāharaṃ sāduṃ karoti patthiva, asāduṃ kayirā tanubandhamuddharaṃ tanuvaṭṭamuddharaṃ (sī. pī.).

O ruler of the earth, just as one with a knife can make a rough-skinned wood-apple bitter by improper handling; one who peels the skin too thinly would make it unpalatable; but one who prepares it well makes it palatable.

5.

5.

Evampi [T 1.0212] gāmanigamesu paṇḍito, asāhasaṃ rājadhanāni saṅgharaṃ;

Dhammānuvattī paṭipajjamāno, sa phāti kayirā aviheṭhayaṃ paraṃ.

So too, a wise king in villages and towns, collecting the royal revenues without violence, practicing in accordance with the Dhamma, would bring about prosperity without harming others.

6.

6.

Odātamūlaṃ [M 1.0156] sucivārisambhavaṃ, jātaṃ yathā pokkharaṇīsu ambujaṃ;

Padumaṃ yathā agginikāsiphālimaṃ, na kaddamo na rajo na vāri limpati.

Just as a lotus born in a pond, with a pure white root, sprung from pure water—a lotus radiant like fire—is not smeared by mud, nor by dust, nor by water.

7.

7.

Evampi vohārasuciṃ asāhasaṃ, visuddhakammantamapetapāpakaṃ;

Na limpati kammakilesa tādiso, jātaṃ yathā pokkharaṇīsu ambujanti.

So too, a king who is pure in conduct and non-violent, whose actions are virtuous and who is devoid of evil—such a one is not tainted by the defilements of action, just as the lotus born in a pond is unsmeared.

Kukkujātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Kukku Jātaka, the First.

397. Manojajātakaṃ (7-1-2)

397. The Manoja Jātaka (7.1.2)

8.

8.

Yathā cāpo ninnamati, jiyā cāpi nikūjati;

Haññate nūna manojo, migarājā sakhā mama.

As the bow bends down, and the bowstring twangs, surely Manoja is struck—the king of beasts, my friend.

9.

9.

Handa dāni vanantāni, pakkamāmi yathāsukhaṃ;

Netādisā sakhā honti, labbhā me jīvato sakhā.

Well now, I will depart to the forests at my ease. Such as these are not friends. While I live, other friends can be found for me.

10.

10.

Na [V 1.0130] pāpajanasaṃsevī, accantaṃ sukhamedhati;

Manojaṃ [T 1.0213] passa semānaṃ, giriyassānusāsanī ariyassānusāsanī (sī. syā. pī.).

One who associates with evil people does not attain perfect happiness. Behold Manoja lying there, who followed the instruction of the jackal.

11.

11.

Na pāpasampavaṅkena, mātā puttena nandati;

Manojaṃ passa semānaṃ, acchannaṃ sacchannaṃ (ka.) samhi lohite.

A mother does not rejoice in a son associated with evil. Behold Manoja lying down, covered in his own blood.

12.

12.

Evamāpajjate poso, pāpiyo ca nigacchati;

Yo ve hitānaṃ vacanaṃ, na karoti atthadassinaṃ.

Thus a person encounters suffering and attains an evil state, who does not follow the word of those who see what is beneficial and desire one's welfare.

13.

13.

Evañca so hoti tato ca pāpiyo, yo uttamo adhamajanūpasevī;

Passuttamaṃ adhamajanūpasevitaṃ seviṃ (syā.), migādhipaṃ saravaraveganiddhutaṃ.

And so he comes to suffering and is even worse, the superior person who associates with the inferior. Observe the superior one, the lord of beasts, who associated with a base person, pierced by the force of an excellent arrow.

14.

14.

Nihīyati [M 1.0157] puriso nihīnasevī, na ca hāyetha kadāci tulyasevī;

Seṭṭhamupagamaṃ mupanamaṃ (sī. pī. a. ni. 3.26) udeti khippaṃ, tasmāttanā uttaritaraṃ tasmā attano uttariṃ (sī. pī.), tasmā attano uttaraṃ (syā.) bhajethāti.

A person declines by associating with the inferior; one would never decline by associating with equals. By approaching the superior one quickly rises; therefore one should associate with those superior to oneself.

Manojajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Manoja Jātaka, the Second.

398. Sutanujātakaṃ (7-1-3)

398. The Sutanu Jātaka

15.

15.

Rājā te bhattaṃ pāhesi, suciṃ maṃsūpasecanaṃ;

Maghadevasmiṃ makhādevasmiṃ (sī. pī.), māghadevasmiṃ (ka.) adhivatthe, ehi nikkhamma bhuñjassu.

O deity who dwells in the Māghadeva banyan tree, for you the king has sent pure food with meat curry. Come, come out and eat.

16.

16.

Ehi māṇava orena, bhikkhamādāya sūpitaṃ;

Tvañca [T 1.0214] māṇava bhikkhā ca bhakkhosi (syā.), bhakkhāva (ka.), ubho bhakkhā bhavissatha.

Come to this side, young man, bringing the regular food endowed with curry. You, young man, and the food—both of you will be my meal.

17.

17.

Appakena tuvaṃ yakkha, thullamatthaṃ jahissasi;

Bhikkhaṃ te nāharissanti, janā maraṇasaññino.

For a small reason, O yakkha, you will abandon a great advantage. People, perceiving the danger of death, will not bring you food.

18.

18.

Laddhāya yakkhā laddhāyaṃ yakkha (sī. syā. pī.) tava niccabhikkhaṃ, suciṃ paṇītaṃ rasasā upetaṃ;

Bhikkhañca te āhariyo naro idha, sudullabho hehiti bhakkhite khādite (sī. syā. pī.) mayi.

O yakkha, for the sake of your constant food—pure, excellent, and endowed with flavor—[I have come]. If I am eaten, a person who would bring you food here will be very difficult to find.

19.

19.

Mameva mamesa (sī. pī.) sutano attho, yathā bhāsasi māṇava;

Mayā tvaṃ samanuññāto, sotthiṃ passāhi mātaraṃ.

O Sutanu, young man, just as you speak, the benefit is indeed my own. You are permitted by me; see your mother in safety.

20.

20.

Khaggaṃ chattañca pātiñca, gacchamādāya gacchevādāya (sī. syā. pī.) māṇava;

Sotthiṃ passatu te mātā, tvañca passāhi mātaraṃ.

Go, young man, taking the sword, the umbrella, and the golden bowl. May your mother see you in safety, and may you also see your mother.

21.

21.

Evaṃ yakkha sukhī hohi, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Dhanañca me adhigataṃ, rañño ca vacanaṃ katanti.

Thus, O yakkha, be happy, together with all your kinsmen. Wealth has been obtained by me, and the king’s word has been done.

Sutanujātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Sutanu Jātaka, the Third.

399. Mātuposakagijjhajātakaṃ (7-1-4)

399. The Mātuposaka-gijjha Jātaka

22.

22.

Te [V 1.0131][M 1.0158] kathaṃ nu karissanti, vuddhā giridarīsayā;

Ahaṃ baddhosmi pāsena, nilīyassa vasaṃ gato.

How indeed will they fare, the aged ones dwelling in the mountain cleft? I am bound by a snare; I have come into the power of the hunter Nilīya.

23.

23.

Kiṃ gijjha paridevasi, kā nu te paridevanā;

Na [T 1.0215] me suto vā diṭṭho vā, bhāsanto mānusiṃ dijo.

Why do you lament, O vulture? What is this lamentation of yours? A bird speaking with a human voice—such a thing has not been heard of nor seen by me.

24.

24.

Bharāmi mātāpitaro, vuddhe giridarīsaye;

Te kathaṃ nu karissanti, ahaṃ vasaṃ gato tava.

I support my aged parents who dwell in a mountain cleft. As I have come into your power, how indeed will they fare?

25.

25.

Yaṃ nu gijjho yojanasataṃ, kuṇapāni avekkhati;

Kasmā jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhasi.

It is said that a vulture sees a corpse from a hundred yojanas away; why then, when you came upon it, did you not perceive the net and the snare?

26.

26.

Yadā parābhavo hoti, poso jīvitasaṅkhaye;

Atha jālañca pāsañca, āsajjāpi na bujjhati.

When a person is to meet with ruin at the exhaustion of his life, then, even when he comes upon a net and a snare, he does not perceive them.

27.

27.

Bharassu mātāpitaro, vuddhe giridarīsaye;

Mayā tvaṃ samanuññāto, sotthiṃ passāhi ñātake.

Support your aged parents dwelling in the mountain cleft. You are permitted by me; see your kinsmen in safety.

28.

28.

Evaṃ luddaka nandassu, saha sabbehi ñātibhi;

Bharissaṃ mātāpitaro, vuddhe giridarīsayeti.

Thus, O hunter, may you rejoice, together with all your kinsmen. I will support my aged parents dwelling in the mountain cleft.

Mātuposakagijjhajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Mātuposaka-gijjha Jātaka, the Fourth.

400. Dabbhapupphajātakaṃ (7-1-5)

400. The Dabbhapuppha Jātaka

29.

29.

Anutīracārī bhaddante, sahāyamanudhāva maṃ;

Mahā me gahito rohito (ka.) maccho, so maṃ harati vegasā.

O bank-walker, may it be well with you! Run after me, your friend! A great fish has been seized by me, and it carries me away with force.

30.

30.

Gambhīracārī bhaddante, daḷhaṃ gaṇhāhi thāmasā;

Ahaṃ taṃ uddharissāmi, supaṇṇo uragāmiva uragammiva (sī. syā. pī.).

O deep-farer, may it be well with you! Hold on firmly with all your strength! I will pull you out, just as a supaṇṇa pulls out a serpent.

31.

31.

Vivādo no samuppanno, dabbhapuppha suṇohi me;

Samehi [T 1.0216] medhagaṃ medhakaṃ (pī.) samma, vivādo vūpasammataṃ.

A dispute has arisen between us, O Dabbhapuppha, listen to me! Settle the quarrel, friend; may the dispute be pacified.

32.

32.

Dhammaṭṭhohaṃ pure āsiṃ, bahū aḍḍā me tīritā bahuaṭṭaṃ me tīritaṃ (sī.), bahuaṭṭaṃva tīritaṃ (syā.), bahu atthaṃ me tīritaṃ (pī.);

Samemi medhagaṃ samma, vivādo vūpasammataṃ.

I was a judge in the past; many cases have been decided by me. I will settle the quarrel, friend; may the dispute be pacified.

33.

33.

Anutīracāri [M 1.0159] naṅguṭṭhaṃ, sīsaṃ gambhīracārino;

Accāyaṃ athāyaṃ (sī. pī.) majjhimo khaṇḍo, dhammaṭṭhassa bhavissati.

The tail for the bank-walker, the head for the deep-farer. This middle section beyond them will be for the judge.

34.

34.

Cirampi [V 1.0132] bhakkho abhavissa, sace na vivademase;

Asīsakaṃ anaṅguṭṭhaṃ, siṅgālo harati rohitaṃ.

The food would have been ours for a long time, if we had not quarreled. The jackal carries away the rohita fish, without head and without tail.

35.

35.

Yathāpi rājā nandeyya, rajjaṃ laddhāna khattiyo;

Evāhamajja nandāmi, disvā puṇṇamukhaṃ patiṃ.

Just as a khattiya king would rejoice, having obtained a kingdom, so too do I rejoice today, seeing my husband with his mouth full.

36.

36.

Kathaṃ nu thalajo santo, udake macchaṃ parāmasi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kathaṃ adhigataṃ tayā.

My dear, being one born on land, how indeed did you get a fish in the water? Being asked by me, please tell: how was it obtained by you?

37.

37.

Vivādena kisā honti, vivādena dhanakkhayā;

Jīnā uddā vivādena, bhuñja māyāvi rohitaṃ.

Through quarreling, beings become lean; through quarreling, there is loss of wealth. The otters were defeated by a quarrel. Eat the rohita fish, my clever one.

38.

38.

Evameva manussesu, vivādo yattha jāyati;

Dhammaṭṭhaṃ paṭidhāvanti, so hi nesaṃ vināyako;

Dhanāpi tattha jīyanti, rājakoso pavaḍḍhatīti ca vaḍḍhati (pī.).

Just so among humans, wherever a dispute arises, they resort to a judge, for he is their arbiter. There, wealth is lost, and the royal treasury increases.

Dabbhapupphajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Dabbhapuppha Jātaka, the Fifth.

401. Paṇṇakajātakaṃ (7-1-6)

401. The Paṇṇaka Jātaka

39.

39.

Paṇṇakaṃ dasaṇṇakaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) tikhiṇadhāraṃ, asiṃ sampannapāyinaṃ;

Parisāyaṃ [T 1.0217] puriso gilati, kiṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Yadaññaṃ dukkaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

A man swallows in an assembly a sword from Paṇṇaka, sharp-edged, accustomed to drinking fine blood. What is more difficult than that? If there is any other difficult matter, you who are asked, please tell it to me.

40.

40.

Gileyya puriso lobhā, asiṃ sampannapāyinaṃ;

Yo ca vajjā dadāmīti, taṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Sabbaññaṃ sukaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi maddava māgadha (sī. syā. pī.).

A man might swallow out of greed a sword accustomed to drinking fine blood. But whoever might say, 'I will give,' that is more difficult than that. All other matters are easy; know this, O Maddava.

41.

41.

Byākāsi āyuro pañhaṃ, atthaṃ attha (pī. sī. niyya) dhammassa kovido;

Pukkusaṃ dāni pucchāmi, kiṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Yadaññaṃ dukkaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

Āyura, skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma, has answered the question. Now I ask Pukkusa: what is more difficult than that? If there is any other difficult matter, you who are asked, please tell it to me.

42.

42.

Na [M 1.0160] vācamupajīvanti, aphalaṃ giramudīritaṃ;

Yo ca datvā avākayirā, taṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Sabbaññaṃ sukaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi maddava.

Beings do not live on speech, on a fruitless word that is uttered. But whoever, having given, would then regret it, that is more difficult than that. All other matters are easy; know this, O Maddava.

43.

43.

Byākāsi pukkuso pañhaṃ, atthaṃ dhammassa kovido;

Senakaṃ dāni pucchāmi, kiṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Yadaññaṃ dukkaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

Pukkusa, skilled in the meaning of the Dhamma, has answered the question. Now I ask Senaka: what is more difficult than that? If there is any other difficult matter, you who are asked, please tell it to me.

44.

44.

Dadeyya [V 1.0133] puriso dānaṃ, appaṃ vā yadi vā bahuṃ;

Yo ca datvā nānutappe tape (sī. pī.), taṃ dukkarataraṃ tato;

Sabbaññaṃ sukaraṃ ṭhānaṃ, evaṃ jānāhi maddava.

A person should give a gift, whether small or great; but whoever, having given, does not regret it—that is more difficult than the giving. All other matters are easy; know this, O Maddava.

45.

45.

Byākāsi āyuro pañhaṃ, atho pukkusaporiso;

Sabbe [T 1.0218] pañhe atibhoti, yathā bhāsati senakoti.

Āyura answered the question, and also the man Pukkusa; but what Senaka speaks surpasses all the questions. Therefore, as Senaka speaks, so it is.

Paṇṇaka dasaṇṇaka (sī. syā. pī.) jātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Paṇṇaka Jātaka, the sixth.

402. Sattubhastajātakaṃ (7-1-7)

402. The Sattubhasta Jātaka (7-1-7)

46.

46.

Vibbhantacitto kupitindriyosi, nettehi te vārigaṇā savanti;

Kiṃ te naṭṭhaṃ kiṃ pana patthayāno, idhāgamā brahme tadiṅgha brāhmaṇa iṅgha (sī. syā.) brūhi.

You have a wavering mind and agitated senses; streams of tears flow from your eyes. What have you lost? What is it you desire, that you have come here? Come, O brahmin, tell me this.

47.

47.

Miyyetha bhariyā vajato mamajja, agacchato maraṇamāha yakkho;

Etena dukkhena pavedhitosmi, akkhāhi me senaka etamatthaṃ.

The yakkha said that if I go home today, my wife will die; if I do not go, it will be my own death. I am trembling with this suffering. O Senaka, please explain this matter to me.

48.

48.

Bahūni ṭhānāni vicintayitvā, yamettha vakkhāmi tadeva saccaṃ;

Maññāmi te brāhmaṇa sattubhastaṃ, ajānato kaṇhasappo paviṭṭho.

Having considered many possibilities, what I shall say in this matter is the very truth. I believe, O brahmin, that while you were unaware, a black cobra entered your bag of roasted grain.

49.

49.

Ādāya [M 1.0161] daṇḍaṃ parisumbha bhastaṃ, passeḷamūgaṃ uragaṃ dujivhaṃ dijivhaṃ (sī. pī.);

Chindajja kaṅkhaṃ vicikicchitāni, bhujaṅgamaṃ passa pamuñca bhastaṃ.

Take a stick and strike the bag; see the serpent with its saliva-drooling mouth and forked tongue. Cut off your doubt and perplexities today! Untie the bag and see the snake.

50.

50.

Saṃviggarūpo [T 1.0219] parisāya majjhe, so brāhmaṇo sattubhastaṃ pamuñci;

Atha nikkhami urago uggatejo, āsīviso sappo phaṇaṃ karitvā.

Alarmed, in the midst of the assembly, that brahmin untied his bag of roasted grain. Then a serpent of fierce energy came out, a snake of swift venom, spreading its hood.

51.

51.

Suladdhalābhā janakassa rañño, yo passatī senakaṃ sādhupaññaṃ;

Vivaṭṭachaddo vivattacchaddo (sī.), vivaṭṭacchado (syā.), vivaṭṭacchaddā (pī.) nusi sabbadassī, ñāṇaṃ nu te brāhmaṇa bhiṃsarūpaṃ.

It is a well-gained acquisition for King Janaka, who sees Senaka of excellent wisdom. Are you one with the veil removed, one who sees all? O brahmin, is your knowledge so formidable?

52.

52.

Imāni me sattasatāni atthi, gaṇhāhi sabbāni dadāmi tuyhaṃ;

Tayā hi me jīvitamajja laddhaṃ, athopi bhariyāya makāsi sotthiṃ.

I have these seven hundred; take them. I give them all to you. Truly, it is because of you that my life has been saved today, and you have also brought about well-being for my wife.

53.

53.

Na paṇḍitā vetanamādiyanti, citrāhi gāthāhi subhāsitāhi;

Itopi te brahme dadantu vittaṃ, ādāya tvaṃ gaccha sakaṃ niketanti.

The wise do not accept a fee for their intricate and well-spoken verses. Even so, O brahmin, let them give you wealth from here. Taking it, go to your own home.

Sattubhastajātakaṃ senakajātakaṃ (syā.) sattamaṃ.

The Sattubhasta Jātaka, the seventh.

403. Aṭṭhisenakajātakaṃ (7-1-8)

403. The Aṭṭhisena Jātaka (7-1-8)

54.

54.

Yeme [T 1.0220] ahaṃ na jānāmi, aṭṭhisena vanibbake;

Te maṃ saṅgamma yācanti, kasmā maṃ tvaṃ na yācasi.

O Aṭṭhisena, those mendicants whom I do not know come together and beg from me. Why do you not beg from me?

55.

55.

Yācako [V 1.0134] appiyo hoti, yācaṃ adadamappiyo;

Tasmāhaṃ taṃ na yācāmi, mā me videssanā viddesanā (sī. pī.) ahu.

A beggar becomes displeasing to the giver; one who does not give what is asked becomes displeasing to the beggar. Therefore, I do not ask of you, lest aversion arise between us.

56.

56.

Yo [M 1.0162] ve yācanajīvāno, kāle yācaṃ na yācati;

Parañca puññā puññaṃ (syā. ka.) dhaṃseti, attanāpi na jīvati.

Indeed, one who lives by begging yet does not ask at the proper time diminishes the other's merit and does not live well himself.

57.

57.

Yo ca yo ve (ka.) yācanajīvāno, kāle yācañhi yācati yācaṃpi yācati (syā.), yācāni yācati (pī.), yācati yācanaṃ (sī. niyya), yācanaṃ yācati (ka.);

Parañca puññaṃ labbheti, attanāpi ca jīvati.

But one who lives by begging and indeed asks at the proper time causes another to obtain merit and also lives well himself.

58.

58.

Na ve dessanti na ve dussanti (syā.), na ve dissanti (pī.), na videssanti (ka. aṭṭha.) sappaññā, disvā yācakamāgate;

Brahmacāri piyo mesi, vada tvaṃ vara taṃ (sī.), vara tvaṃ (pī.) bhaññamicchasi yaññamicchasi (?).

Indeed, the truly wise are not displeased upon seeing approaching beggars. You are dear to me, O holy man. Speak, what is it that you desire?

59.

59.

Na ve yācanti sappaññā, dhīro ca veditumarahati;

Uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhanti, esā ariyāna yācanā.

Indeed, the truly wise do not beg; a discerning person ought to understand. The noble ones stand with an intention; this is the asking of the noble ones.

60.

60.

Dadāmi te brāhmaṇa rohiṇīnaṃ, gavaṃ sahassaṃ saha puṅgavena;

Ariyo hi ariyassa kathaṃ na dajjā, sutvāna gāthā tava dhammayuttāti.

I give to you, O holy one, a thousand red cows together with a leading bull. For how could a noble one, having heard your verses that are endowed with Dhamma, not give to a noble one?

Aṭṭhisenakajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Aṭṭhisena Jātaka, the eighth.

404. Kapijātakaṃ (7-1-9)

404. The Kapi Jātaka (7-1-9)

61.

61.

Yattha [T 1.0221] verī nivasati, na vase tattha paṇḍito;

Ekarattaṃ dirattaṃ vā, dukkhaṃ vasati verisu.

Where an enemy lives, a wise person should not dwell, neither for one night nor for two. It is painful to live among enemies.

62.

62.

Diso ve lahucittassa, posassānuvidhīyato;

Ekassa kapino hetu, yūthassa anayo kato.

Truly, a fickle-minded person who follows his own whim becomes an enemy to himself; on account of a single monkey, ruin was brought upon the troop.

63.

63.

Bālova ca (sī. syā. pī.) paṇḍitamānī, yūthassa parihārako;

Sacittassa vasaṃ gantvā, sayethāyaṃ passethāyaṃ (ka.) yathā kapi.

A fool who thinks himself wise, a leader of the troop, having come under the sway of his own mind, lies fallen just like this monkey.

64.

64.

Na sādhu balavā bālo, yūthassa parihārako;

Ahito bhavati ñātīnaṃ, sakuṇānaṃva cetako ceṭako (ka.).

A powerful fool is not good as a leader of a troop; he brings no welfare to his kinsmen, just like a fowler to birds.

65.

65.

Dhīrova [M 1.0163] balavā sādhu, yūthassa parihārako;

Hito bhavati ñātīnaṃ, tidasānaṃva vāsavo.

Only a wise and powerful one is a good leader for a troop; he brings welfare to his kinsmen, like Vāsava to the Tāvatiṃsa gods.

66.

66.

Yo ca sīlañca paññañca, sutañcattani passati;

Ubhinnamatthaṃ carati, attano ca parassa ca.

And one who sees in himself virtue, wisdom, and learning, practices for the welfare of both himself and others.

67.

67.

Tasmā tuleyya mattānaṃ, sīlapaññāsutāmiva sīlaṃ paññaṃ sutaṃpiva (syā.);

Gaṇaṃ vā parihare dhīro, eko vāpi paribbajeti.

Therefore, one should weigh oneself against the measure of virtue, wisdom, and learning. Having done so, a wise person should either lead a group or wander alone.

Kapijātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Kapi Jātaka, the ninth.

405. Bakajātakaṃ (7-1-10)

405. The Baka Jātaka (7-1-10)

68.

68.

Dvāsattati [V 1.0135] gotama bho gotama (ka.) puññakammā, vasavattino [T 1.0222] jātijaraṃ atītā;

Ayamantimā vedagū brahmapatti brahmupapatti (syā. ka.), asmābhijappanti janā pajā (ka.) anekā.

O Gotama, we are ones of seventy-two meritorious deeds, masters of our own will, having overcome birth and aging. This is the final attainment in the Brahma world for a knower of the Vedas; many people long for this state of ours.

69.

69.

Appañhi etaṃ appañca hetaṃ (syā.), appaṃsi etaṃ (ka.) na hi dīghamāyu, yaṃ tvaṃ baka maññasi dīghamāyuṃ;

Sataṃ sahassāni sahassānaṃ (sī. pī. saṃ. ni. 1.175), sahassāna (syā. kaṃ.) nirabbudānaṃ, āyuṃ pajānāmi tavāha brahme.

This lifespan that you consider long, O Baka, is in fact short; it is not long at all. I know your lifespan, O Brahmā, to be a hundred thousand nirabbudas.

70.

70.

Anantadassī bhagavāhamasmi, jātijjaraṃ sokamupātivatto;

Kiṃ me purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ sīlavantaṃ (pī. ka.), ācikkha me taṃ yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ.

You claim, 'I am the Blessed One of limitless vision, who has overcome birth, aging, and sorrow.' If so, what was my ancient observance and virtuous conduct? Declare it to me, that I may know it.

71.

71.

Yaṃ tvaṃ apāyesi bahū manusse, pipāsite ghammani samparete;

Taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

That you gave drink to many people who were thirsty and overcome by the heat—that ancient observance and virtuous conduct of yours I recall, as if just awakened from sleep.

72.

72.

Yaṃ [M 1.0164] eṇikūlasmi janaṃ gahītaṃ, amocayī gayhaka niyyamānaṃ;

Taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

That on the bank of the Eṇī river you freed people who had been seized and were being led away captive—that ancient observance and virtuous conduct of yours I recall, as if just awakened from sleep.

73.

73.

Gaṅgāya sotasmiṃ gahītanāvaṃ, luddena [T 1.0223] nāgena manussakappā;

Amocayi tvaṃ balasā pasayha, taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ;

Suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

That in the current of the Ganges you freed a boat seized by a fierce nāga intending to harm humans, liberating it by force and constraint—that ancient observance and virtuous conduct of yours I recall, as if just awakened from sleep.

74.

74.

Kappo ca te baddhacaro patthacaro (syā.), paṭṭhacaro (ka.) ahosi, sambuddhimantaṃ sambuddhivantaṃ (syā. pī.), sambuddhavantaṃ (ka.) vatinaṃ vatitaṃ (syā.), vatidaṃ (ka.) amaññaṃ;

Taṃ te purāṇaṃ vatasīlavattaṃ, suttappabuddhova anussarāmi.

And Kappa was your disciple of steadfast conduct; you regarded me as an ascetic endowed with true wisdom. That ancient observance and virtuous conduct of yours I recall, as if just awakened from sleep.

75.

75.

Addhā pajānāsi mametamāyuṃ, aññampi jānāsi tathā hi buddho;

Tathā hi tāyaṃ tyāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. 1.175) jalitānubhāvo, obhāsayaṃ tiṭṭhati brahmalokanti.

Surely you know this lifespan of mine, and you know other things as well, for you are indeed the Buddha. And so this blazing power of yours stands illuminating the Brahma-world.

Bakajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Baka Jātaka, the tenth.

Kukkuvaggo paṭhamo.

The Kukku Chapter, the First.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse:

Varakaṇṇika cāpavaro sutano, atha gijjha sarohitamacchavaro;

Puna paṇṇaka dasaṇṇaka (sī. syā. pī.) senaka yācanako, atha veri sabrahmabakena dasāti.

The Varakaṇṇika and Cāpavara Jātakas, the Sutana Jātaka, then the Gijjha and Sarohitamaccha Jātakas; again, the Paṇṇaka, Senaka, and Yācanaka Jātakas; then the Veri Jātaka, together with the Brahmabaka Jātaka, make ten.

2. Gandhāravaggo

2. The Gandhāra Chapter.

406. Gandhārajātakaṃ (7-2-1)

406. The Gandhāra Jātaka (7-2-1)

76.

76.

Hitvā [T 1.0224][V 1.0136][M 1.0165] gāmasahassāni, paripuṇṇāni soḷasa;

Koṭṭhāgārāni phītāni, sannidhiṃ dāni kubbasi.

Having abandoned sixteen thousand prosperous villages and overflowing granaries, do you now make a hoard?

77.

77.

Hitvā gandhāravisayaṃ, pahūtadhanadhāriyaṃ dhāniyaṃ (sī. pī.), dhaññanti attho;

Pasāsanato pasāsanito (sī. syā.), pasāsanāto (pī.) nikkhanto, idha dāni pasāsasi.

Having abandoned the land of Gandhāra with its abundant wealth and grain, having gone forth from instructing, do you now instruct here?

78.

78.

Dhammaṃ bhaṇāmi vedeha, adhammo me na ruccati;

Dhammaṃ me bhaṇamānassa, na pāpamupalimpati.

I speak the Dhamma, O Videha; what is not Dhamma is not pleasing to me. While I am speaking the Dhamma, no evil stains me.

79.

79.

Yena kenaci vaṇṇena, paro labhati ruppanaṃ;

Mahatthiyampi ce vācaṃ, na taṃ bhāseyya paṇḍito.

If in any way another might be vexed, a wise person should not utter that speech, even if it has great meaning.

80.

80.

Kāmaṃ ruppatu vā mā vā, bhusaṃva vikirīyatu;

Dhammaṃ me bhaṇamānassa, na pāpamupalimpati.

Let him be vexed or not, as he wishes, or let him be scattered like chaff. For me, who speaks the Dhamma, no evil can stain me.

81.

81.

No ce assa sakā buddhi, vinayo vā susikkhito;

Vane andhamahiṃsova andhamahisova (sī. pī.) careyya bahuko jano.

If one did not have one's own wisdom or well-learned discipline, many people would wander like a blind buffalo in the forest.

82.

82.

Yasmā ca panidhekacce, āceramhi ācāramhi (sī. pī.) susikkhitā;

Tasmā vinītavinayā, caranti susamāhitāti.

But since some here are well-trained by a teacher, therefore, disciplined by the training, they live well-composed.

Gandhārajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Gandhāra Jātaka, the first.

407. Mahākapijātakaṃ (7-2-2)

407. The Great Monkey Jātaka (7-2-2)

83.

83.

Attānaṃ [T 1.0225] saṅkamaṃ katvā, yo sotthiṃ samatārayi;

Kiṃ tvaṃ tesaṃ kime kimo (sī. pī.), kiṃ me (syā.) tuyhaṃ, honti ete hete (syā.), so te (ka.) mahākapi.

You who made yourself a bridge and ferried them across to safety—what are you to them, and what are they to you, O great monkey?

84.

84.

Rājāhaṃ issaro tesaṃ, yūthassa parihārako;

Tesaṃ sokaparetānaṃ, bhītānaṃ te arindama.

I am their king and lord, the protector of the troop. O subduer of foes, it was for them, who were overcome by sorrow and afraid of you.

85.

85.

Ullaṅghayitvā sa laṅghayitvā (pī.), sulaṅghayitvā (ka.) attānaṃ, vissaṭṭhadhanuno sataṃ;

Tato aparapādesu, daḷhaṃ bandhaṃ latāguṇaṃ.

Having tied a strong creeper-vine to my hind feet, I leaped a hundred bow-lengths like an arrow from a released bow.

86.

86.

Chinnabbhamiva [M 1.0166] vātena, nuṇṇo nunno (sī.) rukkhaṃ upāgamiṃ;

Sohaṃ appabhavaṃ tattha, sākhaṃ hatthehi aggahiṃ.

Driven by the wind like a scattered cloud, I went toward the tree. But falling short, I grasped a branch with my hands.

87.

87.

Taṃ [V 1.0137] maṃ viyāyataṃ santaṃ, sākhāya ca latāya ca;

Samanukkamantā pādehi, sotthiṃ sākhāmigā gatā.

And over me, stretched taut between the branch and the vine, the monkeys trod with their feet and went across to safety.

88.

88.

Taṃ maṃ na tapate bandho, mato vadho (sī. syā. pī.) me na tapessati;

Sukhamāharitaṃ tesaṃ, yesaṃ rajjamakārayiṃ.

That bond does not torment me, nor will death torment me. I have brought happiness to those for whom I exercised kingship.

89.

89.

Esā te upamā rāja, taṃ suṇohi arindama atthasandassanī katā (pī.);

Raññā raṭṭhassa yoggassa, balassa nigamassa ca;

Sabbesaṃ sukhameṭṭhabbaṃ, khattiyena pajānatāti.

This is a simile for you, O king; listen to it, O subduer of foes. A wise khattiya should seek the happiness of all: of the country, the beasts of burden, the army, and the towns.

Mahākapijātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Great Monkey Jātaka, the second.

408. Kumbhakārajātakaṃ (7-2-3)

408. The Kumbhakāra Jātaka (7-2-3)

90.

90.

Ambāhamaddaṃ [T 1.0226] vanamantarasmiṃ, nīlobhāsaṃ phalitaṃ phalinaṃ (pī.) saṃvirūḷhaṃ;

Tamaddasaṃ phalahetu vibhaggaṃ, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

Amidst the forest, I saw a mango tree, dark-gleaming, fruitful, and flourishing. I saw it broken for the sake of its fruit. Having seen that, I wander on the alms-round.

91.

91.

Selaṃ sumaṭṭhaṃ naravīraniṭṭhitaṃ naravidduniṭṭhitaṃ (ka.), nārī yugaṃ dhārayi appasaddaṃ;

Dutiyañca āgamma ahosi saddo, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

A woman wore a single bracelet—made of gems, well-polished, fashioned by skilled men—and it was soundless. When a second was added, a sound arose. Having seen that, I wander on the alms-round.

92.

92.

Dijā dijaṃ kuṇapamāharantaṃ, ekaṃ samānaṃ bahukā samecca;

Āhārahetū paripātayiṃsu, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

Many birds, having gathered together, attacked a solitary bird that was carrying a piece of flesh, for the sake of that food. Having seen that, I wander on the alms-round.

93.

93.

Usabhāhamaddaṃ yūthassa majjhe, calakkakuṃ vaṇṇabalūpapannaṃ;

Tamaddasaṃ kāmahetu vitunnaṃ, taṃ disvā bhikkhācariyaṃ carāmi.

In the midst of the herd, I saw a bull with a swaying hump, endowed with beauty and strength. I saw it being tormented on account of sensual desire. Having seen that, I wander on the alms-round.

94.

94.

Karaṇḍako [M 1.0167] karaṇḍunāma (sī. pī.) kaliṅgānaṃ, gandhārānañca naggaji;

Nimirājā videhānaṃ, pañcālānañca dummukho;

Karaṇḍaka of the Kaliṅgas, Naggaji of the Gandhāras, Nimi, king of the Videhas, and Dummukha of the Pañcālas—

Ete raṭṭhāni hitvāna, pabbajiṃsu akiñcanā.

these, having abandoned their kingdoms, went forth without possessions.

95.

95.

Sabbepime [T 1.0227] devasamā samāgatā, aggī yathā pajjalito tathevime;

Ahampi eko carissāmi bhaggavi, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikāni.

O Bhaggavī, all these who are gathered here are like devas; just as a fire blazes, so do they blaze. I too, having abandoned sensual pleasures in their various forms, shall wander alone.

96.

96.

Ayameva kālo na hi añño atthi, anusāsitā me na bhaveyya pacchā;

Ahampi ekā carissāmi bhaggava, sakuṇīva muttā purisassa hatthā.

This is the very time; there is no other. For later, there may not be an instructor for me. I too, O Bhaggava, shall wander alone, like a female bird freed from a man's hand.

97.

97.

Āmaṃ pakkañca jānanti, atho loṇaṃ aloṇakaṃ;

Tamahaṃ disvāna pabbajiṃ, careva tvaṃ carāmahanti.

Children know the raw and the cooked, and also the salted and the unsalted. Having seen that, I went forth. You too should wander, and so shall I.

Kumbhakārajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Kumbhakāra Jātaka, the third.

409. Daḷhadhammajātakaṃ (7-2-4)

409. The Daḷhadhamma Jātaka (7-2-4)

98.

98.

Ahaṃ [V 1.0138] ce daḷhadhammassa daḷhadhammāya (pī.), vahanti nābhirādhayiṃ;

Dharantī urasi sallaṃ, yuddhe vikkantacārinī.

If I, bearing a dart in my breast and striving valiantly in battle, did not please Daḷhadhamma while carrying out my duties...

99.

99.

Nūna rājā na jānāti na ha nūna rājā jānāti (sī. pī.), mama vikkamaporisaṃ;

Saṅgāme sukatantāni, dūtavippahitāni ca.

Surely the king does not know my valorous effort, my well-executed deeds in battle, and my dispatching of envoys.

100.

100.

Sā nūnāhaṃ marissāmi, abandhu aparāyinī aparāyiṇī (sī.), aparāyaṇī (?);

Tadā [T 1.0228] hi tathā hi (pī.) kumbhakārassa, dinnā chakaṇahārikā.

Surely I shall die, without kin, without refuge; for then I, a carrier of dung, was given to a potter.

101.

101.

Yāvatāsīsatī poso, tāvadeva pavīṇati;

Atthāpāye jahanti naṃ, oṭṭhibyādhiṃva khattiyo.

For as long as a person has need of another, for just that long does one attend to them. When their usefulness is gone, they are abandoned, just as a king abandons a camel with a mouth disease.

102.

102.

Yo pubbe katakalyāṇo, katattho nāvabujjhati;

Atthā tassa palujjanti, ye honti abhipatthitā.

Whoever has previously received a kindness but does not recognize the good deed done for him, all the aims he desires come to ruin.

103.

103.

Yo [M 1.0168] pubbe katakalyāṇo, katattho manubujjhati;

Atthā tassa pavaḍḍhanti, ye honti abhipatthitā.

Whoever, having previously had a good deed done for him and a benefit conferred, is grateful; all the aims he desires will prosper.

104.

104.

Taṃ vo vadāmi bhaddante bhaddaṃ vo (sī. syā. pī.), yāvantettha samāgatā;

Sabbe kataññuno hotha, ciraṃ saggamhi ṭhassathāti.

Therefore, good sirs, I say this to all of you who are assembled here: All of you, be grateful. You will long remain in the heavenly world.

Daḷhadhammajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Daḷhadhamma Jātaka, the fourth.

410. Somadattajātakaṃ (7-2-5)

410. The Somadatta Jātaka (7-2-5)

105.

105.

Yo maṃ pure paccuḍḍeti paccudeti (sī. syā. pī.), paccuṭṭheti (ka.), araññe dūramāyato;

So na dissati mātaṅgo, somadatto kuhiṃ gato.

410. The well-proportioned elephant named Somadatta, who formerly came forth from afar in the forest to greet me—that elephant is not to be seen. Where has Somadatta gone?

106.

106.

Ayaṃ vā so mato seti, allasiṅgaṃva vacchito allapiṅkava chijjito (sī. pī.), allapītaṃva vicchito (syā.);

Bhumyā nipatito seti, amarā vata kuñjaro.

This indeed is he, lying dead, like a large shoot of the mālūra creeper cut off and laid upon the ground. He lies fallen on the ground; alas, the elephant is dead.

107.

107.

Anagāriyupetassa, vippamuttassa te sato;

Samaṇassa na taṃ sādhu, yaṃ petamanusocasi.

For you, being one endowed with the homeless life, liberated, a recluse, it is not proper that you grieve for the dead.

108.

108.

Saṃvāsena have sakka, manussassa migassa vā;

Hadaye [T 1.0229] jāyate pemaṃ, taṃ na sakkā asocituṃ.

Indeed, Sakka, through living together with a human or a beast, love is born in the heart. It is not possible not to grieve for that beloved one.

109.

109.

Mataṃ marissaṃ rodanti, ye rudanti lapanti ca;

Tasmā tvaṃ isi mā rodi, roditaṃ moghamāhu santo.

They weep for the dead and the dying, those who weep and wail. Therefore, O sage, do not weep; the good say that weeping is in vain.

110.

110.

Kanditena [V 1.0139] have brahme, mato peto samuṭṭhahe;

Sabbe saṅgamma rodāma, aññamaññassa ñātake.

Indeed, O holy one, if by weeping the departed dead could rise up, we would all gather together and weep for one another's kinsmen.

111.

111.

Ādittaṃ vata maṃ santaṃ, ghatasittaṃva pāvakaṃ;

Vārinā viya osiñcaṃ, sabbaṃ nibbāpaye daraṃ.

You have extinguished all my anguish, for I was blazing like a fire sprinkled with ghee, as if you were sprinkling me with water.

112.

112.

Abbahī vata me sallaṃ, yamāsi hadayassitaṃ;

Yo me sokaparetassa, puttasokaṃ apānudi.

Indeed, you have extracted the dart that was lodged in my heart, you who have dispelled the grief for my son from me, who was overcome by sorrow.

113.

113.

Sohaṃ abbūḷhasallosmi, vītasoko anāvilo;

Na socāmi na rodāmi, tava sutvāna vāsavāti.

I am one whose dart has been extracted, free from sorrow, untroubled. I no longer grieve or weep, having heard you, O Vāsava.

Somadattajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Somadatta Jātaka, the fifth.

411. Susīmajātakaṃ (7-2-6)

411. The Susīma Jātaka (7-2-6)

114.

114.

Kāḷāni [M 1.0169] kesāni pure ahesuṃ, jātāni sīsamhi yathāpadese;

Tānajja setāni susīma susima (ka.) disvā, dhammaṃ cara brahmacariyassa kālo.

Formerly the hairs on my head were black, growing in their proper place. Seeing them white today, O Susīma, practice the Dhamma! It is time for the holy life.

115.

115.

Mameva deva palitaṃ na tuyhaṃ, mameva sīsaṃ mama uttamaṅgaṃ;

“Atthaṃ [T 1.0230] karissa”nti musā abhāṇiṃ abhāsiṃ (ka.), ekāparādhaṃ khama rājaseṭṭha.

411. The grey hair is mine, O lord, not yours; it is my head, my chief limb. Thinking, ‘I will do him a service,’ I spoke falsely. Forgive this single offense, O best of kings.

116.

116.

Daharo tuvaṃ dassaniyosi rāja, paṭhamuggato hosi hohi (sī.), hoti (ka.) yathā kaḷīro;

Rajjañca kārehi mamañca passa, mā kālikaṃ anudhāvī janinda.

You are young and handsome, O king, like a newly emerged bamboo shoot. Rule your kingdom and look after me; do not pursue an untimely course, O lord of people.

117.

117.

Passāmi vohaṃ dahariṃ kumāriṃ, sāmaṭṭhapassaṃ sutanuṃ sumajjhaṃ;

Kāḷappavāḷāva pavellamānā, palobhayantīva sā lobhayantīva (pī.) naresu gacchati.

I see a young maiden with a smooth complexion, a beautiful body, and a slender waist. She goes among men, swaying like a dark coral sprout, as if to entice them.

118.

118.

Tamena passāmiparena nāriṃ, āsītikaṃ nāvutikaṃ va jaccā;

Daṇḍaṃ gahetvāna pavedhamānaṃ, gopānasībhoggasamaṃ carantiṃ.

At another time, I see that very same woman, eighty or ninety years of age, going about holding a staff and trembling, bent like a roof-rafter.

119.

119.

Sohaṃ tamevānuvicintayanto, eko sayāmi passāmi (ka.) sayanassa majjhe;

“Ahampi evaṃ” iti pekkhamāno, na gahe rame na gehe rame (sī.), gehe na rame (syā. ka.) brahmacariyassa kālo.

Reflecting on just that, I lie alone in the middle of my bed. Considering, ‘I too will be like this,’ I take no delight in the household life. It is time for the holy life.

120.

120.

Rajjuvālambanī [M 1.0170] cesā, yā gehe vasato rati;

Evampi [T 1.0231] chetvāna vajanti dhīrā, anapekkhino kāmasukhaṃ pahāyāti.

This delight for one dwelling at home is a rope to cling to. Having cut even this, the wise go forth, unconcerned, abandoning sensual pleasure.

Susīmajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Susīma Jātaka, the sixth.

412. Koṭasimbalijātakaṃ (7-2-7)

412. The Koṭasimbali Jātaka (7-2-7)

121.

121.

Ahaṃ dasasataṃbyāmaṃ, uragamādāya āgato;

Tañca mañca mahākāyaṃ, dhārayaṃ nappavedhasi na pavedhayi (ka.).

I have come, having seized a serpent a thousand fathoms long. Seeing that great-bodied one and me who am bearing it, you do not tremble.

122.

122.

Athimaṃ [V 1.0140] khuddakaṃ pakkhiṃ, appamaṃsataraṃ mayā;

Dhārayaṃ byathasi byādhase (sī.), byadhase (pī.), byādhasi (ka.) bhītā bhīto (sī. syā. pī.), kamatthaṃ koṭasimbali koṭisimbali (sī. pī.).

But now, seeing this tiny bird with very little flesh, borne by me, you tremble with fear. For what reason, O Koṭasimbali?

123.

123.

Maṃsabhakkho tuvaṃ rāja, phalabhakkho ayaṃ dijo;

Ayaṃ nigrodhabījāni, pilakkhudumbarāni ca;

Assatthāni ca bhakkhitvā, khandhe me ohadissati.

412. You, O king, are a flesh-eater, but this bird eats fruit. After eating the seeds of the banyan, pilakkha, udumbara, and assattha, it will deposit them on my trunk.

124.

124.

Te rukkhā saṃvirūhanti, mama passe nivātajā;

Te maṃ pariyonandhissanti, arukkhaṃ maṃ karissare.

Those trees will sprout up, born in a sheltered spot at my side. They will completely envelop me and make me no longer a tree.

125.

125.

Santi aññepi rukkhā se, mūlino khandhino dumā;

Iminā sakuṇajātena, bījamāharitā hatā.

There are other trees as well, with roots and trunks, that have been destroyed by seeds brought by this kind of bird.

126.

126.

Ajjhārūhābhivaḍḍhanti ajjhārūḷhābhivaḍḍhanti (sī. pī.), brahantampi vanappatiṃ;

Tasmā rāja pavedhāmi, sampassaṃnāgataṃ bhayaṃ.

Growing upon it, they overwhelm even a great forest tree. Therefore, O king, I tremble, foreseeing the future danger.

127.

127.

Saṅkeyya saṅkitabbāni, rakkheyyānāgataṃ bhayaṃ;

Anāgatabhayā [T 1.0232] dhīro, ubho loke avekkhatīti.

One should be wary of what is worthy of suspicion; one should guard against a future danger. Because of fear of what is yet to come, the wise person has regard for both worlds.

Koṭasimbalijātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Koṭasimbali Jātaka, the seventh.

413. Dhūmakārijātakaṃ (7-2-8)

413. The Dhūmakāri Jātaka (7-2-8)

128.

128.

Rājā apucchi vidhuraṃ, dhammakāmo yudhiṭṭhilo;

Api brāhmaṇa jānāsi, ko eko bahu socati.

The king of the Yudhiṭṭhila clan, a lover of righteousness, asked Vidhura: “Brahmin, do you know who it is that, being one, grieves much?”

129.

129.

Brāhmaṇo [M 1.0171] ajayūthena, pahūtedho bahūtejo (pī. ka.), bahutendo (syā.) vane vasaṃ;

Dhūmaṃ akāsi vāseṭṭho, rattindivamatandito.

A brahmin of the Vāseṭṭha clan, dwelling in the forest with a herd of goats and abundant fuel, diligently made smoke day and night.

130.

130.

Tassa taṃ dhūmagandhena, sarabhā makasaḍḍitā makasadditā (sī. syā.), makasaṭṭitā (pī. ka.);

Vassāvāsaṃ upāgacchuṃ, dhūmakārissa santike.

Drawn by the smell of his smoke, Sarabha deer, tormented by mosquitoes, approached the smoke-maker’s presence to spend the rainy season.

131.

131.

Sarabhesu manaṃ katvā, ajā so nāvabujjhatha;

Āgacchantī vajantī vā āgacchanti vajanti vā (syā. pī.), āgacchantiṃ vajantiṃ vā (ka.), tassa tā vinasuṃ vinassuṃ (sī.) ajā.

413. Having set his affection on the Sarabha deer, he paid no attention to his goats. He did not notice whether they were coming or going; those goats of his perished.

132.

132.

Sarabhā sarade kāle, pahīnamakase vane;

Pāvisuṃ giriduggāni, nadīnaṃ pabhavāni ca.

In the autumn season, when the forest was free of mosquitoes, the Sarabha deer entered the mountain fastnesses and the sources of the rivers.

133.

133.

Sarabhe ca gate disvā, ajā ca vibhavaṃ gatā aje ca vibhavaṃ gate (ka.);

Kiso ca vivaṇṇo cāsi, paṇḍurogī ca brāhmaṇo.

Seeing that the Sarabha deer had gone and that his goats were ruined, the brahmin became thin, discolored, and afflicted with the pale disease.

134.

134.

Evaṃ [V 1.0141] yo saṃ niraṃkatvā, āgantuṃ kurute piyaṃ;

So eko bahu socati, dhūmakārīva brāhmaṇoti.

Thus, whoever, neglecting their own, holds a newcomer dear, that person grieves much alone, like the smoke-making brahmin.

Dhūmakārijātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Dhūmakāri Jātaka, the Eighth.

414. Jāgarajātakaṃ (7-2-9)

414. The Jāgara Jātaka (7.2.9)

135.

135.

Kodha [T 1.0233] jāgarataṃ sutto, kodha suttesu jāgaro;

Ko mametaṃ vijānāti, ko taṃ paṭibhaṇāti me.

“Who here is asleep among the waking? Who here is awake among the sleeping? Who understands this of mine? Who can provide me with an answer?”

136.

136.

Ahaṃ jāgarataṃ sutto, ahaṃ suttesu jāgaro;

Ahametaṃ vijānāmi, ahaṃ paṭibhaṇāmi te.

“I am asleep among the waking; I am awake among the sleeping. I understand this, and I can provide you with an answer.”

137.

137.

Kathaṃ jāgarataṃ sutto, kathaṃ suttesu jāgaro;

Kathaṃ etaṃ vijānāsi, kathaṃ paṭibhaṇāsi me.

“How are you asleep among the waking? How are you awake among the sleeping? How do you understand this of mine? How can you provide me with an answer?”

138.

138.

Ye dhammaṃ nappajānanti, saṃyamoti damoti ca;

Tesu suppamānesu, ahaṃ jaggāmi devate.

“Those who do not know the Dhamma—that is, restraint and self-control—among them, who are heedless and asleep, I am awake, O deity.”

139.

139.

Yesaṃ rāgo ca doso ca, avijjā ca virājitā;

Tesu jāgaramānesu, ahaṃ suttosmi devate.

“Those for whom lust, hatred, and ignorance have faded away—among them, who are awake, I am asleep, O deity.”

140.

140.

Evaṃ [M 1.0172] jāgarataṃ sutto, evaṃ suttesu jāgaro;

Evametaṃ vijānāmi, evaṃ paṭibhaṇāmi te.

“Thus I am asleep among the waking; thus I am awake among the sleeping. In this way I understand this; in this way I provide you with an answer.”

141.

141.

Sādhu jāgarataṃ sutto, sādhu suttesu jāgaro;

Sādhumetaṃ vijānāsi, sādhu paṭibhaṇāsi meti.

“Excellent, you are asleep among the waking. Excellent, you are awake among the sleeping. Excellent that you understand this of mine; excellent that you provide me with an answer.”

Jāgarajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Jāgara Jātaka, the Ninth.

415. Kummāsapiṇḍijātakaṃ (7-2-10)

415. The Kummāsapiṇḍi Jātaka (7.2.10)

142.

142.

Na kiratthi anomadassisu, pāricariyā buddhesu appikā appakā (ka.);

Sukkhāya [T 1.0234] aloṇikāya ca, passaphalaṃ kummāsapiṇḍiyā.
