I have great ministers, counselors, and attendants. They speak of Bārāṇasī as a place with abundant meat, liquor, and rice.

105.

105.

Athopi vāṇijā phītā, nānāraṭṭhehi āgatā;

Tesu me vihitā rakkhā, evaṃ jānāhuposatha.

Moreover, wealthy merchants have come from various countries. For them, I have arranged protection—thus, know, O Uposatha.

106.

106.

Dhammena kira ñātīnaṃ, rajjaṃ kārehi saṃvara;

Medhāvī paṇḍito cāsi cāpi (sī. pī.), athopi ñātinaṃ hito.

O Saṃvara, rule the kingdom of your kinsmen righteously, it is said. You are intelligent and wise, and also a benefactor to your kinsmen.

107.

107.

Taṃ taṃ ñātiparibyūḷhaṃ, nānāratanamocitaṃ;

Amittā nappasahanti, indaṃva asurādhipoti.

You, surrounded by kinsmen and adorned with various jewels, enemies cannot oppress, just as the king of the asuras cannot oppress Inda.

Saṃvarajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Saṃvara Jātaka, the Eighth.

463. Suppārakajātakaṃ (9)

463. The Suppāraka Jātaka (9)

108.

108.

Ummujjanti [M 1.0239] nimujjanti, manussā khuranāsikā;

Suppārakaṃ [T 1.0320] taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo ayaṃ.

Men with noses like razor blades emerge and submerge. O Suppāraka, we ask you, what is the name of this ocean?

109.

109.

Kurukacchā bharukacchā (sī. syā. pī. aṭṭha.) payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, khuramālīti vuccati.

For merchants seeking wealth who have departed from Kurukaccha, when their ship is lost, this ocean is called Khuramālī.

110.

110.

Yathā aggīva suriyova aggi suriyo ca (syā.), aggīva sūriyo (ka.), samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo ayaṃ.

Like fire, like the sun, the ocean appears. We ask you, O Suppāraka, what is the name of this ocean?

111.

111.

Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, aggimālīti vuccati.

For merchants seeking wealth who have departed from Kurukaccha, when their ship is lost, this ocean is called Aggimālī.

112.

112.

Yathā dadhīva khīraṃva dadhi ca khīraṃ ca (syā.), evamuparipi, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo ayaṃ.

Like curds or milk, the ocean appears. We ask you, O Suppāraka, what is the name of this ocean?

113.

113.

Kurukacchā [V 1.0187] payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, dadhimālīti khīramālīti (ka.) vuccati.

For merchants seeking wealth who have departed from Kurukaccha, when their ship is lost, this ocean is called Dadhimālī.

114.

114.

Yathā kusova sassova, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo ayaṃ.

Like kusa grass or a crop, the ocean appears. We ask you, O Suppāraka, what is the name of this ocean?

115.

115.

Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, kusamālīti vuccati.

For merchants seeking wealth who have departed from Kurukaccha, when their ship is lost, this ocean is called Kusamālī.

116.

116.

Yathā naḷova veḷūva, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo ayaṃ.

Like a reed or bamboo, the ocean appears. We ask you, O Suppāraka, what is the name of this ocean?

117.

117.

Kurukacchā payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, naḷamālīti vuccati.

For merchants seeking wealth who have departed from Kurukaccha, when their ship is lost, this ocean is called Naḷamālī.

118.

118.

Mahabbhayo bhiṃsanako, saddo suyyatimānuso samuddo suyyata’mānuso (sī. pī. aṭṭha.);

Yathā [T 1.0321] sobbho papātova, samuddo paṭidissati;

Suppārakaṃ taṃ pucchāma, samuddo katamo ayaṃ.

A greatly perilous, terrifying, inhuman sound is heard. The ocean appears like a great chasm. We ask you, O Suppāraka, what is the name of this ocean?

119.

119.

Kurukacchā [M 1.0240] payātānaṃ, vāṇijānaṃ dhanesinaṃ;

Nāvāya vippanaṭṭhāya, baḷavāmukhīti vaḷabhāmukhīti (sī. syā.), balavāmukhīti (syā. ka.) vuccati.

For merchants seeking wealth who have departed from Kurukaccha, when their ship is lost, this ocean is called Baḷavāmukhī.

120.

120.

Yato sarāmi attānaṃ, yato pattosmi viññutaṃ;

Nābhijānāmi sañcicca, ekapāṇampi hiṃsitaṃ;

Etena saccavajjena, sotthiṃ nāvā nivattatūti.

From when I remember myself, from when I have attained discernment, I do not know of having intentionally harmed even a single living being. By this statement of truth, may the ship return safely.

Suppārakajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Suppāraka Jātaka, the Ninth.

Ekādasakanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Eleventh Nipāta is finished.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Of that, the summary:

Sirimātusuposakanāgavaro, puna juṇhaka dhammamudayavaro;

Atha pāni yudhañcayako ca, dasaratha saṃvara pāragatena navāti.

The Mātuposaka Jātaka; again, the Juṇha, Dhamma, and Udaya Jātakas; then the Pāniya and Yudhañcaya Jātakas; together with the Dasaratha, Saṃvara, and Suppāraka Jātakas, there are nine.

12. Dvādasakanipāto

12. The Twelfth Nipāta

464. Cūḷakuṇālajātakaṃ (1)

464. The Cūḷakuṇāla Jātaka (1)

1.

1.

Luddhānaṃ [T 1.0322][V 1.0188][M 1.0241] khuddānaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) lahucittānaṃ, akataññūna dubbhinaṃ;

Nādevasatto puriso, thīnaṃ saddhātumarahati.

A man not possessed by the deva of passion ought not to trust women who are greedy, fickle-minded, ungrateful, and treacherous.

2.

2.

Na tā pajānanti kataṃ na kiccaṃ, na mātaraṃ pitaraṃ bhātaraṃ vā;

Anariyā samatikkantadhammā, sasseva cittassa vasaṃ vajanti.

They do not recognize a favor done, nor a duty to be done, nor mother, father, or brother. Ignoble, with a nature that transgresses righteousness, they fall under the sway of their own minds.

3.

3.

Cirānuvuṭṭhampi cirānuvutthampi (sī. pī.) piyaṃ manāpaṃ, anukampakaṃ pāṇasamampi bhattuṃ santaṃ (sī. syā. pī.);

Āvāsu kiccesu ca naṃ jahanti, tasmāhamitthīnaṃ na vissasāmi.

Even a husband with whom they have long dwelt, who is dear, pleasing, compassionate, and like life itself—they abandon him in the event of some danger or affair. Therefore, I do not trust women.

4.

4.

Thīnañhi cittaṃ yathā vānarassa, kannappakannaṃ yathā rukkhachāyā;

Calācalaṃ hadayamitthiyānaṃ, cakkassa nemi viya parivattati.

Indeed, the mind of a woman is like that of a monkey; like the ever-shifting shade of a tree. The heart of women is utterly unstable; it revolves like the rim of a wheel.

5.

5.

Yadā tā passanti samekkhamānā, ādeyyarūpaṃ purisassa vittaṃ;

Saṇhāhi vācāhi nayanti menaṃ, kambojakā [T 1.0323] jalajeneva assaṃ.

When they, looking on, see a man's wealth that is ripe for the taking, they lead him on with gentle words, just as the Kambojans lead a horse with a water-reed snare.

6.

6.

Yadā na passanti samekkhamānā, ādeyyarūpaṃ purisassa vittaṃ;

Samantato naṃ parivajjayanti, tiṇṇo nadīpāragatova kullaṃ.

When, looking on, they do not see a man's wealth that is ripe for the taking, they shun him from all sides, just as one who has crossed to the other shore abandons the raft.

7.

7.

Silesūpamā [M 1.0242] sikhiriva sabbabhakkhā, tikkhamāyā nadīriva sīghasotā;

Sevanti hetā piyamappiyañca, nāvā yathā orakūlaṃ parañca.

They are like birdlime, like all-devouring fire; they are sharp in deceit, like a swift-flowing river. They associate with both the dear and the detested, just as a boat serves this shore and the other.

8.

8.

Na tā ekassa na dvinnaṃ, āpaṇova pasārito;

Yo tā mayhanti maññeyya, vātaṃ jālena bādhaye bandhaye (syā. ka.).

They belong not to one or two; they are like a spread-out marketplace. Whoever should think, “They are mine,” might as well try to bind the wind with a net.

9.

9.

Yathā nadī ca pantho ca, pānāgāraṃ sabhā papā;

Evaṃ lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati imissā gāthāya pubbaddhāparaddhaṃ vipariyāyena dissati (ka.).

Like a river, a road, a tavern, a public hall, a drinking-water stand—so indeed are women in this world; for them, no boundary exists.

10.

10.

Ghatāsanasamā etā, kaṇhasappasirūpamā;

Gāvo bahitiṇasseva, omasanti varaṃ varaṃ.

They are like fire, like the head of a black serpent. They consume one choice man after another, just as cows graze upon the abundant grass.

11.

11.

Ghatāsanaṃ kuñjaraṃ kaṇhasappaṃ, muddhābhisittaṃ pamadā ca sabbā;

Ete naro niccayato niccayatto (sī. pī.) bhajetha, tesaṃ have dubbidu sabbabhāvo saccabhāvo (syā.).

Fire, an elephant, a black serpent, an anointed king, and all women—a man should associate with these five with constant mindfulness, for indeed, their entire nature is difficult to fathom.

12.

12.

Naccantavaṇṇā [T 1.0324][V 1.0189] na bahūnaṃ kantā, na dakkhiṇā pamadā sevitabbā;

Na parassa bhariyā na dhanassa hetu, etitthiyo pañca na sevitabbāti.

A woman of excessive beauty, one desired by many, or a clever and enticing woman should not be associated with; nor another's wife, nor one for the sake of wealth. These five types of women should not be associated with.

Cūḷakuṇālajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Cūḷakuṇāla Jātaka, the First.

465. Bhaddasālajātakaṃ (2)

465. The Bhaddasāla Jātaka (2)

13.

13.

Kā tvaṃ suddhehi vatthehi, aghe vehāyasaṃ vehāsayaṃ (sī. pī.) ṭhitā;

Kena tyāssūni vattanti, kuto taṃ bhayamāgataṃ.

Who are you, clad in pure garments, standing unsupported in the sky? For what reason do your tears flow? From where has this fear come to you?

14.

14.

Taveva deva vijite, bhaddasāloti maṃ vidū;

Saṭṭhi saṭṭhiṃ (sī. pī.) vassasahassāni, tiṭṭhato pūjitassa me.

O Deva, in your very own kingdom, they know me as Bhaddasāla. For sixty thousand years I have stood here, being worshipped.

15.

15.

Kārayantā [M 1.0243] nagarāni, agāre ca disampati;

Vividhe cāpi pāsāde, na maṃ te accamaññisuṃ;

Yatheva maṃ te pūjesuṃ, tatheva tvampi pūjaya.

Those lords of the directions, while having cities, houses, and various palaces built, did not treat me with contempt. Just as they worshipped me, so should you, too, worship me.

16.

16.

Taṃ ivāhaṃ tañca ahaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) na passāmi, thūlaṃ kāyena te dumaṃ;

Ārohapariṇāhena, abhirūposi jātiyā.

I do not see another tree as massive in body as you. In height and circumference, you are beautiful by nature.

17.

17.

Pāsādaṃ kārayissāmi, ekatthambhaṃ manoramaṃ;

Tattha taṃ upanessāmi, ciraṃ te yakkha jīvitaṃ.

I will have a delightful palace with a single pillar built. There I will bring you. Your life, O Yakkha, will be long.

18.

18.

Evaṃ cittaṃ udapādi, sarīrena vinābhāvo;

Puthuso maṃ vikantitvā, khaṇḍaso avakantatha.

Since this thought has arisen—that there must be separation from my body—then having cut me up in many ways, cut me into pieces.

19.

19.

Agge [T 1.0325] ca chetvā majjhe ca, pacchā mūlamhi chindatha mūlañca chindatha (sī.), mūlaṃ vichindatha (pī.);

Evaṃ me chijjamānassa, na dukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ siyā.

Having cut the top and the middle, afterwards, cut at the root. For me, being cut in this way, death would not be painful.

20.

20.

Hatthapādaṃ hatthapāde (ka.) yathā chinde chinne (ka.), kaṇṇanāsañca jīvato;

Tato pacchā siro chinde, taṃ dukkhaṃ maraṇaṃ siyā.

Just as if one were to cut the hands and feet, the ears and nose of a living person, and after that cut the head—that would be a painful death.

21.

21.

Sukhaṃ nu khaṇḍaso chinnaṃ, bhaddasālavanappati;

Kiṃ hetu kiṃ upādāya, khaṇḍaso chinnamicchasi.

Is it pleasant to be cut piece by piece, O Bhaddasāla, lord of the forest? For what reason, on what grounds, do you wish to be cut piece by piece?

22.

22.

Yañca hetumupādāya, hetuṃ dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ;

Khaṇḍaso chinnamicchāmi, mahārāja suṇohi me.

O great king, listen to my reason for wishing to be cut piece by piece, a reason that is connected with the Dhamma.

23.

23.

Ñātī me sukhasaṃvaddhā, mama passe nivātajā;

Tepihaṃ upahiṃseyyaṃ, paresaṃ asukhocitaṃ.

My kinsfolk have grown up in comfort, born in a sheltered place beside me. I would harm them too, thus causing sorrow for others.

24.

24.

Ceteyyarūpaṃ [V 1.0190] cetabbarūpaṃ (sī. pī.) cetesi, bhaddasālavanappati;

Hitakāmosi ñātīnaṃ, abhayaṃ samma dammi teti.

You have conceived a worthy thought, O Bhaddasāla, lord of the forest. You desire the welfare of your kinsmen; friend, I grant you safety.

Bhaddasālajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Bhaddasāla Jātaka, the Second.

466. Samuddavāṇijajātakaṃ (3)

466. The Samuddavāṇija Jātaka (3)

25.

25.

Kasanti [M 1.0244] vapanti te janā, manujā kammaphalūpajīvino;

Nayimassa dīpakassa bhāgino, jambudīpā idameva no varaṃ.

Those people plow and sow; humans live by the fruit of their labor. They are not partakers of this island. For us, this very island is better than Jambudīpa.

26.

26.

Tipañcarattūpagatamhi cande, vego [T 1.0326] mahā hehiti sāgarassa;

Uplavissaṃ dīpamimaṃ uḷāraṃ, mā vo vadhī gacchatha leṇamaññaṃ.

When the moon has reached the fifteenth night, there will be a great surge of the ocean. It will flood this excellent island. Let the surge not overcome you; go to another refuge.

27.

27.

Na jātuyaṃ sāgaravārivego, uplavissaṃ dīpamimaṃ uḷāraṃ;

Taṃ me nimittehi bahūhi diṭṭhaṃ, mā bhetha kiṃ socatha modathavho modatha vo (ka.) 6.38 moggallānasuttaṃ passitabbaṃ.

This surge of ocean water will certainly not flood this excellent island. This I have seen through many signs. Do not be afraid! Why do you grieve? Rejoice!

28.

28.

Pahūtabhakkhaṃ bahuannapānaṃ, pattattha āvāsamimaṃ uḷāraṃ;

Na vo bhayaṃ paṭipassāmi kiñci, āputtaputtehi pamodathavho.

You have obtained this excellent dwelling, with abundant provisions and much food and drink. I foresee no danger for you at all. Rejoice with your sons and grandsons!

29.

29.

Yo devoyaṃ dakkhiṇāyaṃ dakkhiṇassaṃ (sī.) disāyaṃ, khemanti pakkosati tassa saccaṃ;

Na uttaro vedi bhayābhayassa, mā bhetha kiṃ socatha modathavho.

That deva in the southern direction who cries out about danger—his word is not true. He is an enemy who is simply afraid. Do not be afraid! Why do you grieve? Rejoice!

30.

30.

Yathā ime vippavadanti yakkhā, eko bhayaṃ saṃsati khemameko;

Tadiṅgha mayhaṃ vacanaṃ suṇātha, khippaṃ [T 1.0327] lahuṃ mā vinassimha sabbe.

As these yakkhas speak in contradiction—one speaks of danger, one of safety—come now, listen to my words, lest we all perish very quickly.

31.

31.

Sabbe [M 1.0245] samāgamma karoma nāvaṃ, doṇiṃ daḷhaṃ sabbayantūpapannaṃ;

Sace ayaṃ dakkhiṇo saccamāha, moghaṃ paṭikkosati uttaroyaṃ;

Let us all gather and build a boat, a strong vessel equipped with all mechanisms. If this southern one speaks the truth, this northern one cries out in vain.

Sā ceva no hehiti āpadatthā, imañca dīpaṃ na pariccajema.

That very boat will be for our sake in time of calamity, and we shall not abandon this island.

32.

32.

Sace ca kho uttaro saccamāha, moghaṃ paṭikkosati dakkhiṇoyaṃ;

Tameva nāvaṃ abhiruyha sabbe, evaṃ mayaṃ sotthi taremu pāraṃ.

And if indeed the northern one speaks the truth, this southern one cries out in vain. Then, all of us, having boarded that very boat, will cross safely to the other shore.

33.

33.

Na ve sugaṇhaṃ paṭhamena seṭṭhaṃ, kaniṭṭhamāpāthagataṃ gahetvā;

Yo cīdha tacchaṃ majjhaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) paviceyya gaṇhati gaṇhi (ka.), sa ve naro seṭṭhamupeti ṭhānaṃ.

One should not easily accept the first statement as true, nor the last statement that one hears. But whoever here investigates and grasps what is true and factual, that person attains the highest state.

34.

34.

Yathāpi te sāgaravārimajjhe, sakammunā sotthi vahiṃsu vāṇijā;

Anāgatatthaṃ paṭivijjhiyāna, appampi nācceti sa bhūripañño.

Just as those merchants in the midst of the ocean water traveled safely by their own effort, so too the person of great wisdom, having foreseen a future matter, does not neglect even the slightest thing.

35.

35.

Bālā [T 1.0328] ca mohena rasānugiddhā, anāgataṃ appaṭivijjhiyatthaṃ;

But fools, greedy for pleasure due to delusion, fail to foresee a future matter.

Paccuppanne sīdanti atthajāte, samuddamajjhe yathā te manussā.

They sink when a present matter arises, like those men in the middle of the ocean.

36.

36.

Anāgataṃ [V 1.0191] paṭikayirātha kiccaṃ, “mā maṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhesi”;

Taṃ tādisaṃ paṭikata paṭikataṃ (ka.), paṭigata (sī. aṭṭha.), paṭikacca (?) kiccakāriṃ, na taṃ kiccaṃ kiccakāle byadhetīti.

One should prepare for a future task in advance, thinking, “Let the task not oppress me when the time for it comes.” For one who has prepared the task in advance, that task does not oppress them when the time for it comes.

Samuddavāṇijajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Samuddavāṇija Jātaka, the Third.

467. Kāmajātakaṃ (4)

467. The Kāma Jātaka (4)

37.

37.

Kāmaṃ [M 1.0246] kāmayamānassa, tassa ce taṃ samijjhati;

Addhā pītimano hoti, laddhā macco yadicchati.

For one desiring sensual pleasure, if that is fulfilled for him, a mortal, having obtained what he wishes, certainly becomes glad of heart.

38.

38.

Kāmaṃ kāmayamānassa, tassa ce taṃ samijjhati;

Tato naṃ aparaṃ kāme, dhamme taṇhaṃva vindati.

For one desiring sensual pleasure, if that is fulfilled for him, then afterwards that person finds even more sensual cravings, just as one afflicted by wind and sun in the summer heat finds thirst.

39.

39.

Gavaṃva siṅgino siṅgaṃ, vaḍḍhamānassa vaḍḍhati;

Evaṃ mandassa posassa, bālassa avijānato;

Bhiyyo taṇhā pipāsā ca, vaḍḍhamānassa vaḍḍhati.

Just as the horn of a horned bull grows as the bull grows, so too for the dull, foolish, and ignorant person, as he grows, craving and thirst increase all the more.

40.

40.

Pathabyā sāliyavakaṃ, gavassaṃ gavāsaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) dāsaporisaṃ;

Datvā ca datvāpi (sī. syā.), datvā vā (pī.) nālamekassa, iti vidvā viddhā (syā.) samaṃ care.

Even having given fields of fine rice and barley on the earth, cattle and horses, and slaves and workers, it is not enough for one person. Knowing this, the wise one should practice a balanced conduct.

41.

41.

Rājā [T 1.0329] pasayha pathaviṃ vijitvā, sasāgarantaṃ mahimāvasanto;

Oraṃ samuddassa atittarūpo atittirūpo (ka.), pāraṃ samuddassapi patthayetha.

A king, having forcibly conquered the earth and ruling over this land bounded by the ocean, being insatiable with this near shore of the ocean, would still long for the other shore as well.

42.

42.

Yāva anussaraṃ kāme, manasā titti nājjhagā;

Tato nivattā paṭikamma disvā, te ve sutittā ye tittā (sī. syā. pī.) paññāya tittā.

As long as one recollects sensual pleasures, one does not attain satisfaction of mind. But they who turn away from them, having seen their fault—those satisfied by wisdom—are indeed well satisfied.

43.

43.

Paññāya tittinaṃ tittīnaṃ (sī. syā.) seṭṭhaṃ, na so kāmehi tappati;

Paññāya tittaṃ purisaṃ, taṇhā na kurute vasaṃ.

Satisfaction through wisdom is supreme; such a one is not tormented by sensual pleasures. Craving does not bring under its control the person who is satisfied by wisdom.

44.

44.

Apacinetheva kāmānaṃ kāmāni (sī. syā. pī.), appicchassa alolupo;

Samuddamatto puriso, na so kāmehi tappati.

One should indeed do away with sensual pleasures; one should have few wishes and not be greedy. A person whose wisdom is vast as the ocean is not tormented by sensual pleasures.

45.

45.

Rathakārova cammassa, parikantaṃ upāhanaṃ;

Yaṃ yaṃ cajati jahati (syā. ka.) kāmānaṃ, taṃ taṃ sampajjate sukhaṃ;

Sabbaṃ ce sukhamiccheyya, sabbe kāme pariccaje.

Just as a leather worker discards the scraps after cutting a shoe from a piece of leather, for whatever part of sensual pleasures one discards, by that very part is happiness attained. If one should wish for complete happiness, one should renounce all sensual pleasures.

46.

46.

Aṭṭha [M 1.0247] te bhāsitā gāthā, sabbā honti sahassiyo sahassiyā (?) upari sutasomajātake tathā dissati;

Paṭigaṇha mahābrahme, sādhetaṃ tava bhāsitaṃ.

O great brahmin, the eight verses spoken by you are all worth a thousand each. Please accept these eight thousand. This speech of yours is excellent!

47.

47.

Na me attho sahassehi, satehi nahutehi vā;

Pacchimaṃ bhāsato gāthaṃ, kāme me na rato mano.

O great king, I have no need for thousands, nor for hundreds, nor for tens of thousands. As I was speaking the final verse, my mind took no delight in sensual pleasures.

48.

48.

Bhadrako [V 1.0192] saddo (sī.) vatāyaṃ māṇavako, sabbalokavidū muni;

Yo [T 1.0330] imaṃ taṇhaṃ yo taṇhaṃ (sī. syā.) dukkhajananiṃ, parijānāti paṇḍitoti.

The wise young man who fully understands this craving, the generator of suffering—that sage, the knower of all the world—is indeed excellent!

Kāmajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Kāma Jātaka, the Fourth.

468. Janasandhajātakaṃ (5)

468. The Janasandha Jātaka (5)

49.

49.

Dasa khalu imāni khalumāni (syā.) ṭhānāni, yāni pubbe akaritvā;

Sa pacchā manutappati, iccevāha iccāha rājā (sī. syā. pī.) janasandho.

There are indeed these ten matters which, not having been done previously, one later regrets. Thus indeed spoke Janasandha.

50.

50.

Aladdhā vittaṃ tappati, pubbe asamudānitaṃ;

Na pubbe dhanamesissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

One is tormented, not having obtained wealth that was not previously acquired. 'I did not seek wealth before!'—thus one later regrets.

51.

51.

Sakyarūpaṃ pure santaṃ, mayā sippaṃ na sikkhitaṃ;

Kicchā vutti asippassa, iti pacchānutappati.

'Though I was able in the past, I did not learn a skill. Difficult is the livelihood for one without a skill!'—thus one later regrets.

52.

52.

Kūṭavedī pure āsiṃ, pisuṇo piṭṭhimaṃsiko;

Caṇḍo ca pharuso cāpi cāsiṃ (sī. syā. pī.), iti pacchānutappati.

'I was formerly a deceiver, a slanderer, and a backbiter; I was also fierce and harsh'—thus one later has remorse.

53.

53.

Pāṇātipātī pure āsiṃ, luddo cāpi cāsiṃ (sī. pī.) anāriyo;

Bhūtānaṃ nāpacāyissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

'I was formerly a destroyer of life, cruel and ignoble; I did not show reverence for living beings'—thus one later regrets.

54.

54.

Bahūsu vata santīsu, anāpādāsu itthisu;

Paradāraṃ asevissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

'Alas, though there were many unclaimed women, I associated with another's wife'—thus one later has remorse.

55.

55.

Bahumhi vata santamhi, annapāne upaṭṭhite;

Na pubbe adadaṃ adadiṃ (sī.) dānaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

'Alas, though much food and drink was present and available, I did not give gifts before'—thus one later has remorse.

56.

56.

Mātaraṃ pitarañcāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ jiṇṇake gatayobbane (sī. syā. pī.);

Pahu [T 1.0331] santo na posissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

'Though I was able, I did not support my mother and father, who were aged and past their youth'—thus one later regrets.

57.

57.

Ācariyamanusatthāraṃ[M 1.0248], sabbakāmarasāharaṃ;

Pitaraṃ atimaññissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

'I disdained my father—the teacher, the constant instructor, the provider of all sensual pleasures'—thus one later regrets.

58.

58.

Samaṇe brāhmaṇe cāpi, sīlavante bahussute;

Na pubbe payirupāsissaṃ, iti pacchānutappati.

'I did not formerly attend upon ascetics and brahmins who were virtuous and of great learning'—thus one later has remorse.

59.

59.

Sādhu hoti tapo ciṇṇo, santo ca payirupāsito;

Na ca pubbe tapo ciṇṇo, iti pacchānutappati.

'It is good to have practiced asceticism, and good to have attended upon the tranquil and virtuous. But I did not practice asceticism before'—thus one later has remorse.

60.

60.

Yo ca etāni ṭhānāni, yoniso paṭipajjati;

Karaṃ purisakiccāni, sa pacchā nānutappatīti.

But whoever practices in accordance with these points wisely, fulfilling a person's duties, does not later have remorse.

Janasandhajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Janasandha Jātaka, the Fifth.

469. Mahākaṇhajātakaṃ (6)

469. The Mahākaṇha Jātaka (6)

61.

61.

Kaṇho [V 1.0193] kaṇho ca ghoro ca, sukkadāṭho pabhāsavā patāpavā (sī. syā. pī.);

Baddho pañcahi rajjūhi, kiṃ ravi dhīra (sī. pī.), vīra (syā.) sunakho tava.

Exceedingly black and fearsome, with white, radiant tusks; bound by five ropes, why does your dog bark?

62.

62.

Nāyaṃ migānamatthāya, usīnaka usīnara (sī. pī.), usīnnara (syā.) bhavissati;

Manussānaṃ anayo hutvā, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

This will not be for the benefit of the deer, O Usinaka. When it has become a calamity for humankind, then Kaṇha will be released.

63.

63.

Pattahatthā samaṇakā, muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā;

Naṅgalehi kasissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When base ascetics, with bowls in hand, shaven-headed, and clad in outer robes, will plow with plows, then Kaṇha will be released.

64.

64.

Tapassiniyo tapanīyā (ka.) dutiyantapadāni hetāni pabbajitā, muṇḍā saṅghāṭipārutā;

Yadā loke gamissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When female ascetics who have gone forth, shaven-headed and clad in outer robes, go about in the world indulging in sensual pleasures, then Kaṇha will be released.

65.

65.

Dīghottaroṭṭhā [T 1.0332] jaṭilā, paṅkadantā rajassirā;

Iṇaṃ codāya vodāya (sī. pī.), codaya (syā.) gacchanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When matted-haired ascetics with long upper lips, grimy teeth, and dusty heads go about demanding debts, then Kaṇha will be released.

66.

66.

Adhicca vede vedaṃ (ka.) sāvittiṃ, yaññatantañca tantrañca (sī. syā. pī.) brāhmaṇā;

Bhatikāya yajissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When brahmins, having studied the Vedas, the Sāvittī, and the ritual texts of sacrifice, perform sacrifices for wages, then Kaṇha will be released.

67.

67.

Mātaraṃ pitarañcāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ;

Pahū santo santā (sī.) na bharanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When people, though capable, do not support their mother and father who are aged and past their youth, then Kaṇha will be released.

68.

68.

Mātaraṃ [M 1.0249] pitarañcāpi, jiṇṇakaṃ gatayobbanaṃ;

Bālā tumheti vakkhanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When children will say to their mother and father, who are aged and past their youth, 'You are fools! You give us no wealth!', then Kaṇha will be released.

69.

69.

Ācariyabhariyaṃ sakhiṃ ācariyabhariyaṃ sakhābhariyaṃ (sī. pī.), mātulāniṃ pitucchakiṃ pitucchayaṃ (sī.), pitucchasaṃ (pī.);

Yadā loke gamissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When people in the world transgress with their teacher's wife, their friend's wife, their maternal uncle's wife, or their paternal uncle's wife, then Kaṇha will be released.

70.

70.

Asicammaṃ gahetvāna, khaggaṃ paggayha brāhmaṇā;

Panthaghātaṃ karissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When brahmins, taking up sword and shield and raising their blades, commit highway robbery, then Kaṇha will be released.

71.

71.

Sukkacchavī vedhaverā, thūlabāhū apātubhā;

Mittabhedaṃ karissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhati.

When men of fine complexion who desire widows, having stout arms yet unable to produce wealth, cause the ruin of friendships, then Kaṇha will be released.

72.

72.

Māyāvino nekatikā, asappurisacintakā;

Yadā loke bhavissanti, tadā kaṇho pamokkhatīti.

When the deceitful, the fraudulent, and those who think the thoughts of wicked men exist in the world, then Kaṇha will be released.

Mahākaṇhajātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Mahākaṇha Jātaka, the Sixth.

470. Kosiyajātakaṃ (7)

470. The Kosiya Jātaka (7)

73.

73.

Neva [V 1.0194] kiṇāmi napi vikkiṇāmi, na [T 1.0333] cāpi me sannicayo ca atthi idhatthi (syā.);

Sukiccharūpaṃ vatidaṃ parittaṃ, patthodano nālamayaṃ duvinnaṃ.

I neither buy nor do I sell, nor do I have any store. Indeed, this small amount was obtained with great difficulty; this single portion of rice is not enough for two.

74.

74.

Appamhā appakaṃ dajjā, anumajjhato majjhakaṃ;

Bahumhā bahukaṃ dajjā, adānaṃ nupapajjati na upapajjati (sī. pī.), nūpapajjati (syā.).

From a little, one should give a little; from a moderate amount, a moderate portion; from much, one should give much. Not giving is not proper.

75.

75.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca.

Ariyamaggaṃ samārūha ariyaṃ maggaṃ samāruha (sī. pī.), nekāsī labhate sukhaṃ.

Therefore I say to you, Kosiya: give gifts and also partake. Ascend the noble path. One who does not eat alone obtains happiness.

76.

76.

Moghañcassa hutaṃ hoti, moghañcāpi samīhitaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, eko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

For one who eats a meal alone while a guest is seated nearby, his offering is in vain and his effort is also in vain.

77.

77.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samārūha, nekāsī labhate sukhaṃ.

Therefore I say to you, Kosiya: give gifts and also partake. Ascend the noble path. One who does not eat alone obtains happiness.

78.

78.

Saccañcassa [M 1.0250] hutaṃ hoti, saccañcāpi samīhitaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, neko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

For him who does not eat a meal alone while a guest is seated nearby, his offering is true, and his effort is also true.

79.

79.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samārūha, nekāsī labhate sukhaṃ.

Therefore I say to you, Kosiya: give gifts and also partake. Having ascended the noble path, one who eats alone does not obtain happiness.

80.

80.

Sarañca juhati poso, bahukāya gayāya ca;

Doṇe timbarutitthasmiṃ, sīghasote mahāvahe.

A person may make offerings at the Sara lake, at the Bahukā river, at Gayā, at the Doṇa landing, at the Timbaru ford, and in the great, swift-flowing river.

81.

81.

Atra cassa hutaṃ hoti, atra cassa samīhitaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, neko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

For him who does not eat a meal alone while a guest is seated nearby, his offering is made right here, and his effort is fulfilled right here.

82.

82.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ [T 1.0334] samārūha, nekāsī labhate sukhaṃ.

Therefore I say to you, Kosiya: give gifts and also partake. Having ascended the noble path, one who eats alone does not obtain happiness.

83.

83.

Baḷisañhi so nigilati niggilati (sī. pī.), dīghasuttaṃ sabandhanaṃ;

Atithismiṃ yo nisinnasmiṃ, eko bhuñjati bhojanaṃ.

Indeed, he who eats a meal alone while a guest is seated nearby swallows a fish-hook, complete with its long line and tackle.

84.

84.

Taṃ taṃ vadāmi kosiya, dehi dānāni bhuñja ca;

Ariyamaggaṃ samārūha, nekāsī labhate sukhaṃ.

Therefore I say to you, Kosiya: give gifts and also partake. Having ascended the noble path, one who eats alone does not obtain happiness.

85.

85.

Uḷāravaṇṇā vata brāhmaṇā ime, ayañca vo sunakho kissa hetu;

Uccāvacaṃ vaṇṇanibhaṃ vikubbati, akkhātha no brāhmaṇā ke nu tumhe.

Indeed, these brahmins are of magnificent appearance! And this dog of yours, for what reason does it manifest various forms, both high and low? Tell us, O brahmins, who then are you?

86.

86.

Cando ca suriyo ca sūriyo ca (ka.) ubho idhāgatā, ayaṃ pana mātali devasārathi;

Sakkohamasmi tidasānamindo, eso ca kho pañcasikhoti vuccati.

Both the Moon and the Sun have come here. This one is Mātali, the divine charioteer. I am Sakka, lord of the gods, and this one is indeed called Pañcasikha.

87.

87.

Pāṇissarā [V 1.0195] mudiṅgā ca mutiṅgā ca (sī. syā. pī., murajālambarāni ca;

Suttamenaṃ pabodhenti, paṭibuddho ca nandati.

The sounds of hand-clapping, kettle-drums, tabors, and other drums awaken him from sleep; and having been awakened, he rejoices.

88.

88.

Ye kecime maccharino kadariyā, paribhāsakā samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ;

Idheva nikkhippa sarīradehaṃ, kāyassa bhedā nirayaṃ vajanti.

Whoever are stingy and miserly, revilers of ascetics and brahmins, having cast off their physical body right here, upon the breaking up of the body, they go to hell.

89.

89.

Ye [M 1.0251] kecime suggatimāsamānā suggatimāsasānā (sī. pī.), suggatāsisamānā (ka.), dhamme [T 1.0335] ṭhitā saṃyame saṃvibhāge;

Idheva nikkhippa sarīradehaṃ, kāyassa bhedā sugatiṃ vajanti.

Whoever, aspiring to a happy destination, are established in the Dhamma of restraint and sharing, having cast off their physical body right here, upon the breaking up of the body, they go to a happy destination.

90.

90.

Tvaṃ nosi ñāti purimāsu jātisu, so maccharī rosako kosiyo (syā. ka.) pāpadhammo;

Taveva atthāya idhāgatamhā, mā pāpadhammo nirayaṃ gamittha appattha (ka. sī. syā. pī.).

You were our relative in former births; you were miserly, wrathful, and of evil nature. For your sake alone have we come here; may you, of evil nature, not go to hell.

91.

91.

Addhā hi maṃ vo hitakāmā, yaṃ maṃ samanusāsatha;

Sohaṃ tathā karissāmi, sabbaṃ vuttaṃ hitesibhi.

Truly, you desire my welfare, in that you instruct me. I shall act thus, according to all that is said by those who seek my welfare.

92.

92.

Esāhamajjeva upāramāmi, na cāpihaṃ na cāpahaṃ (sī. pī.) kiñci kareyya pāpaṃ;

Na cāpi me kiñci adeyyamatthi, na cāpidatvā udakaṃ pivāmi udakampahaṃ pibe (sī.).

This very day I shall abstain from stinginess, and I shall do no evil whatsoever. Nor is there anything of mine that is not to be given, nor shall I drink water without having given.

93.

93.

Evañca me dadato sabbakālaṃ kāle (ka.), bhogā ime vāsava khīyissanti;

Tato ahaṃ pabbajissāmi sakka, hitvāna kāmāni yathodhikānīti.

And as I am thus giving at all times, these possessions of mine, O Vāsava, will be exhausted. Then, O Sakka, I shall go forth, having abandoned sensual pleasures in their entirety.

Kosiyajātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Kosiya Jātaka, the seventh.

471. Meṇḍakapañhajātakaṃ (8)

471. The Jātaka of the Ram's Question (8)

94.

94.

Yesaṃ [T 1.0336] na kadāci bhūtapubbaṃ, sakhyaṃ sakkhiṃ (sī. pī.), sakhi (syā.) sattapadampimasmi loke;

Jātā amittā duve sahāyā, paṭisandhāya caranti kissa hetu.

They for whom there has never before been a friendship of even seven steps in this world—two enemies—have become companions. For what reason do they go about reconciled?

95.

95.

Yadi [M 1.0252] me ajja pātarāsakāle, pañhaṃ na sakkuṇeyyātha vattumetaṃ;

Raṭṭhā pabbājayissāmi vo sabbe, na hi mattho duppaññajātikehi.

If you are not able to state the answer to this question for me today by the time of the morning meal, I will banish all of you from the kingdom, for I have no need for those of little wisdom.

96.

96.

Mahājanasamāgamamhi ghore, janakolāhalasaṅgamamhi jāte;

Vikkhittamanā anekacittā, pañhaṃ na sakkuṇoma vattumetaṃ.

In a fearful, great assembly of people, when a clamorous mingling of the crowd has arisen, with distracted minds and unsteady thoughts, we are not able to state the answer to this question.

97.

97.

Ekaggacittāva ekamekā, rahasi gatā atthaṃ nicintayitvā atthāni cintayitvā (syā. ka.);

Paviveke sammasitvāna dhīrā, atha vakkhanti janinda etamatthaṃ.

Each one with a unified mind, having gone to a secluded place and reflected on the meaning; the wise, having contemplated in solitude, will then, O king, state the meaning of this.

98.

98.

Uggaputta-rājaputtiyānaṃ, urabbhassa maṃsaṃ piyaṃ manāpaṃ;

Na sunakhassa te adenti maṃsaṃ, atha meṇḍassa suṇena sakhyamassa.

For the sons of nobles and princes, the flesh of a ram is dear and pleasing; they do not eat the flesh of a dog, and yet there is friendship between the ram and the dog.

99.

99.

Cammaṃ vihananti eḷakassa, assapiṭṭhattharassukhassa assapiṭṭhattharaṇasukhassa (sī.) hetu;

Na ca te sunakhassa attharanti, atha [T 1.0337] meṇḍassa suṇena sakhyamassa.

They stretch the skin of a goat for the sake of a comfortable covering for a horse's back, but they do not spread the skin of a dog; and yet there is friendship between the ram and the dog.

100.

100.

Āvellitasiṅgiko [V 1.0196] hi meṇḍo, na ca sunakhassa visāṇakāni atthi;

Tiṇabhakkho maṃsabhojano ca, atha meṇḍassa suṇena sakhyamassa.

The ram indeed has twisted horns, while a dog has no horns; one is a grass-eater and the other a meat-eater, and yet there is friendship between the ram and the dog.

101.

101.

Tiṇamāsi palāsamāsi meṇḍo, na ca sunakho tiṇamāsi no palāsaṃ;

Gaṇheyya suṇo sasaṃ biḷāraṃ, atha meṇḍassa suṇena sakhyamassa.

The ram eats grass and leaves, while the dog eats neither grass nor leaves. The dog might seize a hare or a cat, and yet there is friendship between the ram and the dog.

102.

102.

Aṭṭhaḍḍhapado [M 1.0253] catuppadassa, meṇḍo aṭṭhanakho adissamāno;

Chādiyamāharatī ayaṃ imassa, maṃsaṃ āharatī ayaṃ amussa.

This four-footed, eight-hooved ram, unseen, brings food for this four-footed one; this one brings meat for that one.

103.

103.

Pāsādavaragato videhaseṭṭho, vitihāraṃ aññamaññabhojanānaṃ;

Addakkhi addasa (syā. ka.) kira sakkhikaṃ janindo, bubhukkassa [T 1.0338] puṇṇaṃ mukhassa bhobhukkhassa ca puṇṇamukhassa (sī.) cetaṃ.

The excellent Videha king, having gone to his excellent palace, saw with his own eyes, it is said, this mutual exchange of food between the barking one and the full-faced one.

104.

104.

Lābhā vata me anapparūpā, yassa medisā paṇḍitā kulamhi;

Pañhassa gambhīragataṃ nipuṇamatthaṃ, paṭivijjhanti subhāsitena dhīrā.

Indeed, my gains are of no small measure, that in my court there are wise ones such as these. The wise penetrate the profound and subtle meaning of the question with their well-spoken words.

105.

105.

Assatarirathañca ekamekaṃ, phītaṃ gāmavarañca ekamekaṃ;

Sabbesaṃ vo dammi paṇḍitānaṃ, paramappatītamano subhāsitenāti.

To each a chariot drawn by mules, and to each a prosperous, excellent village—to all of you wise ones I give this, my mind exceedingly pleased by your well-spoken words.

Meṇḍakapañhajātakaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ.

The Jātaka of the Ram's Question, the eighth.

472. Mahāpadumajātakaṃ (9)

472. The Mahāpaduma Jātaka (9)

106.

106.

Nādaṭṭhā nādiṭṭhā (ka. sī. syā. ka.) parato dosaṃ, aṇuṃ thūlāni sabbaso;

Issaro paṇaye daṇḍaṃ, sāmaṃ appaṭivekkhiya.

A ruler should not impose punishment without investigating for himself, having not seen for himself the faults of another, all of them, small and great.

107.

107.

Yo ca appaṭivekkhitvā, daṇḍaṃ kubbati khattiyo;

Sakaṇṭakaṃ so gilati, jaccandhova samakkhikaṃ.

Whatever ruler inflicts punishment without investigation, he swallows that which has a thorn, just as one born blind swallows food with a fly in it.

108.

108.

Adaṇḍiyaṃ daṇḍayati daṇḍiyati (syā. pī.), daṇḍiyañca adaṇḍiyaṃ adaṇḍiya (niyya), na daṇḍaye (?);

Andhova visamaṃ maggaṃ, na jānāti samāsamaṃ.

He punishes one who is not to be punished, and leaves unpunished one who is to be punished; like a blind person on an uneven path, he does not know the even from the uneven.

109.

109.

Yo ca etāni ṭhānāni, aṇuṃ thūlāni sabbaso;

Sudiṭṭhamanusāseyya, sa ve voharitu vohātu (pī.) marahati.

But whoever, having well-discerned these matters, both small and great in every way, should instruct accordingly, he indeed is worthy to administer justice.

110.

110.

Nekantamudunā [T 1.0339][M 1.0254] sakkā, ekantatikhiṇena vā;

Attaṃ mahante mahatte (syā. ka.) ṭhapetuṃ ṭhāpetuṃ (sī. syā. pī.), tasmā ubhayamācare.

It is not possible to establish oneself in greatness through exclusive gentleness, nor through exclusive harshness; therefore, one should practice both.

111.

111.

Paribhūto mudu hoti, atitikkho ca veravā;

Etañca ubhayaṃ ñatvā, anumajjhaṃ samācare.

One who is gentle is despised; one who is overly harsh incurs enmity. Knowing both these, one should practice the middle way.

112.

112.

Bahumpi ratto bhāseyya, duṭṭhopi bahu bhāsati;

Na itthikāraṇā rāja, puttaṃ ghātetumarahasi.

An impassioned person may speak much, and a malicious person also speaks much; O king, you should not kill your son for the sake of a woman.

113.

113.

Sabbova [V 1.0197] sabbo ca (ka. sī. pī.) loko ekato ekanto (sī. pī.), itthī ca ayamekikā;

Tenāhaṃ paṭipajjissaṃ, gacchatha pakkhipatheva pakkhipetha (syā. aṭṭha.) taṃ.

The entire populace is on one side, while this woman is alone. Therefore, I shall pass judgment. Go! Throw him down the precipice!

114.

114.

Anekatāle narake, gambhīre ca suduttare gambhīre suduruttare (pī. ka.);

Pātito giriduggasmiṃ, kena tvaṃ tattha nāmari.

Having been thrown down the mountain precipice into the deep and very-hard-to-cross chasm, many palm-trees in depth, for what reason did you not die there?

115.

115.

Nāgo jātaphaṇo tattha, thāmavā girisānujo;

Paccaggahi maṃ bhogehi, tenāhaṃ tattha nāmariṃ.

There, a powerful Nāga with a spread hood, native to the mountain, caught me with its coils. For that reason, I did not die there.

116.

116.

Ehi taṃ paṭinessāmi, rājaputta sakaṃ gharaṃ;

Rajjaṃ kārehi kāresi (sī.) bhaddante, kiṃ araññe karissasi.

Come, O prince, I will lead you back to your own home. Rule the kingdom, may it be well with you. What will you do in the forest?

117.

117.

Yathā gilitvā baḷisaṃ, uddhareyya salohitaṃ;

Uddharitvā sukhī assa, evaṃ sukhaṃ (pī. ka.) passāmi attanaṃ attani (pī. ka.), attanā (syā.), evaṃ ahampi puna sotthibhāvappattaṃ gilitabaḷisaṃ purisamiva attānaṃ passāmīti (aṭṭha. saṃvaṇṇanā).

Just as one, having swallowed a fishhook, would bring it up with blood, and having brought it up, would be happy—so do I see myself.

118.

118.

Kiṃ nu tvaṃ baḷisaṃ brūsi, kiṃ tvaṃ brūsi salohitaṃ;

Kiṃ nu tvaṃ ubbhataṃ brūsi, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito.

What is it that you call a 'fishhook'? What do you call 'with blood'? What is it that you call 'what has been brought up'? Being asked, please tell me that.

119.

119.

Kāmāhaṃ baḷisaṃ brūmi, hatthiassaṃ salohitaṃ;

Cattāhaṃ ubbhataṃ brūmi, evaṃ jānāhi khattiya.

Sensual pleasures I call the 'fishhook'; elephants and horses, 'with blood'; renunciation I call 'what has been brought up'. Know this, O Khattiya.

120.

120.

Ciñcāmāṇavikā [T 1.0340] mātā, devadatto ca me pitā;

Ānando paṇḍito nāgo, sāriputto ca devatā;

Rājaputto ahaṃ āsiṃ ahaṃ tadā rājaputto (sī. syā. pī.), evaṃ dhāretha jātakanti.

Ciñcāmāṇavikā was the mother, and Devadatta was my father; Ānanda was the wise Nāga, and Sāriputta was the deity; I was the prince. Thus should you bear this Jātaka in mind.

Mahāpadumajātakaṃ navamaṃ.

The Mahāpaduma Jātaka, the ninth.

473. Mittāmittajātakaṃ (10)

473. The Mittāmitta Jātaka (10)

121.

121.

Kāni [M 1.0255] kammāni kubbānaṃ, kathaṃ viññū parakkame;

Amittaṃ jāneyya medhāvī, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito.

O wise one, by what actions being performed may an intelligent person, having seen and heard, know an enemy? And how should a discerning person strive to know this?

122.

122.

Na naṃ umhayate disvā, na ca naṃ paṭinandati;

Cakkhūni cassa cakkhūnissa (syā. ka.) na dadāti, paṭilomañca vattati.

Upon seeing him, one does not smile, nor does one welcome him; one does not give him one's eyes, and one acts in a contrary way.

123.

123.

Amitte tassa bhajati, mitte tassa na sevati;

Vaṇṇakāme nivāreti, akkosante pasaṃsati.

One associates with that person's enemies and does not attend to his friends. One prevents those who wish to praise him and commends those who revile him.

124.

124.

Guyhañca tassa nakkhāti, tassa guyhaṃ na gūhati;

Kammaṃ tassa na vaṇṇeti, paññassa nappasaṃsati.

One does not tell one's own secret to that person, and one does not keep that person's secret. One does not praise his deeds, nor does one commend his wisdom.

125.

125.

Abhave [V 1.0198] nandati tassa, bhave tassa na nandati;

Accheraṃ acchariyaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) bhojanaṃ laddhā, tassa nuppajjate sati;

Tato naṃ nānukampati, aho sopi ahāsopi (ka. sī. syā. ka.) labheyyito.

One delights in that person's misfortune and does not delight in his prosperity. Having obtained excellent food, the thought of him does not arise. Therefore, one feels no compassion for him, nor thinks, 'Oh, may he also obtain this!'

126.

126.

Iccete soḷasākārā, amittasmiṃ patiṭṭhitā;

Yehi amittaṃ jāneyya, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito.

These sixteen characteristics are established in an enemy, by which a wise person, having seen and heard, may know an enemy.

127.

127.

Kāni kammāni kubbānaṃ, kathaṃ viññū parakkame;

Mittaṃ [T 1.0341] jāneyya medhāvī, disvā sutvā ca paṇḍito.

O wise one, by what actions being performed may an intelligent person, having seen and heard, know a friend? And how should a discerning person strive to know this?

128.

128.

Pavutthaṃ tassa sarati, āgataṃ abhinandati;

Tato kelāyito hoti, vācāya paṭinandati.

One thinks of him when he is away and rejoices when he has returned. One is affectionate towards him and welcomes him with speech.

129.

129.

Mitte tasseva bhajati, amitte tassa na sevati;

Akkosante nivāreti, vaṇṇakāme pasaṃsati.

One associates only with that person's friends and does not attend to his enemies. One prevents those who revile him and praises those who wish to speak his praise.

130.

130.

Guyhañca tassa akkhāti, tassa guyhañca gūhati;

Kammañca tassa vaṇṇeti, paññaṃ tassa paññamassa (syā. ka.) pasaṃsati.

One tells one's own secret to that person and keeps that person's secret. One praises his deeds and commends his wisdom.

131.

131.

Bhave ca nandati tassa bhave nandati tassa ca (ka.), abhave tassa na nandati;

Accheraṃ acchariyaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) bhojanaṃ laddhā, tassa uppajjate sati;

Tato naṃ anukampati, aho sopi pahāsopi (ka. sī. syā. ka.) labheyyito.

One delights in that person's prosperity and does not delight in his misfortune. Having obtained excellent food, the thought of him arises. Therefore, one feels compassion for him, thinking, 'Oh, may he also obtain this!'

132.

132.

Iccete [M 1.0256] soḷasākārā, mittasmiṃ suppatiṭṭhitā;

Yehi mittañca jāneyya mittaṃ sujāneyya (pī. ka.), disvā sutvā ca paṇḍitoti.

These sixteen characteristics are well-established in a friend, by which a wise person, having seen and heard, may know a friend.

Mittāmittajātakaṃ dasamaṃ.

The Mittāmitta Jātaka, the tenth.

Dvādasakanipātaṃ niṭṭhitaṃ.

The Book of the Twelves is finished.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Lahucitta sasāla kasanti puna, atha kāma dasakhaluṭṭhānavaro;

Atha kaṇha sukosiya meṇḍavaro, padumo puna mittavarena dasāti.

The Cūḷakuṇāla, the Bhaddasāla, and the Samuddavāṇija Jātakas; furthermore, the Kāma and Janasandha Jātakas; furthermore, the Mahākaṇha, Kosiya, and Meṇḍaka Jātakas; the Paduma Jātaka, and again, the Mittāmitta Jātaka. These are the ten.

13. Terasakanipāto

13. The Book of Thirteens

474. Ambajātakaṃ (1)

474. The Amba Jātaka (1)

1.

1.

Ahāsi [T 1.0342][V 1.0199][M 1.0257] āhāsi (?) me ambaphalāni pubbe, aṇūni thūlāni ca brahmacāri;

Teheva mantehi na dāni tuyhaṃ, dumapphalā pātubhavanti brahme.

Before, you brought me mango fruits, O celibate one, both small and large; but now, with those same spells, O brahmin, the tree's fruits do not appear for you.

2.

2.

Nakkhattayogaṃ paṭimānayāmi, khaṇaṃ muhuttañca mante na passaṃ khaṇaṃ muhuttaṃ na maṃ tosayanti (sī. pī.);

Nakkhattayogañca khaṇañca laddhā, addhāharissambaphalaṃ athāharissambaphalaṃ (sī. pī.) pahūtaṃ.

I am waiting for the right conjunction of the stars; I do not see the right moment or instant for the spells. Having obtained the right conjunction and moment, I will surely bring forth abundant mango fruit.

3.

3.

Nakkhattayogaṃ na pure abhāṇi, khaṇaṃ muhuttaṃ na pure asaṃsi;

Sayaṃ harī athāharī (sī. syā. pī.) ambaphalaṃ pahūtaṃ, vaṇṇena gandhena rasenupetaṃ.

Previously, you did not speak of a conjunction of the stars, nor did you mention a moment or an instant; you yourself brought forth abundant mango fruit, endowed with color, fragrance, and flavor.

4.

4.

Mantābhijappena pure hi pura’ssa (sī. pī.), purepi (syā.) tuyhaṃ, dumapphalā pātubhavanti brahme;

Svājja na pāresi jappampi mantaṃ japampi mante (sī. pī.), ayaṃ so ko nāma tavajja dhammo.

Previously, by your recitation of spells, the tree's fruits would appear, O brahmin. But today you are not able, even while reciting the spell. What is this nature of yours today?

5.

5.

Caṇḍālaputto [T 1.0343] mama sampadāsi, dhammena mante pakatiñca saṃsi;

Mā cassu me pucchito nāmagottaṃ, guyhittho atthaṃ mā taṃ (sī. syā. pī.) vijaheyya manto vijaheyyumantā (syā.).

The son of a caṇḍāla gave the spells to me righteously, and he stated the customary rule: 'When asked, do not conceal my name and clan. The spell would then lose its benefit.'

6.

6.

Sohaṃ [M 1.0258] janindena janamhi puṭṭho, makkhābhibhūto alikaṃ abhāṇiṃ;

“Mantā ime brāhmaṇassā”ti micchā, pahīnamanto kapaṇo rudāmi.

I, being asked by the king in the midst of the people and overcome by ingratitude, spoke a falsehood. Falsely saying, 'These spells are from a brahmin,' I, having lost the spell, now weep, wretched.

7.

7.

Eraṇḍā pucimandā vā, atha vā pālibhaddakā;

Madhuṃ madhutthiko vinde, so hi tassa dumuttamo.

Be they castor-oil plants, neem trees, or coral trees, should a seeker of honey find honey in them, that for him is indeed the best of trees.

8.

8.

Khattiyā brāhmaṇā vessā, suddā caṇḍālapukkusā;

Yamhā dhammaṃ vijāneyya, so hi tassa naruttamo.

Be they Khattiyas, Brahmins, Vessas, Suddas, Caṇḍālas or Pukkusas—from whomever one may learn the Dhamma, that one is indeed the best of men for him.

9.

9.

Imassa daṇḍañca vadhañca datvā, gale gahetvā khalayātha balayātha (syā.), galayātha (ka.) jammaṃ;

Yo uttamatthaṃ kasirena laddhaṃ, mānātimānena vināsayittha.

As for this wretch who, through pride and conceit, destroyed the supreme benefit obtained with difficulty—having administered punishment and a beating, seize him by the neck and drive him out!

10.

10.

Yathā samaṃ maññamāno pateyya, sobbhaṃ guhaṃ narakaṃ pūtipādaṃ;

Rajjūti vā akkame kaṇhasappaṃ, andho [T 1.0344] yathā jotimadhiṭṭhaheyya;

Evampi maṃ tvaṃ khalitaṃ sapañña sapaññā (pī.), pahīnamantassa punappadāhi puna sampadāhi (syā.), punappasīda (sī. pī.).

Just as one, thinking the ground level, might fall into a pit, a cave, a chasm, or a rotten tree-hole; or as one, thinking it a rope, might step on a black cobra; or as a blind man might walk into a fire—even so, O wise one, forgive me who has stumbled. To me, who has lost the spell, please give it again.

11.

11.

Dhammena mantaṃ mante (sī. syā. pī.) tava sampadāsiṃ, tuvampi dhammena tvampi dhammeneva (ka.) pariggahesi;

Pakatimpi te attamano asaṃsiṃ, dhamme ṭhitaṃ taṃ patiṭṭhaṃ (ka.) na jaheyya manto.

Righteously I gave the spell to you, and righteously you received it. Well-pleased, I also told you the customary rule. The spell would not have abandoned you, had you remained established in righteousness.

12.

12.

Yo [V 1.0200] bāla mantaṃ balamantaṃ (ka.) kasirena laddhaṃ, yaṃ dullabhaṃ ajja manussaloke;

Kiñcāpi laddhā jīvituṃ appapañño kicchā laddhaṃ jīvikaṃ appapañño (sī. syā.), kacchāpi laddhā jīvikaṃ appañña (pī.), vināsayī alikaṃ bhāsamāno.

Whatever foolish person of little wisdom, having obtained with difficulty a spell rare in this human world, destroys it by speaking a falsehood.

13.

13.

Bālassa [M 1.0259] mūḷhassa akataññuno ca, musā bhaṇantassa asaññatassa;

Mante mayaṃ tādisake na dema, kuto mantā gaccha na mayha ruccasīti.

To one who is foolish, deluded, and ungrateful, who speaks falsehood and is unrestrained—to such a one we do not give spells. From where would spells come for you? Go! You do not please me.

Ambajātakaṃ paṭhamaṃ.

The Amba Jātaka, the First.

475. Phandanajātakaṃ (2)

475. The Phandana Jātaka, the Second.

14.

14.

Kuṭhārihattho [T 1.0345] kudhārihattho (ka.) puriso, vanamogayha tiṭṭhasi;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ dāruṃ chetumicchasi.

O man with an axe in hand, having entered the forest, you stand. Friend, being asked, tell me: what wood do you wish to cut?

15.

15.

Isso iso (sī.), īso (syā. pī.) vanāni carasi, samāni visamāni ca;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, kiṃ dāruṃ nemiyā daḷhaṃ.

O bear, you wander through forests, both even and uneven. Friend, being asked, tell me: what wood is strong for a wheel-rim?

16.

16.

Neva sālo na khadiro, nāssakaṇṇo kuto dhavo;

Rukkho ca rukkhova (sī. pī.) phandano nāma, taṃ dāruṃ nemiyā daḷhaṃ.

Neither the Sāl tree is strong, nor the Khadira, nor the Assakaṇṇa; how then the Dhava? There is a tree named Phandana; that wood is strong for a wheel-rim.

17.

17.

Kīdisānissa pattāni, khandho vā pana kīdiso;

Puṭṭho me samma akkhāhi, yathā jānemu phandanaṃ.

Friend, what are its leaves like, and what is its trunk like? Being asked, tell me, so that we may know the Phandana.

18.

18.

Yassa sākhā palambanti, namanti na ca bhañjare;

So rukkho phandano nāma, yassa mūle ahaṃ ṭhito.

The tree whose branches hang down and bend but do not break, that tree is named Phandana, at whose root I am standing.

19.

19.

Arānaṃ cakkanābhīnaṃ, īsānemirathassa ca;

Sabbassa te kammaniyo, ayaṃ hessati phandano.

For spokes, for wheel-hubs, and for the pole and rim of the chariot, this Phandana will be suitable for all your work.

20.

20.

Iti phandanarukkhopi, tāvade ajjhabhāsatha;

Mayhampi vacanaṃ atthi, bhāradvāja suṇohi me.

Thus the deity of the Phandana tree also spoke at that moment: 'I too have a word to say, O Bhāradvāja, listen to me.'

21.

21.

Issassa imassa (ka. sī. ka.) upakkhandhamhā upakhandhamhā (ka. sī. pī. ka.), ukkacca caturaṅgulaṃ;

Tena nemiṃ pasāresi pariharesi (sī. pī.), evaṃ daḷhataraṃ siyā.

Having cut a four-finger-width of hide from the nape of this bear, bind the rim with it. Thus, it would be much stronger.

22.

22.

Iti phandanarukkhopi, veraṃ appesi tāvade;

Jātānañca ajātānaṃ, issānaṃ dukkhamāvahi.

Thus the deity of the Phandana tree also created enmity at that moment; for bears both born and yet to be born, it brought suffering.

23.

23.

Iccevaṃ [M 1.0260] icceva (sī. pī.) phandano issaṃ, isso ca pana phandanaṃ;

Aññamaññaṃ [T 1.0346] vivādena, aññamaññamaghātayuṃ.

Thus the Phandana deity and the bear, through mutual dispute, caused each other to be killed.

24.

24.

Evameva manussānaṃ, vivādo yattha jāyati;

Mayūranaccaṃ naccanti, yathā te issaphandanā.

Just so among humans, where a dispute arises, they dance the peacock's dance, just like that bear and the Phandana deity.

25.

25.

Taṃ [V 1.0201] vo vadāmi bhaddaṃ vo bhaddante (ka.), yāvantettha samāgatā;

Sammodatha mā vivadatha māvivadittha (sī. syā. pī.), mā hotha issaphandanā.

This I say to you—may it be well with you, all who are assembled here: Rejoice together, do not dispute, and do not be like the bear and the Phandana deity.

26.

26.

Sāmaggimeva sāmagyameva (syā. ka.) sikkhetha, buddhehetaṃ pasaṃsitaṃ;

Sāmaggirato dhammaṭṭho, yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatīti.

You should train only in harmony; this is praised by the Buddhas. One who delights in harmony, established in the Dhamma, does not fall away from security from the yokes.

Phandanajātakaṃ dutiyaṃ.

The Phandana Jātaka, the Second.

476. Javanahaṃsajātakaṃ (3)

476. The Javanahaṃsa Jātaka, the Third.

27.

27.

Idheva haṃsa nipata, piyaṃ me tava dassanaṃ;

Issarosi anuppatto, yamidhatthi pavedaya.

O goose, alight right here; the sight of you is dear to me. You have arrived as a lord; declare what you desire here.

28.

28.

Savanena ekassa piyā bhavanti, disvā panekassa viyeti vineti (syā.), viheti (pī.), vigeti (ka. aṭṭha.) chando;

Disvā ca sutvā ca piyā bhavanti, kaccinnu me pīyasi piyyasi (sī. pī.) dassanena.

To some, one becomes dear by hearing of them; but for another, upon seeing them, affection fades. Some become dear by both seeing and hearing of them. I wonder, am I dear to you by sight?

29.

29.

Savanena piyo mesi, bhiyyo cāgamma dassanaṃ;

Evaṃ piyadassano me evaṃ piyadassano samāno (sī. syā. pī.), vasa haṃsa mamantike mama santike (sī. syā. pī.).

You were dear to me by hearing of you, and even more so now that you have come into sight. Since you are so pleasant to behold, O goose, dwell here in my presence.

30.

30.

Vaseyyāma tavāgāre, niccaṃ sakkatapūjitā;

Matto ca ekadā vajje vajjā (sī. pī.), “haṃsarājaṃ pacantu me”.

We would dwell in your house, always honored and revered. But one day, being intoxicated, you might say: 'Let them cook the goose-king for me!'

31.

31.

Dhiratthu [T 1.0347] taṃ majjapānaṃ, yaṃ me piyataraṃ tayā;

Na cāpi majjaṃ pissāmi pivissāmi (syā.), pāyāmi (sī. pī.), yāva me vacchasī ghare.

Shame on that drinking of intoxicants, that it should be dearer to me than you! I shall not drink any intoxicant for as long as you dwell in my house.

32.

32.

Suvijānaṃ [M 1.0261] siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca sakuntānañca (sī. syā. pī.) vassitaṃ;

Manussavassitaṃ rāja, dubbijānataraṃ tato.

The cry of jackals and of birds is easy to understand; but the speech of humans, O king, is far more difficult to understand than that.

33.

33.

Api ce maññatī poso, ñāti mitto sakhāti vā;

Yo pubbe sumano hutvā, pacchā sampajjate diso.

A person who was formerly well-disposed, one might think of as 'kinsman,' 'friend,' or 'companion'; yet later, that same person can become a foe.

34.

34.

Yasmiṃ mano nivisati, avidūre sahāpi so;

Santikepi hi so dūre, yasmiṃ nāvisate yasmā vivasate (sī. syā. pī.) mano.

One in whom the mind settles, even if far, is indeed close by. One in whom the mind does not settle, even if close by, is indeed far away.

35.

35.

Antopi so hoti pasannacitto, pāraṃ samuddassa pasannacitto;

Antopi so hoti paduṭṭhacitto, pāraṃ samuddassa paduṭṭhacitto.

One with a serene mind, though on the far shore of the ocean, is as if within. One with a corrupt mind, though within, is as if on the far shore of the ocean.

36.

36.

Saṃvasantā vivasanti, ye disā te rathesabha;

Ārā santo saṃvasanti, manasā raṭṭhavaḍḍhana.

Those who are foes, though living together, live apart, O lord of charioteers. The virtuous, though far apart, live together in mind, O increaser of the kingdom.

37.

37.

Aticiraṃ nivāsena, piyo bhavati appiyo;

Āmanta kho taṃ gacchāma gacchāmi (syā.), purā te homa appiyā homi appiyo (syā.).

By dwelling for too long, a dear one becomes undear. We now take our leave of you and shall go, before we become undear to you.

38.

38.

Evaṃ [V 1.0202] ce yācamānānaṃ, añjaliṃ nāvabujjhasi;

Paricārakānaṃ sataṃ santānaṃ (sī. syā.), sattānaṃ (pī.), vacanaṃ na karosi no;

Evaṃ taṃ abhiyācāma, puna kayirāsi pariyāyaṃ.

If you do not heed the folded hands of us who entreat you thus, if you do not follow the word of us who are your attendants, then we implore you: may you make a return visit again.

39.

39.

Evaṃ ce no viharataṃ, antarāyo na hessati;

Tuyhañcāpi [T 1.0348] vāpi (syā. pī. ka.) mahārāja, mayhañca vā (bahūsu) raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Appeva nāma passemu passema (sī. syā. pī.), ahoratānamaccayeti.

If, as we go on living, no obstacle should befall either you, O great king, or me, O increaser of the kingdom, then perhaps, with the passing of days and nights, we may see each other again.

Javanahaṃsajātakaṃ tatiyaṃ.

The Javanahaṃsa Jātaka, the Third.

477. Cūḷanāradajātakaṃ (4)

477. The Cūḷanārada Jātaka, the Fourth.

40.

40.

Na te kaṭṭhāni bhinnāni, na te udakamābhataṃ;

Aggīpi te na hāpito hāsito (sī. syā.), kiṃ nu mandova jhāyasi.

Your firewood is not split, your water is not fetched, and your fire is not kindled. Why do you brood as if you were dull-witted?

41.

41.

Na [M 1.0262] ussahe vane vatthuṃ, kassapāmantayāmi taṃ;

Dukkho vāso araññasmiṃ, raṭṭhaṃ icchāmi gantave.

O Kassapa, I address you: I am not able to dwell in the forest. Dwelling in the wilderness is suffering; I wish to go to the country.

42.

42.

Yathā ahaṃ ito gantvā, yasmiṃ janapade vasaṃ;

Ācāraṃ brahme brahmaṃ (ka.) sikkheyyaṃ, taṃ dhammaṃ anusāsa maṃ.

So that I, having gone from here and dwelling in whichever country, might train in the noble conduct, please instruct me in that practice.

43.

43.

Sace araññaṃ hitvāna, vanamūlaphalāni ca;

Raṭṭhe rocayase vāsaṃ, taṃ dhammaṃ nisāmehi me.

If, having abandoned the wilderness and the forest roots and fruits, you delight in dwelling in the country, then listen from me to that practice.

44.

44.

Visaṃ mā paṭisevittho paṭisevittha (syā. ka.), papātaṃ parivajjaya;

Paṅke ca mā visīdittho paṅko ca mā visiyittho (ka.), yatto cāsīvise care.

Do not partake of poison; avoid the precipice. Do not sink into the mire, and conduct yourself with diligence among vipers.

45.

45.

Kiṃ nu visaṃ papāto vā, paṅko vā brahmacārinaṃ;

Kaṃ tvaṃ āsīvisaṃ brūsi, taṃ me akkhāhi pucchito;

What, pray, is poison, or a precipice, or mire for one who leads the holy life? What do you call a venomous serpent? Being asked, please declare it to me.

46.

46.

Āsavo tāta lokasmiṃ, surā nāma pavuccati;

Manuñño manuññā (sī. syā. pī.) surabhī vaggu, sādu madhu (sī. syā.) khuddarasūpamo rasūpamā (sī. syā. pī.);

Visaṃ tadāhu ariyā se, brahmacariyassa nārada.

Dear son, in the world there is an intoxicant called liquor. It is pleasing, fragrant, and emboldening; it is sweet, like the taste of honey. O Nārada, the noble ones call that poison for the holy life.

47.

47.

Itthiyo [T 1.0349] tāta lokasmiṃ, pamattaṃ pamathenti tā;

Haranti yuvino cittaṃ, tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva māluto;

Papāto eso akkhāto, brahmacariyassa nārada.

Dear son, in the world, women torment the heedless. They carry away the mind of a youth, just as the wind carries away a fallen tuft of cotton. O Nārada, this is called a precipice for the holy life.

48.

48.

Lābho siloko sakkāro, pūjā parakulesu ca;

Paṅko eso ca esova (sī. syā. pī.) akkhāto, brahmacariyassa nārada.

Gain, renown, honor, and offerings in the families of others—O Nārada, this is called the mire of the holy life.

49.

49.

Sasatthā [V 1.0203] mahantā (syā. ka.) tāta rājāno, āvasanti mahiṃ imaṃ;

Te tādise manussinde, mahante tāta nārada.

Dear son, kings with weapons rule this earth. Do not associate, dear Nārada, with such mighty lords of men.

50.

50.

Issarānaṃ adhipatīnaṃ, na tesaṃ pādato care;

Āsīvisoti āsīviso so (sī. pī.) akkhāto, brahmacariyassa nārada.

Of lords and rulers, do not walk in their footsteps. O Nārada, such a one is called a venomous serpent to the holy life.

51.

51.

Bhattattho bhattakāle ca yaṃ (sī. pī.), yaṃ gehamupasaṅkame;

Yadettha kusalaṃ jaññā, tattha ghāsesanaṃ care.

Being in need of food, at the time for the meal, whichever house one may approach—whatever therein one should know to be suitable and blameless, there one should practice the seeking of sustenance.

52.

52.

Pavisitvā [M 1.0263] parakulaṃ, pānatthaṃ pānattho (syā. pī.) bhojanāya vā;

Mitaṃ khāde mitaṃ bhuñje, na ca rūpe manaṃ kare.

Having entered another's family for the sake of drink or food, one should eat in moderation and consume in measure, and not set one's mind on forms.

53.

53.

Goṭṭhaṃ majjaṃ kirāṭañca kirāsañca (sī. syā.), kirāsaṃ vā (pī.), sabhā nikiraṇāni ca;

Ārakā parivajjehi, yānīva visamaṃ pathanti.

Cattle pens, taverns, swindlers, assemblies, and places where treasures are stored—avoid these from afar, just as a vehicle avoids an uneven path.

Cūḷanāradajātakaṃ catutthaṃ.

The Cūḷanārada Jātaka, the fourth.

478. Dūtajātakaṃ (5)

478. The Dūta Jātaka (5)

54.

54.

Dūte [T 1.0350] te brahme dūte brāhmaṇa (ka.) pāhesiṃ, gaṅgātīrasmi jhāyato;

Tesaṃ puṭṭho na byākāsi, dukkhaṃ guyhamataṃ guyhaṃ mataṃ (sī.), tuyhaṃ mataṃ (syā. ka.) nu te.

O brahmin, I sent messengers to you as you were brooding on the bank of the Ganges. Though asked by them, you did not speak. Is your suffering a secret known only to you?

55.

55.

Sace te dukkhamuppajje, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhana;

Mā kho naṃ tassa akkhāhi, yo taṃ dukkhā na mocaye.

O promoter of the Kāsi kingdom, if suffering should arise for you, do not tell it to one who cannot free you from that suffering.

56.

56.

Yo tassa yo ca tathā (pī.) dukkhajātassa, ekaṅgamapi bhāgaso ekantamapi bhāsato (sī. pī.);

Vippamoceyya dhammena, kāmaṃ tassa pavedaya pavedaye (sī.).

But whoever could righteously relieve even a single part of that arisen suffering—to him you may certainly declare it.

57.

57.

Suvijānaṃ siṅgālānaṃ, sakuṇānañca vassitaṃ;

Manussavassitaṃ rāja, dubbijānataraṃ tato.

The cry of jackals and the calls of birds are easy to understand; but the speech of humans, O king, is far harder to understand than that.

58.

58.

Api ce maññatī poso, ñāti mitto sakhāti vā;

Yo pubbe sumano hutvā, pacchā sampajjate diso.

Even one whom a person might consider a kinsman, a friend, or a companion—one who was formerly well-disposed can later become an enemy.

59.

59.

Yo attano dukkhamanānupuṭṭho, pavedaye jantu akālarūpe;

Ānandino tassa bhavantimittā bhavanta’mittā (sī. pī.), hitesino tassa dukhī bhavanti.

The person who, unasked and at an improper time, declares their own suffering—their enemies become joyful, while their well-wishers become sorrowful.

60.

60.

Kālañca ñatvāna tathāvidhassa, medhāvīnaṃ ekamanaṃ viditvā;

Akkheyya tibbāni tippāni (sī. syā. pī.) parassa dhīro, saṇhaṃ giraṃ atthavatiṃ pamuñce.

Knowing the right time, and having understood a wise person to be of like mind, a steadfast person may tell their intense sufferings to another, uttering gentle and meaningful speech.

61.

61.

Sace [T 1.0351][M 1.0264] ca jaññā avisayhamattano, na te hi mayhaṃ nāyaṃ nīti mayha (sī. pī.) sukhāgamāya;

Ekova tibbāni saheyya dhīro, saccaṃ hirottappamapekkhamāno.

And if one should know one's suffering to be irremediable, reflecting, 'These things are not for my happiness,' the steadfast person, alone, should endure what is intense, having regard for truth, moral shame, and fear of wrongdoing.

62.

62.

Ahaṃ [V 1.0204] raṭṭhāni vicaranto, nigame rājadhāniyo;

Bhikkhamāno mahārāja, ācariyassa dhanatthiko.

O great king, desiring wealth for my teacher, I went about begging, wandering through kingdoms, towns, and royal cities.

63.

63.

Gahapatī rājapurise, mahāsāle ca brāhmaṇe;

Alatthaṃ satta nikkhāni, suvaṇṇassa janādhipa;

Te me naṭṭhā mahārāja, tasmā socāmahaṃ bhusaṃ.

From householders, royal men, and wealthy brahmins, I obtained seven nikkhas of gold, O lord of men. Those have been lost, O great king; therefore, I grieve intensely.

64.

64.

Purisā te mahārāja, manasānuvicintitā;

Nālaṃ dukkhā pamocetuṃ, tasmā tesaṃ na byāhariṃ.

Your men, O great king, were considered in my mind. They are not able to free me from suffering; therefore, I did not speak to them.

65.

65.

Tvañca kho me mahārāja, manasānuvicintito;

Alaṃ dukkhā pamocetuṃ, tasmā tuyhaṃ pavedayiṃ.

But you, O great king, were considered in my mind. You are able to free me from suffering; therefore, I have declared it to you.

66.

66.

Tassādāsi pasannatto, kāsīnaṃ raṭṭhavaḍḍhano;

Jātarūpamaye nikkhe, suvaṇṇassa catuddasāti.

Then the promoter of the Kāsi kingdom, with a pleased mind, gave to him fourteen nikkhas of gold, made of wrought gold.

Dūtajātakaṃ pañcamaṃ.

The Dūta Jātaka, the fifth.

479. Kāliṅgabodhijātakaṃ (6)

479. The Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka (6)

67.

67.

Rājā [T 1.0352] kāliṅgo cakkavatti, dhammena pathavimanusāsaṃ manusāsi (syā. ka.);

Agamā agamāsi (syā. ka.) bodhisamīpaṃ, nāgena mahānubhāvena.

King Kāliṅga, a wheel-turning monarch, ruling the earth righteously, approached the vicinity of the Bodhi tree with a great-powered elephant.

68.

68.

Kāliṅgo bhāradvājo ca, rājānaṃ kāliṅgaṃ samaṇakolaññaṃ;

Cakkaṃ vattayato pariggahetvā pariṇetvā (pī.), pañjalī idamavoca.

Kāliṅga of the Bhāradvāja clan, having investigated the area, with joined palms spoke this to King Kāliṅga, who was of the lineage of ascetics and was causing the wheel to turn.

69.

69.

Paccoroha mahārāja, bhūmibhāgo yathā samaṇuggato samanugīto (sī. syā. pī.);

Idha anadhivarā buddhā, abhisambuddhā virocanti.

Descend, O great king, to this portion of the earth which is praised by ascetics. Here the Buddhas, who are unsurpassed and fully enlightened, shine forth.

70.

70.

Padakkhiṇato [M 1.0265] āvaṭṭā, tiṇalatā asmiṃ bhūmibhāgasmiṃ;

Pathaviyā nābhiyaṃ puthuviyā ayaṃ (sī.), paṭhaviyā ayaṃ (syā.), puthaviyā’yaṃ (pī.) maṇḍo, iti no sutaṃ mante mahārāja sutaṃ mahārāja (sī. syā. pī.).

On this portion of the earth, the grass and creepers turn clockwise. This is the navel of the earth, the very essence. Thus, O great king, have we heard in the sacred texts.

71.

71.

Sāgarapariyantāya, mediniyā sabbabhūtadharaṇiyā;

Pathaviyā ayaṃ maṇḍo, orohitvā namo karohi.

Of this earth, bounded by the ocean, fertile, the supporter of all beings, this is the essential place. Descend and pay homage.

72.

72.

Ye te bhavanti nāgā ca, abhijātā ca kuñjarā;

Ettāvatā padesaṃ te, nāgā neva mupayanti.

Whatever high-born elephants there are, of the kuñjara breed, those elephants cannot approach even this much of the region.

73.

73.

Abhijāto nāgo abhijāto te nāgo (sī. pī. aṭṭha.) kāmaṃ, pesehi kuñjaraṃ dantiṃ;

Ettāvatā padeso padeso ca (syā. ka.), sakkā na sakkā (syā.) nāgena mupagantuṃ.

Though you have a high-born elephant, by all means, urge on the tusked kuñjara. It is not possible for the elephant to approach even this much of the region.

74.

74.

Taṃ sutvā rājā kāliṅgo, veyyañjanikavaco nisāmetvā;

Sampesesi nāgaṃ ñassāma, mayaṃ yathimassidaṃ yathā idaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) vacanaṃ.

Having heard that, King Kāliṅga, heeding the words of the expert, urged on the elephant, thinking, ‘We shall know if these words of his are so.’

75.

75.

Sampesito [V 1.0205] ca raññā, nāgo koñcova abhinaditvāna;

Paṭisakkitvā [T 1.0353] paṭiosakkitvā (ka.) nisīdi, garuṃva bhāraṃ asahamāno.

Urged on by the king, the elephant, having trumpeted loudly like a crane, drew back and sat down, as if unable to bear a heavy burden.

76.

76.

Kāliṅgabhāradvājo, nāgaṃ khīṇāyukaṃ viditvāna;

Rājānaṃ kāliṅgaṃ, taramāno ajjhabhāsittha;

Aññaṃ saṅkama nāgaṃ, nāgo khīṇāyuko mahārāja.

Kāliṅga Bhāradvāja, knowing that the elephant's life was exhausted, hastening, addressed King Kāliṅga: 'Change to another elephant, O great king, this elephant's life is at an end.'

77.

77.

Taṃ sutvā kāliṅgo, taramāno saṅkamī nāgaṃ;

Saṅkanteva raññe, nāgo tattheva pati patito (ka.) bhumyā;

Veyyañjanikavaco, yathā tathā ahu nāgo.

Hearing that, King Kāliṅga, hastening, changed to another elephant. As soon as the king had changed over, the elephant fell to the ground right there. It happened to the elephant just as the expert had said.

78.

78.

Kāliṅgo rājā kāliṅgaṃ, brāhmaṇaṃ etadavoca;

Tvameva asi sambuddho, sabbaññū sabbadassāvī.

King Kāliṅga said this to the Kāliṅga brahmin: ‘You yourself are the fully enlightened one, the all-knowing, the all-seeing.’”

79.

79.

Taṃ anadhivāsento kāliṅgaṃ kāliṅgo (sī. syā. pī.), brāhmaṇo idamavoca;

Veyyañjanikā hi mayaṃ, buddhā sabbaññuno mahārāja.

Not enduring that, the brahmin said this to King Kāliṅga: ‘We are merely experts in signs, O great king; it is the Buddhas who are all-knowing.’

80.

80.

Sabbaññū sabbavidū ca, buddhā na lakkhaṇena jānanti;

Āgamabalasā āgamapurisā (pī.) hi mayaṃ, buddhā sabbaṃ pajānanti.

The Buddhas are all-knowing and all-discerning; they do not know by means of signs. We know by the power of tradition, whereas the Buddhas thoroughly know all things.

81.

81.

Mahayitvā [M 1.0266] sambodhiṃ mahāyitvāna sambodhiṃ (sī. pī.), pahaṃsitvāna sambodhiṃ (syā.), mamāyitvāna taṃ bodhiṃ (ka.), nānāturiyehi vajjamānehi;

Mālāvilepanaṃ abhiharitvā mālāgandhavilepanaṃ āharitvā (sī. pī.); pākāraparikkhepaṃ kāresi; atha rājā pāyāsi (sī. syā. pī.) atha rājā manupāyāsi pākāraparikkhepaṃ kāresi; atha rājā pāyāsi (sī. syā. pī.).

Having honored the great enlightenment with various musical instruments being played, and having offered garlands and unguents, the king then departed.

82.

82.

Saṭṭhi vāhasahassāni, pupphānaṃ sannipātayi;

Pūjesi [T 1.0354] rājā kāliṅgo, bodhimaṇḍamanuttaranti varuttameti (sī.).

Sixty thousand cartloads of flowers he gathered; King Kāliṅga honored the unsurpassed Bodhi-maṇḍala.

Kāliṅgabodhijātakaṃ chaṭṭhaṃ.

The Kāliṅgabodhi Jātaka, the sixth.

480. Akittijātakaṃ (7)

480. The Akitti Jātaka (7)

83.

83.

Akittiṃ akattiṃ (ka.) disvā sammantaṃ, sakko bhūtapatī bravi;

Kiṃ patthayaṃ mahābrahme, eko sammasi ghammani.

Having seen the tranquil Akitti, Sakka, the lord of beings, said: 'O great brahmin, desiring what do you dwell alone and peacefully in this hot place?'

84.

84.

Dukkho punabbhavo sakka, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ;

Sammohamaraṇaṃ dukkhaṃ, tasmā sammāmi vāsava.

Rebirth is suffering, O Sakka, and the breaking up of the body; dying in delusion is suffering. Therefore, O Vāsava, I dwell peacefully.

85.

85.

Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and fine utterance of yours, I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.

86.

86.

Varaṃ ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Yena putte ca dāre ca, dhanadhaññaṃ piyāni ca;

Laddhā narā na laddhā naññāni (ka.) tappanti, so lobho na mayī vase.

If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: that greed, by which people, having obtained sons and wives, wealth and grain, and other dear things, are not satisfied—may that greed not dwell in me.

87.

87.

Etasmiṃ [V 1.0206] te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ [T 1.0355] kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and fine utterance of yours, I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.

88.

88.

Varaṃ ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Khettaṃ vatthuṃ hiraññañca, gavassaṃ dāsaporisaṃ;

Yena jātena jīyanti, so doso na mayī vase.

If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: that hatred, by which, when it has arisen, fields, land, gold, cattle and horses, and servants are lost—may that hatred not dwell in me.

89.

89.

Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and fine utterance of yours, I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.

90.

90.

Varaṃ [M 1.0267] ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Bālaṃ na passe na suṇe, na ca bālena saṃvase;

Bālenallāpa bālenā’lāpa (?) sallāpaṃ, na kare na ca rocaye.

If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may I not see a fool, nor hear of one, nor associate with a fool; may I not engage in talk or conversation with a fool, nor delight in him.

91.

91.

Kiṃ nu te akaraṃ bālo, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa bālassa, dassanaṃ nābhikaṅkhasi.

What, pray, has a fool done to you? Speak, Kassapa, the reason. Why, Kassapa, do you not desire to see a fool?

92.

92.

Anayaṃ nayati dummedho, adhurāyaṃ niyuñjati;

Dunnayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto pakuppati;

Vinayaṃ so na jānāti, sādhu tassa adassanaṃ.

The one of little wisdom leads to a wrong course; he engages in what is not his duty. A wrong course seems better to him; when spoken to rightly, he becomes angry. He does not know discipline; therefore, not seeing him is good.

93.

93.

Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and fine utterance of yours, I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.

94.

94.

Varaṃ ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Dhīraṃ passe suṇe dhīraṃ, dhīrena saha saṃvase;

Dhīrenallāpasallāpaṃ, taṃ kare tañca rocaye.

If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may I see the wise, may I hear of the wise, may I dwell together with the wise; may I have talk and conversation with the wise, and may I delight in him.

95.

95.

Kiṃ nu te akaraṃ dhīro, vada kassapa kāraṇaṃ;

Kena kassapa dhīrassa, dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhasi.

What, pray, has a wise one done for you? Speak, Kassapa, the reason. Why, Kassapa, do you long for a sight of the wise one?

96.

96.

Nayaṃ nayati medhāvī, adhurāyaṃ na yuñjati;

Sunayo seyyaso hoti, sammā vutto na kuppati;

Vinayaṃ so pajānāti, sādhu tena samāgamo.

The intelligent one leads to a right course; he does not engage in what is not his duty. A good course seems better to him; when spoken to rightly, he does not become angry. He understands discipline; good is association with him.

97.

97.

Etasmiṃ te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ [T 1.0356] kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and fine utterance of yours, I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.

98.

98.

Varaṃ ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Tato ratyā vivasāne vivasane (sī. syā. pī.), sūriyuggamanaṃ suriyassuggamanaṃ (sī. syā. pī.) pati;

If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: then at the end of the night, towards the rising of the sun—

Dibbā bhakkhā pātubhaveyyuṃ, sīlavanto ca yācakā.

may divine foods appear, and virtuous supplicants.

99.

99.

Dadato [V 1.0207] me dadato ca me (pī.) na khīyetha, datvā nānutapeyyahaṃ;

Dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādeyyaṃ, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

May my provisions not be exhausted while I am giving, may I not regret having given; while giving, may I gladden my mind. This, O Sakka, is the boon I choose.

100.

100.

Etasmiṃ [M 1.0268] te sulapite, patirūpe subhāsite;

Varaṃ kassapa te dammi, yaṃ kiñci manasicchasi.

For this well-spoken, fitting, and fine utterance of yours, I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your mind.

101.

101.

Varaṃ ce me ado sakka, sabbabhūtānamissara;

Na maṃ puna upeyyāsi, etaṃ sakka varaṃ vare.

If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, lord of all beings: may you not approach me again. This, O Sakka, is the boon I choose.

102.

102.

Bahūhi vatacariyāhi vattacariyāhi (sī. syā. ka.), narā ca atha nāriyo;

Dassanaṃ abhikaṅkhanti, kiṃ nu me dassane bhayaṃ.

By many observances, both men and women long for a sight of me. What fear, pray, is there in seeing me?

103.

103.

Taṃ tādisaṃ devavaṇṇaṃ devavaṇṇiṃ (pī.), sabbakāmasamiddhinaṃ;

Disvā tapo pamajjeyya disvā tapo pamajjeyyaṃ (sī. syā. pī.), disvānahaṃ pamajjeyyaṃ (cariyāpiṭakaṭṭhakathā), etaṃ te dassane bhayanti.

Seeing such a divine form, endowed with all sensual pleasures, one might neglect ascetic practice. This is the fear in seeing you.

Akittijātakaṃ sattamaṃ.

The Akitti Jātaka, the Seventh.

481. Takkāriyajātakaṃ (8)

481. The Takkāriya Jātaka (8)

104.

104.

Ahameva dubbhāsitaṃ bhāsi bālo, bhekovaraññe ahimavhāyamāno mavhayāno (sī. pī.);

Takkāriye sobbhamimaṃ sobbhamhi ahaṃ (ka.) patāmi, na [T 1.0357] kireva sādhu ativelabhāṇī sādhūtyativelabhāṇī (ka.).

I myself, being a fool, have spoken ill-spoken words, like a frog in the forest calling a snake. O Takkāriya, I shall fall into this pit. Indeed, it is said that one who speaks excessively is not good.

105.

105.

Pappoti macco ativelabhāṇī, bandhaṃ vadhaṃ sokapariddavañca;

Attānameva garahāsi ettha, ācera yaṃ taṃ nikhaṇanti sobbhe.

A mortal who speaks excessively obtains bondage, killing, and sorrow and lamentation. O teacher, blame your own self in this matter, for you yourself have created the reason for which they will bury you in the pit.

106.

106.

Kimevahaṃ tuṇḍilamanupucchiṃ, kareyya saṃ kareyyāsaṃ (syā.), kareyya sa (ka.), bhareyya saṃ (?) bhātaraṃ kāḷikāyaṃ kāḷikāya (syā. ka.);

Naggovahaṃ naggoca’haṃ (?) vatthayugañca jīno, ayampi attho bahutādisova.

Why did I ever ask Tuṇḍila? I treated Kāḷī's brother with courtesy. Deprived of my pair of cloths, I am now naked. This matter, too, is very much like that.

107.

107.

Yo [M 1.0269] yujjhamānānamayujjhamāno yujjhamānena ayujjhamāno (ka.), meṇḍantaraṃ accupatī kuliṅgo;

So piṃsito meṇḍasirehi tattha, ayampi attho bahutādisova.

The drongo bird that, while not fighting among those who were fighting, flew in between the rams, was crushed there by the rams' heads. This matter, too, is very much like that.

108.

108.

Caturo janā potthakamaggahesuṃ, ekañca posaṃ anurakkhamānā;

Sabbeva te bhinnasirā sayiṃsu, ayampi attho bahutādisova.

Four persons, while protecting one man, seized a hempen cloth. All of them lay down with shattered heads. This matter, too, is very much like that.

109.

109.

Ajā yathā veḷugumbasmiṃ baddhā bandhaṃ (syā. ka.), avakkhipantī asimajjhagacchi;

Teneva [T 1.0358] tassā galakāvakantaṃ galayā vikantuṃ (ka.), galakaṃ vikantā (syā.), ayampi attho bahutādisova.

Just as a goat, tied in a bamboo clump, while struggling, came upon a sword; by that very sword her throat was cut. This matter, too, is very much like that.

110.

110.

Ime na devā na gandhabbaputtā, migā ime atthavasaṃ gatā me atthavasābhatā ime (sī. syā. pī.);

Ekañca naṃ sāyamāse pacantu, ekaṃ punappātarāse ekañca naṃ pātarāse (ka. sī. pī.) pacantu.

These are not devas, nor sons of gandhabbas; these are beasts that have come into my power. Let them cook one for the evening meal, and another for the morning meal.

111.

111.

Sataṃ sahassāni dubhāsitāni, kalampi nāgghanti subhāsitassa;

Dubbhāsitaṃ saṅkamāno kileso kilissati (?), tasmā tuṇhī kimpurisā kiṃpuriso (sī. syā.) na bālyā.

A hundred thousand ill-spoken words are not worth even a sixteenth part of a well-spoken word. Speaking ill-spoken words is a defilement; therefore, the Kinnarī is silent, not out of foolishness.

112.

112.

Yā [V 1.0208] mesā byāhāsi byākāsi (sī. syā. pī.) pamuñcathetaṃ, giriñca naṃ giriṃ varaṃ (ka.) himavantaṃ nayantu;

Imañca kho dentu mahānasāya, pātova naṃ pātarāse pacantu.
